The components in the diagram have these roles:

  • The PEP is the FSC Inway of the source. Its AuthZEN plugin sends every request, with its raw body, to the PDP. The plugin forwards the request only on allow (fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml#L769-L775). No separate PEP service exists (F-35). The PEP passes the request unchanged and never parses it (REQ-42).
  • The PDP is OpenFTV release v0.1.0 with embedded OPA/Rego. The demo builds it from the tag and patches in the FTV GraphQL mapper (Dockerfile#L3-L9). The mapper builds the field list and does nothing else (ftvgraphql.go#L1-L13). It does not verify consent, does not call BSNk, and reads no flow. The policy establishes every fact that it decides on (REQ-18).
  • PIP 1 is the consent register (toestemmingsregister). During evaluation, the policy calls the register for the status of the consent. The call goes over FSC, through the own Outway of the PDP (docker-compose.yml#L141-L142). The policy gets the verification keys (JWKS) directly from the register.
  • PIP 2 is the admission register. Every 5 seconds, OpenFTV pulls the participants as data.entities.dvtp_participant. Each participant has the attributes name, active, allowed_source_peer_ids, and acts_for (dvtp-onboarding.yaml). The contract policy reads this data. The request policy reads it for integrator mandates (acts_for).

The same PDP serves two enforcement points. Each point has its own policy tree. FSC Inways send data requests (package authz). FSC Managers send contract proposals (package doelbinding.auto_sign_contract).

The EUDI adapter and the ASIP call the source over FSC, like every other consumer. They translate between protocols. The decision on source data stays with the PDP of the source (REQ-44).

The source gateway is behind the Inway. Only the Inway can reach the gateway. As a result, the gateway does all its work after the decision (REQ-04, ADR-0033).

docs.title: Regime selection
docs.text:
The PDP judges a request under one of two regimes. The evidence in the request selects the regime (REQ-74, ADR-0031). A declared regime plays no part. Each kind of evidence has its own outcome:

Evidence in the request Regime Rules that bind One X-GBO-Consent-Token, verified or not consent DVT0001, LVG0001 No consent token PID EUD0001, EUD0002, ASI0001 Two consent tokens — denied: CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID

The selection code is in engine.rego#L168-L181. The code that reads the token is in consent.rego#L44-L62. FSC grants carry no properties. No component reads a flow.

The regime only decides which reasons the PDP reports. Access depends on the rules, because each rule still checks its own basis. If no verified consent is present, DVT0001 denies. If a consent token is present, the PID rules deny.

Only consent is positive evidence (F-70). A request enters the PID regime because no token is present. This asymmetry has two consequences:

  • The PID regime needs its own positive evidence: a verified PID disclosure, bound to the subject of the query (REQ-45). In demo v0.9.0, the EUDI adapter does not authenticate the callback that carries the PID (#133).
  • The actor lists of the PID rules (designated_issuers, asip) must stay disjoint from the consent consumers in every environment. If the lists overlap, a consumer can skip consent: it leaves out the token. A test checks this condition for the seeded peers only (engine_test.rego#L366-L376).

A Gov-to-Gov regime on a legal basis needs its own positive evidence. It cannot be a third regime that the absence of evidence defines.

docs.title: Wallet approval is not a legal basis
docs.text:
In DvTP, the consent of the citizen is the legal basis for delivery to a private consumer. In the EUDI route, the citizen chooses in the wallet which data to present. The ARF says that this approval is never a legal basis for the relying party (F-83). In the ASI route, the citizen approves each request by logging in (REQ-90). This approval is not a stored, revocable consent either.

As a result, no single "consent" covers all routes. The PID regime cannot use a DvTP consent as its basis. The consent regime cannot use a wallet presentation as its basis. If a consumer gets data both through DvTP and through the wallet, it needs its own legal basis for the wallet route. The GO and the PSA do not separate the two terms.

docs.title: Rule model
docs.text:
Each rule is a plain Rego package under policies/gbo/rules/ (ADR-0009). A rule declares three things:

  • rule_id, regime (consent or pid), and services (the FSC services that the rule applies to).
  • covers_fields and covers_types: the fields that the rule can grant.
  • Its reasons to refuse: deny for the whole request and deny_field[i] for one field.

If a rule gives no reason, it grants the field. Each rule checks actor and scope itself (REQ-48). The file lib.rego only reads the request and holds no checks.

Demo v0.9.0 has five rules:

Rule Regime Service What it grants Own reasons to refuse DVT0001 consent bri Income declaration fields under consent consent codes, SCOPE_NOT_ALLOWED, CONSTRAINT_MISMATCH, YEAR_NOT_COVERED, CONSENT_ACTOR_MISMATCH LVG0001 consent lvg Ownership check at the LVG, scope lvg:vbo:eigendom consent codes, SCOPE_NOT_ALLOWED, CONSTRAINT_MISMATCH EUD0001 pid bri Income statement (inkomensverklaring) to the wallet, years 2024 and 2025 PID_NOT_PRESENT, ACTOR_NOT_ALLOWED, YEAR_NOT_ALLOWED EUD0002 pid brp Death certificate (akte van overlijden) to the wallet PID_NOT_PRESENT, ACTOR_NOT_ALLOWED ASI0001 pid brp BRP fields for the ASIP PID_NOT_PRESENT, ACTOR_NOT_ALLOWED

The consent codes are the outcomes of the proof verification and the status lookup. For more information, see Consent verification in policy.

docs.title: How the engine binds rules to fields
docs.text:
The engine (engine.rego) decides each data field of the field list separately, in these steps:

  1. Only the rules of the active regime bind.
  2. Only the rules that serve the FSC service of the request bind (REQ-97). The service is the service_name from the FSC access token. The Manager of the source signed this token (engine.rego#L183-L192).
  3. A field binds to the rules that name its key ParentType.field. An argument-free leaf outside the root types also binds to the rules that cover its parent type.
  4. Every delegated call needs an integrator mandate for the represented party and the granting rule (engine.rego#L246-L267). The engine adds this check to every rule. No rule can leave it out.
  5. For each field, the first bound rule without reasons grants the field (engine.rego#L269-L306).
  6. The engine allows the request only if it allows every data field.

Service binding is necessary because a field key is unique only within one schema. Query.ingeschrevenPersoon is in both bri and brp. If the binding is absent, a rule for one service grants the same key on the other service (F-90). A test requires every rule to name its services (engine_test.rego#L497-L501).

The world is closed. If no rule covers a field, the engine denies the field with NO_APPLICABLE_RULE. No separate catalog exists: the rule is the catalog. If the engine cannot make a decision for a field, it refuses the field as RULE_NOT_EVALUABLE. The request then fails as a configuration error (engine.rego#L18-L23). The engine never leaves a field out of the decision.

docs.title: Constraints inside the query
docs.text:
Field coverage answers "which fields". Two more checks answer "whose records" and "which part of the records". Both checks read the arguments of the query. So the selectors must be inside the query, where the PDP can see them. The two checks work as follows:

  • The subject check. Under consent, the query names the citizen with a placeholder: consent:identity for a BSN API, consent:pseudonym for a source-pseudonym API (lib.rego#L43-L53). Each rule lists the placeholders that it accepts. DVT0001 and LVG0001 accept only consent:identity. The PDP denies three cases with CONSTRAINT_MISMATCH: a literal value, another placeholder, and a placeholder without a verified proof (dvt0001.rego#L72-L80).

    The PDP does not check who the subject is. It checks that the subject comes from the proof (REQ-79, F-77).

  • The year check. Every requested tax year (belastingjaren) needs a consented bd:ib:<year> scope. If a query has no year filter, it fails too, because the source then returns every year (dvt0001.rego#L82-L96). An argument that comes from a schema default counts as missing.

The source returns only the fields that the query selects (REQ-08).

docs.title: Consent verification in policy
docs.text:
The policy verifies the consent proof itself (ADR-0032, consent.rego). The request mapper has no part in this verification. The policy ignores a pip.consent in the input. The PDP decides only on a consent for which it established the origin, the binding, and the status at evaluation time itself (REQ-68).

For each evaluation, the policy does three steps in this order:

  1. It verifies the ES256 signature against the JWKS of the register. It caches the JWKS for 300 seconds and fetches the JWKS again on an unknown kid.
  2. It verifies the claims, with 30 seconds of clock skew.
  3. Only then does it call the register for the status of the consent_id. This call goes over FSC, with no cache and a 2-second timeout.

Each failure maps to its own reason code (consent.rego#L174-L186):

Code Cause CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID Two tokens. A wrong type, issuer, or audience. A missing claim or no encrypted_subject. A valid_until that is not equal to exp CONSENT_SIGNATURE_INVALID The token is no JWT, the algorithm is other than ES256, the key is unknown, or the signature does not verify CONSENT_KEYS_UNAVAILABLE The policy cannot fetch the JWKS CONSENT_TOKEN_EXPIRED The time is more than 30 seconds after exp CONSENT_STATUS_UNAVAILABLE The status lookup failed or timed out CONSENT_NOT_FOUND The register does not know the consent CONSENT_WITHDRAWN The status is REVOKED CONSENT_EXPIRED The time is after valid_until, within the clock skew CONSENT_ACTOR_MISMATCH The consent names a party other than the represented party of the call

The consent binds the represented party. On a delegated call, this party is the FSC delegator. On other calls, it is the calling peer (lib.rego#L55-L72). The integrator gets no mandate from the consent (REQ-106, ADR-0034).

The policy fetches the status during evaluation. As a result, the input, the policy, and the data do not reproduce the decision. The engine copies the resolved consent into its response for the console decision log (engine.rego#L25-L29). The ADL does not contain this copy (F-72). For the proof, the status interface, and the freshness rules, see Consent.

docs.title: Query mapping (FTV GraphQL profile)
docs.text:
The GraphQL query of the consumer is the authorization object. The PEP sends the raw body. The request mapper inside the PDP turns the body into the field list of the FTV GraphQL profile for AuthZEN (ftv-graphql/0.1). The mapper is a separate Go module, services/ftv-graphql-mapper, with a thin OpenFTV adapter (ADR-0013).

The mapper applies four rules:

  • It parses the body. It gives each field its parent type from the bundled schema of the FSC service of the request. It gives each field its arguments as the source executes them.
  • It accepts only a query. A mutation or a subscription gives OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED (mapper.go#L194).
  • It enforces limits: body 1 MiB, nesting depth 64, 100 fragment definitions, and selection depth 64. Further limits are 1000 field records, 100 aliased selections, and 1 second of validation (mapper.go#L252-L268).
  • It never accepts persistedQuery.

If the mapper cannot build a complete field list, it marks the request Unverifiable with a code and a subcode (mapper.go#L27-L43). The engine then denies the whole request (REQ-17). The mapper uses these codes and subcodes:

Code Subcodes COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE UNSUPPORTED_TRANSPORT, INVALID_BODY, PARSE_ERROR, INVALID_QUERY, NO_OPERATION, OPERATION_NOT_FOUND, OPERATION_AMBIGUOUS, VARIABLE_ERROR, LIMIT_EXCEEDED OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED — CONFIG_ERROR SCHEMA_UNAVAILABLE

Three controls keep the judged request equal to the executed request:

  • Schema pins: the policy bundle pins the digest of the schema of each service in graphql_schemas.rego. If a schema is not pinned, the PDP denies with CONFIG_ERROR SCHEMA_MISMATCH (engine.rego#L129-L141).
  • Drift check: a CI job compares the bundled schemas with the schemas that the sources run (check-schema-drift.sh).
  • Transport subset at the source: the source gateway accepts only POST with a JSON body on one path. It accepts no query string, no Upgrade, and no Content-Encoding (transport.go#L9-L13). A request that the PDP never judged cannot run.

For future sources, how the PDP models fields, recursion, and arguments is an open question (Q-14).

docs.title: Reason codes: two layers
docs.text:
A denial carries a machine-readable reason in two layers (REQ-06). The consumer gets a coarse code. The administrator of the source gets the detail per field. The consumer code never shows which field the PDP denied, whether a field exists, or which check failed. Otherwise the consumer can map the schema by trying names. The two layers differ in audience, route, and codes:

Layer Who sees it Where it goes Codes Consumer code (graphql.client) Consumer, ADL reason → reason_user.en in the AuthZEN answer. The ADL stores it FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED, ACCESS_DENIED, COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE <subcode>, OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED, NO_DATA_FIELDS Administrator codes (graphql.admin) Administrator of the source OPA console decision log only (observability) Request code, plus per denied field: the bound rules, their reasons in order, and the field code

Each administrator request code maps to one consumer code (engine.rego#L95-L118, authz.rego#L42-L51):

Administrator request code Consumer code Fields denied by rules (FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED) FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE INVALID_QUERY FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE with another subcode COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE <subcode> OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED, NO_DATA_FIELDS the same code PIP_UNAVAILABLE (the consent register, its keys, or the admission register did not answer) ACCESS_DENIED CONFIG_ERROR (MAPPER_OUTPUT_MISSING, SCHEMA_MISMATCH, SCHEMA_UNAVAILABLE, RULE_NOT_EVALUABLE) ACCESS_DENIED

To the consumer, a fault at the source looks like a normal denial. For one field, a rule can give several reasons. The rule reports the first reason in a fixed order (engine.rego#L321-L344). The order is the token, then the state of the consent, then the question, then the caller. As a result, if the consent is revoked and the year check also fails, the code is CONSENT_WITHDRAWN.

Demo v0.9.0 has two limits for reason codes:

  • The FSC Inway loses the reason. It reads reasonUser, but the PDP sends reason_user. Upstream has a fix that was not released at the time of demo v0.9.0 (ftv-graphql-profile.md#L93-L96).
  • The consumer backend shows the citizen only FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED, with an offer to consent again. Every other code becomes UNAVAILABLE (denial.go).

The ADL is the audit source (ADR-0036). It holds only the consumer code. As a result, a supervisor can reconstruct from the ADL only what the consumer can know (F-72). For the full list of deny paths per scenario, see the runtime view, for example DvTP query.

docs.title: Admission and contract acceptance
docs.text:
Admission to the system is data in a register. The decision policy holds no admissions (REQ-61). The FSC Manager of the provider sends every contract proposal to the PDP. The contract policy (autosign.rego) reads the admission register and runs eight checks. The first check that fails names the refusal (ADR-0015, autosign.rego#L165-L175). The policy runs the checks in this order:

# Code Refuses when 1 NOT_AN_AUTOSIGN_REQUEST The input is not a well-formed autosign request 2 GRANT_TYPE_NOT_ALLOWED The grants are not all type 2 (service connection) or all type 3 (delegated service connection) 3 NO_COUNTERPARTY The contract has no party other than the provider itself 4 ADMISSION_REGISTER_UNAVAILABLE The PIP pull supplied no register 5 PARTY_NOT_IN_REGISTRY A party is not in the register 6 PARTY_NOT_ACTIVE A party is suspended 7 SOURCE_NOT_ALLOWED The party is not admitted for this source peer 8 DELEGATION_NOT_REGISTERED A delegated grant has no registered integration

A missing register and an empty register are different (autosign.rego#L51-L53). An empty register is available data that admits nobody. After a refusal, the contract stays proposed, so the party can submit it again (REQ-63).

The contract question and the request question are separate rule sets (REQ-62). A contract decides who can connect at all. A request decides which field the party can read at request time. The two rule sets share no rules and no reason codes. They do share one availability object: one broken module stops both (F-52).

Four points are open:

  • A suspended consumer keeps its existing contract. It can still send queries, also with a valid consent (REQ-110, Q-53).
  • No component logs changes to admissions, mandates, and activations (REQ-123).
  • The autosign input of the Manager carries only peer IDs and grant types. As a result, the policy judges only the parties of a contract. It has no input about the content of the contract (F-56).
  • The task to run the admission register is assigned to the management organization (Q-22).

For the scenario, see Admission and activation.

docs.title: Data scope: demand side and supply side
docs.text:
What a consumer can request depends on two sides (F-74):

  • Supply side: the source publishes what it offers. GBO validates and activates this description (REQ-64, Source onboarding). The EUDI and ASI routes work this way.
  • Demand side: for DvTP, a statutory service catalog (dienstencatalogus) sets the legal ceiling of what a consumer can request, per use case. The sector need defines this catalog.

What is technically allowed is the intersection of both sides. No text in the GO, the PSA, or the FR-DvTP names that intersection. In demo v0.9.0, the DvTP scopes are spread over the rules, the portal, and the field coverage. The proposal is one DvTP catalog as the single source for scopes, fields, and portal text. The proposal also adds an intersection check at activation (REQ-121, #382).

docs.title: Consent
docs.text:
In DvTP, the consent of the citizen is the legal basis for delivery of source data to a private consumer (afnemer). A consent proof carries the consent to the source, and the PDP of the source verifies that proof on every request. A consent has a lifecycle of validity, revocation, and repeated use. The consent model realizes capability S01 for the consent register (toestemmingsregister) and capability S02 for the consent portal (toestemmingsportaal).

The main decision is ADR-0032. It defines the consent proof in five points:

  • The register signs the proof.
  • The proof carries a value per source.
  • The consumer can name the citizen only with a placeholder.
  • The status stays online over FSC.
  • The policy verifies the proof.

For the scenarios, see the runtime view: DvTP consent, DvTP query, and DvTP citizen access.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Five roles take part in consent:

Role Component in the demo Does Consent portal (S02) toestemmingsportaal-frontend, consent portal backend Shows the request, logs the citizen in, makes the values per source at BSNk, and lets the citizen view and revoke consents Consent register (S01) consent-register Stores the consent record, signs the proof, and answers the status over FSC Consumer dienstverlener-backend Starts the request, receives the proof, and sends it unchanged with every query PDP of the source OpenFTV PDP, consent.rego Verifies the proof and gets the status at every request Source gateway bron-sidecar After the allow, decrypts its own value from the proof

It is an open question whether the register and the portal backend are one system (Q-49). For the requirements on the roles, see Consent roles.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Active: citizen gives consent<br/>register signs the proof Active --> Active: consumer queries<br/>(repeated use) Active --> Revoked: citizen revokes Active --> Expired: valid_until passes Revoked --> [*] Expired --> [*] classDef active fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#0F172A classDef stop fill:#FEDCD8,stroke:#E28F80,color:#1E293B class Active active class Revoked,Expired stop

The register stores the status ACTIVE or REVOKED. The status Expired follows from valid_until. The citizen overview shows Active, Expired, and Revoked. Demo v0.9.0 does not build a "retrieved" status. Two points are open: when a consent counts as retrieved, and how the register learns this (Q-42). The FR-DvTP texts name the statuses with different words (F-97).

A consent is bound to one consumer, one service, and named data sets (REQ-12). It covers a whole data set. Within a set, the citizen does not pick fields (REQ-10). The portal shows only the data sets that the consumer asks for. It refuses a data set that it cannot describe. For the record model, see consent register.

docs.title: The consent proof
docs.text:
When the citizen gives consent, the consent register signs a JWT with these parts (consent_token.go#L130-L152):

Part Content Header alg=ES256, typ=gbo-consent+jwt, kid. The public keys are in the JWKS of the register consent_id, jti The consent and a unique token ID scopes, scope_entries The data sets, per source dienstverlener_oin The represented party. In the demo, this field holds the FSC Peer ID (Q-68) valid_until, exp The end of the validity. The two values are equal iss, aud, iat, nbf Issuer, audience (default gbo:dvtp:pdp), and times encrypted_subject For each source OIN: a pseudonym (VP) and, only for a source on the BSN authorization list, an identity (VI). Each value has its key_set_version

The proof holds no BSN and no PI (REQ-20). Only the source that a value in encrypted_subject was made for can read that value (REQ-80). The register refuses a proof without a pseudonym for every party (consent_token.go#L45-L64). The PDP denies such a proof too, with CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID. For how the values are made, see Pseudonymization.

The portal returns the proof to the consumer in the URL fragment of the return redirect. The consumer frontend removes the proof from the visible URL at once (consent-flow.md#L130-L133). The question of what the return redirect gives back is partly answered (Q-44).

The consumer sends the proof unchanged in X-GBO-Consent-Token (AV-05). In its query, the consumer names the citizen only with a placeholder: consent:identity for a BSN API, consent:pseudonym for a source-pseudonym API (REQ-79). The consumer can read consent_id and scopes from the proof. It cannot read who the citizen is (F-76).

docs.title: The integrator is not in the proof
docs.text:
An integrator calls the source for a consumer under FSC delegation (ADR-0034). The proof binds only the represented party, which is the consumer. The integrator needs its own mandate for each consumer and rule in the admission register (REQ-106). If this mandate is absent, the PDP denies with INTEGRATOR_NOT_REGISTERED.

It is an open question whether the proof must also bind the integrator (Q-46). The working assumption is that it does not. If the integrator is in the proof, a change of integrator makes all running consents unusable. If the integrator is not in the proof, every registered integrator of that consumer can use the proof.

docs.title: Bearer token
docs.text:
The proof is a bearer token. The actor binding stops use by another consumer. It does not stop replay by the same consumer (consent-flow.md#L268-L273). Production needs a shorter validity and proof-of-possession binding to the FSC identity (Risks).

The location and the rotation of the signing key are open (Q-55). If the register uses a persistent store, it needs a fixed signing key (CONSENT_SIGNING_KEY_PATH). Then proofs stay valid after a restart (main.go#L84-L86).

docs.title: Verification and status
docs.text:
The PDP of the source decides only on a consent that it checked itself (REQ-68). It establishes the origin, the binding, and the status at evaluation time. The policy does this work. The request mapper has no part in it (consent.rego). The policy verifies the proof and gets the status in this sequence:

sequenceDiagram box rgb(220,252,231) GBO Basis participant IN as Source Inway (PEP) participant PDP as PDP policy (consent.rego) participant OUT as PDP Outway participant CRIN as Register Inway end box rgb(254,220,216) DvTP participant CR as Consent register end IN->>PDP: AuthZEN evaluation with X-GBO-Consent-Token opt JWKS not cached, older than 300 s, or unknown kid PDP->>CR: GET /.well-known/jwks.json end Note over PDP: verify ES256 signature,<br/>then claims (30 s skew) PDP->>OUT: GET /consent-status/consents/{id}/status<br/>(no cache, 2 s timeout) OUT->>CRIN: FSC (mTLS + access token) CRIN->>CR: status listener (port 4012) CR-->>PDP: ACTIVE, REVOKED or 404 Note over PDP: actor binding, scope,<br/>placeholder, years, fields PDP-->>IN: allow or deny

The policy handles keys, claims, and status as follows:

  • Keys: the policy gets the JWKS directly from the register. It caches the JWKS for 300 seconds and fetches it again on an unknown kid, so a new key works at once. No stale-key fallback exists, because the register that serves the keys also answers the status (consent.rego#L70-L90).
  • Claims: the policy verifies type, issuer, audience, required claims, nbf, iat, and valid_until == exp, with 30 seconds of clock skew. The policy reads the claims only after the signature verifies, so a forged token never reaches the register (consent.rego#L169-L186).
  • Status: the policy gets the status for each evaluation, with no cache, a 2-second timeout, and raise_error: false. The call carries traceparent and Fsc-Transaction-Id (consent.rego#L190-L200). It goes over FSC, from the Outway of the PDP (peer …0800) to the Inway of the register (peer …0700, FSC service consent-status).

The register serves the status on its own listener. This listener serves nothing else (status.go#L13-L26). A lookup without an FSC peer gets 401. The register logs each lookup as a processing, with the calling peer as processor (REQ-76).

The FSC Manager of the register signs a contract only for the peer of the PDP. Still, any connected peer can get the status of a consent if it holds the consent ID. Demo v0.9.0 does not restrict lookups to the PDP of the source that the consent is for.

Each failure has its own reason code. For the table of codes, see Authorization.

docs.title: Freshness is asymmetric on purpose
docs.text:
The legal basis travels as a proof, and the status stays online (F-61). Each part has its own freshness:

What Freshness Why Proof content (scopes, party, validity) Fixed at consent, verified locally The register signed it. The PDP needs no lookup for it Verification keys Up to 300 seconds old Keys change rarely. An unknown kid causes a fetch at once Status Live at every request A revocation must deny the next request (REQ-14)

If the status is unknown, the PDP denies. So the register is a dependency of every DvTP request (REQ-75). The values for propagation time, availability, and latency are open (Q-47). The question of who is authoritative for revocation and expiry is answered: the register, with the status online and fail closed (Q-05).

The status answer is not in the PDP input. As a result, the input, the policy, and the data do not reproduce a decision. The ADL does not hold the answer (F-72).

docs.title: Validity
docs.text:
A consent has a finite validity. After the validity ends, the PDP denies (REQ-19). Three rules set the validity:

  • The register sets valid_until at creation, and the proof has exp = valid_until.
  • The PDP checks both values. Within 30 seconds after valid_until, it denies with CONSENT_EXPIRED. After that, the token check denies first, with CONSENT_TOKEN_EXPIRED.
  • In the demo, the consumer chooses the period with validity_seconds. The default is one year, with no upper bound (main.go#L48-L51, main.go#L421-L424). The citizen cannot change the period (F-11, #380).

Since November 2, 2026, the question of who sets the validity period is open again (Q-13). Under FR-11, the default can come from the service catalog, and the citizen can adjust it within bounds. It is a policy and UX choice whether the citizen must be able to do this. It is also open whether the validity can differ per source within one consent (Q-76). The working assumption is one validity per consent.

docs.title: Revocation
docs.text:
The citizen views and revokes consents in the portal (REQ-38). Before it revokes a consent, the portal backend derives the reference of the citizen. It then checks that the consent belongs to that citizen (portal.go#L268-L293, REQ-40). Viewing and revoking need no BSNk call.

The register sets the status to REVOKED and keeps the record. It writes the processing record in the same transaction (main.go#L585-L596). For the next request on that proof, the status is REVOKED, and the PDP denies with CONSENT_WITHDRAWN (REQ-14). Another active consent of the same citizen cannot take its place, because the PDP checks only the consent_id from the signed proof.

Three points on revocation are open:

  • Revocation of a valid consent only (REQ-109).
  • Whether the register records the moment of revocation (Q-48).
  • A pointer to the rights of the citizen at the consumer after revocation (REQ-120).

docs.title: Repeated use, not single use
docs.text:
Within its validity, a consumer can use a consent again (REQ-19). The design removed single use (Q-04, answered, after FR-11). The demo has no reuse check. The status machine of SL-01b waits for the "retrieved" status (Q-42).

The LVG pilot uses repeated use. The Installatie Register keeps the proof. It sends a new request at every installer access, under one consent. Revocation stops this use (lvg-ir.md#L59-L61).

docs.title: The proof freezes at consent
docs.text:
BSNk transforms only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04). So all values in the proof are made at consent time. Parties, key versions, BSN authorization, and proof form are fixed for the whole validity period (F-78). This has four consequences:

  • A source that joins later needs a new consent.
  • If a source gets a new key version, it keeps its old keys while proofs for the old version are valid (AV-09).
  • A source that joins the BSN authorization list later has only a pseudonym in older consents.
  • A new proof form makes every outstanding proof fail with CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID. The proof has no version field.

It is an open question what counts as a change of a consent (Q-77). When consent is given, the register must know the OIN, the key version, and the BSN authorization of each source (REQ-82).

docs.title: Consent in other routes
docs.text: DvTP consent is a registered, revocable legal basis. Approval in the wallet (EUDI) and login at the ASI authorization server are a different thing. They are the choice of the citizen for each presentation or each request. Neither is a legal basis, and neither replaces the other (F-83, Authorization).

docs.title: What travels where
docs.text:
Each tag names a kind of data that a hop carries. The runtime view uses the same tags. The tags are in order of sensitivity:

Tag Meaning Sensitivity Where query and variables GraphQL query and variables. They select data sets and carry no identity data under consent low Every transport hop OIN / Peer ID Organization identifier of the consumer low FSC token, PDP input, decision logs scope Data-set code, for example bd:ib:2025 low Every DvTP and EUDI hop FSC token Certificate-bound JWT of the FSC Manager of the provider. It carries no grant properties medium (transport authentication) Outway, Inway, PDP. The source gateway reads only the caller, for its logbook consent_id Handle to the consent record medium (linkable to the citizen through the register) Inside the proof. Alone, only in the status lookup and the citizen UI consent proof Signed (ES256), audience-bound JWT with consent_id, encrypted_subject, scopes, dienstverlener_oin, and valid_until medium-high (carries the values per source and the legal basis) Consumer → FSC → PDP → source gateway, in X-GBO-Consent-Token. Never in observer or history payloads VI (encrypted identity) Value that BSNk makes for one party and key version. That party decrypts it to the BSN. Only for a party on the BSN authorization list high at the recipient, unreadable for others (readable in the demo: the mock does not encrypt) Only inside the proof. The source gateway takes its own value after the allow VP (encrypted pseudonym) Value that BSNk makes for one party and key version. That party decrypts it to its own pseudonym of the citizen. Every party gets one medium at the recipient, unreadable for others (readable in the demo) Only inside the proof. Demo v0.9.0 does not build a VP for the consumer (#478) placeholder consent:identity or consent:pseudonym in the place of the subject none (identifies nobody) Consumer → FSC → PDP → source gateway, which replaces it PI / PP Polymorphic identity and pseudonym of BSNk. Only the requester can use them medium (only BSNk can transform them) Portal backend. Stored in the register under subject_ref (route D) subject_ref HMAC of the BSN with the secret key of the portal medium (computable from a BSN with the key) Portal backend, register BSN Plain citizen service number high (personal data) DvTP: the portal backend at login, and the source after the allow. EUDI and ASI: through the flow, and in both PDP decision logs (ADR-0043)

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
Nine points on consent are open:

  • Purpose binding in the proof (Q-69).
  • Proof of what the citizen saw at consent (Q-51, REQ-107, REQ-117).
  • Mandatory minimal data sets (Q-45).
  • Consent by an authorized representative (Q-73, REQ-118).
  • Recording of a refusal (Q-43).
  • Recording of the first use of a consent, which the FR-22 usage status needs (F-19).
  • Durability and recovery of the register storage (Q-54).
  • What the management organization records or delivers for the consent process (Q-62).
  • Security requirements for the portal UI inside MijnOverheid, and what MijnOverheid must deliver or allow (Q-59, Q-61).

docs.text:

  • Findings: F-11 (closed), F-19 (open), F-61 (closed), F-72 (open), F-76 (open), F-78 (open), F-83 (open), F-97 (open)

docs.title: Identity and trust
docs.text:
GBO must know which organization it deals with, and which certificate the chain uses for which purpose. The design keeps two questions apart:

  • Who is this organization? This is the legal identity (OIN and name) and the technical identity on FSC.
  • Which certificates does EUDI need? These are the trust roles of attestation issuance and of the Authentic Source Interface.

The capabilities are S04 and F1, under P-07 (trust through recognized admission and trust anchors). These decisions apply:

  • ADR-0003: FSC for all connectivity.
  • ADR-0023: part A, organization identity (accepted), and part B, EUDI certificate roles (proposed).
  • ADR-0028: PuB-EAA productization (proposed).

For the requirements, see Identity, trust and transport.

Authorization per request is a separate layer. FSC establishes the organization, but this tells nothing about what the organization can do in one request. For more information, see Authorization.

docs.title: Three identity carriers
docs.text:
An organization in the chain has three identifiers (F-60):

Carrier What it identifies Source FSC Peer ID the FSC peer: the system that sends or receives FSC traffic subject.serialNumber of the FSC certificate OIN the legal organization (bronhouder, consumer) serialNumber of the organization's certificate Organization name the legal name that a wallet or a record shows exactly one O attribute of the same certificate

If the bronhouder runs its own peer, its Peer ID is its OIN. In other cases, the two values can differ. One peer can offer services of more than one bronhouder. Simulation Peer IDs are not OINs, for example 0000009950HYPBV00000. Until SL-49 (PR #242), the demo used one field for both values. In demo v0.9.0, the source configuration keeps provider_peer_id as a separate field (source_configuration.go#L35-L44).

It is open whether policy can read the Peer ID of a consumer as its OIN. The alternative is that policy takes that link from the admission register (toelatingsregister) (Q-68).

docs.title: The legal identity comes from the certificate
docs.text:
A GBO component can put the OIN or name of a bronhouder in an attestation or a decision record. The component takes that value from verified certificate material. A value that an operator can fill in freely is never the source (REQ-67, ADR-0023, part A).

The certificate content decides the result:

Certificate Result 20-digit OIN in serialNumber, exactly one organization name The OIN and the name come from the certificate The configured OIN or name differs from the certificate Refused: the component does not load the set No 20-digit OIN, or not exactly one organization name Refused (CERTIFICATE_SET_INVALID)

The rule is in development_ca_provider.go#L280-L288 and source-registry/onboarding/service.go#L293-L297. The source document also names its source_oin. This value must equal the OIN in the certificate set. If it differs, the onboarding refuses the document (Source onboarding). The issuer name, the description, and the logo that the wallet shows also come from the certificate (PR #321).

This rule has these consequences:

  • The runtime gets leaf material and public CA certificates, but never CA private keys. Provisioning is a separate privileged command.
  • Consents are bound to the identity of the consumer. If that identity changes, the consents become unusable. The migration in PR #244 and PR #277 showed this.
  • In the default demo onboarding, the Belastingdienst peer publishes RvIG with the Belastingdienst OIN. This is a demo shortcut, and it does not show one OIN per bronhouder. The certificate sets still differ per source.

docs.title: Every channel goes through FSC
docs.text:
Every channel that calls a source for an external party goes through FSC, with a valid certificate (REQ-46, ADR-0003). DvTP, EUDI issuance, and the ASIP each call through their own Outway. FSC traffic is mTLS between peers. The Manager of the provider issues the access token with the grant hash of the contract.

FSC refuses a connection with an expired or revoked certificate. open-fsc checks revocation with a CRL cache. An operator can switch off this cache per Inway, Outway, and Manager. The requirement forbids this. The demo does not check this behavior. It is open within which time a revocation must take effect (Q-53).

docs.title: Private parties
docs.text:
A private consumer authenticates in two ways, with separate roles (Q-06, answered):

  • People use eHerkenning at onboarding and for management (FR-03).
  • Systems use an organization certificate from a recognized issuer, linked to the OIN or the KvK number (FR-33, FR-34).

The candidate connection condition has two parts (AV-04):

  • A private consumer runs its own FSC peer with a PKIoverheid certificate.
  • The private consumer uses the OIN as its legal identity.

FR-33 allows an OIN or a KvK number. The link between OIN, KvK, and eIDAS identifiers is an open S04 decision. The trust framework for private parties as a whole is PSA decision B-09 in the decision register.

An integrator connects under FSC delegation. The consent binds the party that the integrator represents (ADR-0034). The consent does not bind the integrator.

docs.title: The PKIoverheid question
docs.text:
The first version of ADR-0023 aimed at one infrastructure, with PKIoverheid as the anchor for all certificates, including EUDI. GO and PSA no longer follow that ambition (Q-07, answered). The roles are separate:

  • PKIoverheid is the Dutch PKI for mTLS, FSC, and organization identity.
  • A PuB-EAA carries a qualified electronic seal, from a certificate that a QTSP issues. Neither PKIoverheid nor an access CA seals it (F-66).
  • An access CA issues access certificates only (ETSI TS 119 411-8). An access certificate authenticates an issuer or relying party to the wallet. It never signs attestations.

Dutch EUDI governance decides which party operates the Dutch access CA. This is a dependency outside the decision scope of GBO.

docs.title: EUDI issuance: a certificate set per source
docs.text:
The issuance facility keeps a certificate set per bronhouder. The set has issuer, reader (access), and status-list certificates. The facility never signs with the set of another bronhouder (REQ-58). The issuer name and the purpose that the wallet shows are bound to these certificates. A fallback to the set of another source made the wallet show the wrong issuer (F-50).

A missing or incomplete set blocks only that source. For the failure cases, see Source onboarding.

docs.title: EUDI trust roles
docs.text:
GBO issues attestations for bronhouders. Each of these bronhouders needs its own certificate per role, and one certificate never fills two roles (ADR-0023, part B, proposed, F-81). The roles are as follows:

Role Purpose Issued by Trust anchor Organization or system certificate mTLS for FSC, and the OIN and name PKIoverheid PKIoverheid root Access certificate Authenticates the issuer to the wallet (OpenID4VCI) An access CA (ETSI TS 119 411-8) The access CA that the member state notifies Registration certificate Proves the registration, per registered service (since Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1730) A provider that the member state appoints Published by the member state Qualified certificate for electronic seal Seals the PuB-EAA. Profile ETSI TS 119 412-6 clause 8. Names the authentic source and the legal basis. Key in a QSCD A QTSP Open (Q-30) Status-list certificate Signs the status list for revocation Open (Q-17) Open

ADR-0028 sets the roles and responsibilities around these certificates:

  • Each bronhouder is the PuB-EAA provider of its attestations. GBO operates the technical issuance facility. GBO is probably the EEAIssuer in the notification of each bronhouder. It is open who designates the Dutch PuB-EAA issuer, and who supervises (Q-28).
  • The issuer registers as relying party with the entitlement PUB_EAA_Provider.
  • It is open on which trust list PuB-EAA providers appear. The options are a List of Trusted Entities (ETSI TS 119 602) or the trusted lists (ETSI TS 119 612). The specifications contradict each other (Q-30). No decision exists for either list.
  • It is open who holds the seal and status-list keys. The options are the central facility, a remote signing service, or an HSM at the bronhouder (Q-17). In the demo, the central issuance server holds them.

To verify the PID that the wallet discloses, the issuance server also trusts PID issuers. Its list of PID trust anchors holds these CAs (issuance_server.toml.example#L3-L9, issuance_release.go#L120-L121):

  • The BZK pre-production PID issuer CA.
  • The GBO development issuer CA.
  • The issuer CA of every source.

That list is too broad. It must hold PID-provider anchors only. The callback from the issuance server to the adapter has no caller authentication (REQ-45, ADR-0018).

docs.title: ASI trust roles
docs.text:
In the ASI route, the QTSP is not an FSC participant. The chain on FSC starts behind the ASIP (F-87). Two trust points apply:

  • Admission of a QTSP: only a QTSP with the QEAA_Provider right in the register becomes a client of the ASIP (REQ-88). That register and the certificate profile do not exist in demo v0.9.0 (F-85). It is open which identifier links the access certificate of a QTSP to its register entry (Q-35).
  • The seal on a result: the ASIP seals every verification result (REQ-83). The format is open (Q-32, ADR-0041). The demo seals with a development certificate. This certificate is not a qualified seal certificate.

ADR-0037 describes the ASI front door.

docs.title: Demo PKI and production
docs.text:
The demo generates its own trust anchors. Git ignores the private keys, and the demo generates them again for each checkout.

The demo and production use different PKI parts:

Area Demo Production FSC group root A self-hosted CA: cfssl with a root and intermediate CA (GBO-DEMO Root CA) (fsc-infra/pki/generate-root-ca.sh) PKIoverheid FSC certificate requests The FSC ca-certportal in front of cfssl (fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml#L60-L72) The PKIoverheid issuance process of each organization Organization certificates Per organization, a group certificate with serialNumber = OIN, and internal mTLS certificates (bootstrap-bd-mock.sh#L48) PKIoverheid certificates of each organization PDP AuthZEN endpoint A self-signed certificate that the Inways pin as CA (generate-pdp-cert.sh) An organization certificate EUDI issuer and reader CAs Two pre-provisioned development CAs. The demo never generates them, and onboarding stops without them (Makefile#L268-L272) A QTSP for the seal, an access CA, and a registration certificate provider Source leaf certificates The development CA provider mints source-bound issuer, reader, and status-list leafs, under a separate privileged command (Makefile#L326-L336) Issued per bronhouder, per role ASIP seal and QTSP client certificates From the same development CAs (Makefile#L276-L283, #L320-L324) A qualified seal certificate, and access certificates of admitted QTSPs PID trust anchor The BZK pre-production PID issuer CA The notified PID providers

In the demo, the development CA fills all EUDI roles at the same time. Production separates the roles. The demo is not tested against these standards (F-81):

  • ETSI TS 119 471.
  • The certificate profile.
  • The checks of ETSI TS 119 472-3.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
These points about identity and trust are open:

  • Can policy read the Peer ID of a consumer as its OIN (Q-68)?
  • The trust list for PuB-EAA providers (Q-30).
  • Custody of the seal and status-list keys (Q-17).
  • Designation of the Dutch PuB-EAA issuer, and supervision (Q-28).
  • The identifier between a QTSP access certificate and its register entry (Q-35).
  • The time limit for a revocation to take effect (Q-53).
  • The trust framework for private parties (PSA B-09).
  • Migration from the self-generated demo CAs.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-45, REQ-46, REQ-58, REQ-67, REQ-83, REQ-88, AV-04
  • Findings: F-50 (closed), F-60 (closed), F-66 (closed), F-81 (open), F-85 (open), F-87 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-06 (answered), Q-07 (answered), Q-17 (open), Q-28 (open), Q-30 (open), Q-32 (open), Q-35 (open), Q-53 (open), Q-68 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-34a (done), SL-34c (done), SL-49 (done)
  • Decisions: ADR-0003, ADR-0023, ADR-0028 (proposed)

docs.title: Logging, audit and traceability
docs.text:
Every data exchange must be reconstructable afterwards: who asked for what, under which basis, with which decision, and which organization processed which personal data (P-12, capability S09). The record and correlation model on this page is the model that gbo-demo v0.9.0 implements. The decisions behind the model are ADR-0035 (correlation), ADR-0036 (decision records), and ADR-0026 (processing records).

A controller (Verantwoordelijke) is the organization that is responsible for a processing under the GDPR. A data subject (Betrokkene) is the person whom a processing is about.

docs.title: Three records, one chain
docs.text:
Logius maintains three related logging standards. Each standard records a different thing. GBO uses all three, together with traces and logs (F-63):

Record Standard What it records Writer Store in the demo Role Decision Authorization Decision Log (ADL) each PDP evaluation the PDP (OpenFTV) Postgres database ftv_adl authoritative Processing Logboek Dataverwerkingen (LDV) 1.0.0 each processing of personal data each component, in the logbook of its controller one logbook per controller authoritative Transport FSC-Logging (draft) each FSC transaction FSC Inway and Outway transaction log per FSC peer authoritative Traces OpenTelemetry (OTLP) technical operations all services Jaeger, 7 days observability Logs none operational log lines, including the console decision log of the policy engine all services Loki, 7 days observability

A PDP decision is not a processing, so it gets no LDV record. The LDV records are at three processings (F-64):

  • the consent status lookup at the register
  • the decryption at the source gateway
  • the query at the source

Traces and logs are for debugging. They are sampled or best-effort, and nobody cites them as evidence. The audit records are in separate stores with their own guarantees (REQ-32, OBSERVABILITY.md). The components write their records to these stores:

docs.title: Correlation: trace ID and transaction ID
docs.text:
Two identifiers link the records (REQ-55, ADR-0035):

W3C trace ID Fsc-Transaction-Id Made by the application that starts the processing the FSC Outway (or the entry component) Count per processing one one per FSC transaction Recorded in LDV trace_id, ADL trace_id, spans, operational logs FSC transaction log, ADL adl.fsc.transaction_id, span attribute gbo.fsc.transaction_id

Four rules apply to correlation:

  • Every component takes the trace ID unchanged from the incoming traceparent. The component sets the span of the caller as parent only for a caller in the same trace. It sends traceparent and tracestate on every outbound call.
  • The component looks for the trace ID in a fixed order: traceparent, then Fsc-Transaction-Id, then X-Request-Id, then the ambient span. If none of these is present, it starts a new trace (tracecontext.go#L78, #L181).
  • The transaction ID never replaces an incoming trace. A component that starts or receives an FSC transaction records the transaction ID next to the trace ID.
  • If an entry component receives no traceparent, it can tie its new trace to the UUIDv7 transaction ID that it mints (consumerhttp.go#L166-L182). If a request crosses FSC once, the trace ID and the transaction ID then have the same value. After a second FSC hop, they differ.

The earlier rule "trace ID equals transaction ID" (ADR-0019) broke in three cases (F-67):

  • a caller that sends its own traceparent
  • one processing that calls several sources
  • every extra FSC hop

FSC forwards traceparent on the data path. One hop breaks the context: the Inway calls the PDP over AuthZEN on a fresh context, with only X-Request-Id (F-39, F-41).

The Inway copies the headers of the original request into the AuthZEN context. When the policy calls the consent register (toestemmingsregister) for a status, it reads the trace from this context. The status request carries the trace ID of the request with a new span. It also carries the transaction ID (consent.rego#L190-L245). As a result, the LDV record of the register lands in the trace of the request.

The status lookup goes through the own Outway of the PDP. It is a second FSC transaction, but it sends the transaction ID of the consumer. FSC-Logging says that a transaction ID is unique per transaction. Nobody checked on a running stack whether the Outway accepts a duplicate ID from the client.

Separate units of work keep separate traces. The consent_id joins consent issuance and the later query. The two do not share a trace (F-16).

In most services, operational logs carry the trace ID through structured logging (graphql-server/slogctx.go#L15-L24). Logs and traces join on equal identifiers. Time stamps play no part in the join. In demo v0.9.0, the operational logs of bron-sidecar, eudi-adapter, and asi-provider carry no trace ID.

docs.title: Decision records (ADL)
docs.text:
The PDP writes one ADL record for each evaluation, to the Postgres database ftv_adl (REQ-71, ADR-0036). The PDP does not start without this database, so the ADL runs in every deployment profile (docker-compose.yml#L117-L126). Contract-acceptance decisions are ADL records too. A reader gets a SELECT-only role, adl_reader (adl-reader.sql).

The embedded OPA also writes a console decision log line for each evaluation. This line goes to Loki. It holds the full policy result: for each field, the rule that granted or denied it, and the step trace. The line is observability data. The developer portal shows it as detail next to the ADL record. The portal sets the color of the PDP from the ADL record alone (F-53).

The ADL record holds the AuthZEN request and answer. OpenFTV takes only allow and reason from the policy. On a deny, reason becomes reason_user.en (authz.rego#L42-L51). Per-field detail cannot go in the answer, because the FSC Inway returns the reason to the consumer. So the record can hold only what the consumer can also see (F-72).

The decision record has five known gaps:

  • No correlation behind the Inway: the Inway sends neither traceparent nor Fsc-Transaction-Id to the PDP. The record gets a random trace and no adl.fsc.transaction_id. A reader finds the record through the request headers stored in it (adl.go#L48-L66, #369). The fix is upstream in open-fsc.
  • No policy version: the records carry policies: 0 (REQ-59). A reader cannot see in the record which policy decided. For more information, see Policy lifecycle.
  • Only {allow, reason}: the record lacks the consent status answer (adl.core.information) and the configuration (F-72). Because the policy fetches the consent status during evaluation, nobody can replay a decision from the record.
  • No pointer to the consent logbook (Q-25). For more information, see Reading a chain.
  • A BSN in the EUDI and ASI routes. For more information, see Data handling.

docs.title: Processing records (LDV)
docs.text:
Every GBO-delivered component that processes personal data writes one LDV record per processing and per data subject. It writes to the logbook of its own controller (REQ-72, ADR-0026). Only trace metadata crosses an organization boundary. A shared logbook breaks this rule, so the demo runs one ldv-logboek image as seven logbooks (docker-compose.yml#L410-L598):

Logbook Controller Writers logboek-afnemer Hypotheek-BV (demo consumer) dienstverlener-backend, integrator-backend logboek-ir Installatie Register (demo consumer) ir-backend logboek-bd Belastingdienst bron-sidecar, graphql-server logboek-brp RvIG brp-sidecar, brp-graphql-server logboek-lvg LVG lvg-sidecar, lvg-graphql-server logboek-toestemming GBO consent-register, consent-portal-backend logboek-eudi-adapter GBO eudi-adapter

In production, GBO does not build these logbooks. Each controller runs its own logbook, and GBO ships the client (services/ldv-client). The client holds the parts that are the same everywhere: configuration, the acknowledged write, trace and span IDs, and the attribute map. It also decodes FSC claims and derives the data subject.

Each record carries five elements:

  • Trace context, as defined in ADR-0035.

  • The data subject, never a BSN: dpl.core.data_subject_id names the data subject in the own identifier space of the controller. The field data_subject_id_type makes the type explicit:

    Type Meaning Used by consent-id the consent that the consumer acted under consumer logboek-pseudoniem HMAC over the BSN with a key of this controller sources, EUDI adapter portal-subject the reference that the consent portal (toestemmingsportaal) derives consent register and portal brp-persoon-id the own record ID of RvIG, for a person named in a certificate about another person RvIG only

  • A processing activity: processing_activity_id refers to a versioned, resolvable activity, for example bd-ib-2025@v1. Each logbook serves a stand-in register of processing activities (GET /verwerkingsactiviteiten). The logbook validates writes against this register. The stand-in has no legal status (Q-08).

  • A pointer to the next logbook: if a component calls another party, it sets dpl.read.nextLogbookId to the read API of that party. The consumer does this for each source call. The EUDI adapter does it on the attestation record. The portal points to BSNk. That value is a demo placeholder, because the BSNk mock has no read API.
  • The calling party: on a lookup over FSC, dpl.core.foreign_operation.processor names the FSC peer of the caller. At the consent register, this is the peer verified from Fsc-Authorization (client.go#L441-L452, REQ-76).

The LDV integration rests on six design choices:

  • One record per data subject: a further data subject of the same processing gets a child record under the first record. In the death-certificate flow, every further person that the certificate names gets a child record (ldv_query.go#L218-L285). A query over several tax years gives one record per activity.
  • Each logbook has its own pseudonym space: the pseudonym key is per controller. The same citizen is not recognizable across the logbooks of different controllers. A source logs under its own pseudonym, never under a value that the caller sends (F-69). Since SL-51, no pseudonym travels in the chain at all.
  • The logbook refuses a BSN: it scans every write for a nine-digit run that passes the BSN checksum (elfproef). The scan covers all values, the record name, and the resource. The logbook refuses a match. The check is word-bounded, so a 20-digit OIN passes (validate.go#L141-L157).

  • Durable first, delivered after: a component stores the record in a local outbox, with an fsync, before its response leaves. It delivers the record afterwards with retries (outbox.go#L17-L38). A logbook outage delays records. It does not fail requests and does not lose records.

    If a component cannot store the record locally, it refuses the processing. The reason is that a withheld response does not undo a processing that already happened. The primary key (trace_id, span_id) makes a replay idempotent.

    The consent register keeps its outbox as a table in the same database as the consents. So a consent and its record commit in one transaction.

  • Separate write and read tokens: a component that can write cannot read with that token.

  • A local extension: the consent register, the portal, and the EUDI adapter write dpl.gbo.* attributes. This extension has no approval from Logius. The honest claim is "LDV core with a local extension" (Q-72).

In demo v0.9.0, the ASIP writes no LDV records, although it is a GBO-delivered component that processes personal data.

docs.title: How to read a chain
docs.text:
The LDV read extension is POST /data-processing-operations. It selects records by traceId, processingActivityId, or dataSubjectId. A read starts at the application that started the processing. From there, a reader follows nextLogbookId (docs/ldv/README.md). For one DvTP query, a reader does these steps:

  1. Call the consumer logbook with trace ID T.
  2. Follow nextLogbookId in the consumer record to the read API of the source.
  3. Call the source logbook with T. It returns the records of the source gateway and of the source.
  4. Use the transaction ID for the FSC transaction logs. Find the ADL record through the transaction ID in the stored request headers (#369).
  5. Call the consent logbook with T. No record points there.
sequenceDiagram box rgb(241,239,232) Reader participant R as Reader end box rgb(237,233,254) Records participant LA as Consumer logbook participant LS as Source logbook participant ADL as ADL participant LT as Consent logbook end R->>LA: read traceId T LA-->>R: record, nextLogbookId = source R->>LS: read traceId T LS-->>R: gateway and source records R->>ADL: SELECT on transaction ID (request headers) ADL-->>R: decision record Note over R,LT: no pointer leads here (Q-25) R->>LT: read traceId T LT-->>R: status lookup record

Two gaps limit this route (F-68):

  • The start is at a party that LDV does not bind. In DvTP, a private consumer starts the processing. Without its records, nobody knows which sources one processing touched. A consumer that calls two sources writes two records under one trace ID. Each record has its own pointer and its own transaction ID.

    The minimum for a consumer is trace context and the transaction ID (AV-01). LDV for the consumer is a candidate condition (AV-02). The demo consumer logs under the consent ID, because it has no citizen identifier (Q-27).

    The register records form a second index over the whole chain. Every source call leads to a status lookup, and the register logs this lookup with trace and consent ID.

  • The step from the decision to the consent logbook. The PDP writes only an ADL record and no LDV record. The ADL has no field like nextLogbookId. The demo applies option 3 of Q-25: a reader calls the consent logbook by trace ID. The chain view in the developer portal shows that logbook as "reached without pointer" (dev-portal-backend/ldv.go).

A caller can fill nextLogbookId only if the source publishes the read API of its logbook. In demo v0.9.0, the source metadata does not carry this API. The consumer and the EUDI adapter get it from configuration (REQ-64, Source onboarding).

Citizen access works per controller, through the read extension of each logbook, by data subject. Each controller answers for its own processings (GDPR article 15) (F-65). Demo v0.9.0 does not build a view of the processings per consent.

docs.title: Data handling
docs.text:
Logging holds no BSN that the processing does not need. Masking in the decision log is never the only safeguard (REQ-60). Each record type handles the BSN as follows, per route:

Record Consent route (DvTP) EUDI and ASI routes LDV no BSN. The logbook refuses one no BSN. The logbook refuses one ADL and console decision log a placeholder, no identity (SL-51) the plain BSN, from the PID or the token Spans and operational logs no BSN no BSN

In the consent route, the PDP input holds a placeholder for the subject. The source gateway replaces the placeholder after the allow (ADR-0033, Pseudonymization).

In the EUDI and ASI routes, the query variables hold the plain BSN (eudi-adapter/source_metadata.go#L273, asi-provider/internal/graphqlsource/source.go#L94). Neither decision log masks anything. The ADL has no masking option, and the console log ignores the OPA mask policy (F-54).

Earlier, the request mapper pseudonymized the BSN before evaluation. PR #370 removed this step when the mapper became a pure mapper. Until #368 decides, the demo accepts the BSN in both decision logs. The proposal is to keep identifiers out of the PDP input (ADR-0043).

docs.title: Protection and retention
docs.text:
REQ-32 requires three things of audit records: protection against change and deletion, no sampling, and separation from operational logs. Demo v0.9.0 has this status for each property:

Property ADL LDV logbooks FSC transaction logs Separate store yes yes, SQLite per logbook, synchronous = FULL yes, per peer Never sampled yes yes, acknowledged per record yes Read access SELECT-only role read token intra-organization API or the remote Manager (F-42) Tamper evidence (WORM, hash chain, notary) no no no Retention period not set not set not set

Two points are open: who can read which records, and how long the records are kept (Q-08). The ADL source-reference model adds a constraint: a source that a record points to must stay available as long as the record exists.

docs.title: Policy lifecycle
docs.text:
Each bronhouder owns, writes, and publishes the policy that its own PDP evaluates. GBO supplies a reference policy set, an engine choice, and guidelines. GBO does not supply a central policy service. The following sections show how a policy travels from version control to a decision in demo v0.9.0, and which points are open.

The policy lifecycle realizes capability S06. The decision is ADR-0021. For the management-plane scenario, see Policy distribution.

docs.title: Ownership per bronhouder
docs.text:
The PAP and the PDP are at each bronhouder. The PDP is behind the FSC Inway of the bronhouder, and the management function serves only that PDP. The policy belongs to the source (P-10).

The question of who can manage and publish the policy of a bronhouder has an answer: the bronhouder itself (Q-21, October 28, 2026). PSA S06 sets the norm for publication control. The norm asks for these items:

  • An owner.
  • An approver.
  • An effective date.
  • A change history.
  • Tests before publication.
  • An emergency and rollback procedure.

Authority over policy is with competent public parties. As a result, GBO sets no requirements on the policy installation of another party. The management practices are guidelines (RL-01 to RL-05, in the guidelines table later on this page). A guideline becomes a requirement only if GBO delivers the management setup itself (Policy management guidelines).

In the demo, all components run in one compose stack. This is a demo artifact and makes no statement about the architecture.

docs.title: Policy authoring
docs.text:
All authorization policies are Rego in version control (policies/), with tests next to the rules. The set has four parts:

Part Files Role Entrypoint authz.rego The package that OpenFTV evaluates. It maps the engine response to allow and reason Engine and readers gbo/engine.rego, gbo/lib.rego, gbo/consent.rego, gbo/graphql_schemas.rego Generic machinery: regime and service binding, the closed world, reason codes, the consent proof, schema pins Rules gbo/rules/dvtp/, gbo/rules/eudi/, gbo/rules/asi/ One package per access verdict: DVT0001, LVG0001, EUD0001, EUD0002, ASI0001 Contract policy fsc/autosign.rego Contract acceptance for the provider's FSC Manager (ADR-0015)

A new access verdict is a new rule file with tests. The engine does not change. For the rule model, see Authorization.

Scripts generate two files, and CI checks them:

  • The schema pins (scripts/gen-graphql-pins.sh).
  • The rule list that the developer portal shows (scripts/gen-rules-json.sh). OpenFTV has no data API, so the portal reads a generated file.

docs.title: Validation before activation
docs.text:
The PDP compiles the policy set as a whole. One bad module does not give a deny. Instead, it breaks every decision (F-52). The demo had this type of fault several times:

  • A stale policy declared the same package as an existing rule. Every request got HTTP 500.
  • A non-Rego file under policies/ silently removed every policy after it in walk order.
  • A second file with the same name replaced the first, because the PAP keys policies by file name.
  • The PAP reports a module that does not compile as loaded, while the old policy continues to decide (#151).

The local safety net is make policy-check (Makefile#L92-L106). It refuses non-Rego files and duplicate file names under policies/. Then it runs opa check. Every make target that starts the PDP depends on it.

make policy-test adds opa fmt --diff and opa test (Makefile#L115-L117). CI repeats these steps. CI also checks that the generated files are up to date (ci.yml#L135-L182).

Validation and a visible fallback at activation are not built (RL-05). If a PDP gets a broken bundle, it does not keep the last valid set. It also does not report that a later version did not load. Source metadata has this lifecycle in demo v0.9.0: validation before activation, atomic promotion, and rollback (F-59, REQ-66). For policy, this lifecycle is a backlog item.

The contract policy is in the same set. As a result, one broken module also stops the admission of new participants. The contract policy has a fixed package name (doelbinding.auto_sign_contract). If someone renames it, it resolves to nothing, and every contract stays pending.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text:
The demo distributes policy in two modes:

Mode How When Mount (default) The PDP image carries the policies (Dockerfile#L62-L67). Compose mounts ./policies over them (docker-compose.yml#L157) Every make demo* target. Edit and save while you write Rego Bundle (opt-in) The OpenFTV Manager stores the policies in Postgres. Bundle gbo-pdp collects every policy with tag gbo-authz, with a version. If PDP_BUNDLE_MANAGER is set, the PDP pulls the bundle at start (docker-compose.yml#L145-L149) make demo-manager, make manager-seed sequenceDiagram autonumber box rgb(237,233,254) Version control participant GIT as Version control (policies/) end box rgb(241,239,232) Deployment participant SEED as seed-openftv-manager.py<br/>(deployment identity) participant IDP as Keycloak (realm gbo) end box rgb(220,252,231) GBO Basis participant MGR as OpenFTV Manager (PAP) participant PDP as OpenFTV PDP end box rgb(237,233,254) Records participant PG as postgres-ftv end SEED->>IDP: token request (deployment identity) IDP-->>SEED: short-lived access token SEED->>GIT: read policies/**/*.rego SEED->>MGR: POST/PUT /v1/policy/{id}, tag gbo-authz MGR->>PG: store policy and audit trail SEED->>MGR: GET /v1/policies: what left version control? SEED->>MGR: PUT /v1/policy/{id}, tag gbo-retired Note over SEED,PDP: make demo-manager restarts the PDP PDP->>MGR: GET /v1/bundle/gbo-pdp (internal port) MGR-->>PDP: bundle {version, policies} PDP->>PDP: compile and activate the whole set PDP->>PG: decision records to the ADL

Version control is the source of the content. The Manager is the distribution mechanism. Policy enters the Manager only through its API. An administrator in the management interface uses the same path.

The distribution has these properties:

  • The PDP pulls, and nothing pushes. The PDP authorizes its own management endpoints with the decision policy. That policy denies every request that is not a data request, so a push gets 403 (F-51, gbo-pdp.yaml#L18-L32). The bundle has no push targets. The PDP pulls at start, so a new seed needs a PDP restart.
  • The seed script retires policy and does not delete it. A delete fails upstream on a foreign key to the audit trail. The seed script removes the bundle tag from every policy that left version control (seed-openftv-manager.py#L116-L122). Without that reconciliation, a renamed rule stays in the bundle (RL-04).
  • Cedar policies authorize the management API. The Manager authorizes its own API with Cedar policies, separate from the Rego decision policy: admin.cedar, auditor.cedar, and pdp-bundle.cedar. Since OpenFTV v0.1.0, the bundle pull runs through the same authorizer. The PDP shows no identity, so pdp-bundle.cedar allows only GET on the one bundle path (RL-02).
  • The Cedar store seeds once. The Manager seeds its Cedar policies into Postgres only while the store is empty. After that, the Manager uses the store as the source of truth. An existing volume does not pick up a changed Cedar file (CHANGELOG). While its policy store is empty, the engine switches authorization off.
  • Writing and publishing are separate. The realm has the roles admin, author, and auditor. Publication uses a non-personal deployment identity with a short-lived token (RL-03).
  • The bundle has no signature. The bundle has an ID and a version. A bundle gets a signature only when it crosses an organization boundary. Inside one organization, signing is not planned (#426, closed as not planned). If a bronhouder lets another organization build or host its bundles, signing and verification become a requirement (F-09).

Two components have the name Manager. The OpenFTV Manager manages policy. The FSC Manager manages contracts and issues access tokens. Always name which Manager you mean.

The ADL database (postgres-ftv) runs in every profile, because the PDP does not start without it. Only the OpenFTV Manager, its management interface, and Keycloak are opt-in.

docs.title: Policy data
docs.text:
Rules use data from four sources, each with its own lifecycle:

Source Examples Lifecycle In the rule allowed_years of EUD0001, designated_issuers shared by the EUDI rules (eudi_helper.rego#L13-L20), the asip peer of ASI0001 Changes with the policy set In the bundle Schema digests per FSC service (graphql_schemas.rego) Generated from the bundled schemas. CI checks drift PIP pull Admission register: active, allowed_source_peer_ids, integrator mandates acts_for (dvtp-onboarding.yaml) Refreshed every 5 seconds Per request The consent proof and its status, resolved by the policy itself (consent.rego) Status live, keys cached 300 seconds (Consent)

A place on a PID actor list (designated_issuers, asip) is an admission decision with authorization weight. In every environment, those lists must stay disjoint from the consent consumers (F-70, Authorization). In demo v0.9.0, the lists are policy data and not register data.

docs.title: Guidelines for bronhouders
docs.text:
Each guideline has a demo status in demo v0.9.0:

Guideline Demo status RL-01 Deliver policy as a versioned bundle. Do not bake it into the PDP Opt-in only (make demo-manager). The default mounts the policies. No signature RL-02 Authorize the management API with its own policy set. Deny on an empty store Built for the Manager (Cedar). The PDP itself does not obey it (F-51). The engine opens up on an empty store RL-03 Separate writing from publishing. Publish with a non-personal, short-lived identity Deployment identity built. The author role grants no action, so writing and publishing are not separate RL-04 Withdraw policy, and do not delete it. Reconcile with version control Built: retire_stale at every seed RL-05 Validate a bundle before activation. Fall back visibly to the last valid set Local check built (make policy-check). Visible fallback not built

Each guideline is a SHOULD for the bronhouder. A promotion rule names when the guideline becomes a requirement.

docs.title: Policy version and the decision record
docs.text:
The decision record must name the policy version that decided (REQ-59). This is not built. The ADL records show no policy version, also when the PDP runs on a versioned bundle. Without the version, nobody can trace a decision back to the rule text.

Withdrawn policy stays in the Manager. This is a precondition for the trace (RL-04). For the ADL itself, see Logging.

docs.title: Divergence: Rego, not ODRL
docs.text: PSA S06 names ODRL as a policy language option. GBO uses Rego for every decision, and the OpenFTV Manager uses Cedar for its own API. GBO keeps this choice. Risks and technical debt records the deviation. Per D-13, the deviation must go to the standards bodies. It is open how the reference policy shows that it is not tied to one language or engine (Q-78).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: RL-01, RL-02, RL-03, RL-04, RL-05, REQ-59, REQ-66
  • Findings: F-09 (closed by ADR-0021), F-51 (open), F-52 (open), F-59 (closed), F-70 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-02 (answered), Q-21 (answered), Q-78 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-13 (done), SL-44 (done)

docs.title: Pseudonymization
docs.text:
Private consumers must not process the BSN (P-04). In DvTP, they still request data about one citizen from government sources. For this, GBO uses the BSNk PP polymorphic pseudonym scheme. GBO calls BSNk only at consent time (ADR-0005). In the consent route, the consumer holds no identifier of the citizen: no BSN and no pseudonym (REQ-20). After the PDP allows the request, only the source turns its own value back into the BSN (ADR-0033).

Pseudonymization realizes capability S03. For the BSNk rules that shape this design, see BSNk preconditions. For the consent proof that carries the values, see Consent.

docs.title: Identifiers
docs.text:
Each identifier of the citizen or the consent has its own maker and holder:

Identifier What it is Made by Held by BSN The citizen service number DigiD login, or PID disclosure (EUDI, ASI) The portal backend during the login. The source, inside its own boundary PI, PP Polymorphic identity and polymorphic pseudonym. Only the requester can get them transformed (BSNK-03) BSNk Activate, once per citizen The portal backend. The register stores them under subject_ref (REQ-69) VI (encrypted identity) A value for one recipient OIN and key version. It decrypts to the BSN. It exists only for a recipient on the BSN authorization list (BSNK-06) BSNk Transform, at consent Inside the consent proof, encrypted_subject[<OIN>].identity VP (encrypted pseudonym) A value for one recipient OIN and key version. It decrypts to the own pseudonym of that recipient for the citizen. Every recipient gets one BSNk Transform, at consent Inside the consent proof, encrypted_subject[<OIN>].pseudonym Placeholder consent:identity or consent:pseudonym: the name of the subject in a consent-based query Fixed values (lib.rego#L43-L53) The consumer query and the PDP input. The source gateway replaces it subject_ref HMAC of the BSN with the secret, versioned key of the portal Portal backend (subjectref.go#L38-L42) Portal backend and register: the key to the consents of the citizen consent_id The consent record Consent register (toestemmingsregister) Consumer: its only handle on "this person"

PI and PP belong to the portal. VI and VP belong to their recipient. No other party can read them. In the demo, every party can read them because the mock does not encrypt. For more information, see Demo mock and production BSNk.
