docs.title: Values made at consent time
docs.text:
BSNk transforms values only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04). A query comes later. As a result, the portal makes every value that a source needs while the citizen gives consent (portal.go#L119-L192). The portal does these steps:

  1. It derives subject_ref from the BSN.
  2. It looks up PI and PP under subject_ref in the register. At the first consent of this citizen, it activates the BSN once at BSNk and stores PI and PP (portal.go#L296-L314).
  3. It reads the BSN authorization list from a copy. The copy is at most BSN_AUTHORISATION_LIST_MAX_AGE old (default 1 hour).
  4. It transforms PP to a VP for every source. It transforms PI to a VI for every source on the list (portal.go#L197-L224). Each BSNk request names at most four parties (BSNK-05, bsnk.go#L102-L115).
  5. It sends the values to the register. The register signs them into the proof and does not store them.

For each source, the portal must know the OIN, the key version, and the BSN authorization (REQ-82). In the demo, this is configuration: CONSENT_SOURCES=<OIN>@<key set version> (docker-compose.yml#L1005). If no source is configured, the portal gives no consent. A service catalogue that carries these facts is not built (#382).

The portal makes all values at consent, so the proof freezes. For more information, see Consent (F-78).

docs.title: Citizen recognition: route D
docs.text:
To show and revoke the consents of a citizen without a BSN, the consent facility (toestemmingsvoorziening) needs a stable key. A stored PI or PP is not a stable key, because BSNk gives other values at every activation. The proposed solution is route D (ADR-0040, proposed, route D). Route D works as follows:

  • The service recognizes the citizen by an HMAC of the BSN, with a secret, versioned key. Every record keeps the key version.
  • The service activates once and stores PI and PP under that reference.
  • To show or revoke consents, the service does not call BSNk.

The register stores PI and PP, but no BSN and no per-party value (REQ-69, REQ-23). This is an intentional deviation from FR-35, criterion 1 (F-98). For the other routes, see BSNk preconditions.

Route D has these open points:

  • Are the register and the portal backend one BSNk participant (Q-49)? In the demo, the backend activates and the register stores.
  • A changed HMAC key gives every citizen a different reference. Then the service does not show older consents. Migration is not built (Q-56).
  • The protection of the stored PI and PP is open (Q-57). Retention is also open (Q-63).

docs.title: Where the boundary is enforced
docs.text:
The BSN is in three places only. All three places are inside the government:

  1. Portal backend, at login: the backend derives subject_ref. At the first consent, it sends the BSN to BSNk. After that step, no component holds a BSN, because the draft consent has no field for one (portal.go#L116-L118). It is open how the backend inside MijnOverheid gets the verified identity (Q-50).
  2. BSNk, at activation: BSNk records every activation in its inspection register, the Inzageregister (BSNK-10).
  3. The source, after the allow: the source gateway takes the value for its own OIN from the proof. The decryption component of the source reads the value with the keys of the source. The gateway accepts the result only if the value names the OIN of the source as recipient (substitution.go#L213-L251, REQ-80). Then the gateway replaces the placeholder. BSNk is not in the query path (REQ-21).

The register never gets a BSN, not even for a short time (REQ-23). The consumer never gets a BSN in the proof or in the response.

Like the PDP, the gateway acts on the evidence. If the request carries a consent token, the gateway takes the subject from the token. If the request has no consent token, the gateway passes it through unchanged (PID regime). The gateway reads no grant property. The value for the requested form can be missing, for example no VI for a source that is not on the list. In that case, the gateway does not forward the request.

docs.title: Network isolation is the control
docs.text:
The gateway does not verify the proof again (substitution.go#L105-L107). A second check adds nothing, because a consumer holds real proofs. The rule "after the decision" holds only while the Inway is the only component that reaches the gateway (REQ-81, F-79).

In the demo, the gateways publish no port. They are on two networks only:

  • source-gateways, shared with the source Inways.
  • sources, shared with the source services, the decryption component, and the logbooks (docker-compose.yml#L829-L836).

No consumer is on either network. Outside Docker Compose, this isolation needs a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy or an equivalent control. The Helm chart in demo v0.9.0 has no NetworkPolicy. A nonce that binds a value to one consent, as a second line, is not built. For the zones, see Deployment.

docs.title: Subject binding
docs.text:
Under a consent, the PDP does not compare identifiers. The query names the subject with a placeholder. The source can fill in only the subject from the proof (REQ-79, F-77). For the rule, see Authorization. Subject binding has these consequences:

  • No policy at the PDP can depend on who the citizen is.
  • One request names one subject. A question about two persons does not fit. This needs a design decision.
  • Substitution works only on variables. If the query text holds a literal placeholder, the placeholder passes the PDP. The gateway does not replace it, and the query finds nobody.
  • The PDP input and the decision logs have no identifier. They do hold the proof with the encrypted values.

docs.title: The consumer has no identifier
docs.text:
The consumer reads only consent_id and scopes from the proof (F-76). This goes further than the "BSN-free" rule of P-04, because the consumer is free of all identifiers. This has three effects:

  • Logging: the consumer logbook names the data subject by the consent ID, with subject type consent-id (logbook.go#L20-L22). In the logbook, one citizen with two consents is two data subjects. It is open whether this fits LDV (Q-27).
  • Access requests: a citizen can ask the consumer what it processed. The consumer can find the citizen only through the consents of the citizen.
  • Recognition: through GBO, the consumer cannot tell that two consents are from the same person. This is data minimization, and a design choice.

With its own VP, the consumer has a pseudonym to log under. This option is in the design and not built (#478, Q-01). A source API that answers on a pseudonym is also not built. No demo rule accepts consent:pseudonym (#474).

docs.title: Exception: the BSN in the EUDI and ASI routes
docs.text:
The EUDI adapter and the ASIP put the plain BSN from the PID or the token into the query variables. As a result, the BSN is in the PDP input and in both decision logs: the ADL and the console log (source_metadata.go#L273, source.go#L94). The PDP does not call BSNk. This is a known violation of REQ-60. The demo accepts it until #368 decides between masking and "transform first" (CHANGELOG).

The proposed decision keeps identifiers out of the PDP input and uses masking only as a second line (ADR-0043, proposed). Earlier, masking in the policy engine had no effect (F-54). LDV records never hold a BSN, because the logbook refuses one (Logging).

docs.title: Demo mock and production BSNk
docs.text:
The demo uses bsnk-mock (README). The mock follows the BSNk interface (/v2/activate, /v2/transform, /v2/bsn-authorisation-list, and more), but as JSON instead of SOAP. The mock enforces these rules:

  • Only the requester can use the PI.
  • The BSN authorization list applies.
  • A request names at most four parties.
  • The mock reads values per key version.

The mock and production BSNk differ in these properties:

Property Demo Production Encryption None: any party that holds a PI or VI can read the BSN Encrypted values, unlinkable between parties Values Stable by default. Random with RANDOMIZE_VALUES=true, as real BSNk Different at every request Interface JSON over HTTP SOAP with PKIoverheid (BSNK-11) Who can activate Not checked: the mock takes the requester from the request Only a recognized participant (BSNK-01, F-75, Q-26) Activation input The BSN. The mock does not check it against a population register The BSN and check data (BSNK-02) Recipient keys Demo keys in the gateway image Per recipient through an Access Service or Key Requester (BSNK-09, #467) Key versions The mock accepts any key set version A value belongs to one key version. The source keeps older keys while proofs for them are valid (BSNK-08, AV-09) Decryption component One, shared by the three demo sources, which also share one OIN One per source, each with its own OIN (BSNK-07)

The same image, started with DECRYPTION_COMPONENT_ONLY=true, is the decryption component of the sources (docker-compose.yml#L773-L786). The mock does not encrypt and the sources share one OIN. As a result, the demo does not show unlinkability between parties. For the certificates and keys per party at onboarding, see BSNk preconditions.

docs.title: Source onboarding
docs.text:
A GBO component must know, for each source, which data service to call, with which query, and what to do with the answer. That knowledge comes from the source itself, and GBO takes a source into use in a fixed set of steps. The decisions are ADR-0016 (mechanism), ADR-0017 (mapping profile for attestations), and ADR-0039 (attributes for the ASIP). For the requirements, see Source metadata and activation. For the components, see the building block view. For the step-by-step flow, see Admission and activation.

The behavior on this page is the behavior of gbo-demo v0.9.0 (docs/source-onboarding.md, docs/source-metadata-cache.md).

docs.title: Why the source owns its description
docs.text:
The bronhouder keeps control of its data (P-10). It can add services through its source-specific GBO configuration (S07). Central GBO facilities read the part of this configuration that they need. They read it in machine-readable form, validated and versioned (S10).

As a result, a GBO component takes the service description of a source only from what the source publishes itself (REQ-64, F-57):

  • The component does not keep the description, add to it, or carry it per source in code.
  • A new service or attestation type needs no code change in GBO.
  • The source does not publish its GraphQL schema. It publishes the queries and mappings that it takes responsibility for.

Before this mechanism, every new source, attestation type, or tax year was a change in GBO code or in a GBO catalog file. With this mechanism, the adapter parameters come from the source (Q-19). In GO terms, the document is the service catalog (dienstencatalogus) that the bronhouder manages. The validation rules of the reconciler are the common profile.

The mechanism (publish, validate, activate, roll back) is a GBO design decision. The document format gbo-source-metadata-v1 is the proposal of the demo for the open PSA S10 decision. It is not a final interface agreement.

Three inputs together describe a source. Each input has a different owner:

Item Owner Where source_id, transport, metadata location, FSC Peer ID GBO operator source configuration file (sources/configured/<source_id>.yaml) Legal OIN, organization name, issuer name and logo bronhouder, through its certificate certificate set under the key source_id (Identity and trust) Access to the metadata and data services bronhouder and GBO, by agreement FSC contracts and grant hashes Data service, query, parameters, offers, display, claims, attributes bronhouder the source document at /.well-known/gbo Shape of an ASI attribute value (value_schema) GBO, until the EU catalog of attributes exists schemas/asi-attributes.json SD-JWT VC Type Metadata GBO generates it from the document source registry Candidates, states, releases, active pointer GBO source registry (PostgreSQL)

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart LR A[1 Configure<br/>source file] --> B[2 Discover<br/>FSC contracts] B --> C[3 Fetch or read<br/>the document] C --> D[4 Validate] D --> E[5 Candidate<br/>rollout_required] E --> F[6 Promote] F --> G[7 Immutable<br/>release] G --> H[8 Active<br/>pointer] H --> I[9 Runtime<br/>reload] D -- invalid --> X[source stale<br/>or blocked] %% GBO diagram palette: the same colors as the Globaal Ontwerp classDef basis fill:#DCFCE7,stroke:#16A34A,color:#0F172A classDef dvtp fill:#FEDCD8,stroke:#E28F80,color:#1E293B classDef eudi fill:#FFEDD5,stroke:#EA580C,color:#0F172A classDef source fill:#DDEBF7,stroke:#6F94B8,color:#1E293B classDef ext fill:#F1EFE8,stroke:#5F5E5A,color:#444441 classDef store fill:#EDE9FE,stroke:#7C3AED,color:#1E1B4B classDef mock fill:#F3F4F6,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#374151,stroke-dasharray:4 3 classDef planned fill:#FFFFFF,stroke:#9CA3AF,color:#6B7280,stroke-dasharray:6 4 classDef zoom stroke-width:3px class A,B,C,D,E,F,I,X basis class G,H store

Onboarding goes through nine steps:

  1. Configure: the operator adds one file per source in sources/configured/. The file name is the stable source_id. The file names the transport, the location of the metadata, and the FSC Peer ID of the provider (source_configuration.go#L16-L28). It does not name the OIN or the organization name. These come from the certificate set.
  2. Discover the contracts: for the fsc transport, the reconciler looks in the existing FSC contracts. There it finds the metadata contract and the data contract of the configured peer. It does not discover sources: a contract without a source file activates nothing.
  3. Fetch or read: only the reconciler fetches source metadata. It uses ETag and If-None-Match. A 304 only extends freshness. The reconciler validates every 200 in full. The runtime never fetches metadata.
  4. Validate: the reconciler validates schema, origin, version, validity window, query, mapping, offers, claims, and the binding to the data contract. The source_oin in the document must equal the OIN in the certificate set (source-registry/onboarding/service.go#L403-L413).
  5. Candidate: a valid result becomes a complete candidate with state rollout_required. This candidate is not active. An invalid result does not replace the last complete candidate.
  6. Promote: an operator promotes a complete candidate set. In the demo, the reconciler can do this itself (--auto-promote). Promotion is a separate step (reconcile_command.go#L134-L151).
  7. Immutable release: promotion writes one release from the complete candidate set. The SHA-256 of the content identifies the release. A release never changes (postgresregistry/store.go#L300-L390).
  8. Active pointer: in the same database transaction, promotion sets the singleton active_release_id. If a promotion fails, the previous release stays active.
  9. Runtime reload: the readers poll the active pointer with a read-only role. They build the new release in memory and swap it atomically. The nl-wallet issuance server reads its configuration only at startup. So a new release needs a controlled restart of that server.

Four readers use the active release:

Reader What it derives Reload EUDI adapter source snapshot (source, query, mapping, FSC grant, validity window), Type Metadata, offer catalog /eudi-offers.json live, by polling Issuance init container issuance_server.toml: offers, disclosure, certificates, trust anchors at a restart of the issuance server ASIP per data service: query, attribute mapping, legal name of the authentic source, discovery records live, every 5 seconds (asi-provider/main.go#L101) Developer portal and landing page the offers that a citizen can start, from the adapter live

The source registry is a shared module, services/source-registry (onboarding, postgresregistry, asisnapshot). The reconciler writes to it with the writer role. The adapter, the issuance init container, and the ASIP read it with the reader role. The reconciler has no Kubernetes API rights. It reads certificates and contracts and writes only to the registry.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
A source has two legs: the metadata leg and the data leg. Each leg selects its own transport (service.go#L18-L28):

Transport Metadata leg Data leg Authenticated fsc fixed path /.well-known/gbo through a separate FSC metadata service the data service named in the document, under its contract yes unsecured an absolute HTTP or HTTPS URL, with no FSC headers and no redirects an absolute URL no file a document in the metadata directory of the operator (--metadata-dir). The path cannot leave that directory not possible: a file cannot answer a query no

Five rules apply when the two legs combine transports:

  • If no data_access block is present, the data leg uses the metadata transport.
  • fsc metadata with unsecured data is refused.
  • file metadata needs an explicit data_access.
  • If both legs use fsc, the two services must differ.
  • provider_peer_id is on the leg that speaks FSC, never on both.

The registry reports both legs separately, as transport_authenticated and data_transport_authenticated (service.go#L56-L66). A single flag hides an FSC-authenticated data call whose description came over an unauthenticated channel. The party that controls the document decides the query, the mapping, and the wallet claims.

The intended form is fsc on both legs. The other combinations are for an onboarding phase:

  • file is for a source that publishes no /.well-known/gbo. The operator then keeps the description of the product of another party. This is an exception under D-13. The transport flag makes the exception visible, and expires_at makes it temporary.

    The exception is admissible only with recorded agreement of the bronhouder (AV-08, F-71). The demo does not record this agreement. The need for agreement is only an instruction in source-metadata/README.md.

  • unsecured is for local demonstrations. Only the local compose file mounts that source (sources/local-demo/). Deployments use only sources/configured/.

Four bounds stay in place with every transport:

  • The Peer ID comes from the GBO configuration.
  • The grant hash pins the contract.
  • The reconciler compares the OIN with the certificate.
  • Promotion is a separate step.

The trust model for each transport is an open point in demo issue #221.

docs.title: Contract and activation
docs.text:
A valid FSC contract does not take a source into use. It also does not put the offer of the source in the wallet (REQ-65, F-58). Transport and mandate are two decisions with two owners. If a contract alone activates a source, admission becomes automatic again through a back door (F-55). Each situation has a fixed result:

Situation Result Valid metadata contract, no source file nothing happens Source file, no metadata contract source blocked: METADATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND Source file, no contract for the data service source blocked: DATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND FSC Manager unreachable source blocked: FSC_MANAGER_UNAVAILABLE Validated candidate without promotion not active

The reason codes are in service.go#L141-L152. Automatic promotion is off by default (reconcile_command.go#L197). Compose and the Helm example turn it on for the demo. Then the source file is the management action. Demo v0.9.0 does not build two things: control over who can do that action, and a record of the admission decision (PSA B-09 in the decision register, REQ-123).

docs.title: Versions, freshness and isolation
docs.text:
Source metadata fails closed for each source and ages within fixed bounds. An operator can roll it back (REQ-66). The mechanism has five parts:

  • Freshness: a successful check is fresh for at most 15 minutes. After that, it is stale for at most one hour. At acceptance, a document must be valid for at least one more hour (source_metadata_cache.go#L10-L14). The issuance route shows X-GBO-Metadata-Cache: fresh|stale.
  • States per source: each source has one of five application states. Kubernetes conditions are a separate thing.
    • pending: the check started.
    • rollout_required: a complete candidate waits.
    • active: the source is in use.
    • stale: the refresh fails, and the previous snapshot is within grace.
    • blocked: no usable snapshot exists, or the grace is over.
  • Per-source refusal: if a source is past its grace, only the requests for that source get HTTP 503.
  • Version rule: activation refuses a lower version than the last validated candidate. It also refuses the same version with other content (source_registry_backend.go#L163-L175). The rule has no test (#610).
  • Rollback: an operator activates a stored release with activate-source-release --release-id. The command refuses a release that the adapter cannot load. An auto-promoter respects the rollback until new candidate content arrives.

Demo v0.9.0 has two deviations from the isolation rule (#606):

  • Promotion needs a valid version of every configured source (registry.go#L133-L158). The aim of this design is that no source leaves the wallet offer without notice. As a side effect, one broken source freezes new releases for all sources.
  • The offer list /eudi-offers.json takes the shortest grace of all sources (source_release_runtime.go#L95-L100). So the list fails for all sources at the same time.

Source releases have the lifecycle that policy bundles lack: validation before activation, bounded staleness, atomic promotion, and rollback (F-59). For the policy side, see Policy lifecycle and ADR-0021.

docs.title: A certificate set per source
docs.text:
Every source has its own certificate set for issuance: issuer, reader (access), and status-list certificates. GBO never shares a set between sources and never substitutes one (REQ-58). The issuer name and the purpose that the wallet shows are bound to the signing and reader certificates. A fallback to the set of another source made the wallet show the wrong issuer (F-50).

If material is missing, onboarding fails hard for that source only:

Situation Result No set for the source_id source blocked: CERTIFICATE_SET_NOT_FOUND Set without OIN or organization name source blocked: CERTIFICATE_SET_INVALID Mounted material differs from the active release GBO generates no issuance configuration (issuance_release.go#L113-L116) Two sources behind one FSC peer each source has its own set

The reconciler gets only public leaf certificates and public CA certificates. Only the issuance init container gets the private keys of the leaf certificates. Provisioning is a separate privileged command. For where these certificates come from and how they map to EUDI trust roles, see Identity and trust.

docs.title: The source document
docs.text:
The document is JSON, validated against gbo-source-metadata-v1.schema.json. The format is closed: validation refuses unknown fields. The envelope has these fields:

Field Meaning schema_version 1.0 or 1.1. Version 1.1 adds the asi capability (#L17-L23) source_oin 20-digit OIN. It must equal the OIN in the certificate set version Numeric version. One version identifies one content issued_at, expires_at Validity window. At acceptance, at least one hour must remain capabilities.eudi attestations for EUDI issuance capabilities.asi attributes for verification through the ASIP (1.1 only)

docs.title: The eudi capability: claims once, Type Metadata generated
docs.text:
Each attestation has type_id, type_version, offers, graphql, mapping_profile, display, and claims. Four of these fields hold structured content:

  • offers are the concrete wallet offers, each with fixed parameters (for example jaar: 2024). A request with parameters outside the published offers is refused with HTTP 400.
  • graphql holds service_reference, endpoint, one read operation in document, subject_variable, declared parameters, and result_pointer.
  • display is keyed by language. It holds a name, a description, a summary with {{claim}} placeholders, and rendering.
  • claims defines each claim once. A claim has one gbo-simple-v1 rule in source (pointer, datatype, optional optional), a label, an optional description, and sd (always by default, allowed, or never).

Earlier versions had separate mapping, attribute_schema, and type_metadata blocks. The format removed them. GBO derives the mapping from claims. It generates the SD-JWT VC Type Metadata from display and claims (type_metadata.go#L64). Each Type Metadata field has a fixed origin in the document:

Type Metadata Derived from name, description the first language in display display[] display, with lang from the key claims[].path, svg_id the claim name claims[].display[] label and description claims[].sd sd schema.properties source.datatype (date becomes a string with format: date) schema.required every claim without optional: true, plus vct and vct#integrity

Because the schema comes from the same rules as the projection, a source cannot publish a schema that differs from what the mapping fills. Five validation rules apply to the claims (source_claims.go#L216-L242):

  • A summary placeholder must be a claim name.
  • Validation refuses reserved names (vct, vct#integrity, iss, status, cnf, iat, nbf, exp, sub, attestation_qualification).
  • The order of the claims is the order in which the wallet shows them.
  • Validation refuses the datatype number for EUDI, because nl-wallet v0.5 cannot show a non-integral value.
  • Only scalar datatypes pass. GBO does not support nested claims (REQ-78).

The VCT of a type version is /types/{source-id}/{type-id}/v{type-version}. The value vct#integrity covers the exact bytes that GBO serves at that URL. A change to claims or display changes those bytes, so the change needs a new type_version. GBO never deletes published type versions automatically.

For how an answer of the source becomes an attestation, and for the error codes if the answer does not fit, see ADR-0017 (REQ-116).

docs.title: The asi capability (schema 1.1)
docs.text:
From schema 1.1 on, a source can also describe the attributes that it offers for verification through the ASIP (ADR-0039, Q-38). The asi capability has three parts:

  • authentic_source: the legal name and the country. The ASIP uses them in responses and discovery records (REQ-94).
  • graphql: one query that ends in only ...Selected, the subject variable, and the result pointer. For each request, the ASIP replaces ...Selected with the fields of the requested attributes (REQ-92).

  • attributes: for each attribute, an identifier, an optional type condition on, and fields. Each member of the value has exactly one operation:

    Operation Meaning pointer copy a field join with separator concatenate two or more fields, without empty parts const a fixed value of the member type each with pointer for each element of a list, the field at pointer

The identifier must exist in the attribute catalog of GBO, schemas/asi-attributes.json. The catalog gives a value_schema for each identifier. The identifiers are placeholders until the EU catalog of attributes exists (Q-31).

The profile gbo-simple-v1 applies only to the eudi capability. The asi capability composes values, because a source cannot always deliver a catalog value with a copy. For example, a house number is three BRP fields. The BRP document shows this composition (brp-graphql-server/config/gbo-source-metadata.json#L204).

Onboarding applies six rules to asi (source_registration.go#L396-L406):

  • If asi has an error, onboarding refuses the whole source, also if eudi is valid. The active release stays.
  • The asi query uses the same data service as the attestations: one document, one data service.
  • Onboarding also refuses a document with only asi, because onboarding requires the issuance certificate sets.
  • If the reconciler cannot read the catalog, it refuses only the sources with asi.
  • A source with asi gets release snapshot version 4.0. A source without asi stays at 3.0.
  • Onboarding validates only the form. It does not validate the GraphQL schema of the source, or whether the policy of the source allows the selection. A difference becomes visible at the first request.

If the description is absent, has no asi, or is stale, the ASIP answers 503 for verify, retrieve, and discovery (REQ-93). If no registry is available, the ASIP can read a release file (asi-provider write-release-file).

docs.title: Connection conditions for bronhouders
docs.text:
GBO asks three things of a bronhouder, as candidate connection conditions:

  • The bronhouder publishes a machine-readable, versioned description for each data service at the fixed location. The description includes the read API of the logbook of the bronhouder (AV-07).
  • If the bronhouder has no endpoint of its own, it agrees provably with the description that the operator keeps (AV-08).
  • The bronhouder provides a certificate set that carries its OIN and organization name (REQ-67).

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
Seven points are open:

  • The document is not signed. The origin depends on the authenticated transport plus the OIN from the certificate set.
  • The description lacks three items: the read API of the logbook of the source, a reference to the DCAT-AP-NL description, and central findability (F-57, F-68, AV-07). Without the read API, a caller cannot fill dpl.read.nextLogbookId from the description.
  • DvTP does not use the description. The DvTP offer of a source is in the GBO rules. DvTP scope comes from the demand side. EUDI scope comes from the supply side (F-74).
  • Traceability of versions: no record shows which versions of the mapping, the source schema, and the attestation schema an attestation used (REQ-124).
  • Key custody: the central issuance server holds the private keys of the issuer and status-list certificates of every source (Q-17).
  • ASI resource list: in demo v0.9.0, the ASI authorization server takes its data services from configuration. It does not use the descriptions (#592).
  • Scale: how many sources the ASIP must connect, and how fast, is open (Q-38, sub-question 1).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:

  • Findings: F-50 (closed), F-55 (closed), F-57 (open), F-58 (closed), F-59 (closed), F-68 (open), F-71 (open), F-74 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-17 (open), Q-19 (answered), Q-31 (open), Q-38 (partly answered)

docs.title: Architecture decisions
docs.text:
The decision log holds every architecture decision of GBO in MADR format. It contains the decisions of the archived reference architecture v0.6.2. It also contains the decisions that the GBO team made during the build of the demo.

Each ADR names the PSA or GO constraint that it satisfies and the deliberation that produced it. Each ADR also links to its implementation in gbo-demo at release v0.9.0. A "Traceability" section at the end of each ADR lists the requirements, findings, open questions, and demo increments that the ADR depends on.

If a later decision replaces an earlier one, both stay in the log. At the top of its body, the superseded ADR gives the reason. It keeps its text as history.

The column "Serves" names the main requirements of each decision. The full list is in the ADR.

docs.title: ADR-0001: GraphQL as the source access interface
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (ported from reference architecture v0.6.2)
  • Satisfies: P-02, D-09, GO: GraphQL as a selective query mechanism
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 1, and its GraphQL + PBAC proposal (archived and unpublished)
  • Implemented in: services/graphql-server, services/brp-graphql-server, services/lvg-graphql-server

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: Data minimization (dataminimalisatie) requires a different set of fields for each consent scope. With REST, each scope needs a separate endpoint or separate filter parameters. Policies must then also state who can use which filter. As a result, the API layer and the policy layer hold the same logic twice.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Bronhouders expose GraphQL endpoints. The selection set of the consumer is the data minimization: the query names exactly the fields that the consumer wants. The policy engine authorizes that query field by field.

Selectors that matter for authorization, such as the belastingjaren year filter, must travel inside the query. Then the PDP can enforce them.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The query is the authorization object. For more information, see ADR-0009 and ADR-0013.
  • GraphQL runs over HTTP, so FSC proxies it unchanged (ADR-0003).
  • GraphQL is not a recognized type of FDS data service (datadienst). ADR-0025 proposes to standardize it. The iWlz/nID production precedent supports the pattern.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-08, REQ-11, REQ-17
  • Findings: none
  • Open questions: Q-11 (answered), Q-14 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-03a (done), SL-03b (done)

docs.title: ADR-0002: OPA/Rego in OpenFTV, the FSC Inway as PEP, AuthZEN with the FTV GraphQL profile
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: includes the decision "the FSC Inway is the PEP")
  • Satisfies: S05, P-09, GO: consent and legal basis as an enforceable authorization mechanism
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, authorization models analysis (archived and unpublished), F-35, Q-16, demo PR #60, PR #482, PR #337
  • Implemented in: fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml (Inway AuthZEN plugin, with body), services/openftv-pdp/Dockerfile (OpenFTV v0.1.0), mapper/ftvgraphql.go, services/ftv-graphql-mapper, docs/ftv-graphql-profile.md, policies/

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
GBO needs one policy engine and one PEP-PDP protocol for all routes. Then the authorization logic is in policy and not in application code.

Every source also needs an enforcement point in front of it. The interface of that point is the same at every source, so bronhouders must know it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The PDP is OpenFTV (Federatieve Toegangsverlening) release v0.1.0 with embedded OPA/Rego. The same PDP does two jobs:

  • It evaluates data requests. FSC Inways call it for these.
  • It decides on contract acceptance. FSC Managers call it for these (ADR-0015).

The FSC Inway of the source is the PEP. There is no separate PEP service. The AuthZEN plugin of the Inway sends every request to the PDP as an AuthZEN question, with the request body (AUTHZEN_WITH_BODY=true). Then the Inway enforces the answer.

The PEP-PDP interface is OpenID AuthZEN 1.0 (POST /authzen/v1/evaluation). For GraphQL, the request follows the FTV GraphQL profile for AuthZEN (ftv-graphql/0.1). The PEP passes the raw body unchanged and never parses it (REQ-42). The PDP side builds the field list (ADR-0013).

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
The GBO team compared three places for the PEP:

  1. FSC Inway as PEP (chosen). Every call to the source already goes through the Inway, and the Inway has an AuthZEN plugin (F-35).
  2. A separate PEP service between the Inway and the source (the earlier pep-service). It duplicates the PEP role. It also adds a hop. If that hop is in the wrong place, a request can go around it.
  3. A PEP at the source gateway. The gateway then makes the decision call and does the substitution. Enforcement and data transformation then mix in one component.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• All authorization decisions come from Rego policies. The policies are versioned in Git and have tests.
  • If the source gateway is reachable outside the Inway, a request can skip the decision. So the gateway must be reachable only through the Inway (REQ-04, ADR-0033).
  • The demo patches the FTV GraphQL profile mapper into the OpenFTV v0.1.0 build. Each patch step checks that it changed something. When the upstream project includes the profile mapper, the demo removes the patch (#331). CI keeps the PDP ref and the Manager image tags on one release tag.
  • The PDP writes every decision to the ADL (ADR-0036).
  • The PSA mentions ODRL in S06. This design does not use ODRL. Risks and technical debt tracks the deviation.
  • GBO follows the FTV GraphQL profile and AuthZEN. This answers the question of which profile GBO follows (Q-16).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-04, REQ-42, REQ-44, REQ-17. This ADR replaces the removed REQ-52.
  • Findings: F-02 (closed), F-27 (closed), F-31 (closed), F-35 (resolved in demo)
  • Open questions: Q-16 (answered)
  • Demo increments: SL-17 (done), SL-18 (done), SL-31 (done), SL-40 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0003: FSC for all domestic connectivity
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (ported from the reference architecture, updated 2026-11-02 for REQ-46 and the ASIP peer, gbo-demo v0.9.0)
  • Satisfies: D-03, S04, P-07 (trust through recognized admission and trust anchors)
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 6 (archived and unpublished), REQ-46
  • Implemented in: fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml (OpenFSC v2.4.0 group: a directory peer and nine organization peers, among them the ASIP peer …1200 at #L1664-L1669). Each channel has its own Outway in dienstverlener-backend/main.go#L82, eudi-adapter/main.go#L115, and asi-provider/main.go#L83-L85.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: Bronhouders must implement one connectivity stack for all routes, and not one stack for each route.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
FSC (Federated Service Connectivity) carries all domestic traffic. FSC gives these functions:

  • mTLS with group certificates
  • contracts with grant hashes
  • access tokens from the Manager of the provider
  • transaction logs for each hop

A channel that calls a source for an external party uses its own FSC Outway with a valid certificate (REQ-46). FSC establishes the identity of the calling organization. The authorization of each request stays a separate layer (ADR-0031).

External protocols end at the edge of GBO:

  • A bridge at the edge translates cross-border OOTS traffic to FSC (ADR-0020).
  • Wallet protocols end at the EUDI chain (ADR-0018). The EUDI adapter is an FSC consumer.
  • QTSP protocols (ETSI TS 119 478 clause 6.1) end at the ASIP (ADR-0037). The QTSP is not an FSC participant. The ASIP is an FSC consumer with a peer of its own (…1200), so the source sees the ASIP as the actor.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A bronhouder connects once (Inway plus contracts) and serves every route.
  • The Inway is also the PEP (ADR-0004).
  • No channel goes directly into a source service or into its authorization.
  • FSC refuses a connection with an expired or revoked certificate. open-fsc checks revocation with a CRL cache. The Inway, the Outway, and the Manager each have a switch that turns this check off. That switch must stay on. The demo does not check the revocation behavior.
  • FSC does not propagate W3C trace context. The correlation model of ADR-0035 compensates for this.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text: There is no decision on the time within which a certificate revocation or a suspension takes effect (Q-53).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-46
  • Open questions: Q-53
  • Demo increments: SL-34, SL-39, SL-42

docs.title: ADR-0004: Five authorization concerns, federated evaluation, no central authorization server
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02)
  • Satisfies: D-01, S05, P-01
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 5 (archived and unpublished), Q-02, Q-10, F-02
  • Implemented in: fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml (concerns ① ②), services/openftv-pdp and policies/gbo (concerns ③ ④ ⑤)

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
The question "May this request proceed" splits into five questions. Each question changes at its own rate and has its own decision makers:

  • organization identity
  • organization permission
  • access basis
  • data scope
  • request validity

A central authorization server couples all five questions and is a single choke point.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
GBO evaluates each concern where it belongs, federated per organization:

  • mTLS and PKI answer identity at every connection.
  • The FSC Manager of the provider answers permission when it issues a token. Contract acceptance itself is a policy decision (ADR-0015).
  • The PDP at the Inway of the provider answers access basis, data scope, and request validity for each request.

There is no central authorization server. An FSC access token never contains consent. Instead, the consumer presents a consent proof, and the PDP verifies it for each request (ADR-0032). The regime follows from the evidence that the request carries (ADR-0031).

For legal-basis routes (Gov-to-Gov), the design evaluates the legal basis (grondslag) locally from policy data, without a PIP call. The demo does not implement this path. The path needs its own positive evidence, because a declared flow is not sufficient (ADR-0031). For more information, see Risks and technical debt.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A revocation takes effect on the next request. No token needs to be invalidated.
  • In the consent regime, each request depends on two network calls:
    • the consent status, asked over FSC and never cached
    • the JWKS of the register, cached for five minutes
  • Concern ② also has a part at request time for integrators. A delegated call needs a mandate in the admission register (ADR-0034).
  • For the mapping of the concerns to the components, see Authorization.
  • The demo does not implement rate limiting (part of concern ⑤). Risks and technical debt tracks this gap.

docs.text:

docs.title: ADR-0005: BSNk PP polymorphic pseudonyms for private-sector access
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: BSNk only at consent time)
  • Satisfies: P-04, S03, PSA open decisions: choice of BSNk PP
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 4 (archived and unpublished), BSNk preconditions, F-75, demo #364, PR #469, PR #477
  • Implemented in: consent-portal-backend/bsnk (activate, transform, BSN authorization list), consent/portal.go (values per party), services/bsnk-mock (mock of the BSNk interface, also the sources' decryption component)

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: Private parties are not allowed to process the BSN. But DvTP lets them request data from government sources about a specific citizen. Plain encryption of the BSN still gives them a universal correlation key.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
GBO uses the BSNk PP polymorphic pseudonym infrastructure and calls it only at consent time. The decision has these parts:

  • The consent facility (toestemmingsvoorziening) activates the BSN of the citizen once, into a PI and a PP. These belong to the consent facility only (BSNK-03). ADR-0040 (proposed) describes how the consent facility recognizes the citizen later.
  • At each consent, while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04), the consent facility asks BSNk to transform the PI and the PP. BSNk returns values for each recipient OIN:
    • an encrypted pseudonym (VP) for every source
    • an encrypted identity (VI) only for a source on the BSN authorization list (BSNK-06)
  • The consent facility splits the call into requests of four parties at most (BSNK-05).
  • The values travel in the consent proof (ADR-0032). After the allow, each recipient decrypts its own value locally, with its own keys (ADR-0033).
  • BSNk is not in the query path. The consumer gets no identifier.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The values of different parties cannot be linked. No party outside government can derive the BSN.
  • The consent facility must be a recognized BSNk participant (BSNK-01, F-75, Q-26).
  • At consent, the parties, the key versions, and the form of the proof become fixed for the whole validity period (F-78).
  • Every recipient needs its keys in advance, as a step of admission (BSNK-09, #467).
  • A pseudonym for the consumer itself is optional. The demo does not build it (#478, Q-01).
  • The demo mock follows the BSNk interface, but uses JSON instead of SOAP (BSNK-11). The mock enforces the requester-only PI, the BSN authorization list, and the four-party limit. The mock does not encrypt, so anyone can read the values. The three demo sources share one OIN and one decryption component.
  • For the identifier flow at each boundary, see Pseudonymization.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:

  • Findings: F-15 (closed), F-75 (open), F-78 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-01 (partly answered), Q-26 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-02 (done), SL-51 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0006: Consent register as runtime PIP
docs.text:
• Status: superseded by ADR-0007, which ADR-0032 supersedes in turn
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (ported from reference architecture v0.6.2)
  • Satisfies: S01, P-01
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 2, and its DvTP PBAC alignment proposal (archived and unpublished)
  • Implemented in: superseded before implementation

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: DvTP draft v0.1 authorized requests through a custom gateway that checked consent twice. GBO replaces this gateway with the standard PEP-PDP chain. Then the question is how the consent evidence gets to the decision.

docs.title: Decision (superseded)
docs.text: A register records the consent and acts as a Policy Information Point (PIP). For each request, the PDP looks up the consent by consent_id. The consent proof that the service provider (dienstverlener) receives is an opaque reference.

docs.title: Why it was superseded
docs.text:
With a pure lookup, the authorization evidence depends only on the availability and integrity of the register. The consumer gives the PDP nothing that the PDP can verify.

The implemented design keeps the register and its status check for revocation on each request. But the consent itself becomes a signed artifact that the consumer presents and that the PDP can verify. For this design, see ADR-0007.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-68, REQ-18
  • Findings: F-24 (resolved in demo)

docs.title: ADR-0007: Consent as a signed token with a live status check
docs.text:
• Status: superseded by ADR-0032
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (superseded 2026-11-02)
  • Satisfies: S01, S02, P-01
  • Supersedes: ADR-0006
  • Superseded by: ADR-0032
  • Deliberation: signed, actor-bound consent proof (PR #238, SL-47)
  • Implemented in: changed in gbo-demo. Since PR #469, the token does not carry pi. Verification moved from the request mapper into the policy (#330, PR #371). The status goes over FSC (#383).

docs.title: Why superseded
docs.text:
The demo changed three parts of this decision:

  • The token carries no PI. It carries an encrypted value for each source (encrypted_subject). The consumer names the citizen with a placeholder (SL-51).
  • The policy verifies the token and gets the status itself. The request mapper only maps.
  • The PDP asks for the status over FSC, through its own Outway, and not directly at the register.

For this reason, ADR-0032 records the consent proof again. The signed token, the live status check for each request, and the bearer-token consequence stay. The following sections keep the original decision as history.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: The PDP needs consent evidence that it can verify and that can be revoked. The evidence must work without exposing the BSN. Also, one consent must cover more than one bronhouder.

docs.title: Decision (superseded)
docs.text:
The consent register (toestemmingsregister) issues an ES256-signed JWT of type gbo-consent+jwt with these claims:

  • consent_id
  • pi
  • scopes
  • scope_entries (per bronhouder)
  • dienstverlener_oin
  • valid_until (= exp)

The service provider (dienstverlener) presents the token in the X-Gbo-Consent-Token header. For each request, the PDP does three things:

  1. It verifies the signature against the JWKS of the register.
  2. It cross-checks the claims.
  3. It gets the live status of exactly that consent_id. Thus a revocation takes effect immediately.

The register stores no BSN and no PI.

docs.title: Consequences (at the time)
docs.text:
• The decision binds to verified claims:
    • actor binding (subject.id == dienstverlener_oin)
    • subject binding (the PI in the query equals the PI in the token)
    • scope and year coverage
  • The token is a bearer token. Actor binding blocks use by another consumer. It does not block replay by the same consumer. Production needs a shorter validity and a proof-of-possession binding to the FSC identity. Risks and technical debt tracks this.
  • The register stays a runtime dependency only for the status check. This check fails closed (CONSENT_STATUS_UNAVAILABLE).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-68, REQ-79
  • Findings: F-04 (closed), F-44 (resolved in demo)
  • Open questions: Q-05 (answered)
  • Demo increments: SL-23 (done), SL-47 (done), SL-51 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0008: Service catalog as a data-driven policy ceiling
docs.text:
• Status: superseded by ADR-0009
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (ported from reference architecture v0.6.2)
  • Satisfies: P-02, GO: service catalog
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 3 (archived and unpublished)
  • Implemented in: superseded before implementation

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: GBO needs a ceiling that applies to all individual consents. The ceiling limits what a consent screen can ask for and what a query can select.

docs.title: Decision (superseded)
docs.text: GBO keeps a statutory service catalog (dienstencatalogus) as a separate register with a legal anchor. The register maps each scope to its allowed fields (data.dienstencatalogus[scope].allowed_fields). The PDP checks every query against the catalog. The consent portal (toestemmingsportaal) shows only catalog entries.

docs.title: Why it was superseded
docs.text:
A separate catalog is a second authorization source. It can drift away from the rules that enforce it. The implemented model puts the ceiling into the rules themselves: the coverage declarations in closed-world rules are the catalog (ADR-0009).

The question of the legal anchor stays open: a catalog based on a general administrative order (AMvB), with its own governance. Risks and technical debt tracks this question.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-08, REQ-121
  • Findings: F-21 (closed), F-23 (closed), F-38 (closed)
  • Open questions: none
  • Demo increments: SL-14 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0009: Closed-world per-field rules: the rule is the catalog
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: plain-Rego rules bound by regime and service)
  • Satisfies: P-02, D-11
  • Supersedes: ADR-0008
  • Deliberation: engine.rego (design notes in comments), REQ-48, REQ-97, F-90, demo commit 80af776 (rules as plain Rego), PR #527 (service binding)
  • Implemented in: policies/gbo: engine.rego (regime and service binding), lib.rego (reads the request only), rules/, engine_test.rego (every rule names its services)

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
For each requested field, the PDP must decide whether an authorization basis covers the field. The PDP must do this without a separate catalog, because a catalog can drift away from enforcement.

A field key (ParentType.field) is unique only within one schema. Two services can share a key: Query.ingeschrevenPersoon is in both bri and brp (F-90).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Each rule is plain Rego. A rule declares these items:

  • rule_id, regime (consent or pid), and services (the FSC services that the rule applies to)
  • covers_fields and covers_types: the fields that the rule can grant
  • its reasons to refuse: deny for the whole request and deny_field[i] for one field

If a rule gives no reason, it grants the field. Each rule checks the actor and the scope itself (REQ-48). lib.rego only reads the request. It holds no checks.

The engine binds rules to fields in four steps:

  1. Only the rules of the active regime bind (ADR-0031).
  2. Only the rules that serve the FSC service of the request bind. The service is the service_name from the FSC access token. The Manager of the source signed this token (REQ-97).
  3. A field binds to the rules that name its key. An argument-free leaf outside the root types also binds to the rules that cover its parent type.
  4. For each field, the first bound rule without reasons grants the field.

The rule set is a closed world:

  • If no rule covers a field, the PDP denies the field with NO_APPLICABLE_RULE.
  • If the PDP cannot make the decision for a field, it refuses the field as RULE_NOT_EVALUABLE. The request then fails as a configuration error.
  • If the field list of a request is uncertain, the PDP denies the whole request (REQ-17, ADR-0013).

The demo has five rules, as the following table shows:

Rule Regime Service Grants DVT0001 consent bri Income declaration fields under consent LVG0001 consent lvg Ownership check at the LVG, scope lvg:vbo:eigendom EUD0001 pid bri Income statement (inkomensverklaring) to the wallet, years 2024 and 2025 EUD0002 pid brp Death certificate (akte van overlijden) to the wallet ASI0001 pid brp BRP fields for the ASIP

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One artifact defines what is allowed and why. A new access decision needs a new rule file with tests.
  • A test requires every rule to name its services. A rule for one service cannot grant a field of another service with the same key.
  • Consent per year works because each scope covers one year (bd:ib:2025). Also, the year selector must travel inside the query. If the filter is missing, the request fails closed.

  • Reasons have two layers (REQ-06):

    • The consumer and the ADL get only a client code, such as FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED.
    • The rule codes for each field go only to the console decision log for the operator, in a fixed order.

    For more information, see Authorization.

  • The service catalog (dienstencatalogus) with a legal anchor from ADR-0008 stays an open governance question. Risks and technical debt tracks it.

  • gbo-demo v0.9.0 has no test that makes sure that every rule checks the actor itself (#604).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-48, REQ-97, REQ-17, REQ-06, REQ-74, REQ-08
  • Findings: F-21 (closed), F-23 (closed), F-90 (resolved in demo)
  • Open questions: Q-14 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-03b (done), SL-13 (done), SL-33 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0010: BSN resolution inside the PEP
docs.text:
• Status: superseded by ADR-0011, which ADR-0033 supersedes in turn
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (ported from reference architecture v0.6.2)
  • Satisfies: P-04
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 4 (archived and unpublished)
  • Implemented in: superseded before implementation

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: After the PDP allows a pseudonymous DvTP request, a component must resolve the pseudonym to the BSN. The API of the source requires the BSN.

docs.title: Decision (superseded)
docs.text: The PEP intercepts the query of the consumer. After the policy decision, the PEP resolves consent_id → PI → BSNk Transform → BSN. Then it puts the BSN into the internal query of the bronhouder.

docs.title: Why it was superseded
docs.text:
With this decision, the PEP becomes a middlebox that transforms data. Also, a component with BSN authorization sits in shared infrastructure.

In the implemented design, the PEP (the FSC Inway) only enforces decisions. The source owns the identifier resolution. For this design, see ADR-0011.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-21, BSNK-04
  • Findings: F-30 (resolved in demo), F-37 (resolved in demo)
  • Open questions: none
  • Demo increments: SL-02 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0011: Source-owned sidecar resolves pseudonyms, and the PDP never sees a BSN
docs.text:
• Status: superseded by ADR-0033
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (superseded 2026-11-02)
  • Satisfies: P-04, P-10
  • Supersedes: ADR-0010
  • Superseded by: ADR-0033
  • Deliberation: source gateway de-pseudonymization (SL-22, F-30)
  • Implemented in: changed in gbo-demo. The source gateway does not call BSNk and does not read subject_id_type any more (PR #469, #473). The request mapper does not pseudonymize any more (#364). Code in gbo-demo v0.9.0: services/bron-sidecar

docs.title: Why superseded
docs.text:
The mechanism changed in three places:

  • The source gateway does not call BSNk Transform at query time. It takes the value for its own OIN from the consent proof. The decryption component of the source reads this value.
  • The source gateway acts when a consent proof is present. The demo removed the subject_id_type grant property (ADR-0031).
  • The PDP request mapper does not pseudonymize a disclosed BSN any more. In the EUDI and ASI routes, the PDP input holds the plain BSN (ADR-0043, proposed). So the claim "the PDP never sees a BSN" in the title is true only for the consent route.

For this reason, ADR-0033 records the mechanism again. The resolution by the source after the allow stays. The following sections keep the original decision as history.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: A component between the allow decision and the source API must resolve the pseudonym to the BSN. Shared infrastructure must not get BSN authorization. The BSN must not leak into policy inputs or logs.

docs.title: Decision (superseded)
docs.text:
A source gateway that the source owns sits between the Inway and the GraphQL API. The source gateway does the resolution. It reads the subject_id_type claim from the FSC access token:

  • For pseudonym, it transforms the PI to the BSN through BSNk, with its own OIN. Then it substitutes the query variable.
  • For direct, it passes the request through.

In addition, the PDP request mapper pseudonymizes any disclosed BSN (EUDI flows) before policy evaluation. So the engine input and the decision log contain only the PI.

docs.title: Consequences (at the time)
docs.text:
• Each role stays separate, in line with data sovereignty:
    • The PEP stays a pure enforcement point.
    • The PDP does no data transformation.
    • Only the bronhouder holds BSN authority.
  • The meaning of the identifier is a grant property that both peers countersign (ADR-0030). So a caller cannot choose how the source interprets its subject identifier.
  • A pseudonym that cannot be resolved is a hard error (HTTP 400). The fail-safe default is pass-through (direct).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-21, REQ-60
  • Findings: F-30 (resolved in demo), F-37 (resolved in demo), F-54 (open)
  • Open questions: none
  • Demo increments: SL-02 (done), SL-22 (done), SL-29 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0012: Query AST inspection with OPA's graphql.parse_query
docs.text:
• Status: superseded by ADR-0013
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (ported from reference architecture v0.6.2)
  • Satisfies: P-02
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, component architecture "GraphQL schema registry and scope-driven field authorization", and its GraphQL + PBAC proposal (archived and unpublished)
  • Implemented in: superseded before implementation

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: For authorization per field, the PDP must read the structure of the incoming GraphQL query, in addition to its metadata.

docs.title: Decision (superseded)
docs.text: Rego parses the query with the built-in OPA function graphql.parse_query(). The policy code then walks the AST. This follows the nID/iWlz production pattern.

docs.title: Why it was superseded
docs.text:
If Rego walks a raw AST, the parsing mechanics go into every rule. Rego also cannot resolve parent types, verify consent proofs, or pseudonymize identifiers.

The implemented design moves the request preparation into a mapper inside the PDP service, before policy evaluation. The rules then use clean facts for each field. For this design, see ADR-0013. The intent stays the same: the query is the authorization object.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-17
  • Findings: F-25 (closed)
  • Open questions: Q-14 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-03a (done)

docs.title: ADR-0013: GraphQL request mapping in the PDP ahead of policy evaluation
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: the mapper only maps)
  • Satisfies: P-02, S05
  • Supersedes: ADR-0012
  • Deliberation: REQ-17, REQ-42, demo #364, #330, PR #370, PR #371, PR #482, FTV GraphQL profile
  • Implemented in: mapper/ftvgraphql.go (OpenFTV adapter), services/ftv-graphql-mapper (profile mapper), schemas/pdp-mirror (schema per FSC service), graphql_schemas.rego (schema pins), scripts/check-schema-drift.sh

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
Rules need clean, typed facts about the request instead of a raw query string. These facts are the fields, with their parent types and with their arguments as the source executes them.

The PEP passes the raw body unchanged (ADR-0002). So a component on the PDP side must turn the body into a field list. That list must be complete. If it is not complete, the PDP denies the request (REQ-17).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A request mapper inside the OpenFTV PDP implements the mapping function of the FTV GraphQL profile (ftv-graphql/0.1) and nothing else. The mapper does these things:

  • It parses the GraphQL body and builds the field list. The parent type of each field comes from the bundled schema of the FSC service of the request. The arguments are as the source executes them.
  • It accepts only a query operation. A mutation or subscription gives OPERATION_NOT_SUPPORTED.
  • It enforces these limits:
    • body: 1 MiB
    • nesting depth: 64
    • fragment definitions: 100
    • selection depth: 64
    • field records: 1000
    • aliased selections: 100
    • validation time: 1 second
  • If a step fails, it marks the request COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE with a subcode (for example PARSE_ERROR, LIMIT_EXCEEDED). The engine denies the request.

The mapper does not verify the consent proof. It does not call BSNk, does not pseudonymize, and reads no flow. The policy verifies the consent itself (ADR-0032). The regime follows from the evidence (ADR-0031).

The profile mapper is a separate Go module. A thin adapter connects it to OpenFTV.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Rules stay declarative. Parsing happens once, in one place, in tested Go code. The conformance vectors of the profile run as tests.
  • The PDP loads one schema for each FSC service. The policy bundle pins the digest of each schema and denies a schema that is not pinned (CONFIG_ERROR SCHEMA_MISMATCH). A CI job checks for drift between the pinned schema and the schema that the source executes.
  • The source gateway accepts only the request shape that the PDP evaluated (ADR-0033).
  • The mapper is a patch on OpenFTV v0.1.0. The patch stays until the upstream project includes the profile mapper (#331). For more information, see Risks and technical debt.
  • The mapper does not pseudonymize any more. So the EUDI and ASI routes put the plain BSN into the PDP input (ADR-0043, proposed).
