docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-17, REQ-42, REQ-18, REQ-60
  • Findings: F-25 (closed), F-54 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-14 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-03a (done), SL-18 (done), SL-31 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0014: Flow and subject identifier semantics through a provider-side Additional Claims service
docs.text:
• Status: superseded by ADR-0030, which ADR-0031 supersedes in turn
  • Date: 2026-08-24
  • Satisfies: P-01, D-11
  • Deliberation: gbo-demo CHANGELOG, v0.6.11, F-62
  • Implemented in: removed from gbo-demo in v0.6.11 (September 2026)

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: The PDP selects rules by the flow of the request (dvtp:query, eudi:attestation, gbo:source-metadata). The source gateway interprets the subject identifier (pseudonym or direct). If callers supply these values as headers, a caller can choose the authorization regime that applies to its request.

docs.title: Decision (superseded)
docs.text: An Additional Claims service that the provider owned mapped each validated connection grant (outway peer, service peer, service name) to an add claim object. The FSC Manager of the provider signed this object into the access token. The PDP mapper and the source gateway read only the add claim.

docs.title: Why it was superseded
docs.text:
The mechanism was a workaround for a version limit. The simulation environment ran OpenFSC v1.44, which is older than grant properties. The mechanism had two costs:

  • Only the provider signed the regime. The consumer never countersigned it.
  • The mapping file from grants to claims was outside the contracts. People had to maintain it by hand, and it broke twice during the Peer-ID migration.

When OpenFSC v2.4.0 became available, the regime moved into the contract itself, as FSC-normative grant properties. For this design, see ADR-0030.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-74
  • Findings: F-32 (resolved in demo), F-45 (closed), F-62 (resolved in demo)
  • Open questions: Q-15 (answered)
  • Demo increments: SL-48 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0015: FSC contract acceptance by policy
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: ordered refusal codes, delegated grants)
  • Satisfies: S04, P-07
  • Deliberation: autosign.rego (design notes in comments), REQ-61, F-55, F-56, demo #491, PR #464
  • Implemented in: policies/fsc/autosign.rego (ordered checks), services/dvtp-onboarding-register, pip-pull/dvtp-onboarding.yaml, fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml (Manager autosign call)

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: An FSC Manager can sign all incoming contracts automatically, or it can require a manual review. Neither option scales to an admission model. DvTP participation is a governed status, and a provider must accept contracts only from admitted parties. Admission comes from a register and not from decision policy (REQ-61).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The Manager of each provider sends every submitted contract through the PDP. The AuthZEN autosign call of the Manager evaluates a dedicated contract-acceptance policy (package doelbinding.auto_sign_contract).

The policy reads the admission register (toelatingsregister). OpenFTV pulls this register every 5 seconds (attributes name, active, allowed_source_peer_ids, acts_for).

The policy accepts grant type 2 (service connection) and grant type 3 (delegated service connection, ADR-0034). It runs eight checks in a fixed order, and the first check that fails names the refusal:

# Code Refuses when 1 NOT_AN_AUTOSIGN_REQUEST The input is not a well-formed autosign request 2 GRANT_TYPE_NOT_ALLOWED The grants are not all type 2 or all type 3 3 NO_COUNTERPARTY The contract has no party other than the provider itself 4 ADMISSION_REGISTER_UNAVAILABLE The PIP pull supplied no register 5 PARTY_NOT_IN_REGISTRY A party is not in the register 6 PARTY_NOT_ACTIVE A party is suspended 7 SOURCE_NOT_ALLOWED The party is not admitted for this source peer 8 DELEGATION_NOT_REGISTERED A delegated grant has no registered integration

A missing register (check 4) differs from an empty register (check 5). An empty register is available data that admits nobody.

After a refusal, the contract stays proposed, so it can be submitted again (REQ-63). The contract does not become rejected.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Admission is data. If an operator activates or deactivates a participant in the register, the contract outcomes change without a policy edit. The register deactivates participants and does not delete them.
  • The contract question ("may these parties connect at all") stays separate from the request question ("may this field be read now") on purpose (REQ-62). The request policy reads the same register only for integrator mandates.
  • The autosign input of the Manager carries only peer IDs and grant types. So the policy decides about the parties and not about the services. Admission per service is a known limitation (F-56). Risks and technical debt tracks it.
  • The Manager fixes the package name. If someone renames the package, the policy resolves to nothing and every contract stays pending.
  • A suspended consumer keeps its existing contract and can still send queries (REQ-110, Q-53). Changes to admissions are not logged (REQ-123).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-61, REQ-62, REQ-63, REQ-110, REQ-123, AV-06
  • Findings: F-55 (closed), F-56 (closed), F-52 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-22 (answered), Q-53 (open), Q-74 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-09 (mostly covered), SL-45 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0016: Source-owned metadata and reconciliation-based onboarding
docs.text:
• Status: accepted (mechanism). The document format is a proposal for PSA S10.
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-09-07 for the source registry and split transports in gbo-demo v0.6.11, and updated 2026-11-02 for the claims model, schema 1.1 with asi, the shared registry, activation, and certificate sets in gbo-demo v0.9.0)
  • Satisfies: P-10, D-04, S10, S07, S04
  • Deliberation: F-57, F-58, SL-46, docs/source-onboarding.md, docs/source-metadata-cache.md
  • Implemented in: eudi-adapter reconcile command, source registry backend, shared registry module services/source-registry (onboarding, postgresregistry, asisnapshot), gbo-source-metadata-v1 schema, certificate set per source in issuance_config.go#L159-L180, ASIP reader in asi-provider/main.go#L101

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
To connect a source, GBO must not need code on the GBO side or a central catalog of source capabilities. The source owns its schema, its queries, and its attestation definitions (REQ-64). Also, a valid transport contract alone must not be enough to take a source into use (F-58).

PSA S10 leaves the content and the interface of the source-specific GBO configuration open. The following mechanism (publish, validate, activate, roll back) is a GBO design decision. The document format gbo-source-metadata-v1 is the proposal of the demo for that open S10 decision. It is not a final interface agreement.

docs.title: Publication
docs.text:
Each source publishes its own machine-readable metadata at /.well-known/gbo. The metadata is versioned, expires, and is validated against a schema. The GBO configuration names only where to fetch it. Identity comes from certificates. Access comes from FSC contracts.

The document holds capabilities for each channel:

  • eudi (schema 1.0 and 1.1): for each attestation, type_id, type_version, offers, graphql, mapping_profile, display (per language), and claims. Each claim has one gbo-simple-v1 rule in source, a label, an optional description, and sd. GBO generates the SD-JWT VC Type Metadata from display and claims (ADR-0017). The document has no separate mapping, attribute_schema, and type_metadata blocks any more.
  • asi (schema 1.1 only): the attributes that a source offers to the ASIP (ADR-0039).

For more information about the structure, see Source onboarding.

docs.title: Validation into a registry
docs.text:
A reconciler validates the fetched metadata into candidate records in a PostgreSQL source registry. It validates the schema, the origin, the version, the validity window, and the binding to the data contract. The source_oin must equal the OIN in the certificate set. If it does not, the result is METADATA_INVALID.

The registry is a shared module (services/source-registry). The EUDI adapter writes it. The adapter, the issuance configuration step, and the ASIP read it.

docs.title: Activation as a separate management action
docs.text:
Activation is a separate management action (REQ-65). A valid FSC contract activates nothing. A source becomes active only through an explicit source configuration file, a validated candidate, and a promotion.

If a configured source has no contracts, it is blocked with METADATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND or DATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND. If the FSC Manager is unreachable, the result is FSC_MANAGER_UNAVAILABLE. Automatic promotion is off by default. Compose and the Helm example turn it on for the demo.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
Promotion creates one immutable release from the complete candidate set. It activates the release in the same transaction. The SHA-256 of the content document identifies the release.

These products derive from the active release:

  • the adapter activation snapshot
  • immutable type metadata
  • the issuance-server configuration (an init step writes it)
  • the offer catalog
  • the description of each data service for the ASIP

The runtime path never fetches metadata. The adapter and the ASIP poll the active release through a read-only database role.

docs.title: Lifecycle per source
docs.text:
The lifecycle rules are in REQ-66. Metadata is fresh for 15 minutes at most and has one hour of stale grace. It must be valid for at least one hour.

The source states are pending, active, stale, blocked, and rollout_required. If a source is past its grace, it gets HTTP 503. This applies to that source only. A lower version is not activated. The same version with other content is not activated either.

docs.title: Certificate set per source (fail-hard)
docs.text:
Issuance keeps one certificate set for each bronhouder (REQ-58). The set holds the issuer, reader (access), and status-list certificates. Issuance never shares or substitutes a set.

The checks fail hard:

  • If a set is missing, the source is blocked with CERTIFICATE_SET_NOT_FOUND.
  • If a set has no OIN or organization name, the result is CERTIFICATE_SET_INVALID.
  • If the mounted material differs from the active release, the configuration generation is blocked.

If two sources are behind one FSC peer, each source gets its own set. The certificate binds the issuer identity and the purpose. So a shared set shows the wrong issuer (F-50).

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
The two legs of a source choose their transport independently:

  • The metadata leg (metadata_endpoint) is fsc, unsecured, or file. The file transport reads a document that an operator manages from a confined directory. It is for sources that publish no endpoint.
  • The data leg (data_access) is fsc or unsecured. If data_access is omitted, the data leg inherits the metadata transport.

FSC metadata with unsecured data is refused. With file metadata, an explicit data_access is required. Both legs report their authentication status separately (transport_authenticated, data_transport_authenticated).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• To onboard a source, an operator needs only configuration and contracts. There is no GBO catalog of sources, years, or schemas to maintain.
  • Version rollbacks, byte drift, and expired metadata are refused. If metadata is unavailable, issuance fails closed (HTTP 503).
  • Published versions of type metadata are immutable (vct#integrity covers the exact bytes). They are never deleted automatically. A change to claims or display needs a new type_version.
  • An operator can roll back with activate-source-release --release-id. An auto-promoter that watches the registry keeps that choice while the candidate set stays the same.
  • Two deviations from REQ-66 remain (ICTU/GBO-demo#606):
    • Promotion needs a valid version of every configured source. So one broken source stops new releases for all sources.
    • The offer list /eudi-offers.json takes the shortest grace of all sources and fails for all sources at once.
  • The version rule has no test (ICTU/GBO-demo#610).
  • The origin depends on the authenticated transport and the OIN from the certificate set. The document itself is not signed.
  • With the file transport, the operator maintains the description instead of the source. This is a D-13 exception. data_transport_authenticated makes the exception visible, and expires_at makes it temporary. The exception needs recorded consent of the bronhouder (AV-08, F-71). The demo does not record that consent.
  • If the GraphQL service of a source is already on FSC, the source can be onboarded before it publishes /.well-known/gbo. The data call stays bound to the contract.
  • The central issuance server holds the private keys of the issuer and status-list certificates of every source. There is no decision on whether that is allowed (Q-17).
  • The issuance server reads its configuration only at startup. A new release needs a controlled restart (state rollout_required).

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
The following points are open:

  • The description does not contain the read API of the logbook of the source, a reference to the DCAT-AP-NL description, or central findability (F-57, F-68, AV-07).
  • In demo v0.9.0, DvTP does not use the description. The DvTP offer of a source is in the GBO rules. The DvTP scope comes from the demand side (F-74).
  • Who can do the activation action, and how the admission decision is recorded (PSA B-09 in the decision register).
  • The final form of the source configuration. This is the open PSA S10 decision.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-64, REQ-65, REQ-66, REQ-58, REQ-67, AV-07, AV-08
  • Findings: F-50 (closed), F-57 (open), F-58 (closed), F-59 (closed), F-68 (open), F-71 (open), F-74 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-17, Q-19, Q-38
  • Demo increments: SL-46

docs.title: ADR-0017: Gbo-simple-v1 as the attestation mapping profile
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: scope eudi only, claims model, error contract, gbo-demo v0.9.0)
  • Satisfies: S10, S11
  • Deliberation: docs/gbo-simple-v1.md, REQ-116
  • Implemented in: internal/gbosimplev1/profile.go, gbo-simple-v1 schema, claims validation in source_claims.go#L216-L242, generated Type Metadata in type_metadata.go#L64, error codes in profile.go#L33-L37, runtime in main.go#L302-L316

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
Source data must become attestation claims through a mapping. The source must be able to declare this mapping in its metadata. GBO must be able to execute the mapping without trusting logic from the source.

The bronhouder stays responsible for the attestation content. So GBO must not add to the content or convert it (REQ-116).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
GBO defines gbo-simple-v1 under a fixed URN. It is a mapping profile that is minimal on purpose and fails closed. The profile has these properties:

  • It projects one source object to flat claims through RFC 6901 pointers.
  • It has six data types and hard limits.
  • It has no conversions, filters, joins, defaults, expressions, or I/O.
  • Zero source rows give a no_data outcome (no credential). More than one row is an error.
  • Unknown mapping properties are refused.

The profile applies only to the eudi capability of the source metadata. The asi capability has its own operations (pointer, join, const, each) against a value schema that GBO keeps (ADR-0039).

docs.title: Claims model
docs.text:
A source defines each claim once, in claims. Each claim carries these items:

  • its gbo-simple-v1 rule as source (pointer, datatype, optional optional)
  • a label for each language
  • an optional description
  • sd (always by default, allowed, or never)

GBO derives the mapping from the claims. GBO also generates the SD-JWT VC Type Metadata from display and claims. In this metadata, schema.required is exactly the non-optional claims, and every claim gets svg_id. The claim order is the display order in the wallet. Reserved claim names (vct, iss, status, cnf, and others) are refused.

docs.title: No partial attestation
docs.text:
If the answer of the source does not fit the mapping, the adapter issues nothing. This includes the claims that do fit. The adapter gives these outcomes:

Case Outcome A mandatory claim is missing HTTP 502, GBO_SIMPLE_PATH_MISSING A mandatory claim is null or has another type HTTP 502, GBO_SIMPLE_TYPE_MISMATCH The result is not a list HTTP 502, GBO_SIMPLE_RESULT_TYPE There is more than one result HTTP 502, GBO_SIMPLE_RESULT_AMBIGUOUS There is no result HTTP 404 (no_data), and the adapter still logs it An optional claim is missing or null The claim is left out, and the rest is issued

The consumer sees only the HTTP status. The code is in the adapter log.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Mappings are data. They can be validated against a JSON Schema. They have an independent set of conformance fixtures (testdata/cases.json).
  • More expressive needs (derivations, unit conversions) require a later version of the profile and not ad-hoc extensions. A source that needs another form delivers that form itself.
  • A change to claims or display changes the integrity value of the Type Metadata. Therefore the change needs a new type_version.
  • The profile supports number, but EUDI onboarding refuses it. The reason is that nl-wallet v0.5 cannot show an amount that is not an integer. Risks and technical debt tracks this.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
• The profile does not support nested claims (objects and lists) with selective disclosure for each element. Only scalar data types pass validation (REQ-78).
  • In demo v0.9.0, nobody can trace which versions of the mapping, the source schema, and the attestation schema an attestation used (REQ-124).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-64, REQ-78, REQ-116, REQ-124
  • Open questions: Q-20, Q-38
  • Demo increments: SL-46

docs.title: ADR-0018: EUDI issuance through disclosure-based OpenID4VCI on the nl-wallet stack
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (updated 2026-11-02: no flow or subject identifier type, PID verification and the callback gap, gbo-demo v0.9.0)
  • Satisfies: P-06, S11, GO: PuB-EAA issuance
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, PuB-EAA Provider (archived and unpublished), REQ-45, SL-25, demo constraints in AGENTS.md
  • Implemented in: services/eudi-adapter, services/eudi-issuance-server (nl-wallet v0.5.0), PID trust anchors in issuance_server.toml.example#L3-L9, adapter route in source_release_runtime.go#L69

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
Citizens must receive attestations from government sources into their EUDI wallet. The reference architecture called this function the shared PuB-EAA provider (PubEAA-voorziening). The protocol stack and the identification mechanism were open.

PSA v1 treats the wallet as a hook (P-06). The demo proves the route, but the route is outside the v1 scope of the PSA.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
GBO realizes the issuance function on the open-source nl-wallet issuance server (pinned version), with disclosure-based issuance. The issuance has five steps:

  1. The wallet discloses its PID over OpenID4VP. The issuance server verifies the disclosure against its PID trust anchors.
  2. The issuance server calls the GBO EUDI adapter (POST /attestations/{sourceID}/{typeID}). The adapter reads the BSN from the disclosed PID.
  3. The adapter gets the source data over FSC through the standard PEP-PDP chain. It uses the query from the source metadata (ADR-0016). The adapter is a channel adapter, and the PDP of the source decides (REQ-44).
  4. The request carries no consent proof. So the PDP evaluates it under the PID regime (ADR-0031). Grants carry no flow or subject_id_type property.
  5. The adapter projects the answer with gbo-simple-v1 (ADR-0017). The server issues the credential as dc+sd-jwt with immutable type metadata. It uses the certificate set of the bronhouder (ADR-0016).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Issuance is a full GBO route. It uses the same source API and the same authorization chain as DvTP. The source carries no logic that is specific to the wallet.

  • The issuance policy enforces three things:

    • the presence of a PID
    • an actor allowlist (designated_issuers)
    • limits for each type (EUD0001, EUD0002)

    These checks replace the abstract subject.bsn == resource.bsn rule of the reference architecture.

  • The issuance server verifies the PID. The demo removed a separate check in the adapter (SL-25). The demo does not test this verification independently.

  • The main gap is the callback from the issuance server to the adapter. The adapter route has no caller authentication. Any caller that reaches the adapter can post any BSN. The adapter then calls the source as the designated issuer peer, and the PDP allows the request. Nothing binds the BSN in the query to a verified disclosure (REQ-45, ICTU/GBO-demo#133). Risks and technical debt tracks this gap.
  • In addition to the PID providers, the PID trust list holds the GBO development CA and the issuer CA of every source.
  • The BSN from the PID stays in the PDP input and is in both decision logs (REQ-60, ADR-0043).
  • The validity is 365 days for every type. Each type has one status list. For the productization, see ADR-0028.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
The following points are open:

  • Trust in the callback and positive PID evidence (Q-18, REQ-45). Two solutions meet REQ-45:

    • The adapter verifies the SD-JWT itself.
    • The issuance server authenticates the callback and delivers signed evidence.

    Both solutions also need the binding of the disclosure to the request. The PID trust list must hold only PID-provider anchors. A revocation check of the PID is a recommendation (SHOULD). The legal status of a BSN from a PID is part of Q-18.

  • Attestations about a related person. They follow a relation that the source declares, starting from the verified requester (REQ-57, F-47, Q-14). The demo uses a source view. The alternative is filter arguments that the policy requires with fixed values (ICTU/GBO-demo#425).

  • Validity and revocation for each type. The bronhouder sets them. If an attestation is valid for more than 24 hours and the source data changes, the attestation must be revoked. GBO has no change feed (REQ-77, F-82).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-44, REQ-45, REQ-57, REQ-58, REQ-60, REQ-74, REQ-77
  • Findings: F-47 (open), F-70 (open), F-82 (open), F-83 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-14, Q-18
  • Demo increments: SL-19, SL-25, SL-26, SL-29, SL-43

docs.title: ADR-0019: FSC transaction ID as the end-to-end correlation key
docs.text:
• Status: superseded by ADR-0035
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (superseded 2026-11-02)
  • Satisfies: P-12, S09
  • Superseded by: ADR-0035
  • Deliberation: OBSERVABILITY.md, FSC txlog observability (SL-38)
  • Implemented in: changed in gbo-demo (PR #366). If no traceparent arrives, entry components still tie the trace to the transaction ID: consumerhttp.go, eudi-adapter/main.go. Txlog viewer: fsctxlog.go

docs.title: Why superseded
docs.text:
If the two IDs are equal, the design breaks in three cases (F-67):

  • A caller sends its own traceparent.
  • One processing calls more than one source.
  • The request passes an extra FSC hop.

LDV and the ADL require that a component takes over the trace ID unchanged. FSC-Logging gives every transaction its own ID. Also, FSC forwards traceparent on the data path. Only the AuthZEN call from the Inway to the PDP drops it (F-41).

ADR-0035 makes W3C Trace Context the correlation key and records the transaction ID next to it. One part stays: an entry component without an incoming traceparent can tie its trace to the transaction ID that it mints. The following sections keep the original decision as history.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: FSC does not propagate W3C trace context across the Inway. As a result, the trace of a consumer and the records on the provider side carry unrelated identifiers.

docs.title: Decision (superseded)
docs.text: Consumers generate a UUIDv7. They use it as the Fsc-Transaction-Id and also as the OpenTelemetry trace ID. The PDP records it in every decision log line. The FSC transaction logs of every hop carry it natively.

docs.title: Consequences (at the time)
docs.text:
• One identifier links the consumer request, the policy decision, and the audit record of each hop. A deny reason can be traced to the exact exchange.
  • Debug stores (Jaeger, Loki) keep data only for a short time. The FSC txlog stays the authoritative record. For more information, see Logging and traceability.
  • If a later FSC version supports trace-context propagation, GBO can change this convention without breaking the txlog linkage.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-55
  • Findings: F-39 (resolved in demo), F-41 (resolved in demo), F-67 (resolved in demo)
  • Open questions: none
  • Demo increments: SL-07 (done), SL-38 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0020: AS4 bridge for SDG-OOTS
docs.text:
• Status: accepted (not implemented in gbo-demo v0.9.0)
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (ported from the reference architecture)
  • Satisfies: S08, GO pattern B, SDG regulation (EU 2018/1724)
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, decision 7 and OOTS bridge (archived and unpublished)
  • Implemented in: not implemented. gbo-demo v0.9.0 has no implementation.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: The Single Digital Gateway Regulation requires cross-border evidence exchange through the Once-Only Technical System (OOTS). OOTS uses eDelivery AS4 transport, OOTS-EDM payloads, and SMP discovery. This is an EU obligation, so GBO has no architectural choice here.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
GBO builds an OOTS adapter at its edge. The adapter has three parts:

  • A Domibus access point receives AS4 messages.
  • An OOTS-EDM adapter maps evidence requests.
  • An FSC translator forwards the requests to bronhouders over the standard FSC and PEP-PDP chain.

The bronhouder sees a normal FSC request. AS4 exists only at the edge, in line with the national Basisinrichting OOTS.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Bronhouders serve cross-border requests without work that is specific to OOTS.
  • The mapping of evidence types depends on canonical semantic models (ADR-0024).
  • The route needs a legal-basis policy path in the Gov-to-Gov style. This path is not implemented either. Risks and technical debt tracks both gaps.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text: • Open questions: Q-79

docs.title: ADR-0021: Policy management and distribution per bronhouder
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (proposed as "Policy distribution through a central PAP with signed bundles", rewritten and accepted 2026-11-02)
  • Satisfies: S06, D-01, P-10
  • Deliberation: Reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 1 "authorization policy lifecycle" (archived and unpublished), Q-21 (answered October 28, 2026), F-09, F-51, F-52, demo #426 (bundle signing, closed as not planned), PR #337
  • Implemented in: opt-in Manager profile: bundles/gbo-pdp.yaml, authz/pdp-bundle.cedar, scripts/seed-openftv-manager.py (retire, never delete), and validation in Makefile (policy-check, policy-test)

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
Each bronhouder runs its own PDP (ADR-0004). Someone must write the policy for that PDP, publish it, and deliver it to the PDP with integrity. The earlier proposal put a central PAP at GBO: a central registry, signed bundles, and governance in the GBO standards bodies.

Q-21 asked who can manage and publish the policy of a bronhouder. The answer is that policy management stays with each bronhouder. The policy belongs to the source (P-10). Bundle signing inside one organization is not planned (#426).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• The PAP and the PDP are at each bronhouder. The bronhouder writes, approves, and publishes its own policy. GBO has no central PAP.
  • GBO supplies guidance and no service. The guidance is a reference policy set, the engine choice (ADR-0002), and the guidelines RL-01 to RL-05:
    • Deliver policy as a versioned bundle, and do not bake it into the PDP (RL-01).
    • Authorize the management API with its own policy set, and deny on an empty store (RL-02).
    • Separate writing from publishing. Publish with a non-personal, short-lived identity (RL-03).
    • Withdraw policy instead of deleting it. Reconcile the deployed set with version control (RL-04).
    • Validate a bundle before activation, and fall back visibly to the last valid set (RL-05).
  • A bundle is signed only when it crosses an organization boundary. Inside one organization, signing is not planned. If a bronhouder lets another organization build or host its bundles, signing and verification become a requirement.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
This decision compared three options:

  1. Policy management per bronhouder (chosen). This option fits P-10 and the federated PDP. Each bronhouder carries the governance cost.
  2. A central PAP with signed bundles (the earlier proposal). This option gives one place to author and approve policy. But it puts the policy of the bronhouder under another organization, and it needs signing across that boundary.
  3. Policy baked into the PDP image. This option has no lifecycle: no version, no withdrawal, and no validation before activation (F-09).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• This decision closes the design gap of F-09: signing is required only across an organization boundary. The guidelines and their adoption remain.
  • The demo shows the guidelines with the OpenFTV Manager (opt-in, make demo-manager):
    • The bundle gbo-pdp is tagged and has a version. The PDP pulls it at start.
    • Seeding withdraws stale policies and never deletes them.
    • A Cedar policy limits the pull of the PDP to one bundle and to GET.
    • By default, the PDP loads ./policies from a mount.
  • Push distribution does not work. The PDP authorizes its own management endpoints with the decision policy. That policy denies everything that is not a data request (F-51). So the PDP pulls instead.
  • The policy store is cumulative and cannot delete. One duplicate or broken module stops every decision (F-52). Before every PDP start, make policy-check refuses non-Rego files and duplicate file names, and compiles the set. A visible fallback to the last valid set is not built (RL-05).
  • The ADL does not record the policy version that made the decision (REQ-59).
  • The PSA mentions ODRL. This mention stays a deviation (Risks and technical debt).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:

docs.title: ADR-0022: Sector-level grants with organizational attribute verification
docs.text:
• Status: deferred
  • Date: 2026-08-24 (proposed), deferred on 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: S04, P-16
  • Deliberation: reference architecture v0.6.2, authorization models analysis §9.5 (archived and unpublished), F-36, SL-05
  • Implemented in: not implemented. gbo-demo removed the sector-pip scaffolding (#378, CHANGELOG).

docs.title: Why deferred
docs.text: In gbo-demo v0.9.0, admission runs through the admission register (toelatingsregister) and the contract decision of the PDP (REQ-61, ADR-0015). No component called the sector PIP, so the demo removed it. A sector grant is not a native FSC concept (F-36). The proposal stays in the log for one case: per-organization admission does not scale. Work on it starts only after a new decision.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: PKI proves which organization calls (OIN). PKI does not prove what kind of organization it is. Per-organization contracts do not scale to sectors. For example, 800 notary offices need 800 contracts with each source.

docs.title: Proposed decision (deferred)
docs.text:
The proposal extends contract acceptance and token issuance with organizational attributes:

  • Sector PIPs (KvK SBI, KNB, BIG, AFM) verify sector membership.
  • A sector-level grant type expresses "this sector may use this service".
  • The access token carries verified sector claims.

This proposal builds on contract acceptance by policy (ADR-0015). The autosign input then must carry more than peer IDs.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
The proposal leaves three points open:

  • An extension of the FSC grant schema, through the Logius standards process.
  • The freshness of sector register data, and the liability for it.
  • The relation with the admission register: admission versus membership.

docs.title: ADR-0023: Organization identity from the certificate, and separate EUDI certificate roles
docs.text:
• Status: accepted (part A, organization identity), proposed (part B, EUDI certificate roles)
  • Date: 2026-08-24, rewritten on 2026-11-02 for gbo-demo v0.9.0. The rewrite split the ADR into organization identity and EUDI certificate roles, and moved the BSNk production part out.
  • Satisfies: P-07 (trust through recognized admission and trust anchors), S04, S11, F1
  • Deliberation: reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 2 and trust model comparison (archived and unpublished), F-60, F-66, F-81, SL-49, and demo PR #242, PR #247, PR #321
  • Implemented in:
    • Part A: the OIN and the name come from the certificate in development_ca_provider.go#L280-L288. The refusal of a set without OIN or name is in source-registry/onboarding/service.go#L293-L297. The Peer ID is separate from the OIN in source_configuration.go#L35-L44.
    • Part B: not implemented. One development CA stands in for every role (issuance_config.go#L159-L180).

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
The first version of this ADR had one goal: a single "converged" trust and identity story. That story had three parts:

  • PKIoverheid as the basis for all certificates.
  • One common anchor for all organization identifiers.
  • The production BSNk PP.

GO and PSA dropped that goal. P-07 does not name PKI any more (Q-07). Two separate questions remain.

Question A is: who is this organization? The demo had three identity carriers side by side: the FSC Peer ID, a configured OIN, and the certificate. One field mixed two identities, and the runtime held CA private keys (F-60). Simulation Peer IDs are not OINs (0000009950HYPBV00000).

Question B is: which certificates does EUDI issuance need? The analysis first confused the PuB-EAA seal and the access CA with PKIoverheid (F-66). Since August 2026, PuB-EAA issuance falls under ETSI TS 119 471. That standard has its own registration and certificate profile (F-81).

The BSNk production part of the first version is not in this ADR. ADR-0005 covers pseudonymization. ADR-0040 covers citizen recognition and the BSNk participant.

docs.title: Part A: organization identity (accepted)
docs.text:
The decision for organization identity has five parts:

  1. The legal identity of a bronhouder (OIN and organization name) comes from its verified certificate material. It does not come from configuration (REQ-67). The OIN is the 20-digit serialNumber. The name is exactly one O attribute.
  2. GBO refuses a configured OIN or name that differs from the certificate. GBO also refuses a certificate without a 20-digit OIN, or without exactly one organization name.
  3. The configuration holds the FSC Peer ID separately from the OIN (provider_peer_id). One peer can offer services of more than one bronhouder.
  4. The runtime gets leaf material and public CA certificates, never CA private keys. A separate privileged command does the provisioning.
  5. FSC participants use PKIoverheid certificates (ADR-0003).

docs.title: Part B: EUDI certificate roles (proposed)
docs.text:
GBO issues attestations for a bronhouder. Each such bronhouder needs its own certificates, one per role. One certificate never fills two roles. The roles are as follows:

Role Purpose Issued by Trust anchor Organization or system certificate mTLS for FSC, and organization identity (OIN, name) PKIoverheid PKIoverheid root Access certificate Authenticates the issuer to the wallet (OpenID4VCI) An access CA (ETSI TS 119 411-8) The access CA that the member state notified Registration certificate Proves the registration of the service, one per registered service (since Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1730) A provider of registration certificates that the member state appoints Published by the member state Qualified certificate for electronic seal Seals the PuB-EAA. The profile is ETSI TS 119 412-6 clause 8. It names the authentic source and the legal basis (eIDAS art. 45f(1)(b)). The key is in a QSCD A QTSP Open: Q-30 Status-list certificate Signs the status list for revocation Open: Q-17 Open

PKIoverheid is not an EUDI access CA. It is also not the seal infrastructure for PuB-EAAs. An access CA issues access certificates only, and it never signs attestations. REQ-58 makes the certificate set per source fail-hard (ADR-0016).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• An attestation and a decision record name the bronhouder with an identity that an operator cannot fill in freely.
  • Consents are bound to the identity of the consumer. If that identity changes, the consents become unusable. The migration in PR #244 and PR #277 showed that the binding is real.
  • In the default demo onboarding, the demo publishes RvIG through the Belastingdienst peer with the Belastingdienst OIN. That is a demo shortcut, so it does not show one OIN per bronhouder. The certificate sets still differ per source.
  • The demo development CA stands in for all EUDI roles at once. Production separates the roles.
  • The choice of the party that operates the Dutch access CA depends on Dutch EUDI governance. That choice is outside the decision scope of GBO.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
These points are open:

  • Can policy read the FSC Peer ID of a consumer as its OIN, or must policy take that link from the register (Q-68)?
  • On which trust list do PuB-EAA providers appear: a List of Trusted Entities (ETSI TS 119 602) or the trusted lists (ETSI TS 119 612)? The specifications contradict each other (Q-30).
  • Who holds the keys of the seal and status-list certificates: the bronhouder, or the central issuance facility (Q-17)?
  • How does the migration from the self-generated CAs of the demo work?

  • Open questions: Q-06, Q-07, Q-17, Q-30, Q-68

docs.title: ADR-0024: Canonical semantic models per bronhouder
docs.text:
• Status: proposed
  • Date: 2026-08-24
  • Satisfies: S10, D-14, GO F4
  • Deliberation: reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 3 (archived and unpublished)
  • Implemented in: partially. The GraphQL schemas of the sources come from the gbo-semantiek source profiles. No route serializations other than SD-JWT VC exist.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
The same data must appear in three forms:

  • GraphQL responses (DvTP).
  • Attestation claims (EUDI).
  • OOTS-EDM evidence (cross-border).

If no canonical model per source exists, every route grows its own mapping.

docs.title: Proposed decision
docs.text:
The source profile GraphQL schema is the canonical model per source. The GBO-Semantiek track maintains this schema. GBO generates or defines the route serializations from it:

  • Attestation attribute schemas and type metadata. The sources already publish these, as ADR-0016 decides.
  • OOTS-EDM evidence-type mappings for ADR-0020.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
These points are open:

  • The governance between the schemas of the bronhouders and the central semantics track.
  • The mapping coverage for the evidence types of the OOTS Semantic Repository.
  • Is gbo-simple-v1 (ADR-0017) sufficient as the projection language for richer models?

docs.title: ADR-0025: GraphQL as a recognized FDS data service type
docs.text:
• Status: proposed
  • Date: 2026-08-24
  • Satisfies: D-08, D-13, PSA: REST versus GraphQL note
  • Deliberation: reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 4 (archived and unpublished)
  • Implemented in: not applicable (standardization action)

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: FDS mandates the REST API Design Rules. GraphQL is not a recognized data service (datadienst) type in FDS. The data access pillar of GBO (ADR-0001) depends on GraphQL. For this reason, GBO must bring the deviation to the standards bodies under the comply-or-explain rule ("pas toe of leg uit").

docs.title: Proposed decision
docs.text:
GBO proposes GraphQL as an additional data service type through the FDS and Forum Standaardisatie processes. The proposal includes a Digikoppeling GraphQL profile. The proposal positions GraphQL as follows:

  • GraphQL runs over FSC, and the transport does not change.
  • The iWlz/nID production deployment and gbo-demo are the precedent.
  • The AuthZEN mapping of the query structure to the authorization input is the enforcement story.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
These points are open:

  • The owner and the timeline of the standardization submission.
  • The scope of a Digikoppeling GraphQL profile (pagination, errors, introspection policy).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text: • Requirements: none directly. The data access pillar it supports is ADR-0001.

docs.title: ADR-0026: Each controller logs its own processing in an LDV logbook
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-08-24, proposed as "Logboek Dataverwerkingen integration". Rewritten and accepted on 2026-11-02.
  • Satisfies: P-12, P-13, P-10, S09
  • Deliberation: reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 5 "traceability correlation" (archived and unpublished), REQ-72, F-64, F-65, F-68, F-69, and demo PR #303 (#302), PR #366, docs/ldv/README.md
  • Implemented in:
    • services/ldv-logboek: the logbook stand-in, one instance per controller.
    • services/ldv-client: the shared client (outbox.go).
    • validate.go: the BSN refusal.
    • docker-compose.yml: the seven logbooks.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
A citizen and an auditor must be able to see which organization processed which personal data, and why. The decision log records decisions. It does not record processings, because a PDP decision is not a processing (F-63). The gap is at the processing itself (F-64):

  • The consent status lookup at the register.
  • The decryption at the source gateway.
  • The query at the source.

The Logius standard Logboek Dataverwerkingen (LDV, v1.0.0) records each processing in the logbook of its controller (verantwoordelijke). Only trace metadata crosses an organization boundary.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The decision has four parts:

  • Every component that GBO delivers and that processes personal data writes one LDV record per processing and per data subject. The record goes to the logbook of the controller of that component (REQ-72).
  • The record carries these values:
    • The trace context, as ADR-0035 decides.
    • The data subject in the pseudonym space of that controller, with an explicit data_subject_id_type. The data subject is never a BSN.
    • A versioned, resolvable processing_activity_id.
    • dpl.read.nextLogbookId, if the processing calls another party.
    • The FSC peer that the Inway verified, if the component is a processor on a lookup over FSC (REQ-76).
  • GBO ships the client. Each controller owns its logbook (P-10).
  • A component stores the record durably in a local outbox before the processing delivers. If the logbook is down, the record arrives later. The outage never loses the record, and it does not fail the request.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
1. A logbook per controller, written by a shared client (chosen).
  2. One central GBO logbook. Not chosen: LDV keeps records at each controller, and only trace metadata crosses a boundary.
  3. OpenTelemetry spans, relabeled as LDV records. Not chosen: spans are sampled, and their delivery is not acknowledged (REQ-32).
  4. A failed request when the logbook is down (the first demo version). The outbox replaced this option, because a withheld response does not undo a processing that already happened.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The demo runs one ldv-logboek image as seven logbooks: Belastingdienst, BRP, consent (register and portal), EUDI adapter, consumer (Hypotheek-BV and the integrator), LVG, and Installatie Register. Twelve components write to them.
  • The decryption at the source gateway is a processing at the source. Each logbook uses its own pseudonym space. As a result, a pseudonym does not travel between the logbooks of different controllers (F-69).
  • LDV records never hold a BSN. The logbook refuses any record with a run of nine digits that passes the BSN check digit test (elfproef).
  • A reader follows a chain forward from the start logbooks through nextLogbookId. In DvTP the chain starts at the consumer, and LDV does not bind the consumer (F-68, AV-02).
  • The consumer has no citizen identifier, so it logs under the consent ID (Q-27).
  • Citizen access works per controller, through the read extension of each logbook (F-65). A view of the processings per consent is not built in demo v0.9.0.

These points are open:

  • The register of processing activities is a stand-in without legal status. Retention and read access are open (Q-08).
  • Components write a local dpl.gbo.* extension that nobody ratified (Q-72).
  • No pointer leads from the decision at the source to the logbook of the consent register (toestemmingsregister) (Q-25).
  • In demo v0.9.0, the ASIP writes no LDV records.
  • Production needs WORM storage, hash chaining, or a notary for the logbooks (REQ-32).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-72, REQ-32, REQ-55, REQ-60, REQ-76, AV-02
  • Findings: F-07 (closed), F-63 (closed), F-64 (resolved in demo), F-65 (closed), F-68 (open), F-69 (resolved in demo)
  • Open questions: Q-08 (open), Q-24 (closed), Q-25 (open), Q-27 (open), Q-72 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-50 (exploration done, build delivered)

docs.title: ADR-0027: Bronhouder onboarding toolkit
docs.text:
• Status: proposed
  • Date: 2026-08-24, updated on 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: D-06, GO §6: impact on bronhouders
  • Deliberation: reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 6 "bronhouder onboarding toolkit" (archived and unpublished)
  • Implemented in: partially. These parts of the demo are reusable starting points: the Helm chart, the source metadata contract (ADR-0016), the source gateway (ADR-0033), and the contract seed scripts.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: GBO has one API and one connectivity stack. Even so, the connection of a bronhouder involves PKI, FSC components, a source gateway, policies, and metadata. Smaller bronhouders, for example municipalities, can lack the capacity for this work.

docs.title: Proposed decision
docs.text:
GBO packages the source-side stack as a deployable toolkit. The toolkit has these parts:

  • FSC Inway and Manager.
  • The source gateway (bron-sidecar).
  • Contract seeds.
  • Policy templates per route.
  • A reference onboarding process: certificate, FSC registration, metadata publication, contract, and activation.

Some sources cannot host their own GraphQL endpoint. For these sources, GBO offers a GBO translation layer (GBO-vertaallaag) as a shared service.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
These points are open:

  • Who operates the shared instances of the translation layer?
  • The policy templates are guidance. Each bronhouder owns and publishes its own policy (ADR-0021).
  • How does a source get its BSNk decryption keys as an onboarding step (BSNK-09, #467)?
  • Who builds the registration and onboarding facility (Q-74)?
  • The support model and the conformance testing for onboarded sources.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-64, REQ-65, AV-07, AV-09, BSNK-09
  • Findings: F-57 (open), F-71 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-74 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-09 (mostly covered), SL-46 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0028: PubEAA Provider productization
docs.text:
• Status: proposed
  • Date: 2026-08-24, rewritten on 2026-11-02. The rewrite made the bronhouder the PuB-EAA provider and GBO the technical issuance facility, and added the regulatory frame of F-81.
  • Satisfies: S11, P-06, GO: PuB-EAA issuance
  • Deliberation: reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 7 (archived and unpublished), F-81, F-82, REQ-77
  • Implemented in: demo grade. The issuance chain of ADR-0018 works end to end with development CAs. issuance_config.go#L166-L168 fixes the validity at 365 days.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
The government issues no PuB-EAAs. For this reason, the Netherlands relies on commercial QTSPs for attestations from government sources. The demo proves the issuance chain. Production status needs trust anchoring and governance. The demo leaves these out on purpose.

The first version of this ADR made the shared GBO facility the PuB-EAA provider that the member state notifies. That choice does not fit the regulation or the GO:

  • eIDAS article 3(46) names two possible issuers. One is the body that is responsible for the authentic source. The other is a public sector body that the member state designates on behalf of that body.
  • The notification specification (EUDI TS2) assumes that the bronhouder is the provider. A party that issues on behalf of the bronhouder goes in the field EEAIssuer.
  • The GO describes GBO as a technical, central, and optional issuance facility. Legally, GBO is not a PuB-EAA provider. The bronhouder stays legally responsible (PSA S11).

Since August 2026, PuB-EAA issuance also falls under the same standard as QEAA issuance (F-81).

docs.title: Proposed decision
docs.text:
The proposal has seven parts:

  1. Roles. Each bronhouder is the PuB-EAA provider of its attestations. GBO operates the technical issuance facility. GBO is probably the EEAIssuer in the notification of each bronhouder. The designation of GBO or the management organization under article 3(46) is an open decision (Q-28).
  2. Conformity. The facility conforms to ETSI TS 119 471 with EN 319 401. Implementing Regulation 2026/1735 requires this for QEAA and PuB-EAA providers. Issuance follows OpenID4VCI as ETSI TS 119 472-3 specifies. The issuance checks the wallet instance attestation and the key attestation.
  3. Certificates per bronhouder:
    • The facility seals the attestation in a QSCD, with a qualified seal certificate as ETSI TS 119 412-6 clause 8 specifies. The certificate names the authentic source and the legal basis (eIDAS article 45f(1)(b)).
    • Each registered service has its own access certificate and registration certificate.
    • The issuer registers as relying party with the entitlement PUB_EAA_Provider.
    • ADR-0023 describes the roles.
  4. Rulebook per type. Each Dutch attestation type gets a rulebook. The rulebook uses the template of the rulebooks catalogue.
  5. Validity and revocation per type. The bronhouder sets them (REQ-77):
    • If an attestation is valid for more than 24 hours, it carries a status reference.
    • The facility revokes the attestation on instruction of the bronhouder, and when the source data changes.
    • GBO only queries and gets no change signal (F-82). For this reason, each type chooses one of two forms: short-lived (less than 24 hours), or long-lived with a change feed from the source and revocation.
  6. The callback gap of ADR-0018 is closed with positive PID evidence and an authenticated callback (REQ-45).
  7. The facility is optional per bronhouder. Sources with capacity can run their own credential issuer.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The legal responsibility for content, validity, and revocation stays with the bronhouder. GBO revokes technically, on instruction of the bronhouder (AV-12, AV-13).
  • Notification and registration happen per bronhouder. They do not happen once for GBO.
  • Nobody tested the demo against ETSI TS 119 471, the certificate profile, or the checks of ETSI TS 119 472-3.
  • The development CA of the demo stands in for all certificate roles at once. Production separates the roles.
  • The central facility holds the private keys of the issuer and status-list certificates of every source. That needs a decision on key custody (Q-17).

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
These points are open:

  • Who holds and uses the seal and status-list keys of a bronhouder (Q-17)? The options are the central facility, a remote signing service, or an HSM at the bronhouder.
  • Who designates the Dutch PuB-EAA issuer, and who supervises (Q-28)?
  • On which trust list do PuB-EAA providers appear: a List of Trusted Entities or the trusted lists (Q-30)? This point is open, and no fact settles it.
  • Does every source answer get one seal, regardless of the channel (Q-75)?
  • The governance of the attestation schema per attestation type.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-45, REQ-58, REQ-77, AV-12, AV-13
  • Findings: F-66 (closed), F-81 (open), F-82 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-17, Q-28, Q-30, Q-75
  • Demo increments: SL-26

docs.title: ADR-0029: Authentic Source Interface per ETSI TS 119 478
docs.text:
• Status: superseded by ADR-0037
  • Date: 2026-08-24, superseded on 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: eIDAS Article 45e, GO: verification and retrieval service for QTSPs, PSA open decisions: central verification and retrieval service
  • Superseded by: ADR-0037
  • Deliberation: reference architecture v0.6.2, gap 8 and ASI design (archived and unpublished)
  • Implemented in: not implemented in this form. The built route is ADR-0037.

docs.title: Why superseded
docs.text:
The demo built the Authentic Source Interface after this ADR (SL-28). Three core points of this proposal changed:

  • Retrieve is implemented. The ASIP offers clause 6.1.2 next to 6.1.1. EUDI issuance does not replace retrieve, because the QTSP issues the QEAA, and GBO does not (REQ-101, REQ-112).
  • The QTSP is outside FSC. This proposal saw the ASI as a protocol adapter "in front of" the FSC chain. The ASI is an OAuth front door with its own trust model. The authorization server admits the QTSP, and the PDP does not. The generic chain starts behind the ASIP, which is an FSC peer of its own (F-87).

  • Clause numbers replace the labels I1 to I5. The labels came from the reference architecture:

    • I1 is clause 5 (discovery).
    • I2 is 6.1.1 (verify).
    • I3 is 6.1.2 (retrieve).
    • I4 is 6.1.3 (authorization server).
    • I5 is citizen identification inside 6.1.3.

    The TO uses the ETSI clause numbers and roles.

ADR-0037 records the decision that replaces this ADR. ADR-0038, ADR-0039, ADR-0041, and ADR-0042 record the details. The following sections hold the original proposal as history.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: Article 45e of the amended eIDAS regulation obliges member states to let QTSPs verify attributes against authentic sources at the request of the user. ETSI TS 119 478 specifies the interfaces. Without this interface, QTSPs cannot issue QEAAs based on Dutch government registers.

docs.title: Proposed decision
docs.text:
The proposal builds the ASI provider as a GBO edge service, in the HTTP/OAuth variant:

  • Implement I2 (Verify). The service translates verification requests into GraphQL queries over FSC, through the standard PEP-PDP chain, and compares the values.
  • Implement I4 and I5: citizen authorization through OAuth, with a wallet or eID.
  • Skip I3 (Retrieve), because the EUDI chain covers direct issuance (ADR-0018).
  • Register the data services in the EU catalogue of attributes (I1).

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
The proposal left these points open:

  • The PDP policy set for QTSP verification (Trusted List check, citizen authorization, attribute scope).
  • The design of the authorization server (I4), and its relation to the consent facility (toestemmingsvoorziening).
  • The timeline pressure from the Article 45e deadline. For more information, see Risks and technical debt.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-101, REQ-112
  • Findings: F-80 (open), F-87 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-28

docs.title: ADR-0030: Flow and subject identifier semantics as FSC grant properties
docs.text:
• Status: superseded by ADR-0031
  • Date: 2026-09-07, superseded on 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: P-01, D-11, D-08
  • Supersedes: ADR-0014
  • Superseded by: ADR-0031
  • Deliberation: gbo-demo CHANGELOG, v0.6.11, and issues #244, #277, #279
  • Implemented in: removed from gbo-demo. #334 removed the flow property (PR #363). #473 removed the subject_id_type property (PR #475). In gbo-demo v0.9.0, the seeds create grants without properties (CHANGELOG).

docs.title: Why superseded
docs.text:
The regime does not need a declaration. The regime follows from the evidence that the request carries (ADR-0031):

  • A consent proof puts the request in the consent regime.
  • A request without a consent proof is in the PID regime.

After that change, no component read the flow property. The subject_id_type property also lost its reader. The source gateway takes the subject from the consent proof, and not from the contract (ADR-0033). The demo removed both properties. The following sections hold the original decision as history.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: The PDP judges a request under an authorization regime. The regime has two parts: the flow, and the way to read the subject identifier (subject_id_type). The regime must be bound to the connection and signed, and the caller must not control it. ADR-0014 describes the mechanism that this ADR replaced.

docs.title: Decision (superseded)
docs.text:
The decision put flow and subject_id_type as properties in the GRANT_TYPE_SERVICE_CONNECTION grant of the FSC contract (fsc-core, section Properties). It worked as follows:

  • The properties are inside the grant, so they are part of the grant hash. Both peers countersign the regime when they sign the contract.
  • The Manager of the provider puts the properties in the access token, as the FSC-normative prp claim.
  • The PDP request mapper reads the flow from prp only. It uses no header and no default.
  • If a token has no prp, the flow is empty. An empty flow matches no rule, so the PDP denies with NO_APPLICABLE_RULE.
  • The source gateway reads subject_id_type from the same claim.

The demo seeded three property sets:

Contract Properties EDI issuer → data services (bri, brp) {"flow": "eudi:attestation", "subject_id_type": "direct"} Mortgage lender (Hypotheek-BV) → bri {"flow": "dvtp:query", "subject_id_type": "pseudonym"} EDI issuer → metadata services {"flow": "gbo:source-metadata"} (not subject-bound)

docs.title: Consequences (at the time)
docs.text:
The decision had these consequences:

  • The provider needed no mapping file and no extra service. The contract was the single source of truth for the regime.
  • Contracts are immutable, so a regime change meant a new contract. The seed scripts matched on properties and moved the grant link to the new contract.
  • Every peer on a contract needed OpenFSC 2.0 or later. If the contract of a peer carried no properties, the PDP denied the peer until a new seed.
  • If subject_id_type was missing, the fail-safe default of the source gateway was direct (pass-through). If the flow was missing, the default of the PDP was deny. This difference was safe, because the PDP decided first.

docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-74
  • Findings: F-32 (resolved in demo), F-43 (superseded), F-62 (resolved in demo), F-70 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-15 (answered)

docs.title: ADR-0031: The authorization regime follows from the evidence a request carries
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: S05, P-01, D-11
  • Supersedes: ADR-0030
  • Deliberation: REQ-74, F-70, Q-15, and demo #334, PR #363, CHANGELOG
  • Implemented in:
    • engine.rego (regime selection) and consent.rego (token read).
    • The rule regimes in dvt0001.rego, eud0001.rego, and asi0001.rego.
    • The tests in engine_test.rego.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
The PDP judges a request under one of two regimes:

  • In the consent regime (DvTP), the consent of a citizen is the access basis.
  • In the PID regime (EUDI issuance, ASI), a verified PID disclosure of the citizen is the basis.

Each regime has its own rules and its own reasons to deny.

A component must select the regime. If the consumer selects it, the consumer chooses the basis for its own judgment. Earlier designs put the selection in three places:

  • A header.
  • A signed claim of the provider (ADR-0014).
  • An FSC grant property (ADR-0030).

All three are a declaration about the request. None of them is evidence in the request.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The regime follows from the evidence that the request carries:

  • If a consent token is present (X-GBO-Consent-Token, verified or not), the request is in the consent regime. Only the rules with regime := "consent" bind: DVT0001 and LVG0001.
  • If no consent token is present, the request is in the PID regime. Only the rules with regime := "pid" bind: EUD0001, EUD0002, and ASI0001.
  • If two consent proofs are present, the policy denies with CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID. The policy does not pick one of them.

Every rule declares its regime. Only the rules of the active regime bind, so the deny reason also comes from that regime. FSC grants carry no properties. No component reads a flow.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
1. Evidence in the request (chosen). The request carries no declaration that a party can forge or must maintain. Each rule still checks its own basis, so a wrong regime cannot give access.
  2. flow as an FSC grant property (ADR-0030). Both peers sign it, but it is a declaration per contract. Each consumer needs one contract per regime, and a change needs a new contract.
  3. Dispatch from component metadata or from the certificate (SL-24, dropped). This option binds the regime to the caller, and not to the request. A party that acts in both regimes does not fit.
  4. A request header or a default regime (SL-48). With this option, the consumer chooses the regime. Not chosen.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The rules already did the security work. DVT0001 and LVG0001 deny without a verified consent. The PID rules deny without a PID subject. The regime decides which reasons the PDP reports. The regime does not decide access. Engine tests pin the reason in both directions.
  • Only consent is positive evidence. A request enters the PID regime because it has no consent proof (F-70). For this reason, the PID regime needs its own positive evidence: a verified PID disclosure (REQ-45). In demo v0.9.0, the adapter callback that carries this evidence is not authenticated (#133).
  • The actor lists of the PID rules (designated_issuers, asip) must stay disjoint from the consent consumers in every environment. A test pins this for the seeded peers only (engine_test.rego).
  • A Gov-to-Gov regime on a legal basis needs its own positive evidence. It cannot be a third regime that rests on an absence.
  • The source gateway uses the same evidence. If a consent token is present, the source gateway takes the subject from it. If not, the source gateway passes the request through (ADR-0033).

docs.text:

  • Findings: F-70 (open), F-32 (resolved in demo), F-43 (superseded), F-49 (premise lapsed), F-62 (resolved in demo)
  • Open questions: Q-15 (answered)
