docs.title: ADR-0032: The consent proof: signed, a value per source, a placeholder in the query, status online over FSC, verified in policy
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: S01, S03, S05, P-01, P-04
  • Supersedes: ADR-0007
  • Deliberation: REQ-68, REQ-79, REQ-80, F-44, F-61, and demo PR #238, PR #371 (#330), PR #390, PR #469, #383, #473
  • Implemented in:
    • consent_token.go: the proof.
    • consent.rego: the verification and the status check in policy.
    • status.go: the status listener behind the register Inway.
    • lib.rego: the placeholders.
    • docker-compose.yml: the status call over the PDP Outway.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
In DvTP, the consent of the citizen is the access basis. The PDP at the source must establish three facts itself (REQ-68):

  • The consent comes from the consent register (toestemmingsregister) and is unchanged.
  • The consent is bound to this consumer, this data set, and this citizen.
  • The consent is valid at the time of the request, also after a revocation one second before.

The consumer must not hold a citizen identifier (REQ-20). The consumer also must not choose the subject of its question (REQ-79). BSNk transforms values only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04). For this reason, the register must make every value that a source needs at consent time. These values travel with the proof.

docs.title: The proof
docs.text:
When the citizen gives consent, the consent register signs a JWT with these properties:

  • The algorithm is ES256. The header has typ=gbo-consent+jwt and kid. The public keys are in the JWKS of the register.
  • The claims are consent_id, scopes, scope_entries (per source), dienstverlener_oin, valid_until, iss, aud (default gbo:dvtp:pdp), iat, nbf, exp (equal to valid_until), and jti. The dienstverlener_oin is the represented party (ADR-0034).
  • The encrypted_subject claim holds a pseudonym (VP) per source OIN. If the source is on the BSN authorization list, it also holds an identity (VI) for that source. Each value carries its key_set_version. Only that source can read the value (REQ-80).

The proof holds no PI and no BSN. If a proof has no pseudonym for every party, the register refuses it.

docs.title: The consumer
docs.text:
The consumer sends the proof unchanged in X-GBO-Consent-Token (AV-05). In its query, the consumer names the citizen only with a placeholder:

  • consent:identity for a BSN API.
  • consent:pseudonym for a source-pseudonym API.

Each rule lists the placeholders that it accepts. If the query has a literal value, or a placeholder without a verified proof, the PDP denies (CONSTRAINT_MISMATCH).

docs.title: The PDP policy verifies the proof itself
docs.text:
The request mapper only maps (ADR-0013). consent.rego does these steps per evaluation:

  1. It verifies the ES256 signature against the JWKS of the register. The policy caches the JWKS for 300 seconds. On an unknown kid, the policy fetches the JWKS again.
  2. It verifies the claims in Rego, with 30 seconds of clock skew.
  3. Only after that, it asks the status of this consent_id. This call uses no cache and a 2-second timeout. It goes over FSC, through the Outway of the PDP, to the Inway of the register (FSC service consent-status).

Keys can be five minutes old. The status cannot be old. Every failure maps to its own reason code:

  • CONSENT_SIGNATURE_INVALID
  • CONSENT_TOKEN_EXPIRED
  • CONSENT_KEYS_UNAVAILABLE
  • CONSENT_CONTEXT_INVALID
  • CONSENT_NOT_FOUND
  • CONSENT_STATUS_UNAVAILABLE
  • CONSENT_WITHDRAWN

The policy ignores a pip.consent in the input.

docs.title: After an allow
docs.text: After an allow, the source gateway takes its own value from the proof. The gateway decrypts the value with its own keys and replaces the placeholder (ADR-0033).

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
1. A signed proof, with the status online (chosen).
  2. Only a consent ID, and the PDP looks up the content at the register (ADR-0006). The register becomes the only source of the evidence. The consumer presents nothing that the PDP can verify.
  3. A status list that the PDP fetches periodically. A revocation takes effect only after the next fetch. REQ-14 needs a deny on the next request.
  4. A verifiable credential or presentation. This is a wallet format for a server-to-server proof. It adds a holder role that the consumer does not have.
  5. A PI in the query, and a BSNk call at the PEP or the source (ADR-0010, ADR-0007). The PI belongs to the requester only (BSNK-03). BSNk transforms only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04).
  6. Consent verification in the Go request mapper (the earlier demo). FTV puts attribute retrieval inside the PDP. With verification in the mapper, the decision rests on facts that the policy did not establish (REQ-18).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Freshness is asymmetric on purpose (F-61). The basis travels as a proof. The status stays online, so the register is a dependency on every request (REQ-75). The values for latency and availability are open (Q-47).
  • The status check is a processing at the register. The register answers only an FSC peer that its Inway authenticated. The register logs that peer as the processor (REQ-76). Any connected peer can still ask the status of any consent whose ID it holds. A restriction to the own PDP of the source is not built in demo v0.9.0.
  • A replay from (input, policy, data) is not possible. The policy fetches the status during the evaluation. The engine copies the resolved consent into its response for the console log. The ADL carries only {allow, reason} (F-72, ADR-0036).
  • The PDP verifies that the subject comes from the proof. The PDP does not verify who the subject is (F-77). One request names one subject. No policy can depend on the identity of the subject.
  • The proof freezes at consent (F-78). The parties, key versions, BSN authorization, and proof form stay fixed for its validity period. The proof has no version. If a source is added or gets new keys later, it needs a new consent, or it keeps its old keys (AV-09).
  • The proof is a bearer token. The actor binding stops use by another consumer, but it does not stop replay by the same consumer. Production needs a shorter validity and a proof-of-possession binding to the FSC identity (Risks and technical debt).
  • The consumer holds no citizen identifier (F-76). What the consumer records about "this person" hangs on the consent ID. A pseudonym for the consumer itself is not built (#478).

These points are open:

  • Where does the signing key live, and how does it rotate (Q-55)?
  • Does the proof bind the purpose (Q-69)?
  • Is the integrator in the proof (Q-46)?
  • Who sets the validity period (Q-13)?

The design came in three steps:

  1. A consent PIP through a PEP pre-fetch (SL-08).
  2. A signed, actor-bound proof (SL-47).
  3. An encrypted value per source and a placeholder (SL-51).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-68, REQ-75, REQ-76, REQ-14, REQ-18, REQ-19, REQ-20, REQ-21, REQ-79, REQ-80, REQ-82, AV-05, BSNK-03, BSNK-04
  • Findings: F-44 (resolved in demo), F-61 (closed), F-72 (open), F-76 (open), F-77 (open), F-78 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-05 (answered), Q-13 (open), Q-46 (open), Q-47 (open), Q-55 (open), Q-69 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-08 (done), SL-23 (done), SL-47 (done), SL-51 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0033: The source gateway decrypts its own value after the allow, and only the Inway reaches it
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: P-04, P-10, S03, S07
  • Supersedes: ADR-0011
  • Deliberation: REQ-21, REQ-81, F-30, F-37, F-79, and demo #364, PR #469, PR #476, PR #477, #473
  • Implemented in:
    • bron-sidecar/main.go: the gateway acts on the consent proof.
    • substitution.go: the own value and the recipient check.
    • decryption.go: the source keys, with older versions kept.
    • transport.go: only the request shape that the PDP judged.
    • docker-compose.yml: the network isolation.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
Under a consent, the query of the consumer names the citizen with a placeholder (ADR-0032). The source API needs a BSN, or the own pseudonym of the source for the citizen. A component must replace the placeholder, under three conditions:

  • Only after the PDP allowed the request (REQ-04).
  • Inside the boundary of the source, with the keys of the source, and without a central party in the query path (REQ-21).
  • Without a BSNk call, because BSNk transforms only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04).

A transformation after the decision is a gateway task. It is not a policy task (F-37).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A gateway that the source owns (bron-sidecar) sits between the source Inway and the source API. The gateway works as follows:

  • The evidence decides. If a consent token is present, the subject comes from the token. Without a token, the request passes through unchanged (PID regime, ADR-0031). Grant properties play no part.
  • Only the own value of the source counts. The gateway takes encrypted_subject[<own OIN>] from the proof: the VI for consent:identity, and the VP for consent:pseudonym. The own decryption component of the source reads the value with the keys of the source.
  • The recipient must match. The decrypted value must name the own OIN of the source as recipient, or the gateway does not accept it. The key in the proof is not evidence. The value that BSNk signed is the evidence.
  • Three cases lead to a refusal, and the request then goes no further:
    • A form is missing, for example no VI for a source that is not on the BSN authorization list.
    • The value is for another recipient.
    • The query has a literal subject under a consent proof.
  • The gateway does not verify the proof again. The PDP verified it on the same request, and the gateway runs only after the allow.
  • Isolation is the control:
    • Only the source Inways reach the gateway (network source-gateways).
    • The gateway reaches only what serves the source (network sources).
    • The gateway publishes no port.
    • The gateway accepts only the request shape that the PDP judged: POST, one path, a JSON body, and no query string.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
1. The source gateway decrypts after the allow (chosen).
  2. BSN resolution in the PEP (ADR-0010). The PEP becomes a middlebox that transforms data in shared infrastructure, with a BSNk call in the query path.
  3. The source gateway calls BSNk Transform per request (ADR-0011). BSNk transforms only while the citizen is logged in, and a query comes later.
  4. Transformation in the PDP. Policy is not a data pipeline (F-37). With this option, the PDP holds BSN authority.
  5. The gateway verifies the proof again. This option adds no protection, because a consumer holds real proofs. The protection is that no request reaches the gateway without the allow of the PDP (F-79).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The query path has no central party and no BSNk. Only the source holds BSN authority, as P-10 requires.
  • "After the decision" holds only while nothing other than the Inway reaches the gateway (REQ-81). The compose networks do this. A Kubernetes deployment needs a NetworkPolicy or an equivalent. In demo v0.9.0, the Helm chart has no such policy.
  • A nonce does not bind a value to one consent. That binding is not built (F-79).
  • A source keeps the decryption keys of an older key version while proofs for that version are valid (AV-09).
  • A source must get its keys in advance, as a step of admission (BSNK-09, onboarding keys, #467).
  • The gateway is a processing. It writes LDV records for the decryption and the forward (ADR-0026).
  • In the demo, the three sources share one OIN and one decryption component. The mock does not encrypt. Production needs one decryption component per source.
  • Two parts are not built: a source API that answers on a pseudonym (#474), and a pseudonym for the consumer itself (#478, Q-01).
  • The gateway is separate from the HTTP handler. For this reason, the gateway can move into an Inway plugin later.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-04, REQ-17, REQ-21, REQ-79, REQ-80, REQ-81, AV-09, BSNK-04, BSNK-07, BSNK-08, BSNK-09
  • Findings: F-06 (closed), F-30 (resolved in demo), F-37 (resolved in demo), F-79 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-01 (partly answered)
  • Demo increments: SL-02 (done), SL-22 (done), SL-51 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0034: An integrator connects under FSC delegation, and the consent binds the represented party
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: S04, S05, P-01, D-11
  • Deliberation: REQ-106, F-20, F-73, Q-12, and demo #379, PR #464, docs/integrator.md
  • Implemented in:
    • lib.rego: the acting party and the represented party.
    • engine.rego: the mandate check.
    • dvtp_helper.rego: the consent binds the represented party.
    • autosign.rego: the delegated grant.
    • onboarding service.go: integrations and acts_for.
    • dvtp-onboarding.yaml: the PIP pull.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
A consumer (afnemer) can let a software party, the integrator, call the source for it. The consent binds a consumer. The policy compared the dienstverlener_oin of the consent with the FSC peer that calls. An integrator breaks that assumption (F-73). The integrator calls, but the citizen gave consent to the consumer.

The integrator acts as processor for the consumer (Q-12, AV-06). The integrator must not get access of its own. It must act only for the consumers that registered it (REQ-106).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The decision has four parts:

  • Transport. The integrator connects over an FSC DelegatedServiceConnection grant (grant type 3). The consumer is the delegator and signs the contract.
  • Contract admission. The contract decision of the source admits a delegated grant only if the admission register has that integration. If not, the decision refuses with DELEGATION_NOT_REGISTERED (ADR-0015).
  • Mandate. The admission register records per integrator the consumers and the rules that it acts for (integrations, pulled into OpenFTV as acts_for). At request time, every delegated call needs a mandate for the represented party and the granting rule:
    • If the mandate is missing, the engine denies with INTEGRATOR_NOT_REGISTERED.
    • If the register data is missing, the engine denies with INTEGRATOR_REGISTER_UNAVAILABLE.
    • The engine applies this check to every rule. No rule can leave it out.
  • Consent binding. The consent binds the represented party. That is the FSC delegator, or the calling peer if there is no delegator. The consent gives the integrator no mandate.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
1. FSC delegation plus a mandate in the admission register (chosen).
  2. The integrator calls with its own direct grant. The source then sees only the integrator. Either the consent binding fails, or the integrator gets access of its own.
  3. The integrator in the consent proof. With this option, the citizen also consents to the integrator. FR-DvTP v0.9 does not ask any more to tell the citizen about the integrator. It stays open whether the proof names the integrator (Q-46).
  4. No integrator role (the earlier TO). Real consumers use software parties, so the design must say how they connect (F-20).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The integrator gets a separate admission and acts as processor (AV-06).
  • In demo v0.9.0, a mandate has no validity period. It ends only when the register entry changes.
  • The admission register is also a request-time input, in addition to a contract-time input. A suspended consumer with a valid contract can still query directly. REQ-110 covers that gap.
  • OpenFSC puts the delegator in act.sub and the connecting peer in sub. That is the reverse of RFC 8693. The demo reads the values as OpenFSC writes them. An upstream issue is due.
  • The autosign input has no grant data. For this reason, the contract decision admits the pair, but not the direction of the delegation. The mandate check at request time closes that gap.
  • In the demo, the path is opt-in (make demo-integrator, peer …1100).
  • One point is open: can policy read the FSC Peer ID as the OIN of the consumer (Q-68)?

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-106, REQ-48, REQ-61, REQ-62, REQ-110, AV-06
  • Findings: F-20 (closed), F-73 (closed)
  • Open questions: Q-12 (answered), Q-46 (open), Q-68 (open)
  • Demo increments: none

docs.title: ADR-0035: W3C Trace Context is the correlation key, and the FSC transaction ID is recorded next to it
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: P-12, S09, D-08
  • Supersedes: ADR-0019
  • Deliberation: REQ-55, F-67, F-41, and demo PR #366 (#365), PR #329
  • Implemented in:
    • ldv-client/tracecontext.go: the rule and the order.
    • consent.rego: the status lookup carries the trace.
    • The entry components consumerhttp.go, eudi-adapter/main.go, and asi-provider tracing.go.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
An auditor must follow one request through the consumer, the PDP, the source gateway, the source, and the consent register (toestemmingsregister). Three standards record parts of the request:

  • LDV (processing records) and the ADL (decision records) require that a component takes the incoming trace ID over unchanged (LDV §3.3.1, W3C Trace Context §3.1).
  • FSC-Logging gives every FSC transaction its own transaction ID, unique per transaction (§3.4.1.1).

ADR-0019 used one value for both. That choice breaks in three cases (F-67):

  • A caller sends its own traceparent.
  • One processing calls several sources.
  • The request takes an extra FSC hop, for example the status lookup of the PDP.

FSC forwards traceparent on the data path. Only the AuthZEN call of the Inway to the PDP drops it (F-39, F-41).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The decision has four parts:

  • Every GBO component takes the trace ID unchanged from the incoming traceparent. If the caller is in the same trace, the component sets the span of the caller as parent. The component sends traceparent and tracestate on every outbound call.
  • The order of sources is fixed: traceparent, then Fsc-Transaction-Id, then X-Request-Id, then the ambient span, and then a new trace.
  • The Fsc-Transaction-Id never replaces an incoming trace. A component that starts or receives an FSC transaction records the transaction ID next to the trace ID. It records the ID as span attribute gbo.fsc.transaction_id, and in the ADL as adl.fsc.transaction_id.
  • If an entry component receives no traceparent, it can tie its new trace to the UUIDv7 transaction ID that it mints. This part of ADR-0019 stays.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
1. W3C Trace Context, with the transaction ID next to it (chosen). This option follows LDV, ADL, and FSC-Logging at the same time.
  2. The transaction ID equals the trace ID (ADR-0019). F-67 showed that this option fails.
  3. A custom correlation header. Not chosen: LDV mandates W3C Trace Context.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One processing has one trace ID and several transaction IDs. Logs and traces join on equal identifiers. They do not join on time stamps.
  • The consent status lookup carries the trace and the transaction ID of the request. The LDV record of the register lands in the trace of the request.
  • Separate units of work keep separate traces. The consent_id joins the consent issuance and the later query. A trace does not join them (F-16).
  • Behind the FSC Inway, the ADL record has its own random trace and no adl.fsc.transaction_id. The cause is that the Inway sends neither header to the PDP. A reader finds the record through the request headers stored in it. The fix is upstream in open-fsc (#369, ADR-0036).
  • A private consumer must send trace context and record the transaction ID (AV-01).
  • In demo v0.9.0, the operational logs of bron-sidecar, eudi-adapter, and asi-provider carry no trace ID.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-55, REQ-71, REQ-72, AV-01
  • Findings: F-16 (closed), F-39 (resolved in demo), F-40 (resolved in demo), F-41 (resolved in demo), F-67 (resolved in demo)
  • Open questions: none
  • Demo increments: SL-07 (done), SL-38 (done), SL-50 (exploration done, build delivered)

docs.title: ADR-0036: The ADL is the authoritative record of authorization decisions
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: P-12, S09, S05
  • Deliberation: REQ-71, F-53, F-63, F-72, and demo PR #337, PR #373 (#332)
  • Implemented in:
    • docker-compose.yml: the ADL is required in every profile.
    • adl-reader.sql: the SELECT-only reader.
    • authz.rego: what the record carries.
    • dev-portal-backend/adl.go: the lookup by transaction ID.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
The PDP produces two decision logs:

  • The Authorization Decision Log (ADL), which OpenFTV writes to Postgres.
  • The console decision log of the embedded OPA, which goes to Loki.

The design did not say which log is the audit source (F-53). The Logius standards family has three records with three roles (F-63):

  • The ADL for decisions.
  • LDV for processings (ADR-0026).
  • FSC-Logging for transport.

A PDP decision is not a processing, so it is not an LDV record.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The decision has four parts:

  • An ADL record holds every PDP decision. OpenFTV writes the record to the Postgres database ftv_adl. The PDP does not start without this database, so the ADL runs in every deployment profile.
  • The ADL record is the audit source for authorization decisions. Contract-acceptance decisions are ADL records too.
  • The console decision log of the engine is observability. Nobody cites it as the record of a decision.
  • A reader gets a SELECT-only database role (adl_reader).

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
1. The ADL as audit source (chosen). It is a standard record with an access model.
  2. The console decision log as audit source. Not chosen: it is a log pipeline that can lose or sample lines, and it has no access model (F-53).
  3. Per-field detail in the reason of the record. Not chosen: the Inway returns the reason to the consumer (F-72).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The record carries only {allow, reason}. On a deny, the reason is the code for the consumer (FIELD_NOT_PERMITTED, ACCESS_DENIED, COVERAGE_UNVERIFIABLE <subcode>, and more). The per-field rule codes and the step trace are only in the console log (REQ-06).
  • The record has these known gaps:
    • The record does not name the policy version (policies: 0, REQ-59).
    • The record does not hold the consent-status answer (adl.core.information) or the configuration (F-72).
    • Behind the FSC Inway, the record does not hold the trace ID or adl.fsc.transaction_id (#369, ADR-0035). The dev portal finds the record through the stored request headers.
    • No pointer leads from the ADL record to the logbook of the consent register (toestemmingsregister) (Q-25).
    • In the EUDI and ASI routes, the record holds the plain BSN (REQ-60, ADR-0043).
  • A replay of a decision from (input, policy, data) is not possible, because the policy fetches the consent status during the evaluation (ADR-0032). A replay needs the non-deterministic built-in cache of OPA, and OpenFTV does not enable this cache.
  • Retention, read access, and tamper evidence are not set (REQ-32, Q-08).

docs.text:

docs.title: ADR-0037: Authentic Source Interface as an OAuth front door per ETSI TS 119 478 clause 6.1
docs.text:
• Status: accepted (demo grade)
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: eIDAS article 45e, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1569 article 9, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1735 Annex IV, GO: verification and retrieval service for QTSPs, S11, S04
  • Supersedes: ADR-0029
  • Deliberation: SL-28, F-80, F-87, and demo epic ICTU/GBO-demo#336
  • Implemented in:
    • services/asi-provider: the ASIP.
    • services/asi-authorization-server and services/asi-wallet-verifier.
    • services/asi-discovery-stub: a stub.
    • services/qtsp-reference: the reference client.
    • asi0001.rego: the rule.
    • The ASIP FSC peer in fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml#L1664-L1669.
    • The conformance matrix and docs/asi-route.md.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
Article 45e of eIDAS lets a qualified trust service provider (QTSP) verify attributes of a citizen at an authentic source. The QTSP does this at the request of that citizen. ETSI TS 119 478 V1.1.1 specifies the interfaces.

Two regulations make clause 6.1.1 (verify) the legal interface: article 9 of Implementing Regulation 2025/1569, and Annex IV of Implementing Regulation 2026/1735. From January 1, 2027, every verification result must be sealed (article 9(4)). The regulations do not designate clause 6.1.3 (authorization) or clause 5 (discovery). For this reason, the design of the authorization part is a national choice (F-80).

The reference architecture placed the interface "in front of" the FSC and PEP-PDP chain (ADR-0029). The demo showed that this placement is not correct. A QTSP is an EU party with an access certificate and a register entitlement. A QTSP has no FSC peer, no OIN, and no PKIoverheid certificate (F-87). GBO needs two parts:

  • A trust model for the QTSP and the citizen that ends before FSC.
  • A chain behind that trust model that a source can judge like any other consumer.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
GBO offers the Authentic Source Interface as an OAuth front door with its own trust model. The generic chain starts behind it. The front door works as follows:

  1. Interface. The Authentic Source Interface Provider (ASIP) offers clause 6.1 only: 6.1.1 verify, 6.1.2 retrieve, and 6.1.3 authorization with the scopes verify and retrieve. The ASIP does not offer clause 6.2 (ISO 15000) (REQ-112, Q-64). Each authentic source gets its own data service under /<data service>/authsrc-api (ADR-0038).
  2. Two services with separate keys. The ASIP and the authorization server are separate services. The ASIP gets the token keys of the authorization server from its RFC 8414 metadata.
  3. The QTSP is an OAuth client. It is not an FSC participant. QTSP admission is not a PDP rule. The authorization server admits a QTSP as follows (REQ-88, REQ-89):
    • The QTSP registers through RFC 7591. The QTSP seals the software statement with its certificate (x5c, registryURI).
    • The server verifies the chain against its trust anchors.
    • Then the server looks up the register entry. The entry must carry the entitlement QEAA_Provider and the organizationIdentifier of the certificate.
    • The client key is the certificate key.
    • The server repeats the lookup periodically. It deactivates a client without entitlement.
  4. Login is approval. Before login, the citizen sees one request page (REQ-91). The page shows the legal name of the QTSP from the register, the operation, the source, and the attributes, if they are bound. The citizen approves by logging in, or refuses without login (REQ-90). The approval is one login per request: it is not a stored consent, and it has no relation to the consent register (toestemmingsregister). Approval in a wallet is not a legal basis (F-83).
  5. Token. The authorization server uses the authorization code flow with PKCE S256 and private_key_jwt. It issues a DPoP-bound RFC 9068 JWT (ES256, 10 minutes). The token carries the identification data and the means used (acr, amr) (REQ-86). The resource parameter names exactly one data service (REQ-95). As an option, the token is bound to the attributes (ADR-0042).
  6. The ASIP takes the citizen only from the token. The ASIP verifies the token and the DPoP proof before anything else (REQ-87). Then the ASIP sends one GraphQL query per request through its own FSC Outway, as peer …1200 (REQ-92, REQ-46). The PDP of the source sees the ASIP as actor, and never the QTSP or the citizen. Rule ASI0001 grants the ASIP peer the fields behind the attributes, on service brp only.
  7. Results. Per attribute, the ASIP answers Match, NoMatch, MatchWithVariation, or Unknown:
    • A verify response contains no source value (REQ-85).
    • Unknown means only that the source has no complete value (REQ-84).
    • If the chain does not answer, the result is 503 or 500, and never Unknown (REQ-93).
    • If a retrieve finds no value, the result is 404, with no partial result (REQ-101).
    • If a request has mandate, the result is 501 (REQ-114).
  8. Seal. The ASIP seals every successful response (REQ-83). ADR-0041 sets the format.
  9. Discovery. The ASIP publishes a dataService record per attribute and data service. The contract of the data service names the metadata of the authorization server (REQ-99, REQ-100).
  10. Conformance. A conformance matrix gives every ETSI requirement ID a status and named tests. If an ID or a test is missing, CI fails.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The ASIP is a channel adapter in the sense of REQ-44. The source decides with its own PDP. The source needs no ASI-specific logic.
  • The source sees only the ASIP. The ASIP passes nothing about the QTSP into the chain, and it writes no LDV record. A citizen cannot see which QTSP verified data (F-87).
  • Rule ASI0001 checks the actor, the service, and the field list. It also checks that the subject is a BSN, and not a placeholder. The rule does not check the token or the QTSP. The BSN is in the PDP input and in the decision log (REQ-60, ADR-0043).
  • EUDI issuance does not replace retrieve, because the QTSP issues the QEAA, and GBO does not.
  • QTSP admission depends on a register and on access certificates that do not exist on November 2, 2026. The demo uses a register file and test certificates (F-85).
  • If a QTSP needs attributes of two sources, it authorizes twice (ADR-0038).
  • The conformance matrix of v0.9.0 has 55 passed, 4 stub, 21 not applicable, and 1 failing. The failing item is REQ-ASIP-6.1.1.1-10-01: fuzzy matching asks for the value, and the ASIP returns none (F-92, Q-29).
  • The route runs locally only. ICTU/GBO-demo#594 tracks a deployment to the simulation environment with an external QTSP.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
The decision considered four other options:

  • Skip retrieve, as ADR-0029 proposed. Not chosen. A QTSP needs the value to issue a QEAA. The EUDI issuance chain does not replace that, because the QTSP issues the attestation, and GBO does not.
  • Make the QTSP an FSC participant. Not chosen. QTSPs are EU parties with access certificates and register entitlements. Clause 6.1 is HTTPS with OAuth.
  • Admit the QTSP in the PDP of the source (a Trusted List check as a rule). Not chosen. The PDP sees only the FSC actor. Admission belongs where the token is issued.
  • Offer clause 6.2 (ISO 15000) as well. Not in demo v0.9.0: Q-64 holds this point open.

docs.title: Security profile of the authorization server
docs.text:
The security profile is open (Q-66). ETSI leaves the profile open and conflicts with FAPI 2.0 on PAR and RS256 (F-84, E8).

The demo uses private_key_jwt and DPoP. It has no mTLS client authentication, no PAR, and no refresh tokens. The authorization server signs with ES256. The ASIP also accepts RS256, because RFC 9068 requires it. security-considerations.md lists the demo choices.

These points of the profile are open:

  • The authorization response has no iss (RFC 9207). A QTSP that uses several ASIPs has no mix-up defense (F-96, E9).
  • Tokens stay valid for up to 10 minutes after the withdrawal of the entitlement (Q-41, E10).
  • If the register is unreachable during a re-check, the client stays active (Q-34).
  • Which identifier links the access certificate to the register entry (Q-35)?

docs.title: Citizen identification at the authorization server
docs.text:
Citizen identification is open (Q-36). The demo accepts two means:

  • The NL Wallet over OpenID4VP, through the nl-wallet verification_server. It asks only the PID attributes of its registration, and it requires a BSN in urn:eudi:pid:nl:1 (REQ-102). The trusted PID issuers are a fixed list, and not a trusted list. The verifier accepts a PID with an undetermined revocation status.
  • A DigiD mock (stub). DigiD supplies only the BSN (F-88).

These related points are open:

  • The NL PID has no place of birth, but the implementing regulation makes it mandatory (F-94).
  • The BSN is in plain text in the token, so the QTSP can read it (F-86, E7, ICTU/GBO-demo#595).
  • Nothing links the citizen who logs in at the QTSP to the citizen who logs in at the authorization server (F-93, Q-40, E6).
  • The same-device wallet login did not run on a phone in demo v0.9.0 (ICTU/GBO-demo#596).
  • P-05 decides which means are recognized at the correct assurance level.

docs.title: Role, legal basis, and registration
docs.text:
These points are open:

  • Who designates the ASI intermediary, and what is the role of GBO (Q-28, Q-37)? The PSA decision register holds this point as open decision B-14.
  • What is the legal basis to verify for private QTSPs, and does the ASIP return the value on a match (Q-29)?
  • Who registers the data services in the catalogue of attributes and the Discover Interface, and how does the contract name the authorization server (Q-31, Q-67, Q-39, F-91)?
  • How do requests on behalf of another person work (Q-65)?

docs.title: ADR-0038: One data service per authentic source, one token per data service
docs.text:
• Status: accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1569 article 9(4), as replaced by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1735 (the result names the body that is responsible for the authentic source), S11, P-10, P-13
  • Deliberation: F-89, and demo PR #529, PR #534, PR #535
  • Implemented in:
    • config/dataservices.json: the data services.
    • handler.go#L99-L105: the routes per data service.
    • main.go#L115-L125 and accesstoken.go#L148: the token audience per data service.
    • service.go#L201-L204: one resource at the authorization server.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
ETSI TS 119 478 lets a verify or retrieve response name one authentic source (authenticSource, REQ-ASIP-6.1.1.2-08 and REQ-ASIP-6.1.2.2-04). Article 9(4) requires that the result names the body that is responsible for that source. GBO offers one ASIP for several sources. For this reason, that ASIP must keep every request inside one source (F-89).

The token has the same problem. The citizen approves a request for one source (REQ-91). If the token is also valid at another source, the QTSP can verify data at a source that the citizen did not see. ETSI does not specify the reach of a token per data service.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The decision has four parts:

  1. An ASIP that serves several authentic sources offers one data service per source. Each data service has its own base URL (/<data service>/authsrc-api), its own contract, its own dataService records, and its own token audience (REQ-94, REQ-99).
  2. Every response names the ASIP (provider) and the one authentic source of the data service (authenticSource). Since step 5 of ICTU/GBO-demo#592, the legal name comes from the description of the source (ADR-0039). A data service without an authentic source is not possible.
  3. If an attribute belongs to another data service, the ASIP answers 404. The ASIP then asks no source.
  4. An authorization request names exactly one data service as resource (RFC 8707):
    • If the request has no resource, two, or an unknown one, the result is invalid_target.
    • The token has the base URL of that data service as aud.
    • The ASIP refuses a token for another data service with 401 (REQ-95).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• If a QTSP needs attributes of two sources, it authorizes twice. The citizen logs in twice.
  • The request page can name one source and its legal name (REQ-91).
  • Every data service needs its own records in the Data Service Directory. It is open who registers them (Q-67).
  • The demo has one data service: brp, with source rvig. A second data service exists only in unit tests.
  • The authorization server takes its list of data services from the configuration (AZSP_RESOURCES). It does not take the list from the source descriptions (ADR-0039, an open part of #592).
  • It is open whether an ASIP for several sources makes GBO an intermediary in the sense of article 9(4) (Q-37).

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
The decision considered three other options:

  • One endpoint for all sources that refuses requests across sources. Not chosen. With this option, the contract, the records, and the token audience do not show which source answers.
  • One authorization for several resources, with a token per resource (RFC 8707 §2.2). Not chosen. This option saves the citizen a login. But the request page then shows several sources at once, and ETSI clients do not expect that.
  • One token for several sources. Not chosen. With this option, the token is valid at a source that the citizen did not see.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-91, REQ-94, REQ-95, REQ-99
  • Findings: F-89 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-37, Q-67
  • Standards feedback: E3
  • Demo increments: SL-28

docs.title: ADR-0039: ASI attributes described by the source (asi capability in source metadata)
docs.text:
• Status: accepted, partly implemented. In demo v0.9.0, the authorization server takes its resource list from configuration (ICTU/GBO-demo#592 is open).
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: S10, S07, S11, P-10, P-02
  • Deliberation: Q-38, and demo ICTU/GBO-demo#592 steps 1 to 5, up to PR #624
  • Implemented in:
    • asiCapability in gbo-source-metadata-v1.schema.json#L95.
    • The attribute catalogue schemas/asi-attributes.json.
    • The mapping module services/asi-mapping.
    • The validation by the reconciler in source_registration.go#L396-L406.
    • The release snapshot in services/source-registry/asisnapshot.
    • The query per request in verification/service.go#L238-L268 and plan.go#L22-L35.
    • The BRP description in gbo-source-metadata.json#L204.
    • The rules in docs/source-onboarding.md#L391-L487.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
Per data service, the ASIP must know three things:

  • Which attributes the source offers.
  • Which source fields make each attribute.
  • How to ask for these fields.

The first demo ASIP had this knowledge in code, as a BRP adapter. That breaks REQ-64: a GBO component works only with the description that the source publishes itself. With the adapter, a new source needs a code change in the ASIP.

Q-38 named three options: code, GBO configuration, or a description that the source publishes. On October 27, the direction became the third option, with a "copy only" mapping. ETSI expects attribute identifiers and value schemas from the EU catalogue of attributes. That catalogue did not exist on November 2, 2026.

This ADR extends ADR-0016 from EUDI issuance to the ASIP.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The decision has seven parts:

  1. The source describes its attributes. Source metadata schema 1.1 adds the capability asi next to eudi. The capability holds these parts:
    • authentic_source: the legal name and country, used in responses and discovery records.
    • graphql: one query document that ends in ...Selected, the subject variable, and the result pointer.
    • attributes: per attribute identifier, the source fields per member of the value.
  2. GBO keeps the shape of each value. GBO keeps a value_schema per attribute identifier in schemas/asi-attributes.json, until the EU catalogue of attributes provides it. The identifiers are provisional. The value schemas use only type, properties, required, items, and format.

  3. The source composes values with four operations. Each member of a value has exactly one operation:

    • pointer: copy a field.
    • join with separator: concatenate fields.
    • const: a fixed value.
    • each with pointer: per list element.

    Pointers are RFC 6901 JSON Pointers over GraphQL field names. This part deviates from the "copy only" direction of October 27. A source cannot always deliver a catalogue value with a copy only. An example is a house number made of three BRP fields.

  4. gbo-simple-v1 stays for the eudi capability only (ADR-0017). The two capabilities have different targets. The eudi target is wallet claims that the source defines. The asi target is values that the catalogue of GBO defines.

  5. The reconciler validates, and the ASIP reads the active release. The reconciler validates asi against the catalogue, as part of the source metadata (ADR-0016). If asi is invalid, the reconciler refuses the whole source. The ASIP reads the active release from the source registry every 5 seconds, with the reader role.
  6. One query per request. The ASIP replaces ...Selected with only the fields of the requested attributes and fragments (REQ-92). If the description does not name an attribute, the ASIP answers 404 and does not ask the source.
  7. Fuzzy matching follows the value schema. A string with a format, such as a date, matches exactly or does not match. Only strings without a format get MatchWithVariation (REQ-113).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A new source for the ASIP needs a description and a configured data service. It needs no code. The discovery records and the legal name of the source follow the description without a restart.
  • If no current description exists (absent, without asi, or stale), the ASIP answers 503 for verify, retrieve, and discovery (REQ-93).
  • A source with asi gets release snapshot version 4.0. A source without asi stays at 3.0. Onboarding still refuses a document with only asi, because onboarding requires the issuance certificate sets.
  • Onboarding validates the form only. It does not validate against the GraphQL schema of the source. It also does not check whether the policy of the source allows the selection. A difference shows at the first request. A demo test holds the BRP description against rule ASI0001.
  • The ASIP still normalizes a code without a format, such as a nationality or a postal code. For codes, demo v0.9.0 does not meet REQ-113 (Q-70).
  • The shape of name and address is provisional (Q-71).

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
These points are open:

  • The authorization server takes its data services from AZSP_RESOURCES (main.go#L105), and not from the descriptions. This is the open part of ICTU/GBO-demo#592.
  • The identifiers and value schemas move to the EU catalogue of attributes when it exists (Q-31).
  • Which normalization applies per kind of value (Q-70)?
  • The document format is part of the open PSA S10 decision on the source-specific configuration (ADR-0016).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-64, REQ-84, REQ-92, REQ-93, REQ-94, REQ-113, REQ-115
  • Findings: F-57 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-31, Q-38, Q-70, Q-71
  • Demo increments: SL-28, SL-46

docs.title: ADR-0040: Citizen recognition and the BSNk participant: route D
docs.text:
• Status: proposed (waits for Q-49)
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: S01, S02, S03, P-04
  • Deliberation: Open design choice: how does the register find the citizen again?, route D, routes A, B and C, F-75, F-98, and demo PR #469
  • Implemented in: demo, provisionally:
    • subjectref.go: the HMAC reference.
    • portal.go: one activation per citizen.
    • polymorphic.go: PI and PP stored under the reference.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
The consent facility (toestemmingsvoorziening) needs two things from a citizen who logged in:

  1. A stable key for its own administration. With this key, the service shows and revokes the consents of the citizen without a BSN (REQ-20, REQ-40).
  2. A PI and a PP. With these, the service makes the values for the parties at a new consent (BSNK-03).

A stored PI or PP is not a stable key. BSNk gives other values at every activation, and the service cannot compute these values from a BSN. Every activation goes into the BSNk access register (Inzageregister) (BSNK-10). Only a recognized BSNk participant can activate and transform (BSNK-01).

Two points are open (Q-49):

  • Are the consent register (toestemmingsregister) and the consent portal (toestemmingsportaal) backend one system?
  • Which of them is the BSNk participant?

The working assumption puts the BSNk calls at the register. The demo puts them at the backend. The TO removed the earlier requirement on this point (REQ-22) until a decision on Q-49.

docs.title: Proposed decision
docs.text:
The proposal is route D, under the working assumption that MijnOverheid passes the BSN:

  • The consent facility recognizes the citizen by an HMAC of the BSN, with a secret, versioned key:
    • The key is in an HSM or KMS.
    • The input has a fixed prefix and nine digits with leading zeros.
    • The result is at least 128 bits.
    • Every record keeps the key version.
  • At the first consent, the service activates once at BSNk. It stores PI and PP under that reference. At a later consent, the service only lets BSNk transform values.
  • To show and revoke consents, the service needs no BSNk call.

In the demo, the portal backend derives the reference and activates. The register stores PI and PP. This split fits only if both are one BSNk participant (Q-49).

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
BSNk preconditions describes the routes in full. The design weighed four options:

  1. Route D: an own pseudonym from the BSN (proposed). BSNk is necessary only at the first activation. The route needs the BSN from MijnOverheid and a legal basis (grondslag) for the register.
  2. Route A: an own pseudonym through BSNk. The service activates and transforms at every login, also to show consents. Every login goes into the access register.
  3. Route B: a pseudonym through the login. MijnOverheid passes a VP for the register. The route depends on DigiD and MijnOverheid.
  4. Route C: a reference from MijnOverheid. MijnOverheid must have such a reference and must be allowed to pass it on.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The register stores PI and PP. It stores no BSN and no value per party (REQ-69, REQ-23). This deviates on purpose from FR-35, criterion 1 (F-98).
  • The service processes the BSN briefly at every login, and that needs a legal basis. For every BSN, the service can compute whether consents exist, without a trace elsewhere.
  • The secret key is the whole protection. Without the key, anyone can compute every reference back from the small BSN space.
  • A new key gives every citizen a new reference. A migration of existing records is not built (Q-56).
  • The consent facility must become a recognized BSNk participant (F-75, Q-26).

These points are open:

  • Q-49: one system, and which participant.
  • Q-50: how the backend gets the verified identity.
  • Q-57: the protection of the stored PI and PP.
  • Q-58: does the register authenticate the backend?
  • Q-63: retention.

When Q-49 has a decision, this ADR becomes accepted, or another route replaces it.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-20, REQ-23, REQ-24, REQ-40, REQ-69, BSNK-01, BSNK-02, BSNK-03, BSNK-10
  • Findings: F-75 (open), F-98 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-26 (open), Q-49 (open), Q-50 (open), Q-56 (open), Q-57 (open), Q-58 (open), Q-63 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-51 (done)

docs.title: ADR-0041: Seal format of ASI results
docs.text:
• Status: proposed (waits for Q-32)
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1569 article 9(4), as replaced by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1735, from January 1, 2027, and S11
  • Deliberation: REQ-83, F-80, and demo ICTU/GBO-demo#498, PR #499
  • Implemented in: demo grade, with a development certificate:
    • The seal in seal.go#L18-L57.
    • The seal on successful responses only, in handler.go#L402-L417.
    • The header in the contract, in completions.json#L25-L33.
    • The validation by the reference QTSP, in qtsp-reference/internal/seal/seal.go.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
From January 1, 2027, every verification result of an ASIP must be signed or sealed. The seal is at least an advanced electronic seal based on a qualified certificate. The certificate belongs to the responsible public sector body or to the designated intermediary (F-80). ETSI TS 119 478 defines no seal on the response (E4).

A QTSP that verifies at several ASIPs must validate every seal in the same way. If each ASIP chooses its own format, every QTSP must implement each format. For this reason, the format is an interface agreement. It is not a choice per ASIP (REQ-83). Q-32 asks who decides the format. This ADR stays proposed until that decision.

docs.title: Proposed decision
docs.text:
The proposal has five parts:

  1. The ASIP seals the exact response body with a detached JWS (RFC 7515, Appendix F). The JWS goes in the header X-JWS-Signature (<protected header>..<signature>).
  2. The algorithm is ES256. The protected header carries the certificate chain in x5c, leaf first.
  3. The body stays plain JSON, as the ETSI OpenAPI prescribes. The contract of the data service names the header as an addition.
  4. The ASIP seals every successful verify and retrieve response (200). An error response is not a verification result and gets no seal.
  5. The QTSP validates the signature over the received body, and the chain against its trust anchors. The QTSP does not accept a result without a valid seal.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• With only the response and the trusted lists, the QTSP can establish that the response comes unchanged from this ASIP.
  • The format works with any HTTP client. It leaves the ETSI response schema unchanged.
  • The demo seals with a development certificate. Production needs a qualified certificate for electronic seals (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1943, Annex II). The certificate has the registration number of the organization as organizationIdentifier.
  • It is open who holds that certificate: the bronhouder, or the designated intermediary (Q-17, Q-28).

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
• A detached JWS in a header (proposed). It is simple for a JSON API. The body stays as ETSI specifies.
  • A JAdES baseline signature (ETSI TS 119 182-1). This is the EU format for JSON signatures, with the signing time and the certificate references in the header. It is more work for the QTSP and the ASIP, but it is closer to the eIDAS ecosystem.
  • An enveloping JWS, with the result as the JWS payload. This option changes the response form that the ETSI OpenAPI prescribes.

docs.title: Open points
docs.text:
These points are open:

  • Who decides the format for all Dutch ASIPs, and does ETSI ESI add it to TS 119 478 (Q-32, E4)?
  • Does every source response get one seal, regardless of the channel (DvTP, EUDI, ASI) (Q-75)?

docs.title: ADR-0042: Optional per-attribute token binding for ASI tokens
docs.text:
• Status: proposed (waits for Q-33)
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1569 article 9(5) (a member state can impose access control), S11, P-02
  • Deliberation: REQ-103, F-95, and demo PR #559, ICTU/GBO-demo#571, PR #572
  • Implemented in:
    • The check at the authorization server in authorization_details.go#L31-L79.
    • The request page in pages.go#L109-L111.
    • The token in tokens.go#L70-L72.
    • The mandatory switch in main.go#L109.
    • The check at the ASIP in accesstoken.go#L177-L197 and handler.go#L346-L356.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text: ETSI TS 119 478 clause 6.1.3.2 binds an access token per operation only (verify, retrieve). With one token, the QTSP can ask every attribute of the data service, also when the citizen approved something else (F-95, E5). Article 9(5) of Implementing Regulation 2025/1569 lets a member state impose access control. Q-33 asks whether the Netherlands imposes a binding per attribute. This ADR stays proposed until that decision.

docs.title: Proposed decision
docs.text:
The proposal has four parts:

  1. A QTSP can name the attributes in the authorization request as one RFC 9396 authorization_details entry. The entry has the provisional type https://gbo.example/authorization-details/authentic-source-attributes. The entry has these fields:
    • locations, equal to resource.
    • actions, equal to the scope.
    • attribute_identifiers, with 1 to 50 unique https URIs.
  2. The authorization server validates the entry against the data service and the scope. It refuses an invalid entry with invalid_request. It shows the attributes on the request page and puts the entry unchanged in the token.
  3. If the token carries the entry, the ASIP refuses a request for another attribute with 401 insufficient_scope.
  4. By default, the binding is optional, so a QTSP that implements only ETSI can connect. Without the entry, the authorization is per operation, and the description of the data service is the limit. A configuration switch makes the entry mandatory (AZSP_REQUIRE_AUTHORIZATION_DETAILS=true in the demo).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• With the binding, the citizen sees exactly which attributes the QTSP asks (REQ-91). The token is not valid for other attributes.
  • Only parties that know the GBO type can use the binding. The type identifier is provisional.
  • If the Netherlands makes the binding mandatory, QTSPs that implement only ETSI cannot connect. This stays so until ETSI or a national profile defines the extension.

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
The proposal considered three other options:

  • A binding per operation only, as ETSI specifies. This option is simpler for QTSPs, but the token is wider than the approval.
  • A mandatory binding per attribute. This option is closer to P-02. But it excludes QTSPs that implement only ETSI, until the extension is standard.
  • Attributes in the scope string. Not chosen. ETSI fixes the scopes, and RFC 9396 is the standard place for structured detail.

  • Open questions: Q-33
  • Standards feedback: E5
  • Demo increments: SL-28

docs.title: ADR-0043: Keep identifiers out of the PDP input instead of masking decision logs
docs.text:
• Status: proposed (waits for demo #368)
  • Date: 2026-11-02
  • Satisfies: P-04, P-02, S09
  • Deliberation: REQ-60, F-54, and demo #149, #364, #368, CHANGELOG
  • Implemented in: not implemented. The plain BSN enters the PDP input at eudi-adapter source_metadata.go and asi-provider graphqlsource/source.go.

docs.title: Context and problem statement
docs.text:
Logging must hold no BSN that the processing does not need (REQ-60). Two decision logs record the PDP input: the ADL and the console decision log (ADR-0036). The routes differ:

  • In the consent route, the PDP input holds a placeholder and no identifier (ADR-0032). This route meets the requirement.
  • In the EUDI and ASI routes, the query variables hold the plain BSN from the PID or the token. As a result, both decision logs hold the BSN.

Masking in the policy engine had no effect (F-54). The demo then kept the BSN out through the construction of the input: the request mapper pseudonymized the BSN through BSNk. The demo removed that step when the mapper became a pure mapper (#364). The demo accepts the BSN in both logs until #368 decides between masking and "transform first".

docs.title: Proposed decision
docs.text:
The proposal has three parts:

  • A component that builds PDP input leaves out or replaces every identifying value that the decision does not need.
  • If the component cannot do that, the request does not continue.
  • Masking in the engine or in the log pipeline is a second line only, with a continuous test on the real log output.

docs.title: Why proposed, not accepted
docs.text: In demo v0.9.0, the input side gives no guarantee. If the team picks masking in #368, REQ-60 must change, because it says "never rely only on masking".

docs.title: Considered options
docs.text:
1. Keep identifiers out of the input (proposed). The PDP never receives the value, so no log can hold it.
  2. Mask the decision logs. The value still reaches the engine. A change in the log shape can leak the value again without notice, as F-54 showed.
  3. Transform the BSN to a pseudonym before the PDP, as the earlier mapper did. This option needs a BSNk call in the decision path, and no rule reads the result.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• If the proposal is accepted, the EUDI adapter and the ASIP must build their PDP input without the BSN. The source still needs the BSN after the allow. For this reason, the value must reach the source another way, as in the consent route (ADR-0033).
  • LDV records never hold a BSN. The logbook refuses any record with a run of nine digits that passes the BSN checksum (elfproef) (ADR-0026). This ADR covers the decision logs only.
  • Until a decision on #368, the BSN in the EUDI and ASI decision logs is a known risk (Risks and technical debt).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-60, REQ-71, REQ-20
  • Findings: F-54 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-08 (open)
  • Demo increments: SL-29 (done)

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
A requirement in this technical design is a testable demand on what GBO builds, or on the interfaces between GBO and other parties. It follows from the design (GO, PSA, FR-DvTP), or the GBO team derived it from building the demo. Each requirement states where it comes from.

The arc42 sections explain the design, and the architecture decisions record the choices. A requirement states the need that a section or a decision serves. Each arc42 page and each ADR ends with a traceability footer. The footer lists the requirements that the page explains or depends on. The traceability pages link requirements to findings, open questions, and demo increments.

docs.title: When something is a requirement
docs.text:
A REQ-NN counts as a requirement only with these four properties:

  1. Testable: MUST, MAY, or MUST NOT, with a result that you can observe.
  2. Sourced: it names the passage in the design that it follows from. For a requirement derived from the demo, the source is the principle or capability that it serves, with one sentence about the reason.
  3. Addressed: it is addressed to a component that GBO delivers, or to an interface agreement (see Addressee).
  4. A need: it describes the need and does not describe the chosen solution.

The test for a derived requirement is one question: which principle or capability breaks without this requirement? If there is no answer, it is no requirement.

docs.title: What is not a requirement
docs.text:
Three levels of items are no requirements, and each level lands in its own place:

Level Example Where it lands Demo glue mocks, seeds, provisioning, the fake DigiD nowhere Implementation detail a switch, a design pattern, a library in the code Design decision never cache the status, or keep keys for at most five minutes an ADR, or a note on the requirement that it serves

Need or decision: ask can another solution meet the same need? If yes, the need is the requirement, and the chosen solution is a design decision.

When a design decision becomes an ADR: a design decision becomes an ADR only if all three conditions apply:

  • There were real alternatives.
  • Going back is expensive (an interface, a data model, or another party).
  • Someone outside the team must know about it or agree to it.

If not, the decision is a note "design choice" on the requirement that it serves. Related choices go into one ADR. The ADRs are in Architecture decisions.

docs.title: Entry format
docs.text:
Each requirement entry has this format:

## REQ-NN — Title as a statement {#req-nn}

> The [component] MUST [testable demand].

| Case | Outcome |        (optional: what must hold, with the deny reason)
|---|---|

- **Source**: design — PSA S04, FR-34 criterion 1
             or: derived — serves PSA S01: why, in one sentence
- **Addressee**: GBO-delivered component | interface agreement | guideline for bronhouders
- **Evidence**: demo issue or PR, with a permalink to the test or the code;
               or: not built — issue
- **Related**: links only (REQ, F, Q, ADR)
- **Notes**: only what a builder needs; an open point as a link to the Q
- **Status**: draft | ready for review | approved | covered | withdrawn

The fields have these rules:

  • Source: the value is design if the design already states or sharpens the requirement. The value is derived if the requirement comes from the demo. PSA and GO links go to the published site. FR-DvTP criteria are named without a link until the FRs are public. The archived reference architecture (v0.6.2) is no longer a source. The PSA passage replaces it.
  • Evidence: the place where the demo tests the requirement: an issue or PR in gbo-demo, and a permalink to the test or the code. Later, test tags with coverage from CI will replace this field.
  • Related: only references that work as links.
  • Notes: limits, design choices, and open points. No history: the page describes the design as it is.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
An entry has one of these statuses:

Status Meaning draft written by the analysis team ready for review meets this norm approved accepted in the review with the tech lead covered a test shows the requirement withdrawn an approved requirement that no longer applies. It stays, with the reason and the successor, because others can refer to it candidate a connection condition (AV) that is proposed and not set

If a requirement was never approved and no longer holds, the GBO team removes it and does not withdraw it. Nobody uses its number again. For more information, see Removed numbers.

docs.title: Addressee: a MUST is only about what GBO builds
docs.text:
The system is federative (Q-02), and P-10 puts the bronhouder in control. So a requirement that prescribes how a bronhouder configures its own PDP, PAP, or policy engine is no requirement. Nobody can enforce it in practice. Each requirement names its addressee:

  • GBO-delivered component: software that GBO builds and delivers as a generic component or reference implementation. A MUST applies, because it is a demand on an artifact of GBO itself. Delivery does not mean operation: most of these components run at the source (behind the Inway: PEP and PDP, adapters, request mappers, gateways). The requirement binds the GBO build. It does not limit the freedom of a source to choose something else.
  • Interface agreement: behavior at the outside that every participant must deliver, because it follows from system or legal demands. For example, you can trace which policy version a decision used. A MUST applies, but only to the observable result. It never applies to the internal configuration or the product.
  • Guideline for bronhouders: the internal configuration at a source. At most SHOULD, with the reason, or a selection criterion for a product.

Three other namespaces hold what is not a requirement on GBO:

  • RL-NN: guidelines for bronhouders, on Policy management. Matrix and findings can refer to them like a requirement, without the suggestion that they are one. Each guideline has a promotion rule: the open question that must be answered before it can become a requirement.
  • AV-NN: candidate connection conditions, obligations for other participants, on Connection conditions.
  • BSNK-NN: preconditions that BSNk PP, an external facility, imposes on GBO, on BSNk preconditions.

If you write a requirement, do two checks:

  1. Does the MUST sentence name a product or an implementation form that GBO does not deliver? If so, reword the sentence to the role (PAP, PDP, management API), and change the addressee. The use of a product in the demo is a demo choice. It belongs in the evidence.
  2. Does the requirement assume that GBO runs something? That is almost never certain. It is open which facilities are really central (Q-10, Q-02). The demo runs everything in one stack, and that proves nothing about it. Write the requirement on the artifact or on the interface.

docs.title: Organization of the pages
docs.text: Topic pages are grouped by channel, as in the building block view: GBO Basis (needed for every channel), DvTP, and EUDI. A requirement that belongs to one channel only is on a topic page of that channel. If a requirement moves to another page, its number does not change.

docs.title: Removed numbers
docs.text:
If a requirement was never approved and no longer holds, the GBO team removes it. Nobody uses its number again. Topic pages list their own removed numbers with the reason. Each removed number has a disposition and, where one exists, a successor:

Number Disposition Successor REQ-01 removed — REQ-02 merged into REQ-61 REQ-03 removed — REQ-05 merged into REQ-48 REQ-07 removed — REQ-09 merged into REQ-17 REQ-13 removed REQ-68, REQ-18 REQ-15 merged into REQ-79 REQ-16 merged into REQ-55 REQ-22 removed pending Q-49 REQ-25 removed REQ-79, REQ-17 REQ-26 removed REQ-79, REQ-17 REQ-27 removed REQ-79, REQ-17 REQ-28 merged into REQ-55 REQ-29 merged into REQ-60 REQ-30 never used — REQ-31 merged into REQ-71 REQ-33 removed — REQ-34 removed — REQ-35 merged into REQ-40 REQ-36 removed — REQ-41 merged into REQ-14 REQ-43 removed — REQ-47 removed — REQ-49 removed — REQ-50 merged into REQ-18 REQ-51 removed REQ-44, REQ-64 REQ-52 removed a design decision, not a requirement (see F-35) REQ-53 removed REQ-20, REQ-21 (and F-30, F-37) REQ-54 merged into REQ-55 REQ-56 removed REQ-74 (partly) REQ-70 removed — REQ-73 removed AV-01 REQ-96 merged into REQ-91 REQ-98 removed REQ-48, REQ-74, REQ-97, REQ-79, REQ-17 REQ-104 removed REQ-88 (a duty of the QTSP under ETSI and eIDAS) REQ-105 removed REQ-88 (a duty of the QTSP under ETSI and eIDAS)

docs.title: Admission and connection requirements
docs.text:
These requirements cover who can connect to a source. The first part holds requirements on the admission register (toelatingsregister) and the contract decision. The second part holds candidate connection conditions for the parties that connect. For the design, see Admission of parties.

This page has the following parts:

  • Admission register and contracts
  • Connection conditions (candidates)

docs.title: Admission register and contracts
docs.text:
The admission requirements cover the step before a request. They answer three questions: can this party connect, to which bronhouder, and who decides that. The requirements are generic. They apply to every party that connects through FSC: in DvTP, EUDI issuance, and the ASI route. Authorization covers the authorization of one request.

Admission is a registration and is not a policy rule. An automatic "no" stays reversible (F-55). The contract proposal that the PDP judges is thin. It tells who connects, but it does not tell to what (F-56). The governance side (who runs the register, and which legal protection a refused party has) is in Q-22. The design decision is ADR 0015.

docs.title: REQ-61: Admission comes from a register and not from decision policy
docs.text:
The admission of a participant MUST come from a participant register that the PDP consults as an information source. Admission covers whether a party is allowed to connect, to which bronhouder, and whether that admission is active. If a party is not actively admitted there to the bronhouder, it MUST NOT get a new contract. It MUST be possible to add, suspend, extend, or withdraw an admission without a change of decision policy and without a restart of the PDP. The reference policy MAY co-sign only for grants that the admission decision covers. These grants are a service connection, or a delegated service connection with a registered representation (REQ-106).

Case Outcome Party actively admitted to this bronhouder contract co-signed Party not in the register refused: PARTY_NOT_IN_REGISTRY Party suspended refused: PARTY_NOT_ACTIVE Party admitted, but not to this bronhouder refused: SOURCE_NOT_ALLOWED Register gives no data refused: ADMISSION_REGISTER_UNAVAILABLE Proposal with another kind of grant, with both kinds at the same time, or without a grant refused: GRANT_TYPE_NOT_ALLOWED. The proposal stays pending (code)
  • Status: ready for review
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: design:
    • PSA S04 (participation needs a prior admission decision, "deelname vereist een voorafgaande toelatingsbeslissing", and the facility is a participant register, "deelnemersregister").
    • PSA S05 (the PDP consults the participant status, among other sources).
    • FR-30 criteria 1 and 2, and FR-16 criterion 2.
    • P-16.
  • Addressee: GBO-delivered component: the admission register, its link to the PDP, and the reference policy for co-signing.
  • Evidence: PR #239, PR #228. Code and tests:
    • The register and the PIP link.
    • The refusals are in autosign.rego#L166-L175, tested in autosign_test.rego#L126-L141.
    • PR #579: the policy tells a missing register apart from an empty register in autosign.rego#L50-L52, tested in autosign_test.rego#L86-L99.
  • Related: REQ-62, REQ-106, REQ-110, F-55, Q-22, Q-68, ADR 0015.
  • Notes:
    • The register uses the FSC Peer ID as key. It is thin: name, active, admitted sources, and mandates.
    • The register has no accounts. Whoever can reach the management interface locally is administrator.
    • Production needs administrator authentication and a shielded or mTLS-protected pull endpoint. The form of the data does not change for that.
    • The register deactivates a participant and does not delete it.
    • The pull replaces entities but does not remove them. So a record that disappears leaves the old admission in place.

docs.title: REQ-62: The admission decision on a contract is its own rule set, separate from request policy
docs.text:
A separate rule set MUST decide whether a contract proposal gets a co-signature. This rule set MUST stay apart from the policy that decides on single requests. The two MUST NOT share rules or deny reasons. They MAY read the same admission data from the register.

  • Status: ready for review
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: design. PSA S04 (the setup handles technical identity and admission status apart from the role and authority in one interaction: "de inrichting behandelt technische identiteit en toelatingsstatus apart van de rol en bevoegdheid in een concrete interactie").
  • Addressee: GBO-delivered component: the reference policy.
  • Evidence: PR #228. The rule set is its own package without an import, in autosign.rego#L1-L10. The request policy reads the same register for the mandate in engine.rego#L253-L267 (PR #464).
  • Related: REQ-61, REQ-106, F-52, F-55, F-56, ADR 0015.
  • Notes:
    • Design choice: the contract decision runs as an AuthZEN evaluation through the same PDP as the requests (fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml#L701, #L773). So both decisions are in the same decision log.
    • The FSC Manager selects the policy on doelbinding = "auto_sign_contract". A renamed package switches the policy off without a signal, and every contract stays pending (F-52).
    • The proposal names no service and no direction of delegation. So the decision is about who connects. It does not cover what the party connects to (F-56).

docs.title: REQ-63: An automated refusal of a contract proposal is recoverable
docs.text:
An automated negative decision on a contract proposal MUST leave the proposal pending. A final refusal MUST be a separate, deliberate action. After a correction of the admission data, the submitting party MUST be able to submit again without an action of the other party. The new submission MUST get a new assessment.

Case Outcome Policy refuses the proposal the proposal stays pending, no co-signature Admission corrected, proposal submitted again new assessment, co-signed if allowed
  • Status: draft
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: derived. The requirement serves P-16 and PSA S04. An automatic "no" that nobody can correct turns an error in the register into an exclusion.
  • Addressee: interface agreement: the observable behavior of the admission process.
  • Evidence: PR #228, tested by hand. The co-signature follows only on allow, in autosign.rego#L3-L5. No automated test.
  • Related: REQ-61, F-55, Q-22, ADR 0015.
  • Notes: in the FSC Manager in use, this is product behavior. A refusal by the PDP leaves the proposal at proposed. A new submission is a new proposal with a new contract hash. So the requirement binds the configuration: do not configure an automatic refusal. Q-22 covers the procedural side (reasons, objection).

docs.title: REQ-110: A suspended or departed consumer gets no more data, even with a valid consent
docs.text:
If a consumer is suspended or terminated, it MUST receive no more data within a set period, even with a valid consent. A suspension or termination MUST NOT change any consent. After a suspension ends, the existing consents MUST be usable again.

Case Outcome Active consumer, valid consent allowed Consumer suspended denied within the period, consent unchanged Suspension ended allowed again, without a new consent Consumer terminated denied Consent expires during the suspension expires as always
  • Status: draft
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: design. PSA S04 (a suspension or termination leads in time to a withdrawal of access: "schorsing of beëindiging leidt tijdig tot intrekking van de toegang"), made stricter: the consent does not change. Also FR-31 criterion 2 and FR-36 criterion 4.
  • Addressee: interface agreement between source and management organization: who closes the access, and how fast. The consent function does not need to do anything.
  • Evidence: not built. The demo issue follows after Q-53. Partly built: a suspended party gets no new contract (autosign.rego#L172). At a request, the policy checks only the status of an integrator (engine.rego#L263). So a suspended consumer with an existing contract can still call the source.
  • Related: REQ-61, REQ-106, REQ-123, Q-53.
  • Notes:
    • The requirement fixes the effect and leaves the mechanism open. A status check at every request meets it, and so does the withdrawal of the FSC contract. With the withdrawal, an issued access token stays valid until it expires. A new contract is then necessary after the suspension ends. The deny reason depends on the mechanism (Q-53).
    • In the demo, a status change in the register reaches the PDP within the pull interval of 5 s (dvtp-onboarding.yaml#L9).
    • A suspension or departure does not revoke the consents. The citizen sees them as active (shown as "Actief") while the party cannot use them.
    • A consumer with a new OIN is a new party. Old consents become unusable and do not move to the new party.
    • New consent requests of a suspended consumer belong to the check of the initiator (ICTU/GBO-demo#427).

docs.title: REQ-123: Every change to an admission, mandate, or activation is traceable
docs.text:
A GBO-delivered component that records who is allowed to take part, or what is in use, MUST record every change of that data. The record MUST hold who made the change, when it took effect, what changed, and the value before and after. This covers the admission register (admissions and mandates), the activation of sources in issuance, and the client registration of the ASI authorization server. A change MUST be possible only for an authenticated, authorized administrator, or for a check that the component runs itself. The component MUST protect the record in the same way as the audit records of REQ-32.

Case Outcome Administrator suspends a party record: administrator, moment, active → suspended Change without an authenticated, authorized administrator refused, nothing changed Client deactivated after a re-check (REQ-89) record with the re-check as actor Source activated or rolled back (REQ-65, REQ-66) record with the version before and after
  • Status: draft
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: design:
    • PSA S09 (each component records the events that are relevant to its responsibility, and measures protect log data against unauthorized change and deletion: "iedere component legt de gebeurtenissen vast die voor zijn verantwoordelijkheid relevant zijn", "maatregelen beschermen loggegevens tegen ongeautoriseerde wijziging en verwijdering").
    • PSA S04 (a suspension or termination leads in time to a withdrawal of access: "schorsing of beëindiging leidt tijdig tot intrekking van de toegang").
    • D-11 (management rights are limited, temporary, and provably granted: "beheerrechten zijn beperkt, tijdelijk en aantoonbaar toegekend").
    • P-12.
  • Addressee: GBO-delivered component: the admission register, the activation in the EUDI adapter, and the authorization server of the ASI.
  • Evidence: not built. The register has no accounts (notes of REQ-61).
  • Related: REQ-61, REQ-110, REQ-65, REQ-66, REQ-88, REQ-89, REQ-32, Q-53, Q-74.
  • Notes:
    • These records are data about organizations. They are no LDV processing of a data subject.
    • How the administrator authenticates is a choice of the configuration. The requirement asks only that a change can be attributed to an authorized person or to a check.
    • The component does not delete a record (REQ-61: deactivate, do not delete).
    • Without this record, nobody can test REQ-110 ("within a set period"), because nobody knows when a suspension took effect.

docs.title: Connection conditions (candidates)
docs.text:
The demo asks participants for certain behavior to make the chain work. The TO records these demands as candidate connection conditions (AV-NN). They cover every channel: GBO Basis, DvTP, and EUDI. None of them is an approved condition.

PSA S04 names connection conditions per participant group ("aansluitvoorwaarden per deelnemersgroep") as an agreement that is still open. FR-30 lets the operator of the DvTP facility check selection criteria and connection conditions. The framework falls under PSA open decision B-09.

docs.title: Why the items are candidates and not requirements
docs.text:
A connection condition puts an obligation on a party that is not GBO. The management organization sets the condition. GBO does not. For that reason, each item is a candidate, written as SHOULD. Each candidate has its basis in the demo, the PSA, or the FR, as input for the decision. A candidate can refer to a requirement (REQ) that enforces the same behavior on the GBO side.

The connection conditions name three participant groups: private consumer, integrator, and bronhouder. Each channel puts its candidates on one of these groups:

Channel Obliged party Candidates All channels bronhouder AV-07 DvTP private consumer AV-01, AV-02, AV-03, AV-04, AV-05, AV-14, AV-15 DvTP integrator AV-06 DvTP bronhouder AV-09 EUDI bronhouder AV-08, AV-10, AV-11, AV-12, AV-13

docs.title: AV-01: Consumer sends trace context and records the transaction ID
docs.text:
A private consumer SHOULD send W3C Trace Context with every call to a source, and SHOULD record the Fsc-Transaction-Id.

  • Status: candidate, normative minimum according to S09
Source, evidence and notes
  • Obliged party: private consumer
  • Channel: DvTP
  • Source: PSA S09 (a request identifier across the whole chain) and Q-24. This candidate replaces the removed REQ-73.
  • Related: REQ-55

docs.title: AV-02: Consumer records its processing according to LDV
docs.text:
