A check of the proof by the gateway itself MUST NOT replace this restriction.

Case Outcome Request through the Inway of the source reaches the gateway, after the decision of the PDP Request from the network of a consumer, directly to the gateway not reachable Request from the host not reachable, because the gateway publishes no port
  • Status: ready for review
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: derived. The requirement serves PSA S05 ("iedere gegevensvraag doorloopt een PEP-PDP-keten") and PSA S03 ("de inrichting voert identiteitsvertaling alleen uit voor een toegestane dienst en gegevensvraag"). A party that reaches the gateway outside the PEP has a real proof converted without a decision. A consumer has such proofs.
  • Addressee: GBO-delivered component: the source gateway and the deployment that GBO delivers with it. Guideline for bronhouders: the isolation in their own network.
  • Evidence: PR #469 gives this evidence:
    • The gateways are only on a network with the Inways and on the source network. They publish no port (docker-compose.yml#L829-L836, #L881-L888, #L966-L973, #L1893-L1902).
    • Only the Inways of the sources are on that network (fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml#L744-L748, #L1840-L1844).
    • The gateway relies on the decision and does not check the proof itself (substitution.go#L105-L107).
    • A manual test showed that the gateway is not reachable from the consumer networks and from the host. The Inways can reach it. No automated test exists.
  • Related: REQ-04, REQ-21, REQ-68, REQ-80, F-79, ADR 0033.
  • Notes:
    • Design choice: the isolation is in the network, and the gateway has no own proof check. Such a check does not stop a consumer with a real proof.
    • The isolation exists only in compose. In Kubernetes, the isolation needs a NetworkPolicy or an equivalent.
    • Open point: bind the value to the consent for which it was made, with what BSNk offers in addition. Then the value is unusable under another proof. This binding is not built.
    • In the demo, the source services themselves publish a port for the GraphQL playground (docker-compose.yml#L613-L614). That port falls under REQ-04 and not under this requirement.

docs.title: REQ-82: When consent is given, the consent facility knows the OIN, the key version, and the BSN authorization of each source
docs.text:
Some sources need to find the citizen under a consent. When the consent is given, the consent facility MUST know the identification (OIN) of each of these sources. It MUST also know the current version of the keys of each source and its authorization to process the BSN. The consent facility MUST have a value made for each source, in the form that belongs to that authorization. If no value can be made for one of those sources, a consent MUST NOT be given. If it is not established at that moment which sources are allowed to process the BSN, a consent MUST NOT be given either.

Case Outcome Source on the BSN Authorization List a pseudonym and an identity Source not on the list only a pseudonym No source configured no consent, and BSNk is not called BSNk makes no value for a source no consent, and nothing is kept Copy of the list expired and cannot be renewed no consent
  • Status: draft
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: derived. The requirement serves PSA S03. Without the OIN, the key version, and the BSN authorization of every source, BSNk cannot make a value that the source can read. BSNk cannot make that value later either, because BSNk transforms only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04). Preconditions: BSNK-06, BSNK-07, and BSNK-08.
  • Addressee: GBO-delivered component: the consent portal (S02), which has the values made at BSNk.
  • Evidence: PR #469 and PR #477 give this evidence:
    • The sources come from the configuration (main.go#L153-L189).
    • Without a source, there is no consent (portal.go#L126-L128).
    • The form follows the authorization (portal.go#L197-L224).
    • The BSN Authorization List and its maximum age are in bsnk.go#L84-L100, portal.go#L226-L247, and main.go#L132-L135.
    • The tests are portal_test.go#L459-L491, #L493-L508, #L510-L548, #L550-L562, and #L639-L651.
  • Related: REQ-64, REQ-68, REQ-80, F-74, F-78, Q-26, Q-49.
  • Notes:
    • Design choice (stand-in): the sources are in the configuration of the portal (CONSENT_SOURCES=<OIN>@<key set version>). Every consent gets values for all configured sources, whatever the service.
    • In the target design, the sources come from a service catalog (dienstencatalogus) (ICTU/GBO-demo#382). The keys come from onboarding (ICTU/GBO-demo#467).
    • The mock gives the list without a validity period. So the portal uses its copy for a configurable time at most (BSN_AUTHORISATION_LIST_MAX_AGE), by default one hour. That period is an assumption. Q-26 sub-question 8 covers how the list is delivered.
    • BSNk takes at most four recipients per request (BSNK-05). The portal splits the request (bsnk.go#L102-L115).
    • The proof fixes parties and key versions for its whole life (F-78). If a source changes keys, it must keep the old keys as long as proofs for them are valid. The proof itself carries no version.
    • Q-49 covers who is the BSNk participant: the portal or the register.

docs.title: BSNk PP preconditions for the DvTP design
docs.text:
BSNk PP is the polymorphic pseudonymization of the BSN connection point. Logius runs it. BSNk PP sets preconditions for the DvTP design (ICTU/GBO-demo#364). In that design, the consent proof holds an encrypted value per party. The source decrypts its value itself, after the authorization decision.

This page also holds the analysis of how the consent facility recognizes a citizen at a later login (routes A, B, C, and D). That analysis is the basis of ADR 0040.

GBO does not set the preconditions. BSNk sets them for GBO. They follow from the specification of a provision that GBO does not own, and GBO cannot change them. For this reason, the preconditions have their own namespace, BSNK-NN, and no requirement status. Each entry states what the specification says, why BSNk does it so, and what it means for the design. If the "why" is a reading of the GBO team and not in the specification, the entry says so.

The main source is the BSNk technical specifications v11.2 (December 2025). In this page, "p. n" refers to a page in that document. Two documents describe the Logius decryption component: the Design Specification v1.2 and the Software Architecture Document v1.0. The GBO team wrote this page on September 30, 2026. The working assumptions date from October 5, 2026.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
The design starts from four working assumptions:

  • The design is the one of ICTU/GBO-demo#364.
  • The citizen logs in at MijnOverheid. The consent portal and the consent register are behind MijnOverheid.
  • After the login, MijnOverheid passes the BSN to the consent portal. The variant in which MijnOverheid passes the BSN encrypted for BSNk is part of the open design choice.
  • The consent register becomes a recognized BSNk participant and requests activation and transformation itself.

In the demo, the consent portal backend activates and transforms, and the register stores the polymorphic values. In the rest of this page, "the register" means the party that talks to BSNk. Which component that is, is open (Q-49).

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
The BSNk specification uses the terms in the following table:

Term Meaning Spec Participant (recognized party) A party in the authentication chain that, as the Minister of the Interior and Kingdom Relations (BZK) established, meets the requirements. The roles are Means Issuer (Middelenuitgever), Authentication Service (Authenticatiedienst), Authorization Service (Machtigingsdienst), Access Service (Toegangsdienst), and Key Requester p. 24, 34 Service provider (dienstverlener) Receives and decrypts. A service provider is not a Participant p. 38 Key Requester (Sleutelaanvrager) A Participant that requests the keys at BSNk for a service provider. It has no other role in login or connection p. 26, 37 Polymorphic identity (PI) An encrypted BSN that only the requester can have transformed. Nobody can decrypt the PI itself p. 25, 43 Polymorphic pseudonym (PP) The same as the PI, but it leads to a pseudonym instead of the BSN p. 43 Encrypted identity (VI) A PI transformed for one recipient. Only that recipient decrypts it, to the BSN. The English text says EI p. 29 Encrypted pseudonym (VP) A PP transformed for one recipient. Only that recipient decrypts it, to a pseudonym that is valid only for that recipient. The English text says EP p. 29 Activate Offer a BSN to BSNk and get a PI and PP for it p. 52 Transform Have BSNk convert a PI or PP to a VI or VP for a recipient p. 54 OIN Identifies the recipient. BSNk derives the keys and the pseudonym from it p. 23 BSN Authorization List A list of RvIG with the parties that are allowed to process the BSN. Logius publishes it per OIN as the technical BSN list ("Technische Lijst BSN") p. 17, 28

docs.title: The chain with the preconditions in it
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the basic setup, with the preconditions at each step:

sequenceDiagram box rgb(221,235,247) Citizen participant B as Citizen end box rgb(241,239,232) Portal participant MO as MijnOverheid end box rgb(254,220,216) DvTP participant TR as Consent register end box rgb(241,239,232) External participant K as BSNk participant A as Consumer end box rgb(221,235,247) Source participant BR as Source end B->>MO: logs in MO->>TR: BSN [BSNK-02] TR->>K: activate [BSNK-01, BSNK-02] K-->>TR: PI and PP of the register [BSNK-03] Note over K: activation goes into the inspection register [BSNK-10] B->>TR: gives consent for consumer and service Note over TR: per party: BSN-authorized? [BSNK-06]<br/>which key version? [BSNK-08] TR->>K: transform, citizen is logged in [BSNK-04, BSNK-05] K-->>TR: VI per source, optionally VP for the consumer TR-->>A: signed proof with the values per party A->>BR: request with placeholder and proof Note over BR: first the PDP, then decrypt<br/>with its own key [BSNK-07, BSNK-08, BSNK-09] BR-->>A: data

BSNk takes part only when the citizen gives consent. It has no part in the query. The open design choice covers how the register finds the citizen again at a later login, and whether it keeps the PI.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
BSNk sets 11 preconditions for the design, as listed in the following table:

ID Precondition Kind Status BSNK-01 Only a recognized party can activate and transform administrative fixed, recognition open BSNK-02 Activation needs the BSN and check data technical fixed, delivery to check BSNK-03 A PI belongs to the requester and nobody else technical fixed BSNK-04 Transformation is possible only while the citizen is logged in technical fixed, application to check BSNK-05 At most four recipients per request technical fixed BSNK-06 The BSN Authorization List sets BSN or pseudonym technical fixed BSNK-07 The recipient is an OIN technical fixed BSNK-08 An encrypted value belongs to one key version technical fixed BSNK-09 The recipient gets its keys through an Access Service or Key Requester technical fixed, who fills the role is open BSNK-10 The party that activates has the inspection duty technical fixed BSNK-11 The interfaces are SOAP with PKIoverheid technical fixed

"Fixed" means that the precondition follows directly from the specification.

docs.title: BSNK-01: Only a recognized party can activate and transform
docs.text:
BSNk accepts an activation only from a Means Issuer, an Authorization Service, or the eIDAS message service. It accepts a transformation only from those three or an Authentication Service.

  • Status: fixed, recognition open.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says:
    • BSNk opens the interfaces per role (p. 79, 132).
    • The certificate of the requester must contain its OIN and be in the metadata (p. 75 to 76).
    • A party must not deliver metadata for a role for which it is not recognized. In the test environment, a party can deliver metadata for a role for which it requested recognition (p. 213).
    • Participants must not contact or accept parties that are not in the metadata (p. 211).
  • Why: the metadata is the trust list of the chain. The GBO team reads it as follows: activation and transformation touch the BSN of every citizen, so BSNk admits only assessed parties.
  • Consequence for the design: BZK must recognize the register as a Means Issuer or an Authorization Service. Neither role is written for a consent facility. The specification names future roles, among them attribute services, but does not work them out (p. 34). After the register requests recognition, trials in the test environment are possible.
  • Related: F-75, Q-26, Q-49.
  • Kind: administrative (a decision of BZK).

docs.title: BSNK-02: Activation needs the BSN and check data
docs.text:
BSNk activates on a BSN. It does not activate on an existing polymorphic identity. BSNk checks the BSN with name and date of birth against the Personal Records Database (BRP).

  • Status: fixed, delivery to check.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says:
    • The input is a plain BSN, an encrypted BSN, or an encrypted identity (p. 93). An encrypted BSN can be encrypted directly at the source ("bij de bron al direct versleuteld", p. 53).
    • A BSN alone is not sufficient: check data must come with it. If a party does the identification itself, it goes on an exception list. Then BSNk checks only the BSN (p. 94).
    • The eIDAS message service is exempt, because its link with the BSN already rests on the BRP (p. 97).
    • After registration, the BSN must be erased (p. 44).
  • Why: "Only providing the BSN is not deemed to identify a subject with sufficient assurance" (p. 94). BSNk wants to be sure that the BSN belongs to this person.
  • Consequence for the design:
    • MijnOverheid passes the BSN. The register uses it for a short time and does not keep it (REQ-20, route D). It uses the BSN to derive its own key for the citizen, and to activate at the first consent.
    • The register activates once per citizen. After that, it only transforms.
    • If the register is not on the exception list, it must also send name and date of birth with that one activation. Then the register processes more data about the citizen than REQ-69 wants.
    • If MijnOverheid passes the BSN encrypted for BSNk, the register never sees the BSN. But then it also cannot recognize the citizen by it (routes A, B, and C).
  • To check:
    • Is MijnOverheid allowed to pass the BSN to the consent portal?
    • On which legal basis (grondslag) does the register process the BSN?
    • Can the register get on the exception list?
  • Kind: technical.

docs.title: BSNK-03: A PI belongs to the requester and nobody else
docs.text:
Only the register can have the PI and PP that it receives transformed.

  • Status: fixed.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says:
    • BSNk makes PI and PP with key material specific to the requester (p. 42). The notation is PI@MU (p. 25).
    • Another party can use them only as an Authentication Service with a registered affiliation (p. 56, 214).
    • BSNk signs them, so no other party can make one (p. 42 to 43).
  • Why: the specification says that this makes the solution stronger ("Dit verhoogt de robuustheid van de oplossing", p. 42). A PI that leaks is of no use to another party.
  • Consequence for the design: the PI does not belong in the consent proof. The source and the PDP can do nothing with it. The design of #364 agrees with this: the proof holds only values per recipient. The PI of the DigiD login is not usable for the register either. The register needs an activation of its own.
  • Storing is allowed: the party that activates keeps PI and PP so that they are reliably linked to the natural person ("zodanig dat ze betrouwbaar zijn gekoppeld aan de Natuurlijk persoon", p. 53). Whether storing is useful depends on how the register finds the citizen again. For more information, see the open design choice.
  • Related: REQ-69, REQ-80.
  • Kind: technical.

docs.title: BSNK-04: Transformation is possible only while the citizen is logged in
docs.text:
The requester must have authenticated the user at the requested level of assurance before it requests a transformation.

  • Status: fixed, application to check.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says: "MUST authenticate a User at the requested Level of Assurance before requesting a transformation". A Machtigingsdienst must have authenticated the representative and registered the authorization (p. 135).
  • Why: the specification gives no reason. The GBO team reads it as follows: a transformation delivers an identity to a recipient. The link to a fresh login stops a Participant from handing out identities of citizens who are not present.
  • Consequence for the design: BSNk makes all values in the proof when the citizen gives consent. At query time, days later and without the citizen, no party is allowed to transform. The design of #364 does not transform at query time either. This has two consequences:
    • All parties of a service must be known at consent time (ICTU/GBO-demo#382).
    • To extend a consent to an extra source, the citizen must log in again.
  • To check: does the login at MijnOverheid count as authentication by the register? The register is not an Authentication Service itself.
  • Related: REQ-21, REQ-24, REQ-82, F-78.
  • Kind: technical.

docs.title: BSNK-05: At most four recipients per request
docs.text:
One transformation request serves a limited number of recipients. The initial threshold is four.

  • Status: fixed.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says: "Will be limited. Initial threshold will be set to 4" (p. 133). The requester chooses identity or pseudonym per recipient (p. 134).
  • Why: "To reduce linkability risks […] the number of Relying parties will be limited" (p. 137).
  • Consequence for the design: a service with more than four parties (sources plus consumer) needs more than one request. This is extra work. It does not block the design.
  • In the demo (PR #477): the portal splits the parties over requests of at most four, per form (bsnk.go#L106). A test tried a consent with five sources. It gave two requests for the pseudonyms and one for the identity (bsnk_test.go#L77).
  • Related: REQ-82.
  • Kind: technical.

docs.title: BSNK-06: The BSN Authorization List sets BSN or pseudonym
docs.text:
If a recipient is on the BSN Authorization List, it gets an encrypted identity. Otherwise, it gets an encrypted pseudonym.

  • Status: fixed.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says:
    • Before the requester has a PI transformed, it "MUST check the relying party is listed in the Autorisatielijst BSN" (p. 135).
    • The requester must process the list periodically and automatically. It must not use the list after its validity period (p. 229).
    • BSNk also gives the key to decrypt a VI only to parties on that list (p. 154).
  • Why: BSNk uses the BSN only where that is strictly necessary and allowed by law. In all other cases, it uses a pseudonym (p. 42).
  • Consequence for the design: in #364, "may process the BSN" is a lookup by OIN in a list of RvIG. The GBO team does not make this judgement itself. The register must process that list. The lock is double: if a party is not on the list, it gets no VI and also no key.
  • In the demo (PR #477):
    • The portal reads the list from the mock (bsnk.go#L86).
    • Every source gets a VP. Only a source on the list also gets a VI (portal.go#L197).
    • The list of the mock has no validity period. For this reason, the portal uses its copy for at most BSN_AUTHORISATION_LIST_MAX_AGE (default one hour).
    • If the copy is expired and the portal cannot renew it, the portal gives no consent (portal.go#L228).
    • The period of one hour is an assumption. How the list is delivered in practice is open (Q-26, sub-question 8).
  • Related: REQ-82, REQ-117.
  • Kind: technical.

docs.title: BSNK-07: The recipient is an OIN
docs.text:
An encrypted value is made for one OIN. The keys and the pseudonym are derived from that OIN.

  • Status: fixed.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says:
    • BSNk uses the OIN to derive the keys of the service provider that encrypt the EI and EP. BSNk also uses it for the pseudonym that is unique to the service provider ("voor het afleiden van de DV-sleutels waarmee de EI en EP vercijferd zijn en voor het DV-unieke pseudoniem", p. 23).
    • Separate administrations within one organization have "their own OIN and hence their own Pseudonyms" (p. 108).
    • The transformation request has no parameter for a service. Role and TransactionID are "reserved for future use" (p. 135).
  • Why: compartmentalization is a design goal. A service provider cannot recognize a citizen by the pseudonym of that citizen at another service provider (p. 69).
  • Consequence for the design: this precondition answers the open point in #364 about more than one peer.
    • Two peers with the same OIN share one VI and one key.
    • A peer with another OIN needs its own VI, and must itself be on the BSN Authorization List.
    • A pseudonym per service is possible only with a separate OIN per service. Each OIN then has its own certificate and keys.
  • Related: REQ-80, REQ-82, Q-68.
  • Kind: technical.

docs.title: BSNK-08: An encrypted value belongs to one key version
docs.text:
A VI or VP is encrypted for one key version of the recipient, and that version is the issue date of its certificate.

  • Status: fixed.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says:
    • The transformation request names the key version per recipient (p. 134).
    • For a service provider, the key version is the issue date of the certificate with which it requested the keys, as YYYYMMDD (p. 170, 192).
    • The closing key sets the pseudonym. It has its own version (p. 183).
    • The public key provision list (Sleutelverstrekkingslijst) shows which versions BSNk provided (p. 231 to 232).
  • Why: a party requests the keys with its certificate. A new certificate gives a new set of keys. The Design Specification of the decryption component says: "When SP-keys are renewed/replaced, persisted pseudonyms will change" (use case 5).
  • Consequence for the design: the precondition has three consequences:
    • The register must know the current key version per party. The key provision list gives it.
    • The source must keep old keys as long as proofs encrypted with them are in use. That is as long as the longest consent.
    • If a consumer gets a VP, its pseudonyms change with a new closing key. The decryption component has a conversion function for that.
  • Related: REQ-80, REQ-82, AV-09, F-78.
  • Kind: technical.

docs.title: BSNK-09: The recipient gets its keys through an Access Service or Key Requester
docs.text:
A source or consumer cannot get its keys from BSNk itself.

  • Status: fixed, who fills the role is open.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says:
    • Only an Access Service or a Key Requester calls provideDVKeys, and only for a contracted service provider (p. 146, 155).
    • The service provider needs a PKIoverheid certificate with the OIN (p. 154). The keys come encrypted for that certificate (p. 185 to 186).
    • BSNk publishes every provision with OIN and name (p. 231).
    • The service provider needs no HSM (p. 27).
  • Why: the public list is there for transparency, "like Certificate Transparency" (p. 231).
  • Consequence for the design:
    • Every source needs a connection through an Access Service or a Key Requester. If the consumer gets a VP, it needs such a connection too. As a result, participation is publicly visible.
    • Decryption itself needs no construction work. The Logius decryption component is a container without its own storage. It gets all keys with each call and needs no outgoing connection (Software Architecture Document §2.4, §4.7).
  • Onboarding: the key request is a step in the admission of a source or consumer. For more information, see consequence for onboarding.
  • Related: REQ-80, ADR 0033.
  • Kind: technical.

docs.title: BSNK-10: The party that activates has the inspection duty
docs.text:
BSNk records every activation in the inspection register (Inzageregister). The party that activated must keep the status there up to date.

  • Status: fixed.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says:
    • At activation, BSNk registers the relation between the requester and the citizen in the inspection register (p. 54).
    • A Means Issuer or an Authorization Service MUST keep the status up to date (p. 61) and implement the interface for it (p. 110).
    • The citizen sees the overview in MijnOverheid (p. 39).
    • The registration holds a description that the citizen can read (p. 119).
  • Why: the inspection register exists so that citizens can see if a party issued something in their name without their knowledge (p. 44).
  • Consequence for the design:
    • The consent register appears in the overview of login means and authorizations of the citizen. The register must report status changes.
    • That overview is not made for consent. For this reason, the description must explain what the citizen sees there.
    • This duty is also a reason why the design activates a citizen only once (route D).
  • Kind: technical.

docs.title: BSNK-11: The interfaces are SOAP with PKIoverheid
docs.text:
All interfaces are SOAP 1.1 over mutual TLS with PKIoverheid certificates, with a signature on every message.

  • Status: fixed.
Source, evidence and notes
  • What the specification says:
    • The interfaces use Digikoppeling profile 2W-be, with a WS-Security signature on request and answer (p. 74 to 75).
    • TLS uses the PKIoverheid G1 private root (p. 76).
    • Clocks can differ by two seconds at most (p. 74).
    • Participants must publish DNSSEC (p. 76).
  • Why: interoperability and security based on open standards (p. 73).
  • Consequence for the design: the register needs integration work. This does not block the design. The source and the PDP do not talk to BSNk, so nothing changes for them. The demo mock offers the BSNk interface as JSON instead of SOAP.
  • Kind: technical.

docs.title: Open design choice: how does the register find the citizen again?
docs.text: The preconditions say what must happen. They do not say how the register recognizes a citizen at a later login. The working assumption is that MijnOverheid passes the BSN. With that assumption, the provisional choice is route D. There is no decision (Q-49, ADR 0040, proposed). Routes A, B, and C belong to the variant in which MijnOverheid passes the BSN encrypted for BSNk.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
The register needs two things from a logged-in citizen:

  1. A stable key for its own administration. With this key, the register shows and revokes the consents of this citizen without a BSN (REQ-20).
  2. A PI and PP. With these, the register has BSNk make the values for the parties at a new consent (BSNK-03).

A stored PI or PP is not a stable key itself, for three reasons:

  • The register cannot get the BSN out of it.
  • The register cannot compute it from a BSN.
  • BSNk gives other values at every activation.

As a result, a party that holds only a BSN at a later login cannot find which stored PI and PP belong to that citizen.

docs.title: Route D: an own pseudonym from the BSN (working assumption)
docs.text:
If MijnOverheid passes the BSN, the register derives a stable key itself. The key is an HMAC of the BSN with a secret key of the register. The register keeps PI and PP under that stable key. The following diagram shows route D:

sequenceDiagram box rgb(241,239,232) Portal participant MO as MijnOverheid end box rgb(254,220,216) DvTP participant TR as Consent register end box rgb(241,239,232) External participant K as BSNk end Note over MO,K: every login MO->>TR: BSN Note over TR: HMAC of the BSN = stable key,<br/>looks up PI, PP and consents,<br/>does not keep the BSN Note over MO,K: first consent (onboarding) TR->>K: activate, with check data [BSNK-02] K-->>TR: PI and PP Note over TR: keeps PI and PP under the stable key TR->>K: transform for the parties K-->>TR: VI and VP for the parties Note over MO,K: next consent TR->>K: transform, with the stored PI and PP K-->>TR: VI and VP for the parties

Route D has the following properties:

  • One activation per citizen: the register activates at the first consent and only transforms after that. Viewing and revoking need no BSNk.
  • The stable key exists before onboarding: the register computes the key itself, so it has the key at the first login. If the register finds nothing under that key, the citizen is new.
  • The HMAC must meet four conditions:
    • The secret key is the only protection. There are about a billion BSNs, so without the key, any party can compute every pseudonym back. The key is in an HSM or KMS.
    • The input is unambiguous (nine digits, with leading zeros) and gets a fixed prefix. Thus the pseudonym never equals another HMAC under the same key.
    • The pseudonym is at least 128 bits.
    • Every record keeps the key version with which the register made the pseudonym. With a new key, the register cannot recompute the pseudonyms itself, because it does not have the BSN. At a login it can, with the BSN that comes in at that login.
  • Route D does not need BSNk for the stable key. An own VP of the register is also a stable key. But to get the VP again at a later login, the register must activate again (route A), or MijnOverheid must pass the VP (route B). Route D needs neither.
  • Route D has a cost. The register processes the BSN for a short time at every login, and that needs a legal basis. Also, the register can compute for every BSN itself whether consents exist, without a trace elsewhere. In route A, that is possible only through BSNk, and every activation goes into the inspection register (BSNK-10).

The demo builds route D (PR #469):

  • The consent portal backend derives its stable key with an HMAC of the BSN under its own secret key (SUBJECT_REF_KEY, versioned, subjectref.go#L40).
  • At the first consent, the backend activates and keeps PI and PP under that key in the consent register. At every later consent, it only has values transformed (portal.go#L298-L314, polymorphic.go#L10-L17).
  • Viewing and revoking do not call BSNk.
  • A new secret key gives every citizen a new stable key. For this reason, the key version is part of the key. The demo does not build migration of existing data (Q-56).
  • The protection of the stored PI and PP is Q-57.
  • This setup fits only if the backend and the register are one BSNk participant (Q-49).
  • The setup deviates on purpose from FR-35 criterion 1 (REQ-69, F-98).

docs.title: With an encrypted BSN: three routes to the stable key
docs.text: If MijnOverheid passes an encrypted BSN, that value gives no stable key. The value is different at every login, because the specification demands a new random key per encrypted element (p. 78). Also, the register cannot read it.

docs.title: Route A: own pseudonym through BSNk
docs.text: The register activates and has the PP transformed to a VP for itself. Then it decrypts the VP to its own pseudonym for this citizen. The register needs BSNk at every login (activate and transform). The route depends on nothing extra.

docs.title: Route B: pseudonym through the login
docs.text: At the login, MijnOverheid asks a VP for the register and passes it on. The register decrypts it locally. The register does not need BSNk at every login. The route depends on DigiD and MijnOverheid: both must be able to do this.

docs.title: Route C: reference from MijnOverheid
docs.text: MijnOverheid passes its own stable reference to the citizen. The register does not need BSNk at every login. The route depends on MijnOverheid: it must have such a reference and be allowed to pass it on.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
The four routes compare as follows:

Route How BSNk at every login Depends on A. Own pseudonym through BSNk Activate, VP for itself, decrypt Yes: activate and transform Nothing extra B. Pseudonym through the login MijnOverheid passes a VP for the register No DigiD and MijnOverheid must be able to do it C. Reference from MijnOverheid MijnOverheid passes its own reference No MijnOverheid must have it and be allowed to pass it D. Own pseudonym from the BSN HMAC of the plain BSN No (only the first activation) MijnOverheid passes the BSN, and the register has a legal basis

The routes differ in the following points:

  • A and B give the same pseudonym for the same key version (BSNK-08). A pseudonym is always the same for one citizen at one recipient, whatever the authentication service or the login means ("ongeacht de Authenticatiedienst of het gebruikte Authenticatiemiddel", p. 29).
  • B already exists for another register. MijnOverheid lets the citizen log in for itself and for the inspection register ("voor zichzelf en voor het Inzageregister"). So it gets a value for that register (p. 39). The consent register is as fixed at login as the inspection register.
  • For A and B, the register needs its own keys to decrypt a VP (BSNK-09). In route A, the register counts as one of the four recipients (BSNK-05).
  • C is the simplest, and B gives the strongest separation. With C, the register knows the citizen under a reference that MijnOverheid also knows. With A or B, the register knows the citizen only under a pseudonym that is valid nowhere else.

The route decides whether storing PI and PP is useful:

  • In route A, storing is useless. To compute the pseudonym, the register already activated, so it already holds a fresh PI. The register activates at every login at which it must recognize the citizen, also if the citizen only views the consents. It throws PI and PP away after use.
  • In routes B and C, storing is useful. The register activates once per citizen and keeps PI and PP under the stable key. After that, a new consent needs only a transformation, and viewing or revoking needs no BSNk. The register needs the encrypted BSN only the first time.
  • In route B, the "stable key" is the pseudonym that the register decrypts from the passed VP. In route C, it is the reference of MijnOverheid.

docs.title: What is fixed for every route
docs.text:
Three points do not depend on the route:

  • Transformation is possible only when the citizen gives consent, with the citizen logged in (BSNK-04).
  • The PI stays in the register and does not go into the proof (BSNK-03).
  • The register must be a recognized party (BSNK-01).

docs.title: Questions to answer
docs.text:
The routes depend on answers from other parties, as listed in the following table:

Question For route Addressee Is MijnOverheid allowed to pass the BSN to the consent portal, and on which legal basis does the register process it? D MijnOverheid, lawyer, BZK Can MijnOverheid get a VP for the consent register at the login, as for the inspection register? B MijnOverheid, Logius Does MijnOverheid have its own stable reference to the citizen, and is it allowed to pass it on? C MijnOverheid How does the inspection register handle repeated activation for the same citizen? A Logius If the register gets new keys, does a stored PI stay usable? B, C, D Logius

Q-26 also holds these questions.

docs.title: Consequence for onboarding: certificate and keys per party
docs.text: A source or consumer can read a value from the proof only if it got keys in advance. That follows from BSNK-06, BSNK-08, and BSNK-09. The key request is a step in the admission of a party. It is not a step in the data exchange. The design and demo v0.9.0 do not have this step. ICTU/GBO-demo#467 asks for it.

docs.title: Two kinds of certificate
docs.text:
Both kinds are PKIoverheid certificates with the OIN of the organization. BSNk issues neither kind. A party requests its certificate at a PKIoverheid certificate provider. The following table shows the two kinds:

Certificate Of whom For what Spec Communication certificates The party that calls BSNk: the register, and the party that requests the keys TLS and the signature on every message. The certificate must be in the metadata of that Participant p. 75 to 76 Recipient certificate Every source or consumer that must read a value BSNk encrypts the key files with it, and its issue date becomes the key version. The OIN is in Subject.serialNumber and the certificate allows keyEncipherment p. 154, 192

The recipient certificate is not a decryption key itself. The decryption keys are separate keys that BSNk makes.

docs.title: Who makes and keeps what
docs.text:
Each party makes and keeps different items, as listed in the following table:

What Made by Kept by Spec Certificate and its private key The party itself, through a PKIoverheid certificate provider The party. Only the public certificate goes to other parties p. 154 EP Decryption and EP Closing, to read a VP BSNk key management The party. An HSM is not mandatory p. 27, 155, 188 EI Decryption, to read a VI BSNk key management, only for a party on the technical BSN list The party p. 154 to 155 Key provision list BSNk management organization Public p. 231

The decryption component keeps nothing. The party gives the keys with every call (BSNK-09).

The following diagram shows the key request:

sequenceDiagram box rgb(221,235,247) Party participant P as Source or consumer end box rgb(241,239,232) External participant C as Certificate provider participant S as Key Requester participant K as BSNk end P->>C: requests certificate with OIN C-->>P: certificate, private key stays with the party P->>S: public certificate Note over S: checks certificate and origin,<br/>and the technical BSN list if a VI is needed S->>K: request keys for this OIN K-->>S: key files, encrypted for the certificate Note over K: provision goes on the key provision list S-->>P: encrypted key files Note over P: decrypts with its own private key,<br/>checks the key pairs, keeps them

The party does not talk to BSNk. The Key Requester cannot read the keys, because every file is encrypted with the certificate of the party (p. 185 to 186). The party must check that the private and public key in every file match (p. 195).

The party that requests the keys has duties. The specification states the following duties for an Access Service (p. 155):

  • It requests keys only for a contracted service provider.
  • It establishes that the request comes from that service provider, and records this in a way that it can prove.
  • It checks that the certificate is valid.
  • It makes sure that a party that wants to decrypt the BSN is on the technical BSN list.

The Key Requester role covers only one specific responsibility of the Access Service ("slechts één specifieke verantwoordelijkheid", p. 37). The GBO team reads this as follows: the same duties then apply to a Key Requester.

docs.title: When the step comes back
docs.text:
The key request comes back in three cases:

  • A new certificate: a new certificate gives a new key version and new keys (BSNK-08). The pseudonyms change with it. The register must know the new version before it transforms for that party.
  • Another OIN: another OIN needs separate migration keys. The party requests them the same way (p. 156).
  • A party that becomes BSN-authorized later: BSNk provides the key for a VI only to a party on the technical BSN list (p. 154). The GBO team reads this as follows: if a party gets on the list later, the party must make the request again.

docs.title: What is open
docs.text:
Two points about the key request are open:

  • Who requests the keys for sources and consumers:
    • The GBO parties talk to MijnOverheid and the consent register. They do not talk to BSNk.
    • Thus one of the parties that does talk to BSNk must be an Access Service or a Key Requester. As an alternative, an existing Key Requester comes in between.
    • A Participant can combine roles (p. 34).
    • The register must already be recognized for activation and transformation (BSNK-01), and it already admits parties. These facts argue for giving the role to the register.
    • There is no decision, and recognition is a decision of BZK (Q-26).
  • Where in admission the step goes:
    • The demo has an admission register for DvTP.
    • Per consumer, it records the FSC Peer ID, the name, and the sources to which the consumer is admitted. Sources are in it as configuration.
    • It knows no certificate, key version, or BSN authorization.

docs.title: What BSNk does not offer
docs.text:
BSNk does not offer the following:

  • A pseudonym per service or per consent within one OIN (p. 135).
  • The way back from pseudonym to BSN. A recipient cannot trace its pseudonym back (p. 29). Thus a source cannot look up anybody by the pseudonym of a consumer.
  • A shorter route through the direct variants:
    • BSNk allows the directly encrypted pseudonym only for separate administrations within an Authentication Service, a Means Issuer, or an Authorization Service. It also needs consultation with BSNk (p. 99, 108).
    • The directly encrypted identity is in the notation, but no interface delivers it.
  • A role for a consent facility (p. 34).

docs.title: What the specification offers in addition
docs.text:
The specification offers two things that touch an open point from #364. That point is whether the source checks the signature of the proof again.

  • A VI is signed by BSNk itself and names the recipient (p. 176 to 177). Thus the source can check, apart from the proof, that the value is real and meant for it. The decryption component does that check before decryption (Design Specification, use case 1).
  • BSNk can sign a nonce with the VI. Per recipient, the transformation request can give a nonce of 8 to 128 letters and digits, which goes into the VI (p. 134, 181). With the consent ID as nonce, the VI itself is bound to this one consent, in addition to the signature of the proof. Demo v0.9.0 does not build this nonce (REQ-81).

docs.title: Open: administrative and legal
docs.text:
The following administrative and legal points are open:

  • The recognition of the consent register, and in which role (BSNK-01, Q-26).
  • A private consumer outside the public domain. The specification is written for service providers with a public task (p. 26). This point matters only if the consumer gets a VP. In #364, the VP for the consumer is optional (Q-01).
  • The consumer carries an encrypted BSN. The VI for the source is in the proof that the consumer sends, and the consumer cannot read it. The lawyer must decide whether this counts as processing of the BSN (Q-01).

docs.title: Not verified
docs.text:
The GBO team did not verify the following points:

  • Is MijnOverheid allowed to pass the BSN to the consent portal, or can it encrypt the BSN for BSNk?
  • Can the register get on the exception list for the BRP check?
  • Does the login at MijnOverheid meet BSNK-04?
  • For which recipient must BSNk make an encrypted identity that is the input for activation (p. 93)?
  • How long does a VI stay usable? It carries an issue month and no end date (p. 177). The specification says nothing about this.
  • Do bronhouders already have BSNk keys from their DigiD connection?
  • Can a party use the certificate that it already has for FSC for the key request? The certificate must have the OIN in Subject.serialNumber and allow keyEncipherment (p. 154).
  • Which requirements does BZK set for a Key Requester? Do the duties of an Access Service at a key request (p. 155) apply in full to a Key Requester?
  • The questions under questions to answer: what MijnOverheid can pass at login, and how BSNk handles repeated activation and new keys of the register.
  • Can the mock make the encrypted structures itself? The decryption component contains only the decryption side. The demo mock does not encrypt: anyone can read its values.

docs.title: Source and identity requirements
docs.text:
These requirements cover how a source describes its own services and how GBO activates that description. They also cover how the legal identity of a party follows from its certificate. For the design, see Source onboarding and Identity and trust.

This page has the following parts:

  • Source metadata and activation requirements
  • Identity, trust and transport requirements

docs.title: Source metadata and activation requirements
docs.text:
These requirements cover how a source publishes its service description, and how GBO validates and activates that description. REQ-64 applies to every GBO-delivered component that must know something per source or per service, in every data flow: EUDI issuance, the ASIP, and the consent facility (toestemmingsvoorziening) of DvTP. REQ-65 and REQ-66 describe activation as the issuance route and the shared Source Registry implement it.

The demo builds the description for two channels. EUDI issuance reads the eudi capability. Since ICTU/GBO-demo#592, the ASIP reads the asi capability (schema version 1.1) from the same Source Registry. In demo v0.9.0, the offer of a source for DvTP is in the GBO rules. The source does not publish it.

F-57 and F-58 give the background. ADR 0016 records the mechanism.

Evidence links to gbo-demo point at tag v0.9.0.

docs.title: REQ-64: A GBO component works only with the service description the source publishes itself, after validation
docs.text:
A GBO-delivered component MUST take the service description of a source only from what the source publishes itself. The description covers the data service, the query with declared parameters, the mapping, the attestation schema, the validity per attestation type, and the offer. The component MUST NOT keep that description itself, add to it, or carry it per source in code. This applies to every GBO-delivered component that must know something per source or per service, in every data flow. These data flows are issuance, the ASIP, and the consent facility (the offer of the source per data set). A new service or data set of a source MUST be usable without a code change in such a component.

Before use, the component MUST validate the description on schema, origin (the publishing party is the bronhouder of the certificate set), version, validity window, and binding to the contract for the data service. The runtime MUST work only from a validated, activated version (REQ-66). Every request that follows from it goes through the PDP of the source (REQ-44). The description MUST name the read API of the logbook of the source, and the chain MUST fill dpl.read.nextLogbookId from it.

If the answer of the source does not fit the published mapping exactly, or holds more than one result, issuance MUST refuse. It MUST NOT pick a result, and it MUST NOT add or convert a value.

Case Outcome Valid description, OIN equal to the certificate set, contracts present candidate activated OIN in the description differs from the certificate set not activated: METADATA_INVALID No contract for the data service the description names not activated: DATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND Query is not exactly one read operation, or unknown mapping profile not activated: METADATA_INVALID Valid for less than one hour, or expires_at not after issued_at not activated: METADATA_INVALID Issuance request with parameters outside the published offer refused (HTTP 400) Answer does not fit the mapping (path missing, other datatype, result not a list) no attestation (HTTP 502): GBO_SIMPLE_PATH_MISSING, GBO_SIMPLE_TYPE_MISMATCH, GBO_SIMPLE_RESULT_TYPE (code) Answer with more than one result no attestation (HTTP 502): GBO_SIMPLE_RESULT_AMBIGUOUS (code) Answer without a result no attestation (HTTP 404) (code) Source without its own endpoint, where the operator maintains the document admitted as an exception, visible as unauthenticated transport, lapses after expires_at Read API of the logbook in the description proposal and not built
  • Status: ready for review
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: design:
    • PSA S07 ("the bronhouder can in principle add new services through the source-specific GBO configuration")
    • PSA S10 ("the bronhouder manages a source-specific GBO configuration that records which data services are available for which data flows, and which schemas, mappings and other processing instructions apply", "central GBO facilities can consult the configuration relevant to them in machine readable form", "the configuration can be validated, versioned and traced")
    • PSA S11 (the bronhouder records mapping and attestation schema in its GBO configuration)
    • GO ("the mapping happens centrally with the settings from the decentral configuration component")
    • Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1569, Annex II point 2(b) (verify the identity of the authentic source)
    • P-10
    • for the exception: D-13
  • Addressee: GBO-delivered component: the reconciler and the runtime of the EUDI adapter, the ASIP, and the consent facility. Interface agreement: the form of the publication and the validation rules. What the bronhouder must publish is in AV-07 and AV-08.
  • Evidence: PR #219, PR #224, PR #242, PR #318, PR #463, #592.
    • Publication at /.well-known/gbo: brp-graphql-server/main.go#L938 and graphql-server/main.go#L360, with the document gbo-source-metadata.json.
    • Schema with version 1.0 or 1.1 (1.1 adds asi): gbo-source-metadata-v1.schema.json#L17-L23.
    • Origin and contract: source-registry/onboarding/service.go#L403-L413.
    • Content: one read operation in source_metadata.go#L130-L141. The validity window is in source_metadata_cache.go#L29-L41, tested in main_test.go#L628.
    • Offer: source_metadata.go#L272-L296, tested in main_test.go#L434.
    • GBO generates the SD-JWT VC Type Metadata from display and claims: type_metadata.go#L64, tested in type_metadata_test.go#L120.
    • The ASIP reads the active release: asi-provider/main.go#L101, tested in asi_onboarding_test.go#L152.
    • Exception without endpoint: source-metadata/README.md and service.go#L18-L28, #L56-L66.
  • Related: REQ-44, REQ-57, REQ-65, REQ-66, REQ-67, REQ-72, REQ-77, REQ-78, REQ-116, REQ-121, REQ-124, F-57, F-68, F-71, F-74, Q-14, Q-19, Q-38, ADR 0016, ADR 0017, ADR 0039.
  • Notes:
    • The requirement is built for EUDI issuance and, since #592, for the ASIP. The Source Registry is a shared module in services/source-registry. The ASIP reads the active release every 5 seconds.
    • The eudi capability describes each attestation with type_id, type_version, offers, graphql, mapping_profile, display, and claims. Each claim has one gbo-simple-v1 rule in source, a label, and an sd value. GBO derives the mapping and generates the Type Metadata from it. The schema has no separate mapping, attribute_schema, and type_metadata blocks.
    • The asi capability maps source fields onto GBO-catalogued attribute value schemas with pointer, join, const, and each. gbo-simple-v1 applies to the eudi capability only (ADR 0039).
    • For DvTP, the offer of a source is in the GBO rules (dvt0001.rego#L32-L44). The source does not publish it. For DvTP, the requirement covers the supply side. The legal ceiling per service, and whether a data set is mandatory or optional, come from the catalogue (FR-32, F-74, REQ-121, Q-45).
    • In demo v0.9.0, the origin check is authenticated transport (FSC) plus the OIN from the certificate set. The document itself is not signed.
    • The exception for a source without an endpoint follows D-13. The demo builds the exception as visible (data_transport_authenticated) and temporary (expires_at). The agreement of the bronhouder is only an instruction in the README (AV-08, F-71). The local compose also has a source over unsecured HTTP. Deployments do not mount it (docker-compose.yml#L1868-L1870).
    • Not built: the logbook read API in the description. In demo v0.9.0, the adapter gets it per caller from configuration (docker-compose.yml#L1819, F-68). Also not built: a reference to the DCAT-AP-NL description of the data service (S10: "refers to managed objects where possible").
    • The content and the interface of the source configuration are an open decision of PSA S10. gbo-source-metadata-v1 is the proposal of the demo.
    • The issuance runtime of nl-wallet reads its configuration only at start. That is a product property.

docs.title: REQ-65: Only an explicit management action takes a source into use, and a valid contract is not enough
docs.text:
A valid FSC contract MUST NOT be enough to take a source into use or to publish its offer in the wallet. Taking a source into use MUST be an explicit management action, recorded in configuration apart from the contract. A validated service description MUST apply only after a separate promotion. A component MUST NOT discover and activate a source by itself.

Case Outcome Valid metadata contract, no source configuration nothing activated Source configuration, no metadata contract source blocked: METADATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND Source configuration, no contract for the data service source blocked: DATA_CONTRACT_NOT_FOUND Validated candidate without promotion not active
  • Status: ready for review
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: design: PSA S04 ("participation needs a prior admission decision", "the set-up treats technical identity and admission status apart from the role and authority in a specific interaction") and P-07.
  • Addressee: GBO-delivered component: the reconciler of the issuance facility.
  • Evidence: PR #237, PR #247.
    • Configuration: one file per source in sources/configured/, read in source_configuration.go#L16-L28.
    • No discovery, tested in fsc_contract_discovery_test.go#L143.
    • Missing contract in service.go#L346-L349, tested in fsc_contract_discovery_test.go#L201.
    • Promotion as a separate step in reconcile_command.go#L134-L151.
  • Related: REQ-61, REQ-64, REQ-66, REQ-123, F-58, ADR 0016.
  • Notes: design choice: automatic promotion is off by default (reconcile_command.go#L197). Compose and the Helm example turn it on (docker-compose.yml#L1865). In that case, adding the configuration file is the management action. Not built: who is allowed to do that action, and how the admission decision is recorded (PSA B-09). The configuration is a file in the repository.

docs.title: REQ-66: Source metadata fails closed per source, ages within bounds, and can be rolled back
docs.text:
Source metadata can fail to validate, fall outside its validity, or fail to refresh within a grace period set in advance. In each of these cases, the metadata MUST fail closed for that source: no issuance follows on that metadata. The failure of one source MUST NOT stop issuance for other sources.

An activated version MUST be immutable, MUST be activated as a whole, and MUST be possible to roll back to an earlier valid version. A version number MUST identify one content. A candidate with the same version but other content MUST NOT be activated. A candidate with a lower version than the last validated candidate of that source MUST NOT be activated either. Only the explicit management action of REQ-65 can go back to an earlier version.

Case Outcome Refresh fails, previous version within grace source stale, and issuance on the previous version Refresh fails, no previous version or grace over source blocked Active version of a source past grace issuance for that source refused (HTTP 503) Certificate set of one source missing that source blocked, the others activated One configured source without a valid version no new release for any source, and the active release stays (deviates from the requirement, see notes) One source past grace offer list for all sources HTTP 503 (deviates from the requirement) Roll back to a stored release active. Automatic promotion does not undo that. Roll back to a release the adapter cannot load refused Source publishes the same version with other content not activated (code, no test) Source publishes a lower version than the last validated one not activated (code, no test)
  • Status: ready for review
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: design: PSA S10 ("the configuration can be validated, versioned and traced"). For the isolation, the requirement is derived. It serves P-15 and D-04. If the configuration of one source fails, issuance for other bronhouders must not fail with it.
  • Addressee: GBO-delivered component: the reconciler, the release register, and the runtime of the issuance facility.
  • Evidence: PR #205, PR #276, PR #463. Not built: the test for the version rule (ICTU/GBO-demo#610) and the per-source isolation of promotion and offer list (ICTU/GBO-demo#606).
    • Grace in service.go#L463-L476, tested in fsc_contract_discovery_test.go#L549.
    • Refusal per source in main.go#L221-L225.
    • Isolation tested in service_test.go#L130.
    • Immutable and atomic in store.go#L300-L390, tested in store_test.go#L94 and #L147.
    • Rollback in source_registry_command.go#L120-L143, tested in source_registry_command_test.go#L72 and registry_test.go#L116.
    • Version rule in source_registry_backend.go#L163-L175.
  • Related: REQ-64, REQ-65, REQ-124, F-52, F-59, ADR 0016, ADR 0021.
  • Notes:
    • Design choice: fresh for at most 15 minutes, one hour of grace, and at least one hour of validity (source_metadata_cache.go#L10-L14). The source states are pending, active, stale, blocked, and rollout_required.
    • Design choice: promotion of a new version needs a valid version of every configured source. This way, no source drops out of the release without notice (registry.go#L133-L158). As a result, new metadata of other sources waits until the failing source is repaired, or until the operator removes it from the configuration.
    • The offer list /eudi-offers.json takes the shortest grace of all sources (source_release_runtime.go#L95-L100, #L298-L300). As a result, the list fails for all sources at the same time. That breaks the rule that the failure of one source must not stop issuance for other sources (#606).
    • Policy bundles do not have this lifecycle (F-52, F-59). PSA S06 asks the same for them ("on failure they fall back in a controlled way", "rollback procedure").

docs.title: Removed numbers
docs.text: No numbers of this page were removed. The list of all removed numbers is on the requirements overview.

docs.title: Identity, trust and transport requirements
docs.text:
These requirements cover how GBO establishes who an organization is, and how channels reach a source. FSC establishes the identity of the calling organization on every channel. The legal identity of a bronhouder (OIN and name) comes from its certificate. It does not come from configuration that an operator can fill in. Authorization for each request stays a separate layer: see Authorization.

ADR 0003 records FSC as the transport. ADR 0023 records the certificate roles. Evidence links to gbo-demo point at tag v0.9.0.

docs.title: REQ-46: Every channel that calls a source on behalf of an external party does so through FSC, with a valid certificate
docs.text:
Every channel that calls a service of a bronhouder on behalf of an external party MUST do so through FSC. A channel MUST NOT enter the service of the bronhouder, or the authorization for it, directly. FSC establishes the identity of the calling organization. The authorization for each request (consent, PID binding, legal basis) stays a separate layer of the channel. If the certificate of the calling party is expired or revoked, the connection MUST be refused. The revocation check MUST NOT be disabled.

Case Outcome Certificate of the calling party expired connection refused Certificate of the calling party revoked connection refused, after the revocation propagates. Time limit: Q-53 Revocation check disabled in an Inway, Outway or Manager not allowed (proposal: not checked)
  • Status: ready for review
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: design:
    • GO (FSC as the connectivity standard).
    • PSA S04.
    • FR-34 criterion 3 ("on expiry or revocation of the organization identification means, access to the consent process and the data traffic is blocked immediately").
    • FR-33 criterion 2.
  • Addressee: interface agreement for every channel: DvTP, EUDI issuance (PuB-EAA), and the Authentic Source Interface.
    • the backend of the service provider (dienstverlener) (main.go#L82)
    • the EUDI adapter (main.go#L115)
    • the ASIP (main.go#L83-L85)

    Evidence: all three channels call through their own FSC Outway:

    Nobody checked the revocation behavior.

  • Related: REQ-61, REQ-74, REQ-111, Q-53, Q-60, ADR 0003.

  • Notes:
    • FSC establishes the organization. That says nothing about what the organization is allowed to do in each request. The regime for each request follows from the evidence that the request carries (REQ-74).
    • open-fsc checks revocation with a CRL cache. An operator can switch the check off for each Inway, Outway, and Manager. Without this requirement, that switch is a silent configuration choice.
    • The time within which a revocation must take effect is Q-53.
    • The consent process blocks through the status in the register (REQ-111), as long as the initiation is not bound to the certificate (Q-60).

docs.title: REQ-67: The legal identity of a bronhouder comes from its certificate and not from configuration
docs.text:
A GBO component can put the legal identity of a bronhouder (OIN and organization name) in an attestation or a decision record. The component MUST then take it from verified certificate material of that bronhouder. A value that an operator can fill in freely MUST NOT be the source for it.

Case Outcome Certificate with the OIN in serialNumber and exactly one organization name OIN and name come from the certificate Configured OIN or name differs from the certificate refused: the certificate set is not loaded Certificate without a 20-digit OIN, or without exactly one organization name refused
  • Status: draft
Source, evidence and notes
  • Source: design:
    • PSA S04 ("organizations and systems use recognized identifiers and certificates", "the set-up links the technical identity to the admitted legal organization and role").
    • PSA F1.
    • FR-33 and FR-34.
    • P-07.
  • Addressee: GBO-delivered component: the source registration of the EUDI adapter.
  • Evidence: PR #242, PR #247, PR #321. Code and tests:
    • The derivation is in development_ca_provider.go#L242-L253 and #L280-L288, tested in development_ca_provider_test.go#L152.
    • A set without OIN or name blocks the source: source-registry/onboarding/service.go#L293-L297.
    • The organization description goes into the certificate through onboarding.go#L182.
  • Related: REQ-58, REQ-64, F-60, Q-06, Q-07, Q-68, ADR 0023.
  • Notes:
    • It is open whether policy can read the Peer ID of a consumer as its OIN: Q-68.
    • In FSC the Peer ID is the subject.serialNumber of the FSC certificate. If the peer is the bronhouder itself, the Peer ID is the OIN. One peer can offer services of more than one bronhouder. So the source configuration keeps provider_peer_id apart from the OIN in the certificate (source_configuration.go#L35-L44).
    • The runtime gets leaf material and public CA certificates. It gets no CA private keys (development_ca_provider_test.go#L128).
    • Consents are bound to the identity of the consumer. A change of that identity makes them unusable (PR #244, PR #277).
    • In the default demo onboarding, RvIG is published through the Belastingdienst peer with the Belastingdienst OIN. That is a demo shortcut, and it does not show one OIN for each bronhouder. The certificate sets still differ for each source.

docs.title: Removed numbers
docs.text:
• REQ-01: removed. Organization attributes from a register described FSC and OpenFTV behavior that no longer exists.
  • REQ-02: merged into REQ-61 (admission comes from a register).
  • REQ-03: removed. A verified token before each query described code that no longer exists.

The list of all removed numbers is on the requirements overview.

docs.title: Runtime view
docs.text:
The runtime view shows how the building blocks work together at runtime. Each page covers one scenario or a small group of scenarios. Each page has these parts:

  • a sequence diagram with numbered steps,
  • the data that each hop carries,
  • the error and failure paths, with links to the tests in gbo-demo v0.9.0,
  • the main observations, with links to requirements, findings, and open questions.

A built scenario is a scenario that gbo-demo v0.9.0 implements, with the error paths that its page lists. A design-level scenario has no implementation. A design-level page describes the intended sequence and names the open points.

docs.title: Two planes
docs.text:
The scenarios fall into two planes:

  • Data plane. A request reads source data about a citizen. Every request takes the same route (ADR-0004, ADR-0002), in this order:

    1. the FSC Outway of the consumer (afnemer),
    2. the FSC Inway of the source, as PEP,
    3. the PDP of the source,
    4. the source gateway,
    5. the source API.

    The scenarios differ in the evidence that the request carries.

  • Management plane. No citizen data travels. The scenarios in this plane admit parties, take sources into use, and bring policy to the PDP. These scenarios come before the first request.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
A route is a path from a source to a party that uses the data. The PDP of the source judges each request under one regime. The evidence in the request selects the regime (ADR-0031, Authorization).

Three routes are built in gbo-demo v0.9.0:

  • DvTP. A private consumer reads source data with the consent of the citizen. The request carries a signed consent proof, so the PDP uses the consent regime. The consumer never gets a BSN (Consent).
  • EUDI issuance. The GBO issuance facility reads source data for a citizen who discloses a PID from the wallet. The request carries no consent proof, so the PDP uses the PID regime. The bronhouder is the PuB-EAA provider. GBO operates the technical facility (ADR-0028).
  • ASI verification. A QTSP verifies or retrieves attributes at the ASI provider (ASIP). The ASIP calls the source over FSC under the PID regime. The QTSP itself is not an FSC participant (F-87).

Three routes exist only at design level:

  • Gov-to-Gov. A government consumer reads source data under a legal basis. The regime needs its own positive evidence. No rule set for this regime exists.
  • SDG-OOTS. A competent authority in another member state requests evidence through the Once-Only Technical System. AS4 exists only at the edge. No implementation exists.
  • Relying-party presentation. The citizen presents a wallet attestation to a relying party. No GBO decision component and no source take part.

docs.title: Data classification
docs.text:
The data-per-hop tables use the tags of the classification table in Consent: what travels where. That table gives each data item (for example the consent proof, VI, VP, subject_ref, and BSN) a meaning, a sensitivity, and the hops where it occurs. The runtime pages add only items that the table does not have, for example contract proposals, admission records, and policy bundles. Those items carry no citizen data.

The error tables give administrator codes. The consumer gets only a coarse code (REQ-06, Authorization).

docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-06, REQ-74
  • Findings: F-70 (open), F-87 (open)
  • Open questions: Q-30 (open), Q-79 (open)
