  • Related: F-84, REQ-91, REQ-103, Q-33, E5, ADR-0042.

docs.title: F-96: ETSI does not name RFC 9207, so a QTSP that verifies at several ASIPs has no defense against mix-up
docs.text:
• Status: open

An OAuth client that talks to more than one authorization server needs a defense against mix-up attacks. RFC 9700 prefers the issuer parameter in the authorization response, and FAPI 2.0 requires the server to return it. ETSI only asks to take both into account, and the demo does not return the parameter. A QTSP talks to one authorization server per ASI provider, which is exactly the case where RFC 9700 makes the defense mandatory. The proposal is that a Dutch ASI authorization server returns the issuer parameter and that the QTSP checks it.

Evidence, impact and proposal
  • Type: open point in the specification
  • Trigger: SL-28, part 8 of the demo epic (PR #574): the item-by-item review of RFC 9700 and the FAPI 2.0 Security Profile.
  • Observation:
    • RFC 9700 §2.1 requires a defense against mix-up for a client that talks to more than one authorization server. The preferred defense is the iss parameter in the authorization response (RFC 9207). FAPI 2.0 §5.3.2.2 requires the server to return iss.
    • ETSI TS 119 478 clause 6.1.3.4 only asks to take both "into account" and does not name RFC 9207. Clause 6.1.3.1 does not require it.
    • The demo returns code and state, without iss. The metadata does not announce authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported (security-considerations.md#L23).
  • Why it matters: a QTSP talks to one authorization server per ASIP. In the EU, that is one server per member state or per source. RFC 9700 makes the defense mandatory for exactly this case. Without iss, the QTSP must tell servers apart with its own redirect URI per server (RFC 9700 §4.4.2). That method is a choice of each QTSP. It is part of the profile that ETSI leaves open (F-84).
  • Proposal: record in the PSA (S11, B-14) that a Dutch ASI authorization server returns iss per RFC 9207, and that a QTSP checks it (Q-66). Send the point to ETSI (E9), so that clause 6.1.3 includes it. The return of iss is not built in demo v0.9.0.
  • Related: F-84, Q-66, E9, ADR-0037.

docs.title: F-97: FR-22 to FR-24 name the same statuses with different words, and the rationale of FR-23 contradicts its criteria
docs.text:
• Status: open

FR-22 to FR-24 of FR-DvTP use different words for the same consent statuses. One rationale uses "Openstaand" (pending) next to "Actief" (active). A revoked consent is "Geannuleerd" (cancelled) in one place and "ingetrokken" (revoked) in another. The rationale of FR-23 allows revocation only while the status is "Open", but its criteria also allow it after retrieval. Builders and reviewers therefore get two readings of one rule. The proposal is one set of terms, with "Ingetrokken" for a revoked consent, and a rationale that matches the criteria.

Evidence, impact and proposal
  • Type: contradiction in the source (FR-DvTP v0.9)
  • Trigger: a review of the decision points for the build phase, track B (October 27, 2026).
  • Observation:
    • FR-22, criterion 1, names the statuses active ("Actief"), retrieved and still valid ("Opgehaald (nog geldig)"), expired ("Verlopen"), and cancelled ("Geannuleerd"). The rationale of FR-22 uses "Openstaand" for the same status.
    • FR-23 names the action revoke ("Intrekken") and the outcome "Geannuleerd". FR-24 uses "ingetrokken".
    • The rationale of FR-23 says that revocation is possible only when the status is "Open". FR-23, criterion 1, and FR-24, criterion 1, also allow revocation after "Opgehaald", while the consent is valid.
  • Why it matters: builders and reviewers get two readings of one rule. The demo shows "Actief", "Verlopen", and "Ingetrokken" (StatusChip.tsx#L4-L6). "Opgehaald" is missing, because no decision exists on when a consent counts as retrieved (Q-42, F-19).
  • Proposal: use one set of terms in FR-DvTP: "Actief", "Opgehaald (nog geldig)", "Verlopen", and "Ingetrokken". The last term matches the action "Intrekken". Make the FR-23 rationale match the criteria: revocation is possible on "Actief" and "Opgehaald". The choice for the build (October 27, 2026) is "Actief" for the first status and "Ingetrokken" for a revoked consent (REQ-109).
  • Addressee: owner of FR-DvTP.
  • Related: F-19, REQ-38, REQ-109, Q-42, Q-48.

docs.title: F-98: FR-DvTP v0.9 contradicts decisions and its own criteria on four points, and PSA S02 is ambiguous on one point
docs.text:
• Status: open

FR-DvTP v0.9 conflicts with decisions or with its own criteria on four points, and the PSA is ambiguous on one point. FR-39 and FR-26 put policy and a first check at a central place, while the decisions keep PAP and PDP at each bronhouder. FR-25 assumes that revocation ends at retrieval, and FR-35 describes register contents that differ from the chosen design. The PSA calls pseudonymization "transparent" to the citizen, which can mean invisible or explained. The FR-DvTP owner must make four changes and the PSA authors must fix the meaning, so that builders do not get two conflicting sources.

Evidence, impact and proposal
  • Type: contradiction in the source
  • Trigger: a design round compared FR-DvTP v0.9 and the PSA with the requirements (November 2, 2026).
  • Observation:
    • FR-39 puts the authorization policy at a central policy authority. Its criteria cover centrally managed, sealed bundles (criteria 1 and 2), an RFC process (3), and governance of the authority (4). Criterion 5 puts the mapping of the service catalogue to scopes in that central policy. The decision in demo issue #426 replaced this model (Q-21, closed October 28, 2026). Under that decision, policy management stays at each source, PAP and PDP sit at the bronhouder, and RL-01 to RL-05 stay guidelines. Criterion 5 then belongs in the service description (REQ-121) instead of a central policy.
    • FR-26, dependency 2, says: "the bronhouder receives a request only after the central authorization component (FR-17) did the first check". That conflicts with Q-02 (PEP, PDP, and PAP decentral at the bronhouder) and with REQ-04 and REQ-68: the PDP of the source does the check. The FR-26 criteria themselves are covered.
    • FR-25 applies the pointer to GDPR rights only "when a consent can no longer be cancelled technically (because the data is retrieved)". Its dependency says "only activated when FR-24 is active (revocation no longer possible)". But FR-23 and FR-24, criterion 1, allow revocation after retrieval while the consent is valid (REQ-109). For that reason, REQ-120 shows the pointer with every consent and after every revocation.
    • FR-35, criterion 1, says: "only a party-specific identifier in place of the BSN and the consent proof are recorded". The design chooses otherwise on purpose (REQ-69, consent register data model, route D in ADR-0040). The register keeps the polymorphic PI and PP under its own reference. It keeps no party-specific values, and it signs the proof without keeping it. Both approaches keep no BSN, but they record different data.
    • PSA S02 says: "pseudonymization and technical identifiers are transparent to the citizen. The interface does not present them as a choice of content." The second part is clear and is in REQ-117. "Transparent" can mean two things: the citizen sees nothing of it, or the interface explains it to the citizen (PSA P-13).
  • Why it matters: the requirements follow the decisions (Q-02, Q-21) and the chosen design (route D). If the FR-DvTP text stays, builders and reviewers get two conflicting sources. The S02 UI requirement stays incomplete until the meaning of "transparent" is fixed.
  • Proposal:
    • The owner of FR-DvTP must make four changes:
      • Rewrite FR-39 to policy at the bronhouder, with the catalogue-to-set mapping in the service description.
      • Make FR-26 dependency 2 refer to the PDP of the source instead of a central authorization component.
      • Detach FR-25 from "revocation no longer possible". Apply it to every consent and after a revocation.
      • Make FR-35, criterion 1, describe what the register really keeps: its own reference with PI and PP, no party-specific values, and not the proof.
    • The PSA authors must fix in S02 whether "transparent" means invisible or explained.
  • Addressee: owner of FR-DvTP, and the PSA authors (S02).
  • Related: F-06, F-09, F-97, REQ-04, REQ-68, REQ-69, REQ-109, REQ-117, REQ-120, REQ-121, RL-01, RL-05, Q-02, Q-21, ADR-0021, ADR-0040.

docs.title: Summary for the PSA
docs.text:
The demo shows that the generic chain works end to end for three routes: DvTP, EUDI issuance, and the Authentic Source Interface (ASI). The following sections group the open findings per theme (state of November 2, 2026) and name what the PSA must decide.

An earlier version of this summary named six open design knots. All six are closed: F-02, F-03, F-04, F-06, F-07, and F-08. The requirements and ADRs cover PDP placement, consent atomicity, the consent lifecycle, the fourth validation point, LDV, and mTLS on FSC.

In total, 34 findings are open. The review of September 21, 2026 closed 28 of 39 findings and kept 11 open. After that review, 24 findings were added, and the demo resolves one of them. F-54 is open again, and ADR-0021 closed F-09.

docs.title: Policy management
docs.text:
• Closed: F-09 (signing only across an organization boundary, ADR-0021).
  • Open: F-51 (management endpoints behind the decision policy), F-52 (cumulative store), and F-98 (FR-39 still describes a central policy authority).
  • Decided: policy management stays at each source. PAP and PDP sit at the bronhouder (Q-21). RL-01 to RL-05 are guidelines for bronhouders.
  • PSA to decide: whether bundle signing is required when a bundle crosses an organization boundary (ADR-0021).

docs.title: Consent and its lifecycle
docs.text:
• Open: F-19 (no "retrieved" status), F-74 (scope is the intersection of legal ceiling and source offer), F-78 (the proof freezes at consent), and F-97 and F-98 (FR-DvTP contradictions).
  • Decided: the legal basis travels as a signed proof. The status is checked online and fails closed (F-61, ADR-0032). An integrator connects under FSC delegation, and the consent binds the represented party (F-73, ADR-0034).
  • PSA to decide:
    1. When a consent counts as retrieved, and how the register learns it (Q-42).
    2. A DvTP catalogue per FR-32 as the single source for scopes, with an intersection check at activation (B-03, REQ-121).
    3. A version for the proof, and how long an old version stays valid (REQ-82).
    4. What "transparent" means in S02 (F-98).

docs.title: Authorization regime
docs.text:
• Open: F-70. The regime follows from the proof (ADR-0031), but only consent is positive proof. The PID regime rests on an actor list and an unverified BSN.
  • PSA to decide: what the evidence for the EUDI legal basis is (REQ-45, Q-18). The demo resolves the binding of rules to services (F-90), and this binding is a proposal for S05.

docs.title: Pseudonymization and BSNk
docs.text:
• Open: F-75 (the consent facility must be a recognized BSNk party), F-76 (the consumer has no citizen identifier), F-77 (one subject per request), and F-79 (only the Inway reaches the source gateway, with the roll-out outside Compose and the nonce open).
  • Decided in the TO: the source gateway decrypts its own value after the allow (ADR-0033). Route D for citizen recognition is proposed (ADR-0040).
  • PSA to decide:
    1. Recognition of the consent facility at BSNk, and who the BSNk participant is (Q-26, Q-49).
    2. Whether the consumer gets a pseudonym (VP), with its effects on logging, access, and recognition (Q-01).
    3. Queries about more than one person.

docs.title: Admission and service descriptions
docs.text:
• Open: F-57 (the source owns its description, but the DCAT-AP-NL reference and central findability are missing), and F-71 (an operator takes over a description, and the recorded agreement of the bronhouder is not built).
  • Decided: admission is a register entry instead of a policy rule (F-55).
  • PSA to decide: accept or reject the role split "the source publishes, GBO validates and activates" (S10), and decide where central findability lives.

docs.title: Audit and logging
docs.text:
• Open: F-54 (BSN in both decision logs on the EUDI and ASI routes), F-68 (no route from the ADL at the source to the consent logbook), F-72 (the ADL lacks policy version, consent status answer, and configuration), and F-76 (what the consumer logs under).
  • Decided: three standards give three records. ADL is for decisions (ADR-0036), LDV is per controller (ADR-0026), and FSC-Logging is for transport. W3C Trace Context is the correlation key (ADR-0035). The register index covers the chain start (F-68 point 1).
  • PSA to decide: keep identifiers out of the PDP input instead of masking logs (ADR-0043, proposed). The questions to Logius (Q-25, Q-27) and to OpenFTV (fill the ADL fields) need an owner.

docs.title: EUDI issuance
docs.text:
• Open: F-47 (attestation about a related person), F-81 (designation, TS 119 471, and the certificate profile), F-82 (an issuer must track source changes), and F-83 (wallet approval is no legal basis).
  • PSA to decide:
    1. Who designates the PuB-EAA issuer and who supervises (Q-28). Add art. 3(46) and TS 119 471 to B-13.
    2. Per attestation type: short-lived, or long-lived with a change notification stream from the source.
    3. Separate the terms "consent" (DvTP) and "approval" (wallet) in the GO and the PSA. - The relation in a related-person attestation is enforced through schema filters instead of source code (REQ-57).

docs.title: Authentic Source Interface
docs.text:
• Open: F-80, F-84 to F-89, and F-91 to F-96.
  • Decided in the TO: the ASI is an OAuth front door per ETSI TS 119 478 clause 6.1, and the QTSP is not an FSC participant (ADR-0037). Each source has one data service, with one token per data service (ADR-0038). The source describes its ASI attributes (ADR-0039). Two ADRs are proposed: the seal format (ADR-0041) and the optional per-attribute binding (ADR-0042).
  • PSA to decide (S11, B-14): Annex IV and the seal duty apply from January 1, 2027. The PSA must decide five points:
    1. The role of GBO and the designated intermediary (Q-37, Q-28), and who holds the qualified seal certificate (Q-17, Q-32).
    2. One security profile for Dutch authorization servers, including iss per RFC 9207 (Q-66, F-84, F-96).
    3. The accepted identification means, and identification data in the token that only the ASIP can read (Q-36, F-86, F-88, F-94).
    4. A check that links the QTSP login to the login at the authorization server (Q-40, F-93), and per-attribute binding under art. 9(5) (Q-33).
    5. Whether the ASI returns the value on a match, and fuzzy matching (Q-29, F-92). Also the register and the certificate link for QTSP admission (Q-34, Q-35). - The specification gaps go to ETSI ESI: E1 to E10. The sender is not decided.

docs.title: Source texts
docs.text: • Open: F-97 and F-98. The owner of FR-DvTP makes FR-22 to FR-26, FR-35, and FR-39 match the decisions. The PSA authors fix the meaning of "transparent" in S02.

docs.title: Demo increments
docs.text:
A demo increment (ID SL-NN) is a bounded piece of demo work. Each increment proved part of the design and produced requirements, findings, and open questions. The IDs are stable anchors: the design to demo matrix, the findings, the open questions, and the requirement pages refer to them. The issues and pull requests of ICTU/GBO-demo track the work itself.

Each increment entry uses the same fields:

  • Status values: done, planned, blocked, dropped, merged, or partly covered.
  • Demo work: links go to ICTU/GBO-demo only. The public repository started with v0.1.0 on July 20, 2026. Increments SL-01a to SL-42 were built before that date, so they have no public pull request. The code that they produced is in the public history from v0.1.0.
  • Produced: the IDs that the increment created or changed. If a later increment replaced the result, the entry names the successor.
  • Explained in: the TO page that explains the result.

Demo work outside increments lists the demo work that was not part of an increment.

docs.title: SL-01a: Consent TTL and finer denial reasons
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: the consent register (toestemmingsregister) sets an expiry time, and the policy denies an expired consent. If the expiry time is missing or unreadable, the policy also denies. The policy gives a separate reason code for each failed check (not found, withdrawn, expired, scope mismatch, and field not in consent).
  • Produced: REQ-19, REQ-06 (made more precise), and part of F-04.
  • Explained in: Consent

docs.title: SL-01b: Single use and status machine
docs.text:
• Status: blocked
  • Demo work: none.
  • What it showed: not built. The increment waited on Q-04 (single use or repeatable). Q-04 is answered: FR-DvTP v0.9 makes a consent repeatable within its validity period, so single use is not necessary. The status "retrieved" from FR-22 is open: Q-42 asks who marks a consent as retrieved, and when.
  • Produced: rest of F-04 (closed), F-19.
  • Explained in: Consent

docs.title: SL-02: Pseudonymization in the path
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: the demo kept the BSN away from private consumers without a decision on the pseudonym form (Q-01). The consent register stored a polymorphic identity (PI) instead of the BSN. The PEP resolved the BSN only after an allow. For a denied request, the PEP did not resolve the BSN at all.
  • Produced: REQ-20 and REQ-21. Later, the conversion moved to the source gateway (SL-22). Since SL-51, the proof carries a value per source, and the source decrypts it after the decision.
  • Explained in: Pseudonymization

docs.title: SL-03a: AST field parsing in OPA
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: the policy parses the real GraphQL query, with schema validation, instead of a regex in the PEP. The fields in the query must be a subset of the allowed fields of the scope. If a query does not parse, it gets a deny.
  • Produced: REQ-17, and model B (field allowlist) for Q-14.
  • Explained in: Authorization

docs.title: SL-03b: Constraint axis (4b) and two-schema model
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: the policy checked that the query carried the consent ID and that it matched the authorization context. A consumer-facing schema without BSN stood next to the internal source schema, and the PEP translated between them.
  • Produced: REQ-25 to REQ-27 (removed later, successors REQ-79 and REQ-17), and REQ-06 (new reason codes). Later, the query translation moved to the source gateway (SL-42).
  • Explained in: Authorization

docs.title: SL-04: Persist OPA decision logs
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: the PDP logs every decision with a decision ID, the reason, and the trace ID of the request. Loki stores the log, and a Grafana panel links each decision to its trace.
  • Produced: REQ-32 (REQ-31 merged into REQ-71), and the audit part of F-07.
  • Explained in: Logging

docs.title: SL-05: FSC sector-grant check
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: organization permission is an authorization concern of its own, next to the legal basis. The demo checked a sector-level grant per service. FSC has no sector concept (F-36). #378 removed the sector-pip. Since SL-45, a register gives the admission.
  • Produced: part of F-08 (REQ-33 and REQ-34, removed later).
  • Explained in: ADR-0022, Contract admission and source activation

docs.title: SL-06a: User demo flow A: consent issuance
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: a citizen goes from a mock service provider (dienstverlener) website to the consent portal (toestemmingsportaal) inside a MijnOverheid shell. He logs in with a DigiD mock, gives consent, and returns. The redirect carries the consumer, the service, the purpose, the data sets, and the return address. The result page fetches real data through the whole chain.
  • Produced: REQ-37, F-15, F-16, F-17, and F-18.
  • Explained in: Citizen grants consent

docs.title: SL-06b: User demo flow B: access under MijnOverheid
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: a citizen sees his consents under MijnOverheid, with status active, expired, or revoked, and opens a detail page. He can revoke a consent after he approves the revoke in a dialog. The next request on that consent gets a deny.
  • Produced:
    • requirements REQ-38, REQ-39, REQ-40, and REQ-14 (REQ-41 merged into it)
    • findings F-19, F-20, and F-17 (widened)
  • Explained in: Citizen views and revokes consents

docs.title: SL-07: Restore trace correlation
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: trace context propagates end to end. One trace covered all services of a request.
  • Produced: no requirement. The result is the basis for REQ-55.
  • Explained in: Logging

docs.title: SL-08: Consent PIP through PEP pre-fetch
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: the PEP fetched the consent record and gave it to the policy as input, so the policy engine made no network call. Since PR #371, the flow is reversed: the policy verifies the signed consent proof and asks the register for the status itself.
  • Produced: REQ-18 and F-22. Later, REQ-68 replaced this result.

docs.title: SL-28: Authentic Source Interface (QTSP verification)
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: epic ICTU/GBO-demo#336, closed on October 27, 2026. The numbered list after this entry gives the parts of the epic.
  • What it showed: an ASIP mock to ETSI TS 119 478 clause 6.1, with its own authorization server, a reference QTSP, and a conformance matrix in CI. The QTSP is not an FSC participant. The generic chain (FSC, PDP, source gateway, and source) starts behind the ASIP (F-87). The citizen logs in with a DigiD mock or the NL Wallet.
  • Explained in: QTSP verification (ASI route), ADR-0037, ADR-0038, ADR-0039, Feedback on ETSI TS 119 478

Epic #336 has 14 parts:

  1. Verify and retrieve with a seal (#498, PR #499). The ASIP verifies and retrieves against an in-memory source. It gives the four verification results, the published contract, and a seal on each result. Produced: REQ-83, REQ-84, REQ-85, F-80, and Q-32.
  2. Authorization server (#503, PR #504, PR #522, and refactor PR #505). The authorization server implements clause 6.1.3 with PKCE, private_key_jwt, DPoP, and JWT tokens. It also has dynamic client registration with a sealed software statement, a stub register, and a periodic re-check. Produced: REQ-86 to REQ-89, F-84, F-85, F-86, Q-33, Q-34, and Q-35.
  3. Citizen approves or refuses (#523, PR #524). The transaction is one-time, short-lived, and bound to the browser. The token carries PID attributes. Produced: REQ-90, REQ-91, F-88, and Q-36.
  4. Chain behind the ASIP (#525, PR #526, PR #527, PR #529, PR #530, PR #532). The ASIP is an FSC peer and asks the BRP over FSC under rule ASI0001. Each source has one data service and one token, each request causes one source request, and every rule names its services. Produced: REQ-92 to REQ-95, REQ-97, F-87, F-89, F-90, Q-37, and Q-38. REQ-96 merged into REQ-91, and REQ-98 was removed.
  5. Discovery records: merged into part 6.
  6. Discovery and conformance matrix (#533, PR #534, PR #535, PR #536, PR #537, PR #538, PR #539, PR #540, PR #541, PR #542). The part added a record per data service for the Discover Interface, and a reference QTSP. It also added a conformance matrix per ETSI requirement with a check in CI, and a 404 for a retrieve without a value. Produced: REQ-99 to REQ-101, F-91, F-92, Q-39, and Q-29.
  7. NL Wallet identification (#546, PR #550, PR #551, PR #552). The ASI route uses OpenID4VP with the verifier of nl-wallet. A run with the real NL Wallet is recorded. Produced: REQ-102, F-93, F-94, and Q-40.
  8. Documentation and security notes (PR #574). The documentation tells what is real, stub, interpretation, or shortcut. It gives a choice per point of RFC 9700 and FAPI 2.0. Produced: F-96, Q-41, F-84 (extended), and the ETSI feedback list.
  9. Protect the BSN in the token: not done. #595 tracks the follow-up.
  10. DigiD mock and one request screen (#544, PR #545). The legal name of the QTSP comes from the register. The consent is fixed only after a successful identification. The token carries the means (acr/amr). Produced: REQ-86, REQ-90, REQ-91 (validated), F-88, and Q-36.
  11. House style and consent screen (#547, PR #559, and optional binding in #571, PR #572). The consent screen uses plain language. RFC 9396 authorization_details binds the token to the attributes. Without a configuration that requires it, this binding is optional. Produced: REQ-91, REQ-103, F-95, and Q-33.
  12. Same-device login with the NL Wallet (#548, PR #573). The ASI route accepts the return only in the browser of the transaction. Produced: REQ-102 and F-93. #596 tracks the real run on one phone.
  13. Wallet issuance by the reference QTSP (#549, PR #570, and tools PR #566, PR #567). After a successful result, the reference QTSP issues a marked test attestation. Produced: F-93. REQ-105 was removed.
  14. Citizen logs in at the reference QTSP (#560, PR #562, PR #563, PR #564). Produced: F-93 and Q-40. REQ-104 was removed.

The close of the epic (PR #590, PR #591, PR #593) made the consent page name the QTSP that gets consent (REQ-91). On October 28, 2026, the GBO profile on ETSI TS 119 478 followed (ASI profile). The profile produced REQ-112 to REQ-115 and Q-64 to Q-67.

Epic #336 has four follow-ups:

  • #592: the source describes its attributes in its source metadata. Steps 1 to 5 are in v0.9.0 (PR #623, PR #624, and earlier). In demo v0.9.0, every ASI data service names an authentic source (Q-38, ADR-0039).
  • #594: the ASI route in the simulation environment, and an external QTSP.
  • #595: protect the BSN in the token (F-86).
  • #596: the real run of same-device login.

docs.title: SL-29: BSN out of the EDI decision logs
docs.text:

docs.text:

docs.title: SL-33: EUD0001 explicit scope and actor authorization
docs.text:

docs.text:

docs.title: SL-38: FSC txlog observability and trace ID equal to Fsc-Transaction-Id
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: before the public repository.
  • What it showed: FSC v2.4.0 does not propagate trace context, and its plugins drop the request context. The demo made the trace ID equal to the FSC transaction ID and read the FSC transaction logs. SL-50 reversed the key: W3C Trace Context is the key, and the demo records the transaction ID next to it (F-67).

docs.text:
• Status: done

docs.text:

docs.text:
• Status: done

  • What it showed: DvTP runs over real FSC too, with a second consumer organization. The demo removed the fsc-mock and the PEP service. The PDP is the only policy endpoint for DvTP and EUDI. The source gateway does the conversion after the decision (SL-22, SL-23).

docs.title: SL-43: Death certificate: BRP source and second EUDI attestation (subject differs from discloser)
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: PR #125
  • What it showed: a second source (BRP) and a second attestation. A surviving partner discloses his PID and gets the death certificate of the partner. The subject of the attestation is not the person who discloses. Each bronhouder needs its own certificate set for issuance.
  • Produced:
    • findings F-47, F-49, and F-50

docs.title: SL-44: OpenFTV Manager: policy management and distribution through bundles (PAP)
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: PR #208
  • What it showed: the PAP runs at the source side. Git stays the source of truth, and policy goes to the PDP as an identified, versioned bundle. The management API has its own policy set. If the store is empty, the management API denies. Push distribution, delete, and masking of decision logs do not work in this configuration.
  • Produced:
    • findings F-51, F-52, F-53, and F-54
    • requirements REQ-59 and REQ-60
    • guidelines RL-01 to RL-05
    • open question Q-21
    • most of F-09 closed
  • Explained in: Policy distribution, Policy lifecycle, ADR-0021

docs.title: SL-45: Admission as a register and contract decision by the PDP
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: PR #228, PR #239, PR #241
  • What it showed: admission is a registration instead of a policy rule. The PDP decides each contract proposal in a policy tree of its own, with machine-readable reason codes. An automatic "no" leaves the proposal pending, so it is recoverable. Admission is per bronhouder. The demo has no admission per service.
  • Produced:
    • findings F-55 and F-56
    • requirements REQ-61, REQ-62, and REQ-63
    • open question Q-22
  • Explained in: Contract admission and source activation, ADR-0015

docs.title: SL-46: Generic source metadata: source publishes, GBO validates and activates
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: PR #219, PR #224, PR #237, PR #247, PR #276
  • What it showed: each source publishes its service description on /.well-known/gbo: query, parameters, mapping, attestation schema, and offers. GBO validates the description against a profile and activates it as an explicit step. A valid contract does not activate the description. If a description is bad or old, it fails closed per source, and it can be rolled back.
  • Produced:
    • findings F-57, F-58, and F-59
    • requirements REQ-64, REQ-65, and REQ-66
    • Q-19 answered for EUDI
    • a direction for F-21, F-22, and F-23
    • Q-17 (sub-question 6)
    • in demo v0.9.0, REQ-64 built for EUDI and the ASIP (#592) and not for DvTP
  • Explained in: Source onboarding, ADR-0016

docs.title: SL-47: Signed, actor-bound consent proof
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: PR #238
  • What it showed: the consent register issues a signed consent proof (ES256, with a JWKS). The policy verifies the signature and binds the consumer in the proof to the verified caller. The status check stays online and fails closed. The validity period is in the signed proof, so the consumer cannot change it.
  • Produced: F-61, REQ-68, and REQ-69. The increment closed F-24 and F-44, and sharpened Q-05. REQ-13, REQ-25, and REQ-27 were revised and removed later.
  • Explained in: Consent, ADR-0032

docs.title: SL-48: Flow dispatch cleaned up: no default regime, no flow header
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: PR #236
  • What it showed: the demo removed the default regime, and the regime header that a consumer was able to send. If a request had no signed flow property, it matched no rule and got a deny. PR #363 removed the flow property too (REQ-74).
  • Produced: the premise of F-49 lapsed. REQ-56 was tightened, then removed and replaced by REQ-74.
  • Explained in: ADR-0031

docs.title: SL-49: Identity separation: FSC Peer ID separate from source OIN
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: PR #242, PR #244, PR #247, PR #277
  • What it showed: the FSC Peer ID (transport identity) and the OIN of the source (legal identity) are recorded apart. The OIN and the name of the organization come from the verified issuer certificate. CA private keys stay out of the application runtime.
  • Produced: F-60 and REQ-67. The increment sharpened Q-06 and Q-07.
  • Explained in: Organization identity and trust

docs.title: SL-50: LDV and ADL exploration: three logging standards, one trace ID
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work: build in #302, and review and correction in PR #366.
  • What it showed: three related logging standards apply. The decision log already implements the Authorization Decision Log (ADL). The gap is at the processing: each GBO component that processes personal data writes a Logboek Dataverwerkingen (LDV) log line at its controller (Verantwoordelijke). The trace ID from traceparent links the logs, and each controller logs its own pseudonym.
  • Produced:
    • findings F-63, F-64, F-65, F-67, F-68, and F-69
    • requirements REQ-71, REQ-72, REQ-55 (revised), and AV-01 (was REQ-73)
    • open questions Q-08, Q-23, Q-24, and Q-25
    • F-53 answered
  • Explained in: Logging, ADR-0026, ADR-0035, ADR-0036

docs.title: SL-51: Encrypted identity per source in the consent proof, replaced after the decision
docs.text:
• Status: done
  • Demo work:
    • ICTU/GBO-demo#468 and PR #469, the first part of #364, on the BSNk mock from PR #466.
    • the follow-up in #473: PR #475 removed subject_id_type, and PR #476 added two placeholders, one per form. PR #477 added a pseudonym for each source, an identity for a source on the BSN authorization list, and more than four parties.
  • What it showed: the design works with the BSNk interface. At the consent, the portal backend activates and transforms. The proof carries an encrypted value per source, and the consumer sends a placeholder. The PDP decides on that placeholder. Only after an allow, the source decrypts its own value, without a call to BSNk.
  • Produced:
    • findings F-76, F-77, F-78, and F-79
    • requirements REQ-79, REQ-80, REQ-81, REQ-82, and REQ-21 (revised)
    • open questions Q-27, Q-26 (sub-question 8), and Q-01 (extended)
    • BSNK-05 and BSNK-06, tried on the mock
  • Not built:
    • a pseudonym for the consumer (#478)
    • the subject variable in one place (#479)
    • an API that answers on a pseudonym (#474)
    • onboarding of keys (#467)
  • Explained in: Pseudonymization, Consumer queries under consent, ADR-0032, ADR-0033

docs.title: Demo work outside increments
docs.text:
From September 14 to 16, 2026, the demo work ran through demo issues instead of an increment. This work produced the following IDs:

  • PR #284 and PR #363: the regime follows from the evidence of the request instead of a grant property. Produced: F-70 and REQ-74. F-62 is resolved, and SL-24 is dropped. REQ-56 was partly replaced and removed later.
  • PR #370 and PR #371: the request mapper does only GraphQL mapping. The policy verifies the consent proof and asks for the status. Produced: REQ-68, F-61, Q-05, Q-23, and Q-25. The BSN is in both decision logs on purpose, so REQ-60 is not met (F-54).
  • PR #372: make policy-check is a local safety net. Produced: RL-05 and F-52.
  • PR #373: the ADL is the audit source. Produced: F-72 and REQ-71. The rest of F-53 and F-63 is done. A check against a running stack showed the gap of REQ-59: the records carry no policy version.
  • PR #337: OpenFTV v0.1.0 makes the ADL mandatory (REQ-71). A silent bundle 403 led to F-52 and RL-05.
  • PR #318: the demo has a file transport for source metadata. Produced: F-71, an exception in REQ-64, and Q-06.
  • PR #321: the description of the issuer comes from the certificate (REQ-67).

The same round recorded three observations in issues:

  • #369: the ADL record behind the Inway has no trace and no transaction ID. Related: F-41, REQ-55, and REQ-71.
  • #225: the choice between one shared certificate set and a set per source. Related: REQ-58, Q-07, and Q-17.
  • #133: the callback from the issuance server to the adapter has no authentication. Related: F-70 and Q-18.

Later, PR #464 (#379) added more demo work outside increments. An integrator calls under FSC delegation, and the consent binds the represented party. Produced: REQ-106, F-73, Q-46, and ADR-0034.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: each increment lists the requirements it produced.
  • Findings: each increment lists its findings. For all findings, see Findings.
  • Open questions: each increment lists its open questions. For all questions, see Open questions.
  • Design coverage: Design to demo matrix.

docs.title: Design to demo matrix
docs.text:
This matrix lists the design elements of four sources:

  • the Globaal Ontwerp (GO),
  • the Projectstartarchitectuur (PSA),
  • the functional requirements for DvTP (FR-DvTP v0.9),
  • the EUDI regulation.

For each element, the matrix records if the GBO demo covers it, and gives the evidence. The findings and the open questions give the reverse direction, from demo to design.

Each row has a status, an evidence link, and a note on the state of the demo. The notes link to the requirements, findings, open questions, demo increments, and ADRs that explain the row. The port to the TO on November 2, 2026 brought the evidence and the notes up to demo v0.9.0. No status changed.

docs.title: Coverage summary
docs.text:
The summary counts the rows on this page. It does not count the historical rows of the reference architecture.

Group ✓ ◐ ○ In scope Hook or out Rows P: architecture principles 2 12 1 15 1 16 D: design principles 4 8 2 14 0 14 F: generic functions 1 4 3 8 0 8 S: capabilities 3 7 0 10 1 11 PAT: interaction patterns 1 1 0 2 1 3 EUDI: EUDI wallet and regulation 0 8 3 11 0 11 B: open decisions 0 12 2 14 5 19 FR: FR-DvTP v0.9 8 22 7 37 2 39 Total 19 74 18 111 10 121

Of the 111 in-scope rows, 17% are covered, 67% are partial, and 16% are not covered.

Most partial rows can become covered only after a governance decision or with production infrastructure. Three examples of such rows are:

  • the LDV schema and retention (Q-08),
  • the link of organization identifiers in PSA S04,
  • PKIoverheid certificates instead of the demo CA (the direction is answered in Q-07).

Three items of concrete demo work are open in demo v0.9.0:

  • validate a policy set before activation (F-52),
  • admission per service (#382),
  • the BSN in the ASI token (#595).

docs.title: Legend
docs.text:
The status column uses five symbols:

Status Meaning ✓ Covered: the feature works end to end in the demo, with evidence. ◐ Partial: some parts are covered, and the rest is open. ○ Not covered: in scope, but not built. — Out of scope or hook: deliberately not in v1. ? To be checked against the demo. In demo v0.9.0, no row has this status.

The scope column uses five values:

Scope Meaning Base The shared foundation for all routes: PEP, PDP, PIP, connectivity, audit, and semantics. DvTP Specific to the consent route (data sharing with third parties). EUDI Specific to the EUDI wallet routes: issuance (PuB-EAA) and verification for QTSPs (ASI). Hook Not in v1, but the demo keeps an extension point open. Out Not relevant for the v1 demo.

The evidence column follows three rules:

  • A status is valid only with evidence. The evidence is a link to the demo at v0.9.0, a demo pull request or issue, or a requirement that carries the evidence.
  • Some links pin an older demo commit. They are historical evidence for the state at the time of the check.
  • FR-DvTP v0.9 is not public. The matrix names its criteria without a link.

docs.title: Architecture principles (P-01 to P-16)
docs.text:
Source: PSA architecture principles. These principles are invariants: the demo must not break them.

ID Title Scope Status Evidence Notes P-01 Legal basis before exchange Base ◐ REQ-68, REQ-14, REQ-19 Before an allow, the PDP checks that the consent is valid, unexpired, and not revoked. A legal-basis path (government to government) is out of scope. P-02 Minimal data processing Base ◐ REQ-08, REQ-17 The PDP decides each field of the parsed query (SL-03a). Under a consent, the subject comes only from the proof (REQ-79). P-03 Privacy by design and by default Base ◐ REQ-80, REQ-21, REQ-23, REQ-69, REQ-82 The register holds no BSN. The proof carries an encrypted value per source, and the consumer gets no identifier (SL-51). In the demo, BSNk is a mock, and the pseudonym form is open (Q-01). P-04 BSN-free for private consumers DvTP ✓ consent_token.go#L47 (no plain BSN in the proof), decryption.go#L76 (the source decrypts its own value) The consumer has no identifier at all: it sends a placeholder, and the source replaces it after the allow (REQ-79, REQ-80, SL-51). F-76 describes the effects on logging and recognition. P-05 Recognized authentication means at an adequate level of assurance Base ○ DigiD mock in the consent portal (toestemmingsportaal) (DigiDAuth.tsx), ASI authorization server with DigiD mock and NL Wallet (client.go#L119) The demo has no real means at a set level of assurance. Real means are out of scope. Q-36 asks which level ETSI TS 119 461 requires for the ASI route, and if DigiD meets it. P-06 Support for the EUDI wallet Hook — — The principle row stays a hook. The wallet routes are in the EUDI rows. P-07 Trust through recognized admission and trust anchors Base ◐ fsc-infra/pki, REQ-67 The demo runs real OpenFSC with mTLS and its own CA (SL-34a). The certificate carries the legal identity (SL-49, F-60). Open: PKIoverheid certificates instead of the demo CA (direction answered in Q-07). Also open: the issuing model, with one certificate set or a set per source (#225). P-08 Record once, use many times Base ◐ REQ-11 The source stays authoritative, and GBO components keep no copy. The demo does not show reuse explicitly. P-09 Open standards and vendor independence Base ◐ docker-compose.yml GraphQL, OPA, AuthZEN, OpenFSC with mTLS, OTel, OpenID4VCI, and OpenID4VP are open standards. The GraphQL profile for FSC is a proposal and has no standard status (B-02). P-10 Data sovereignty: the bronhouder keeps control Base ◐ source_metadata.go#L101 (validation of the source description), dvtp-onboarding-register, autosign.rego#L171 The source decides who connects (SL-45), what is available (REQ-64, F-57), and when (REQ-65). The PDP behind the source Inway checks each request (F-06 closed). In demo v0.9.0, REQ-64 is built for EUDI and the ASIP (#592). It is not built for DvTP. P-11 FAIR principles for data Base ◐ REQ-64, AV-07 Findable and accessible: each source publishes a versioned description at a fixed location. Not interoperable or reusable: the mapping is per source, with no canonical model (Q-11). P-12 Logging and non-repudiation Base ◐ docker-compose.yml#L125 (ADL), adl.go, ldv-logboek The ADL is the audit source (REQ-71), with an LDV logbook per system (REQ-72) and one trace ID (REQ-55). Open: the BSN in both decision logs (REQ-60, F-54, #368), field detail only in the console log (F-72), and production guarantees (Q-08, F-07). P-13 Transparency and access for the citizen DvTP ✓ REQ-38, REQ-39, REQ-40 For each consent, the citizen sees who, what, purpose, and duration, and can revoke the consent (SL-06a, SL-06b). Missing: usage status (F-19) and processing per consent (Q-25). P-14 Separation of generic and specific functions Base ◐ REQ-44, REQ-92 Each capability is a service of its own, and the front ends call it directly (SL-11, SL-15). The EUDI adapter holds no use-case knowledge (SL-46). The generic chain also runs behind the ASIP (F-87). P-15 Decoupling for agility Base ◐ gbo-pdp.yaml Policy changes reach the PDP as a bundle, without a new PDP image (SL-44, RL-01). Mostly covered. P-16 Transparent access for private parties Base ◐ dvtp-onboarding-register, autosign.rego#L171 Admission is a registration, and each contract proposal gets an explicit decision with reasons (REQ-61, REQ-62, REQ-63). Missing: the grounds (FR-30), an objection procedure, and admission per service (F-56, #382). Q-22 gives the answer on grounds and granularity.

docs.title: Design principles (D-01 to D-14)
docs.text:
Source: PSA design principles.

ID Title Scope Status Evidence Notes D-01 Decentral where possible, central where necessary Base ◐ fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml#L773 (one shared PDP) One shared PDP behind all Inways is a demo shortcut. A PDP per source is possible with bundles (SL-44). Q-02 is answered: federated, per bronhouder. D-02 Agreements before standards before facilities Base ○ — This is governance, and the demo cannot show it. D-03 Use national generic facilities (GDI) unless Base ○ — DigiD, BSNk and MijnOverheid are mocks. Real GDI facilities are out of scope. D-04 Robust, modular, and flexible design Base ◐ services/ The services are modular. Some services run in memory or as a mock. D-05 Data at the source, no unnecessary copies Base ✓ REQ-11 GBO components fetch per request from the source and keep no copy. D-06 Component-based working Base ✓ services/ The services are separate and reusable. D-07 Open source unless Base ✓ docker-compose.yml All components are open source. D-08 Comply or explain: mandatory open standards Base ◐ — The demo uses GraphQL, JWT, OTel, and FSC with mTLS. The GraphQL profile for FSC is open (B-02). D-09 API-first Base ✓ graphql-server, openftv-pdp All interaction goes through APIs. D-10 Information security and privacy by design Base ◐ PR #242 (CA keys outside the runtime), PR #222, PR #220, REQ-69, REQ-66 The demo has mTLS over FSC, CA keys outside the application runtime, no per-party values in the register, and source metadata that fails closed. Open: there is no penetration test or audit (D-12), and the demo uses its own CA instead of PKIoverheid (Q-07). D-11 Least privilege Base ◐ REQ-48, REQ-81 The demo limits the fields per scope and takes the subject from the proof. Every rule names its services (REQ-97), and only the Inway reaches the source gateway. F-08 is closed: no source requires a certificate-bound token. D-12 Demonstrable security: audit and penetration testing Base ◐ policies/gbo (policy tests), etsi-ts-119478.yaml Policy unit tests and an ETSI conformance matrix with a check in CI. No penetration test or audit. D-13 Standardize where possible Base ◐ dvt0001.rego#L65 The scope convention bd:ib:<year> is ad hoc. D-14 Interoperability: semantic and technical alignment Base ◐ graphql-server The source schemas follow the gbo-semantiek v0.3 source profiles. There is no canonical semantic model.

docs.title: Generic functions (F1 to F8)
docs.text:
Source: PSA generic functions and section 4 of the GO.

ID Title Scope Status Evidence Notes F1 Identity and trust Base ◐ fsc-infra, dvtp-onboarding-register Organizations connect as real FSC peers with mTLS, and a register admits them (REQ-61). Transport identity and legal identity are apart (REQ-67). The citizen login is a mock. The demo uses its own CA, and production uses PKIoverheid (Q-07). F2 Access and interaction Base ✓ REQ-04, REQ-46 The chain FSC Outway → Inway → PDP → source works end to end. F3 Data provision Base ◐ REQ-11, REQ-97 Three sources answer over FSC: BD, BRP, and LVG. Each DvTP consent and each request reaches only one source (FR-38). F4 Semantics and common language Base ○ — No canonical model. The mapping is per source. F5 Data quality and validation Base ○ — The demo has no validation layer. F6 Legal basis and policy Base ◐ REQ-68, REQ-14, REQ-19 Consent works as legal basis, and policy management runs (SL-44). The demo has no legal-basis path. F7 Orchestration and integration Base ○ — The demo has no orchestration or integration layer. An integrator can call under FSC delegation (REQ-106), but there is no FDS broker. F8 Management and continuity Base ◐ openftv-manager-ui, openftv-manager/authz Policy management has roles and a management interface (RL-02, RL-03). Continuity is weak: one bad rule stops every decision (F-52, RL-05).

docs.title: Capabilities (S01 to S11)
docs.text:
Source: PSA capabilities.

ID Title Scope Status Evidence Notes S01 Consent registration DvTP ◐ consent_token.go#L47, postgres_store.go The register issues the signed proof (REQ-68) and keeps the polymorphic values under its own reference (REQ-69). It signs the value per source and does not store it (REQ-80, F-78, REQ-82). The local stack runs in memory (SL-12). S02 Consent portal (citizen interaction) DvTP ✓ REQ-38, REQ-39, REQ-40 The portal has its own backend and front end on a government origin, a DigiD mock token, and an ownership check on revoke (SL-11, SL-06b). Not built: the acknowledgment that the citizen read the text (REQ-107), and the export (REQ-108). S03 Citizen identification and pseudonymization Base ✓ bsnk.go#L65 (activate), bsnk.go#L106 (transform), decryption.go#L76 The portal backend activates and transforms at the consent. The source decrypts its own value after the allow (REQ-21, REQ-81). The BSNk mock follows the BSNk interface. S04 Organization authentication and trust framework Base ◐ fsc-infra, autosign.rego#L171 A register admits organizations to the system, and the PDP decides on contracts (REQ-61, REQ-62). Transport and legal identity are apart (REQ-67, F-60). Open: PKIoverheid certificates in place of the demo CA (Q-07). S05 Authorization (PEP/PDP/PIP) Base ◐ engine.rego#L173 (regime), consent.rego#L268 (status), ftvgraphql.go The regime follows from the evidence (REQ-74, F-70). The policy verifies the proof and asks for the status (REQ-68). The subject must be a placeholder (REQ-79, F-77), and every rule names its services (REQ-97). The contract decision has a policy tree of its own (REQ-62). S06 Policy management and distribution (PAP) Base ◐ gbo-pdp.yaml, seed-openftv-manager.py The PAP runs at the source side and distributes versioned bundles (RL-01 to RL-04). These RL items are guidelines: management stays with each bronhouder (Q-21). Open: validation before activation (F-52, RL-05), push distribution (F-51), and the policy version in the decision record (REQ-59). S07 Data access (source access API) Base ✓ REQ-17, REQ-97 GraphQL source access works for three sources. PSA S07 asks for pre-registered selective queries. The DvTP path lets the consumer send free queries within a field allowlist (Q-14). S08 OOTS adapter Hook — — Not in v1 (ADR-0020). S09 Logging, audit and traceability Base ◐ adl.go, ldv-logboek, request-flow.json The ADL is the audit source (REQ-71). Each system has an LDV logbook (REQ-72), and the trace comes from traceparent (REQ-55, F-67). Open: the BSN in the decision logs (REQ-60), and the record behind the Inway without a trace (#369). Also open: the read route to the consent log (Q-25, F-68), and the register of processing activities (Q-08). S10 Semantics and data catalogue Base ◐ gbo-source-metadata-v1.schema.json, source_metadata.go#L101 The source owns its service description on /.well-known/gbo, and GBO validates and activates it (F-57, REQ-64). In demo v0.9.0, this is built for EUDI and the ASIP. DvTP scopes come from rule files on the GBO side (F-17). There is no DCAT-AP-NL reference and no central findability. F-74 covers the DvTP catalogue per FR-32. S11 Attestation issuance (PuB-EAA / QEAA) EUDI ◐ eudi-issuance-server, eudi-adapter, eud0002.rego Issuance works for products of two sources (SL-43, REQ-57, REQ-58). Missing: a qualified seal and a trust list. F-80 and F-81 cover the regulation, F-82 covers change notification, and Q-30 covers the trust list.

docs.title: Interaction patterns
docs.text:
Source: PSA interaction patterns and section 3 of the GO.

ID Title Scope Status Evidence Notes PAT-A Citizen uses the EUDI wallet EUDI ◐ REQ-45, REQ-64 The route works end to end against a pre-production wallet, with products from offers that the sources publish (SL-46). Missing: a seal, trust lists, and an authenticated adapter callback (#133). For more information, see EUDI-3 to EUDI-5. PAT-B Cross-border SDG/OOTS Hook — — Not in v1 (ADR-0020). PAT-C Data request by a private service provider (dienstverlener) in DvTP DvTP ✓ REQ-68, REQ-14, REQ-19 Consent, query, allow or deny, and revoke work end to end, for the BD and LVG sources, and through an integrator (PR #464).

docs.title: EUDI wallet and regulation (EUDI-1 to EUDI-11)
docs.text:
The EUDI rows have five sources:

  • the GO sections on attestation issuance and on the verification service for QTSPs,
  • PSA S11,
  • eIDAS article 45e,
  • the implementing regulations (EU) 2025/1569 and 2026/1735,
  • ETSI TS 119 478.

The EUDI-NN IDs belong to this matrix.

ID Title Scope Status Evidence Notes EUDI-1 PuB-EAA provider and OpenID4VCI issuance EUDI ◐ REQ-58, REQ-64, REQ-77 Issuance works against mock trust (ADR-0018). PuB-EAA issuance falls under ETSI TS 119 471 and needs designation (F-81, Q-28). EUDI-2 Authentic Source Interface (QTSP verification, art. 45e) EUDI ◐ seal.go#L45, registration.go#L222 (re-check), asi0001.rego#L23, etsi-ts-119478.yaml, asi-route.md SL-28 is done. It built sealed verify and retrieve, its own authorization server, and the chain behind the ASIP over FSC. It also built discovery, a reference QTSP, and login with a DigiD mock and the NL Wallet. The GBO profile is in the ASI profile: REQ-83 to REQ-115. Open: the BSN in the token (#595, F-86), and an external QTSP (#594). The ASIP has no certification and seals with a development certificate. EUDI-3 PID presentation and signature verification EUDI ◐ client.go#L119 (ASI route) ASI route: the nl-wallet verifier verifies the PID against a fixed list of issuers (REQ-102). Issuance route: the issuance server verifies the PID. The callback to the adapter has no authentication, so nothing binds the BSN to the verified disclosure (#133, REQ-45, F-70). EUDI-4 Qualified seal and signing infrastructure (eIDAS2, ARF) EUDI ○ — The demo has no qualified seal. The ASIP seals with a development certificate (REQ-83). For more information, see FR-27. EUDI-5 Trusted lists and trust anchors EUDI ○ — The demo uses mock trust. The list on which PuB-EAA issuers appear is open (Q-30). EUDI-6 Attestation schemas and serialization (SD-JWT VC, mdoc) EUDI ◐ PR #224 (schemas published by the source, fixed per version) Each source publishes its schemas, and GBO validates and activates them (REQ-64). An integrity reference binds the schema to the credential. Q-20 (closed) covers the claim shape for related-person data. EUDI-7 Self-service access basis (subject = resource owner) EUDI ◐ engine.rego#L173, eud0001.rego The regime follows from the evidence (REQ-74). If a request carries no consent proof, it enters the PID regime. The PID regime has no positive evidence of its own (F-70, REQ-45). EUDI-8 Thin channel adapter / protocol translation EUDI ◐ source_metadata.go#L272 (query plan from the source description) The adapter cannot hold use-case knowledge: query, parameters, mapping, and offers come from the validated source description (REQ-64, REQ-44). It projects with gbo-simple-v1. If a result is ambiguous, the adapter fails closed (ADR-0017). EUDI-9 Issuer role and liability (PuB-EAA or QTSP) EUDI ○ — This is governance (Q-17). The reference QTSP issues a test attestation after an ASI verification (SL-28, part 13 of epic #336). Role and liability stay a governance matter. EUDI-10 Shared authorization service for both routes EUDI ◐ engine.rego#L173 One AuthZEN endpoint for DvTP, EUDI issuance and the ASI route. The regime follows from the evidence (REQ-74). Approval in the wallet is not a legal basis (F-83). EUDI-11 Related-person credential (subject of the claim is not the discloser) EUDI ◐ eud0002.rego, brp-graphql-server A surviving partner discloses his PID and gets the death certificate of the partner (SL-43). The source fixes the relation, and the PDP limits the output fields. REQ-57 prefers the relation as enforceable filters in the schema (#425). For more information, see F-47.

docs.title: Open decisions (B-01 to B-19)
docs.text:
Source: the PSA decision register. The status shows how far the demo tries out or follows the preferred direction of the PSA. Governance and organization decisions that the demo cannot try out have the status "—".

ID Title Scope Status Evidence Notes B-01 Governance of GBO agreements Base — — PSA direction: FDS as the base, with GDI and domain governance. This is governance. For more information, see Q-16. B-02 API profile for source access Base ◐ ftv-graphql-profile.md PSA direction: GraphQL, comply or explain. The demo uses GraphQL over FSC for all routes. The profile is a GBO proposal in the OpenFTV working group (#331). For more information, see Q-14. B-03 Service catalogue Base ◐ REQ-64 PSA direction: federated content, with a common profile for central findability. EUDI and ASI are federated. DvTP scopes are on the GBO side, without a ceiling per use case (#382, F-74). The demo has no central findability. B-04 PDP placement Base ◐ fsc-infra/docker-compose.yml#L773 PSA direction: several variants under one PEP-PDP interface. Demo shortcut: one shared PDP. A PDP per source works with bundles (SL-44). For more information, see Q-02 and Q-10. B-05 Policy governance Base ◐ RL-03 PSA direction: content ownership apart from technical management. The PAP splits read, write and publish (SL-44). Management stays with each bronhouder (Q-21). B-06 Consent in DvTP DvTP ◐ REQ-68 PSA direction: a central or nationally coherent facility, anchored in law, with an equivalent alternative. The demo has a central register and portal. Missing: the alternative (AV-15). For more information, see Q-05 and Q-13. B-07 Pseudonymous identity DvTP ◐ bsnk.go#L65, decryption.go#L76 The register holds no BSN (REQ-69). The demo follows the BSNk PP model on a mock (SL-51, REQ-80, BSNK-01 to BSNK-11, F-75). Open: recognition (Q-26), and a consumer pseudonym (Q-27, #478). B-08 Identity matching EUDI — — Not in v1: the PID carries the BSN, so no match is necessary (Q-18). B-09 Trust framework for private parties Base ◐ dvtp-onboarding-register PSA direction: FDS functions plus a legal and organizational framework. Demo: an admission register and FSC peers with certificates (SL-45, SL-49). The connection conditions are candidates for the framework. Q-07 and Q-22 give the answered direction. The PSA decision B-09 is open. B-10 Logging and citizen access Base ◐ REQ-55, REQ-71, REQ-72 PSA direction: logs stay decentral, correlation is federated. Open: the read route from ADL to LDV (Q-25) and the access model for the citizen (F-65, F-68). B-11 Semantic governance Base ○ — The mapping is per source, without shared concepts (F4, S10). For more information, see Q-11. B-12 OOTS function boundaries Hook — — Not in v1 (PAT-B). B-13 PuB-EAA issuance model EUDI ◐ REQ-58 The demo has a central issuance facility with a certificate set per source. Key management and seal are open (Q-17, #225). The issuer is the bronhouder or a designated body (F-81, Q-28). B-14 ASI provider EUDI ◐ see EUDI-2 The ASIP mock and the authorization server are two roles, each with its own keys. Neither is certified. Each source has one data service (REQ-94, F-89), and each data service has a discovery record (REQ-99, F-91). The interface and the seal are law from January 1, 2027 (F-80). Q-37 covers the role of GBO. B-15 Start of attestation issuance EUDI ◐ — PSA direction: several standardized start routes. The demo has one route: a QR code from the developer portal. B-16 GBO translation layer Base ○ — Not in the demo: all sources use GraphQL. B-17 Management of reference components Base — — Organization decision. The demo cannot try it out. B-18 Report of errors or suspected inaccuracies Base — — Not in v1. The PSA does not describe it in detail. B-19 Representation and authority credentials Base ◐ integrator.md First case: an integrator under FSC delegation. The decision uses the acting and the represented party (PR #464, F-73, REQ-106). Q-46 covers the integrator in the proof, and Q-73 covers citizen representation.

docs.title: FR-DvTP v0.9 (FR-01 to FR-39)
docs.text:
Source: the functional requirements for DvTP, v0.9. This version is a draft of July 6, 2026, and it is not public. FR-06 and FR-19 lapsed in v0.9. FR-DvTP is not in the document hierarchy of the GO. If they differ, the GO and the PSA lead.

ID Title Scope Status Evidence Notes FR-01 Citizen authentication with a recognized means DvTP ◐ REQ-24 The DigiD mock gives a token, and the backend takes the identity only from that token. Real DigiD and level of assurance are out of scope. FR-02 Configuration-driven delegation check DvTP ○ — The demo has no delegation check. FR-DvTP v0.9 lets a service allow or exclude delegation (REQ-118). For more information, see B-19. FR-03 Authentication of the private service provider with eHerkenning DvTP ○ — FR-03 is about the person who logs in for onboarding and management. The admission register has only a local operator. FR-33 and FR-34 cover system identity. FR-04 Access through a trusted government domain DvTP ✓ MijnOverheidLayout.tsx The consent screens are inside a MijnOverheid shell on their own origin, apart from the service provider (SL-06a, SL-11). FR-05 Consent details shown to the citizen (scope) DvTP ◐ PortaalConsent.tsx The portal shows who, purpose, source, valid until, and a choice per data set. Criterion 5 (the citizen adjusts the validity within bounds) is not built (#380). REQ-117 covers plain language. FR-06 Transparency about the integrator (lapsed) DvTP — — Lapsed in v0.9. The integrator role is in FR-18 and FR-37. FR-07 Understandable information (language level) DvTP ✓ scopeGroups.ts All texts are at language level B1. The citizen sees no technical terms. FR-08 Acknowledgment of understanding (force to read) DvTP ○ — The demo asks for no acknowledgment. When the citizen chooses one data set, the button becomes active. REQ-107 is the requirement, and #598 tracks the build. Q-51 asks what must be provable. FR-09 Specific consent only DvTP ✓ REQ-12 Each consent is bound to a consumer, a service, and a data scope. FR-10 Atomicity per indivisible data set DvTP ◐ REQ-10 The citizen gives consent per data set, as v0.9 asks (Q-03). Missing: a fixed minimal mandatory set with a legal check (Q-45, #382). FR-11 Validity period (configurable) DvTP ◐ consent.rego#L138 (valid_until must equal exp) The validity is enforced and signed in the proof (REQ-19, REQ-68). Reuse within the validity conforms to v0.9 (Q-04). Missing: a default per service, adjustment by the citizen (Q-13, #380), and the status "retrieved" (Q-42). FR-12 Initiation from the private environment DvTP ✓ Start.tsx, buildPortalUrl.ts The mock service provider website redirects the citizen to the portal, with context (REQ-37). FR-13 Smooth transfer of context DvTP ✓ buildPortalUrl.ts, useRedirectContext.ts The redirect carries the consumer OIN, the service ID, the purpose, the data sets, and the return address (REQ-37). What the citizen sees must come from the registration (REQ-111). FR-14 Automatic return DvTP ◐ PortaalBevestiging.tsx, redirectValidation.ts#L26 The portal returns the citizen with the signed proof in the URL fragment, without BSN. Only the front end checks the return address, against fixed origins (#427, REQ-111). The cancel button (shown as "Annuleren") does not return the citizen (#599, Q-44). FR-15 Support for web and app DvTP ◐ — The demo supports web only. App switching is out of scope. FR-16 Reliable identification of the requesting party and its authority DvTP ◐ REQ-68, REQ-74 Identity (FSC peer with mTLS), admission (SL-45), and consent binding work. An integrator can act for a service provider (REQ-106). Missing: admission per service (#382). FR-17 Fetch data only within a valid consent DvTP ✓ consent.rego#L268, consent_token.go The consumer sends a signed proof. The policy verifies it and checks the status online on every request (REQ-68, F-61). FR-18 Integrator as processor DvTP ◐ service.go#L50 (acts_for) The integrator calls under FSC delegation with a registered mandate, and the consent binds the service provider (REQ-106, F-73). Not enforced: the processor agreement and the rule of no storage (AV-06). Q-46 covers the integrator in the proof. FR-19 Verification of received data (lapsed) DvTP — — Lapsed in v0.9. Transparency goes through FR-20 and FR-31. FR-20 Central overview of consents DvTP ◐ MijnToestemmingenOverview.tsx The citizen has an overview under MijnOverheid with active and expired consents (REQ-40, REQ-69). Not built: the processing per consent from the LDV (Q-25, Q-27) and the export (REQ-108, Q-52). FR-21 Detail view per transaction DvTP ◐ REQ-38 Each consent has a detail page. There is no transaction view. FR-22 Status of the consent shown to the citizen DvTP ◐ REQ-38 The statuses active, expired, and revoked are visible. FR-DvTP v0.9 also asks for "retrieved", and the demo does not have it (F-19, F-97, Q-42). FR-23 Revocation of a valid consent DvTP ✓ portal.go#L269, RevokeModal.tsx Revoke works, and the next request gets a deny (REQ-14). In demo v0.9.0, the backend also accepts a revoke of an expired or revoked consent (REQ-109, #600). FR-24 Revocation works forward: data already retrieved DvTP ✓ consent.rego#L268 (status per request) Revocation works forward and is possible while the consent is valid. Same gap as FR-23 (REQ-109). FR-25 Reference to GDPR rights DvTP ○ — The user interface has no reference to these rights. REQ-120 and AV-14 give the requirement. FR-26 Verification of consent at the source DvTP ◐ REQ-04, REQ-68 Criteria 1 to 3 run at the source. The PDP behind the source Inway verifies the proof and checks the scope. A request without a valid consent gets a deny (F-06 closed). Open: the check does not use the service catalogue (#382). FR-27 Sealing of personal data DvTP ○ — The demo has no qualified seal. Q-75 covers one seal for each source response. FR-28 Connection through common source access DvTP ◐ — This is a meta requirement, and the chain exists. FR-29 Digital registration and onboarding DvTP ◐ dvtp-onboarding-register The operator can admit, pause, widen and reconnect a service provider without a policy change (REQ-61). Missing: the applicant side (Q-74). Q-22 answers the grounds. FR-30 Validation of connection conditions DvTP ◐ autosign.rego#L171 (reason codes) The demo validates at the contract proposal (REQ-62) and at source activation (REQ-65, F-58). Missing: the conditions themselves (connection conditions) and criterion 3 (status "trusted" visible to the citizen). FR-31 Compliance and auditing DvTP ◐ ldv-logboek, adl.go Each system has an LDV logbook (PR #366), the ADL is the audit source (PR #373), and the admission register can pause a party. Open: a chain-wide index (F-68), audit guarantees (F-07), and suspension that ends contracts (REQ-110, Q-53). FR-32 Process for setting up data needs DvTP ◐ dvt0001.rego Scopes are configurable. There is no legal ceiling per use case and no link to service providers (F-74, #382). FR-33 Acquisition and registration of a connection certificate DvTP ◐ REQ-58, REQ-67, AV-04 Certificate material is registered, validated, and decisive. Missing: connection certificates of consumers, and the model for issue, rotation, and revocation (F-60, Q-07, #225). FR-34 Identification of the requesting party during use DvTP ◐ REQ-74 The runtime identity comes from mTLS and the contract. There is no regime header and no default regime (SL-48). Open: criterion 1, because nothing proves that the browser start comes from the service provider (#427, REQ-111, Q-60). FR-35 BSN-free delivery to a private service provider DvTP ◐ consent_token.go#L47 The register stores no BSN. The consumer gets only a placeholder and no identifier (SL-51). The values come from a BSNk mock. The demo does not use the real BSNk PP (Q-01, Q-26). FR-36 Voluntariness and an equivalent alternative DvTP ○ — The consent screen does not say that the route is voluntary and names no alternative (AV-15). FR-37 Onboarding of an integrator or software party DvTP ◐ service.go#L50, autosign.rego#L171 The register lists the integrator with its mandates. If a delegated contract has no registration, it stays proposed (DELEGATION_NOT_REGISTERED) (REQ-106, AV-06). The integrator is not in the service catalogue, and there is no digital onboarding. FR-38 Multi-source scope of a consent DvTP ○ main.go#L83 (one source per backend) The demo does not try out one consent with a rule per bronhouder. Each consumer backend calls one source (BD or LVG). For more information, see F-68 and Q-76. FR-39 Central policy management and distribution DvTP ◐ gbo-pdp.yaml The demo has a PAP and bundles with split roles (SL-44). It has no signed bundles and no policy authority. Management stays with each bronhouder (Q-21).

docs.title: Reference architecture (historical)
docs.text:
Two earlier sources of this matrix were the GBO reference architecture v0.6.2 and the PSA open issues of April 2026 (VR-1 to VR-8). The reference architecture is archived and was never published. Its decisions and gaps became TO architecture decisions. The PSA decision register replaced the VR issues. The summary does not count these rows.

Each historical row gives its last status in the analysis and the TO decision that it was ported to:

ID Title Last status Ported to Notes CDD-1 GraphQL over REST ✓ ADR-0001 The PDP decides per field on the parsed query. Q-14 covers pre-registered queries. CDD-2 Access basis: consent (PIP) or legal basis (bundle) ◐ ADR-0006 → ADR-0032, ADR-0031 The path follows from the evidence (REQ-74). A legal-basis path is out of scope. CDD-3 Consent model: multi-source, service catalogue, integrator ◐ ADR-0008 → ADR-0009, ADR-0034 The data model is multi-source, but each request reaches one source. An integrator acts by mandate (REQ-106). CDD-4 BSNk PP for pseudonymization ✓ ADR-0005, ADR-0010 → ADR-0011 → ADR-0033 The demo calls BSNk only at the consent, and the source decrypts (SL-51). BSNk is a mock. CDD-5 Five-factor authorization, federated PDP ◐ ADR-0004 Organization identity: mTLS, no certificate-bound token. Organization permission: admission and contract. Access basis: consent. Scope: ✓. Constraint: the subject is a placeholder from the proof (REQ-79). Request validity: only presence checks. The demo has one shared PDP. CDD-6 FSC-primary connectivity ◐ ADR-0003 All routes run over OpenFSC with mTLS. The sector-pip is removed (#378). CDD-7 AS4 bridge for SDG-OOTS — ADR-0020 Not in v1. RAGAP-1 Authorization policy lifecycle ◐ ADR-0021 The demo has bundles, versions, and retirement (SL-44). Open: validation before activation (F-52). RAGAP-2 Identity convergence and BSN pseudonymization ◐ ADR-0023 The path has pseudonymization (REQ-80). The demo does not model convergence of sector pseudonyms. RAGAP-3 Semantic mapping ○ ADR-0024 The demo has no canonical model. RAGAP-4 GraphQL standardization within FDS ◐ ADR-0025 The GraphQL profile is a GBO proposal in the OpenFTV working group (#331). RAGAP-5 Traceability correlation ✓ ADR-0026, ADR-0035 One trace ID per request (REQ-55). RAGAP-6 Bronhouder onboarding toolkit — ADR-0027 Not in v1. Source metadata and activation cover a part of it (SL-46). RAGAP-7 PuB-EAA provider — ADR-0028 The demo built issuance anyway (EUDI-1). RAGAP-8 Authentic Source Interface — ADR-0029 → ADR-0037 Built in SL-28 (EUDI-2). VR-1 Identification and authentication of private parties ◐ B-09, B-19 See the open decisions. VR-2 Authorization central or distributed ◐ B-04, B-05 See the open decisions. VR-3 Citizen identification and the BSN ◐ B-07, B-08 See the open decisions. VR-4 Trust framework ◐ B-09 See the open decisions. VR-5 Consent facility SDG-OOTS — B-12 Not in v1. VR-6 Qualified EAA — B-13, B-14, B-15 See the open decisions. VR-7 Central components ◐ B-04, B-06, B-13, B-14, B-16 Q-10 (answered) covers which functions must be central. VR-8 Transformation architecture ◐ B-16, B-12, B-11 The source describes its mapping, and GBO validates it (REQ-64). There is no canonical model.

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: each row links its requirements.
  • Findings: each row links its findings. For all findings, see Findings.
  • Open questions: each row links its open questions. For all questions, see Open questions.
  • Demo increments: each row links its increments. For all increments, see Demo increments.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
An open question is a question that the demo cannot answer. It needs a decision by the PSA, by a system forum (G5, Logius, the standards bodies), or a legal assessment. Each entry names the forum, the options, and the working assumption. The demo and this TO use the working assumption until the forum decides the question. An architecture decision that waits for a question has the status proposed in the decision log.

A question has one of four status values: open, partly answered, answered, or closed. The register never reuses a question number. A renumbered question keeps a history line with its old number.

docs.title: Q-01: Which pseudonym form does the system use?
docs.text:
• Status: partly answered

PSA P-04 asks that a consumer without a statutory power gets a citizen identity that nobody can link outside its context. It is a legal question whether a private consumer without a public task can connect to BSNk as a recipient. It is also open whether an encrypted identity that the consumer cannot decrypt counts as a processing of the BSN. The answer decides how the consumer logs the citizen, gives access, and recognizes one citizen across consents. The working assumption is that the consumer gets no pseudonym, and the consent proof carries an encrypted value per source that each source decrypts itself.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: PSA B-07 (pseudonymous identity). Sub-question 1: Logius (BSNk management organization) and the Ministry of the Interior and Kingdom Relations (BZK). Sub-question 2: lawyer and BZK.
  • Question: PSA and GO set the direction of the form. PSA P-04 says that a consumer without a statutory power gets "a party-specific identity or pseudonym" that cannot be linked outside its context. The GO says the same for the private service provider (dienstverlener). Two sub-questions stay open:
    1. Is a private consumer without a public task allowed to connect to BSNk PP as a recipient? If so, on which legal basis (grondslag)?
    2. The consumer carries an encrypted identity for the source that the consumer cannot decrypt. Is that a processing of the BSN by the consumer?
  • Answer so far:
    • At BSNk, the recipient is the party (OIN). The service is not the recipient.
    • The consent proof carries an encrypted value per party. Each source decrypts its own value locally (REQ-21, REQ-80).
    • The BSNk technical specifications v11.2 agree. The key belongs to the OIN and not to the FSC peer. Two peers with the same OIN share one encrypted value and one key.
    • A pseudonym per service needs a separate OIN (BSNK-07).
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Both sub-questions are legal questions under the BSN General Provisions Act (Wabb) and the GDPR. Technically, BSNk can do it. Every service provider with a PKIoverheid certificate gets keys for pseudonyms. BSNk also supports an OIN derived from a Chamber of Commerce (KvK) number (specification p. 23, p. 67). But the specification is written for service providers with a public task (p. 26). In the reading of the GBO team, a consumer without a public task falls outside it.
  • Options:
    • (a) No pseudonym for the consumer. The consumer then has no citizen identifier at all. This option affects three things:
      • the identifier that the consumer logs under (Q-27),
      • the access of a citizen at the consumer,
      • the recognition of a citizen across consents (F-76).
    • (b) An encrypted pseudonym (VP) from BSNk for the consumer. This option needs a yes on sub-question 1.
  • Current working assumption: The working assumption is option a:
    • The demo gives the consumer no pseudonym (PR #469).
    • Since PR #477, the proof carries a VP for every source. For a source on the BSN Authorization List, it also carries an encrypted identity (VI). Thus sub-question 2 is already the practice of the demo.
    • Issue #478 tracks a pseudonym for the consumer. Issue #377 tracks a test against the real BSNk PP.
    • A point for the choice of form: with a pseudonym per recipient, the LDV dataSubjectId differs per controller (verantwoordelijke). Chain-wide citizen access can then search only by trace ID, from the own organization (F-65). This is a privacy property and not a defect.
  • Related: F-65, F-75, F-76, REQ-20, REQ-21, REQ-80, BSNK-07, Q-26 (recognition of the consent facility (toestemmingsvoorziening) at BSNk), Q-27, ADR 0005, ADR 0033.

docs.title: Q-08: What belongs in the LDV (processing log), and who holds the retention duty?
docs.text:
• Status: open

GBO builds and runs three components: the consent register (toestemmingsregister), the EUDI adapter, and the issuance server. Each component records its own processings in an LDV logbook, and the PDP records every decision in the ADL. Nobody decided how long these records stay, or who can read them. That is a legal and supervision decision, and retention is harder because an ADL record needs its sources to stay available. In the working assumption, the demo keeps separate stores and a read-only role for the ADL, without a retention policy or tamper evidence.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: management organization and privacy officer. PSA S09 ("agreements set retention, access, inspection and destruction explicitly"), B-10.
  • Question: GBO builds and operates three components: the consent register, the eudi-adapter, and the issuance server. Which retention periods apply to the LDV and ADL records of these components? And who can read those records?
  • Answer so far:
    • The field schema is LDV plus ADL (PSA S09).
    • The ADL is the authoritative decision log (PR #373). The policy version goes in adl.core.policies (REQ-59).
    • Logius keeps three related logging standards with one trace ID: LDV, ADL, and FSC logging (F-63).
    • Each component records the events of its own responsibility, decentrally. This also applies on the wallet side (S09, B-10).
    • The citizen access model and central audit aggregation belong to B-10 and the open decisions of S09. This question does not cover them.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Retention periods and read access are a legal and supervision decision. Two points make retention harder:
    • The ADL source-reference model requires that a source stays available as long as a record that points to it exists.
    • LDV deliberately sets no access model for its read API. The access-control module of the API strategy is a candidate.
  • Options: None named. The management organization and the privacy officer give the periods and the access model as input.
  • Current working assumption:
    • The demo has separate stores and a SELECT-only reader role for the ADL.
    • The demo has no retention policy, no WORM storage, and no tamper evidence for ADL, LDV, or FSC transaction logs (REQ-32).
    • The LDV field processing_activity_id needs a register of processing activities. In the demo, this register is a stand-in per logbook, without legal status. The real register is a dependency on the management organization (REQ-72).
    • Since PR #370, the demo deviates on purpose from the S09 minimization norm (REQ-60).
  • Related: F-53, F-54, F-63, F-72, REQ-32, REQ-55, REQ-59, REQ-60, REQ-71, REQ-72, Q-25, Q-27, ADR 0026, ADR 0036.

docs.title: Q-13: Who sets the validity period of a consent?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The functional requirements give each service a default validity period from the service catalog and let the citizen adjust it within bounds. It is open whether the citizen really must be able to change the period, and within which bounds. The choice is a policy and UX question under the GDPR, which the demo can show but cannot decide. The demo deviates from the requirements: the consumer sends the end date, and the citizen cannot change the period. Without an end date, the consent register uses one year.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: FR-DvTP owner, management organization (defaults and bounds in the service catalog), PSA B-06 (consent in DvTP).
