    • FR-11 (FR-DvTP v0.9) says that the default period per service comes from the service catalog (FR-32). It also says that the citizen can adjust the period within the permitted bounds.
    • FR-05, criterion 5, says the same for the screen. Thus FR-05 and FR-11 agree.
    • It is open whether the citizen really must be able to adjust the period. The PSA capabilities only say that the portal shows the period to the citizen.

    Question: Reopened on November 2, 2026.

    Must the citizen be able to change the default validity period of a service? If so, within which bounds? The question which component enforces those bounds is Q-62, sub-question 1.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: It is a policy and UX choice (GDPR art. 7). The demo can show each variant. It cannot decide which variant is lawful and wanted.

  • Options:
    • (a) A fixed default per service from the catalog. The citizen sees the period and does not change it.
    • (b) The citizen adjusts the period within bounds from the catalog, as the text of FR-11 says.
    • (c) The consumer sets the period in the request, within the catalog ceiling. No source names the consumer for this role. The demo does this in v0.9.0.
    • The consumer sends valid_until in the redirect context (REQ-37).
    • The portal turns this value into validity_seconds (PortaalConsent.tsx#L85).
    • If there is no value, the register uses one year (consent-register/main.go#L51).
    • The citizen cannot change the period.

    Current working assumption: No requirement says that the citizen adjusts the period (REQ-19, REQ-117, register data model). The demo deviates from FR-11:

    Issue #380 tracks the deviation. The issue also covers the adjust option that the demo removed earlier.

  • Related: FR-05, FR-11, FR-32, F-11, REQ-19, REQ-37, REQ-117, Q-04, Q-62, Q-76 (per consent or per source).

docs.title: Q-14: Query enforcement model: how does the PDP model fields, recursion, and arguments?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The PSA speaks of pre-registered, selective data requests, and the GO says that the service catalog holds the permitted requests per application. The question is whether queries are fixed per application, or whether a consumer can write its own queries within a schema that the source publishes. The answer decides how rich the catalog gets and how close GBO stays to iWlz (the data exchange of the Dutch Long-term Care Act). The working assumption rejects fixed queries for DvTP, so the consumer writes its own query and the PDP decides every field against an allowlist. If the field list is uncertain, the PDP denies the request.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: PSA and GO authors, through B-02 (API profile) and B-03 (service catalog). The technical enforcement model belongs in the GraphQL profile proposal for OpenFTV (Q-16, issue #331).
  • Question: PSA S07 says that the API supports "pre-registered, selective data requests". The GO says that the service catalog "contains the permitted data requests per application". Are the queries then fixed per application? Or is a different model sufficient, as follows:
    • The source publishes a (partial) schema per service.
    • The consumer writes its own queries within that schema.
    • The PDP validates each query against the schema (fields, nesting, arguments).
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo can show each model. The meaning of S07 is for its authors to say. Three points are design and maintainability choices: which model applies per regime, how rich the catalog gets, and how close GBO stays to iWlz.
  • Options:
    • (A) The consumer picks one of a list of fixed query templates (iWlz, historically).
    • (B) The consumer writes its own query. The PDP parses it and checks each field against an allowlist (the demo).
    • (C) Schema directives say per field which policies run. A PEP preprocessor parses the query once and gives the PDP structured input (iWlz, present practice).
    • (D) The catalog fixes a maximum template or schema per scope. The query of the consumer must be a structural subset of it.
    • A middle form (findings review, September 21, 2026): the source publishes a (partial) schema with filter arguments. Per application, policy requires which paths are mandatory, and which filters with which fixed values. Policy does not look at content. The queries are then free, but the bounds for them are fixed. This form fits the GO and the iWlz network model. Issue #425 tests it for an attestation about another person (REQ-57).
  • Current working assumption: The team does not want fixed queries for DvTP. The DvTP path uses model B. The PDP side builds the complete field list per the FTV GraphQL profile and decides every field separately. If the field list is uncertain, the PDP denies the request (REQ-17). Since SL-13, consent works at scope level, and that makes D a small next step. SL-14 built a proof of concept for D.
  • Related: REQ-17, REQ-57, F-74, Q-16, SL-03a, SL-03b, ADR 0001, ADR 0012.

docs.title: Q-17: EUDI issuance architecture: who owns the issuance server and the adapter?
docs.text:
• Status: open

GBO offers a central, optional facility that issues attestations for the EUDI Wallet, and each bronhouder stays responsible for its attestations. Can the facility hold the seal key of a bronhouder, or must it call a signing facility under control of the bronhouder? It is also open who holds the qualified seal certificate, which names the authentic source, and the status-list certificate. Key custody and certificate holding are legal and governance decisions. As a working assumption, the demo uses one issuance server, a certificate set per source, and keys in files, which decides nothing for production.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK, the Dutch Authority for Digital Infrastructure (RDI), and bronhouders, with a legal review. PSA B-13 and the open decisions of PSA S11, issue #225.
  • Question: The question became a key and seal question, with three parts:
    1. Can a central PuB-EAA facility hold and use the seal key material of a bronhouder? Or must sealing go through a signing facility that the bronhouder manages (remote signing, an HSM at the source)?
    2. Who holds the qualified seal certificate?
    3. Is the status-list certificate of the source or of the facility?
  • Answer so far:
    • The choice "one issuance server per bronhouder or one central server" is obsolete.
    • The GO gives GBO the technical role of a central, optional issuance facility: "GBO is not itself a PubEAA provider".
    • In PSA S11, the bronhouder stays legally and materially responsible.
    • The source publishes its own attestation schema and offer (F-57, REQ-64).
    • Issuer and reader certificates are a set per source. If material is missing, issuance fails hard (REQ-58).
    • Onboarding is REQ-65 and B-09.
    • The regime follows from the evidence and not from a flow field (REQ-74).
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Key custody and the holder of a qualified certificate are legal and governance decisions. The regulation makes them concrete:
    • Attestations: the seal on a PuB-EAA is created in a QSCD (ETSI TS 119 471, REQ-EAASP-7.5.3-02, through CIR 2026/1735). The seal uses a qualified certificate per ETSI TS 119 412-6 clause 8. That certificate names the authentic source and the legal basis (eIDAS art. 45f(1)(b)).
    • ASI results: from January 1, 2027, the public sector body or the designated intermediary seals them. It uses at least an advanced seal on a qualified seal certificate. A QSCD is not required there (CIR 2025/1569 art. 9(4), as amended by 2026/1735).
  • Options:
    • (a) The central facility holds the key of each bronhouder.
    • (b) Remote signing or an HSM under control of the bronhouder, which the facility calls.
  • Current working assumption: One issuance server with a certificate set per source. The demo keeps the keys in files at the facility. This choice decides nothing about production.
  • Related: F-66, F-80, F-81, REQ-58, Q-07, Q-28, Q-32, Q-37, ADR 0028, ADR 0041.

docs.title: Q-18: EUDI flow security: phishing, certificate management, data processing in the adapter, PID verification
docs.text:
• Status: open

Can a bronhouder identify a citizen with a BSN from a verified EUDI Wallet PID, with the legal status of a BSN from DigiD? If so, the chain must show how the verified disclosure binds to the source query. This is a national legal question, because eIDAS does not name the BSN and the member state decides on the number. In the working assumption, the issuance server verifies the PID but passes only plain attributes to the adapter, without an authenticated callback. So nothing in the chain binds the BSN of the source query to a verified PID.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: lawyer and BZK. PSA B-08 (identity matching), PSA S11.
  • Question: The question is about a BSN from a verified PID disclosure (EUDI Wallet). Can a bronhouder use that BSN to identify the citizen in a source query, with the same legal status as a BSN from DigiD? If so, which binding between the verified disclosure and the query must the chain show (issue #133)?
  • Answer so far: The original question was split.
    • Presentation and combination of attestations by verifiers are outside GBO (GO pattern A).
    • The designation of the Dutch PID issuer is an external dependency.
    • The issuance server verifies the PID signature.
    • The security basis for the build covers phishing, certificate rotation and compromise, and trust-list use. It also covers data processing and logging in the adapter, state, and data freshness. See REQ-77 and the checklist in issue #381.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: It is a national legal question.
    • eIDAS does not name the BSN. It requires that the PID "uniquely represents" the person (art. 5a(5)(f)). It forbids use that can be "tracked, linked or correlated" (art. 5a(16)(a)).
    • personal_administrative_number stays optional. The member state sets its policy in its eID scheme (CIR 2024/2977). CIR 2026/1731 did not change this.
    • Without a number, identity matching per CIR 2025/846 applies.
    • (a) The issuance server authenticates its callback to the adapter (mTLS or a signed request).
    • (b) The adapter verifies the SD-JWT disclosure itself.

    Options: For the legal part, the answer is yes or no. For the binding (REQ-45), there are two options:

    In both cases, the disclosure is bound to the request, and the PID trust list holds PID issuers only.

  • Current working assumption: The issuance server verifies the wallet presentation, but gives the adapter only plain attributes. The adapter does not authenticate that callback. Nothing in the chain binds the BSN of the source query to a verified PID disclosure. If a request carries no consent proof, it gets the PID regime (REQ-74, F-70). SL-25 (PID verification in the adapter) is a dropped demo increment.

  • Related: F-70, REQ-45, REQ-74, REQ-77, Q-15, Q-36 (PID without BSN), ADR 0018, ADR 0031.

docs.title: Q-25: How can a reader find the step from the decision at the source to the consent log?
docs.text:
• Status: open

If the PDP of a source checks a consent status, the consent register logs that check in its own LDV logbook. The PDP writes only an ADL decision record, and the ADL has no field that points to another LDV logbook. A reader who follows the standard links therefore cannot get from the decision to the consent log. The question is how the ADL record can point there, and the answer needs Logius or a design choice. The working assumption accepts the gap: an auditor finds the register record by a search on the trace ID.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: Logius (maintainers of ADL and LDV), PSA S09.
    • The caller is the PDP of the source. The PDP writes an ADL record and no LDV record (F-63).
    • Thus no LDV record at the source points to the consent logbook with nextLogbookId. The ADL has no equivalent. A reader who follows the standard route does not get to the consent logbook (F-68, point 2).
    • ADL 1.0.0 gives adl.core.information a reference per information source (PIP). That reference must be "sufficient to retrieve, on demand, the data … that affected the authorization decision".
    • That field is for rebuilding the input of the decision, in a free format. It does not mention LDV or nextLogbookId.
    • If a GBO profile uses the field as a pointer to an LDV logbook, that meaning is a GBO invention. Thus it does not close the gap.

    Question: The status check is a processing of the consent register. The register records it in its logbook under the trace of the request.

    A PDP calls a PIP (the consent register). The register records that call itself as an LDV processing. How does the ADL record point to that LDV logbook, so that an LDV reader can follow the chain across the decision step? Is adl.core.information meant for this, or does a separate link field belong here, like dpl.read.nextLogbookId?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Option 1 adds a component that the design does not have. Option 2 changes the family of standards. Option 3 is a choice not to act. All three are design decisions. Option 2 needs Logius.

  • Options:
    • (1) Record the status query as a processing of the source, through a PIP adapter at the source. That adapter writes LDV with nextLogbookId. This option closes the gap with the means of the standard. It costs a component and a hop.
    • (2) Ask Logius how an ADL record points to the logbook of a PIP source.
    • (3) Accept the gap and document it. An auditor finds the status record through a search of the consent logbook by trace ID.
  • Current working assumption: Option 3. The record of the register is found by trace ID (PR #371), with a verified caller (issue #383). The demo log viewer shows the consent logbook as "reached without pointer".
  • Related: F-63, F-68, REQ-72, REQ-76, Q-08, Q-23, ADR 0026, ADR 0036.

docs.title: Q-26: Can the consent facility become a recognized BSNk party, and in which role?
docs.text:
• Status: open

In the design, the consent facility fetches an encrypted identity or pseudonym per party from BSNk. BSNk serves only recognized parties, such as means issuers and authorization services, and a consent facility is none of these. The minister of BZK decides on recognition and its role. Several practical points are open too, such as how the service recognizes a citizen at a later login and how it gets the Autorisatielijst BSN. The working assumption is that MijnOverheid passes the BSN, and the service derives its own pseudonym under which it stores the encrypted values.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK and Logius (BSNk management organization). Also MijnOverheid for sub-questions 2, 3 and 5, and RvIG for sub-question 8. PSA B-07, S01.
  • Question: In the design of issue #364 the consent facility fetches an encrypted identity or an encrypted pseudonym per party from BSNk. Which part of the consent facility is the BSNk participant (register, portal backend, or both as one) is Q-49. Sub-questions:
    1. In which role can a consent facility be recognized: means issuer, authorization service (Machtigingsdienst), or a new role?
    2. Can the service be exempted from the check data at activation, because the citizen is already identified with DigiD at MijnOverheid (BSNK-02)?
    3. Does the login at MijnOverheid count as authentication by the service, as the specification requires before a transformation (BSNK-04)?
    4. How does the service appear in the overview of login means that the citizen sees in MijnOverheid (BSNK-10)?
    5. How does the service recognize the citizen at a later login? Can MijnOverheid pass an encrypted pseudonym for the service at login, as for the BSNk inspection register (Inzageregister)? Or can it pass a fixed reference of its own? If MijnOverheid passes the BSN itself, the service needs nothing else from MijnOverheid. The question then becomes whether MijnOverheid can legally pass the BSN.
    6. How does BSNk handle repeated activation for the same citizen? Does a stored PI stay usable when the service gets new keys?
    7. Who requests the keys at BSNk for sources and consumers? They do not talk to BSNk themselves (BSNK-09). Can the service also become Key Requester, and which requirements apply?
    8. What does the BSN Authorization List look like in practice (BSNK-06)?
      • Known: RvIG manages the list. Logius publishes it per OIN as the Technical List BSN. The service must process it periodically and automatically. The service must not use it after its validity.
      • Not known: how Logius delivers it (file or service, signed or not, format). Also not known: how long an edition is valid and where that is stated. Further open points are how the service gets access, and how a source gets on the list (request to RvIG, lead time).
  • Why the demo cannot answer it:
    • Recognition is a decision of the minister of BZK (specification p. 24).
    • BSNk allows activation and transformation only to recognized parties: means issuer, authentication service, authorization service, or the eIDAS message service (BSNK-01). A consent facility is none of these.
    • The specification names future roles, among them attribute services, without detail (p. 34).
    • The login cannot deliver the values. The citizen logs in at MijnOverheid, and the sources are known only at consent (F-75).
    • The demo can show the behavior with a mock. It cannot decide the role or its conditions.
  • Options:
    • For sub-question 1: means issuer, authorization service, or a new role.
    • For sub-question 5, there are three options. The first is an encrypted pseudonym from MijnOverheid. The second is a fixed reference from MijnOverheid. The third is the BSN from MijnOverheid, with a pseudonym that the service derives itself (route D).
  • Current working assumption: Since October 5, 2026, MijnOverheid passes the BSN. The service derives its own pseudonym and stores PI and PP under it (route D, ADR 0040, proposed, BSNk preconditions). The demo uses a BSNk mock. It reads the BSN Authorization List at the mock and uses a copy for at most one hour. The form and the period are assumptions (PR #477).
  • Related: PSA P-04, GO (central consent facility, BSNk PP mandatory for DvTP), F-75, BSNK-01, BSNK-02, BSNK-04, BSNK-06, BSNK-09, BSNK-10, Q-01, Q-49, Q-50, ADR 0005, ADR 0040.

docs.title: Q-27: Under what does a consumer without an identifier name the data subject in its processing log?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The consent proof carries the citizen only in values that sources can read, so the consumer has no identifier for its LDV processing log. It is open whether LDV accepts a reference to the legal basis as the data subject. It is also open whether citizen access through the consents meets the GDPR. In the working assumption, the consumer logs under the consent ID. That ID is no pseudonym, so one citizen with two consents shows as two data subjects.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: Sub-question 1: Logius and the LDV working group. Sub-question 2: lawyer or DPO. Variant 2 depends on Q-01. PSA S09.
  • Question: Since SL-51 (PR #469), the consent proof carries the citizen only in values that the sources can read. The consumer has no BSN, no PI, and no pseudonym. If the consumer logs its source calls per LDV (AV-02), dpl.core.data_subject_id must contain something. Two sub-questions follow:
    1. If the controller has no identifier of the data subject, can dpl.core.data_subject_id be a reference to the legal basis?
    2. Is it sufficient for the right of access that the citizen finds his processings at the consumer through his consents?
  • Why the demo cannot answer it:
    • Whether a reference to the legal basis is a valid data_subject_id is an interpretation of the LDV standard.
    • Whether access through the consent register is sufficient is a GDPR question.
    • Nobody checked whether the standard allows a record without a pseudonym of its own.
  • Options:
    • (1) The reference to the legal basis. The consumer holds no extra data. Citizen access goes through the consent register, which knows whose consents they are.
    • (2) A pseudonym for the consumer (a VP from BSNk). The consumer then logs under a pseudonym from its own space, as REQ-72 asks. It also recognizes the citizen across consents. This option needs a yes on Q-01 sub-question 1. The build is in issue #478.
    • (3) The own customer reference of the consumer, which it knows from its own process outside GBO. GBO cannot enforce or check it.
  • Current working assumption: Option 1. The demo consumer puts the consent ID in the field, with its own data_subject_id_type consent-id (logbook.go#L22). The consent ID is not a pseudonym. One citizen with two consents shows as two data subjects (F-76).
  • Related: PSA P-03, P-04, P-12, FR-31, F-68, F-76, REQ-72, AV-01, AV-02, Q-01, Q-08, Q-24, ADR 0026.

docs.title: Q-28: Who designates the PuB-EAA issuer and the ASI intermediary of the Netherlands, and who supervises?
docs.text:
• Status: open

A bronhouder can issue a PuB-EAA itself, or a public body that the member state designates issues it on behalf of bronhouders. For verification of attributes by QTSPs, the law also names a designated intermediary. The question is whether the Netherlands designates GBO or the management organization for one or both roles, and who supervises PuB-EAA issuance. In the working assumption, the bronhouder is the PuB-EAA provider and GBO runs the technical issuance facility. For verification, the demo acts as the designated intermediary, but nobody designated it.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK (system responsibility), RDI (supervision of trust services). PSA B-13, B-14, S11.
    • The bronhouder itself can issue a PuB-EAA. "A public sector body that is designated by the Member State" can also issue it on behalf of bronhouders (art. 3(46)).
    • For verification by QTSPs, Annex VI names "designated intermediaries recognized at national level".
    • CIR 2025/1569 art. 9(4), as amended by 2026/1735, lets "the designated intermediary recognized at national level" seal the result.
    • The member state notifies a PuB-EAA issuer with a conformity assessment report (art. 45f(3)).
    • The acts that the GBO team read do not name a supervisor of PuB-EAA issuers.

    Question: The legal acts give the following background:

    Two sub-questions follow:

    1. Does the Netherlands designate GBO, or the management organization, as PuB-EAA issuer on behalf of bronhouders (eIDAS art. 3(46))? And as the nationally recognized intermediary for verification (eIDAS Annex VI, CIR 2025/1569 art. 9)?
    2. Which body supervises PuB-EAA issuance?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Designation and supervision are administrative decisions.

  • Options:
    • (a) GBO or the management organization gets a designation for both roles.
    • (b) GBO or the management organization gets a designation only for verification.
    • (c) No designation. Each bronhouder issues and verifies itself, and GBO supplies the technology.
  • Current working assumption: The bronhouder is the PuB-EAA provider, and GBO runs the technical issuance facility (ADR 0028). For the ASI the demo acts as a designated intermediary (Q-37). Neither is designated.
  • Related: F-80, F-81, Q-17, Q-30, Q-31, Q-37, ADR 0028, ADR 0037.

docs.title: Q-29: Is there a legal basis to verify attributes for private QTSPs, and does the ASI return the value on a match?
docs.text:
• Status: open

eIDAS lets a QTSP verify attributes at a source in accordance with Union or national law, so the regulation creates no legal basis itself. From January 1, 2027, the ASI can return the stored value on a match with variation, which is more than a yes or no. An ETSI requirement makes that value mandatory for fuzzy matching, which contradicts the optional rule. It is open which Dutch legal basis applies, and whether the GBO ASI does fuzzy matching and returns the value. In the working assumption, the demo reports a match with variation but never returns the stored value.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: A lawyer or DPO, and BZK. PSA B-14, S11.

  • Question: Verification happens "at the request of the user, in accordance with Union or national law" (eIDAS art. 45e(1)). So the regulation does not create a legal basis itself. The UBO architecture states that no policy initiative is known for attribute verification by QTSPs.

    From January 1, 2027, CIR 2026/1735 lets the ASI return the value on Match or MatchWithVariation. With MatchWithVariation, the value is "the value of the attribute as stored in the authentic source". This return is optional, and it gives more than a yes or no answer. On Match, the source value gives no new information, because it equals the value of the QTSP. So sub-question 2 is about MatchWithVariation.

    Annex IV makes the value optional. But REQ-ASIP-6.1.1.1-10-01 still requires the value from an ASIP that supports fuzzy matching (F-92, E2). Three sub-questions are open:

    1. Which Dutch legal basis covers the verification of attributes from government sources for private QTSPs?
    2. Does the GBO ASI also return the value on a match, or only the result?
    3. Does the GBO ASI do fuzzy matching? If so, does it return the stored value with MatchWithVariation?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The legal basis and data minimization are legal trade-offs.

  • Options:
    • (a) Only the result, without MatchWithVariation.
    • (b) Only the result, with MatchWithVariation, and a report of the contradiction to ETSI and the Commission.
    • (c) The stored value with MatchWithVariation.
  • Current working assumption: Option b. The report to ETSI and the Commission is not sent. The demo ASIP gives MatchWithVariation and never returns the stored value (verification/service.go#L127-L128). REQ-85 stays draft until this question is decided.
  • Related: F-80, F-92, REQ-85, REQ-113, E2, Q-18, Q-36, Q-70, ADR 0037.

docs.title: Q-30: On which trust list are PuB-EAA issuers: LoTE or the trusted lists?
docs.text:
• Status: open

Wallets and relying parties check the seal of a GBO attestation against a trust list, and that list also goes into the attestation schema. The EUDI specifications disagree on which list holds PuB-EAA issuers: a List of Trusted Entities or the trusted lists. It is also open who manages that list for the Netherlands. No decision exists, so a TO page that names one list describes an assumption.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK, through the EUDI cooperation group, and the operator of the Dutch trusted list. PSA B-13, S11.

  • Question: EUDI technical specification TS2 lets the member state publish providers in LoTEs per ETSI TS 119 602. TS11 names "Lists of Trusted Lists" per ETSI TS 119 612 for PuB-EAAs. The ARF speaks of the PuB-EAA LoTE (§6.3.2).

    Wallets and relying parties validate the seal of a GBO attestation against this list. The list also sets the value in trustedAuthorities of the attestation schema.

    Is a PuB-EAA issuer published in a List of Trusted Entities (LoTE, ETSI TS 119 602) or in the trusted lists (ETSI TS 119 612)? Who manages that list for the Netherlands?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The specifications contradict each other.

  • Options:
    • (a) A LoTE per ETSI TS 119 602.
    • (b) The trusted lists per ETSI TS 119 612.
  • Current working assumption: There is no decision on the list. If a TO page names one list as fact, that page describes an assumption.
  • Related: F-81, Q-28, ADR 0023, ADR 0028.

docs.title: Q-31: Who registers the Dutch verification points in the catalogue of attributes?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The member state asks the EU to include its verification points in the catalogue of attributes, which tells a QTSP how to use them. Each record can carry a national code that tells Dutch sources apart if more than one source delivers the same attribute. The question is who registers the Dutch attributes and verification points, and who sets that national coding scheme. Both are assignments that BZK makes. In the working assumption, the demo has a local discovery stub and registers nothing in the EU catalogue.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK and the Dutch OOTS coordination. PSA B-14, S10, S11.

  • Question: Under CIR 2025/1569 art. 7(3) and 7(5), the member state asks for inclusion of the Annex VI attributes that rest on a public source. The request also describes how a QTSP uses the verification point.

    Per TS11, every attribute record has a DataService per source. A DataService holds the country, an optional nationalSubID, and the endpoint. The member state sets the coding scheme of nationalSubID. The catalogue runs on the SDG/OOTS infrastructure. TS11 has no management API for the catalogue. Two sub-questions are open:

    1. Who registers the attributes and verification points for the Netherlands?
    2. Who sets the coding scheme for nationalSubID? If more than one Dutch source delivers the same attribute, this scheme is necessary.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Registration and the national coding scheme are administrative choices. The route goes through OOTS, and OOTS is outside the scope of the demo.

  • Options: None named. Both answers are assignments that BZK makes.
  • Current working assumption: The demo has a local discovery stub with a record per attribute and data service (REQ-99). It registers nothing in the EU catalogue.
  • Related: F-80, REQ-99, Q-28, Q-67 (Discover Interface).

docs.title: Q-32: In which format does an ASIP seal the verification result, so a QTSP can validate every ASIP the same way?
docs.text:
• Status: open

From January 1, 2027, every ASI verification result carries a seal, but no rule fixes its format. A QTSP that verifies in several member states must then implement the format of each ASIP separately. The question is whether ETSI or an implementing act will fix a seal profile, or else whether the Netherlands fixes one format for its ASIPs. In the working assumption, the demo seals the response body with a detached JWS in a header. That format is a demo choice, and the reference QTSP had to implement it.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: For sub-question 1: ETSI ESI, and BZK through the EUDI cooperation group. For sub-question 2: BZK and the management organization.

  • Question: From January 1, 2027, the public sector body or the designated intermediary signs or seals every verification result (CIR 2025/1569 art. 9(4), as amended by 2026/1735). The signature or seal is at least advanced and rests on a qualified certificate. Recital 2 of 2026/1735 says that it "introduces the requirements for the signing and sealing of verification results". But these requirements only say who seals and at which level.

    Annex IV points to ETSI TS 119 478 clause 6.1.1, clause 6.2.3, or both, with changes on attributeValue. Annex IV says nothing about the seal. Clauses 6.1.1 and 6.1.2, and the OpenAPI of annex B, define no signature on the response.

    These points are fixed: that a seal is made, who makes it, at which level, and how to validate the certificate through the trusted lists. These points are open: the format (JAdES, CAdES, XAdES, or a plain JWS), the place (header, body, or envelope), and what exactly is signed.

    A QTSP that verifies at ASIPs in more than one member state must find and implement the format of each ASIP. An ASIP can describe its format in the OpenAPI that endpointDescription points to (REQ-DIP-5.3.3-03-02-01). But that OpenAPI is only documentation and is not an agreement. Two sub-questions are open:

    1. Will a next version of ETSI TS 119 478, or an implementing act, give a seal profile for the verification result?
    2. If not, does the Netherlands fix one format for its ASIPs? An example is JAdES baseline (ETSI TS 119 182-1) over the response body.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The format must apply to all ASIPs. That needs an agreement in ETSI, at EU level, or at national level. The demo can only make a proposal.

  • Options:
    • (a) A profile in ETSI TS 119 478.
    • (b) An implementing act.
    • (c) One national format, for example JAdES baseline.
    • (d) Each ASIP describes its own format in its OpenAPI.
  • Current working assumption: The demo ASIP seals the exact response body with a detached JWS in the header X-JWS-Signature (ES256, chain in x5c). This JWS is an addition to the ETSI OpenAPI (PR #499, handler.go#L414). The format is a choice of the demo itself and is not JAdES. The reference QTSP had to implement this format. It accepts only a result with a valid seal (PR #535). ADR 0041 stays proposed until this question is decided.
  • Related: REQ-83, F-80, E4, Q-17 (who holds the seal certificate), Q-28, Q-37, Q-39 (same pattern), Q-75, ADR 0041.

docs.title: Q-33: Does the Netherlands impose per-attribute authorization for ASI requests under art. 9(5)?
docs.text:
• Status: open

Under the ETSI standard, a QTSP gets a token per operation, and that token is valid for every attribute while it lasts. The implementing regulation lets a member state add controls, such as a binding of the token to the attributes that the citizen came for. Such a binding limits what a QTSP can request, but a QTSP that implements only ETSI fails on it. The question is whether the Netherlands imposes this authorization per attribute. In the working assumption, the binding is optional on request of the QTSP, and a setting in the demo makes it mandatory.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK, and a lawyer or DPO.

  • Question: ETSI TS 119 478 authorizes an ASI request per operation, with the scopes verify and retrieve (clause 6.1.3.2, figure 2). The QTSP puts the attributes to verify in the body of the request ("shall set out the attributes", art. 9(3)). The token does not hold them. So a token with scope verify is valid for every attribute while the token is valid.

    Art. 9(5) lets a member state impose "control mechanisms on the use of the verification methods", if the member state publishes them. The article adds: "taking into account … whether the authentic sources contain personal confidential or sensitive data".

    A binding of the token to the attributes that the user came for is such a mechanism. RFC 9396 authorization_details is one way to make this binding. The binding limits what a QTSP can request with one authorization, mainly on /retrieve. But the binding makes a Dutch ASIP stricter than ETSI. A QTSP that implements only ETSI fails on it.

    Does the Netherlands impose an authorization per attribute under CIR 2025/1569 art. 9(5)? Or is the authorization per operation of ETSI TS 119 478 sufficient?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Whether the Netherlands imposes a control beyond ETSI is a policy choice under art. 9(5).

  • Options:
    • (a) Per operation, as in ETSI.
    • (b) Per attribute, mandatory.
    • (c) Per attribute on request of the QTSP, with a setting that makes it mandatory.

  • Current working assumption: Option c. By default, the demo authorizes per operation. If the QTSP sends authorization_details, the token carries the attributes that the citizen saw on the consent screen. The ASIP then refuses other attributes (REQ-103, PR #559).

    PR #572 made the binding optional. The setting AZSP_REQUIRE_AUTHORIZATION_DETAILS=true makes it mandatory (main.go#L109). If a token does not cover the requested operation, the request gets 401 with insufficient_scope. The binding is an extension of ETSI with its own type (F-95). ADR 0042 stays proposed until this question is decided.

  • Related: F-80, F-95, REQ-103, E5, Q-03, Q-29, ADR 0042.

docs.title: Q-34: What happens to admitted QTSPs if the register is unreachable during a re-check, and how often is it checked?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The authorization server of the ASI checks the right of each registered QTSP again at regular intervals in the register of relying parties. No source says how often, or what happens when the register is unreachable. With fail-open, a QTSP whose right was revoked during an outage stays active, and with fail-closed, all QTSPs lose access. That trade-off between availability and timely exclusion is a management and risk choice. The working assumption is fail-open with a check every hour, and the server refuses a new registration while the register is unreachable.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The management organization and BZK.

  • Question: The authorization server of the ASI checks the right of each registered QTSP "again in regular intervals" in the register of relying parties (ETSI TS 119 478 clause 6.1.3.2, figure 2). No source says what happens if the register is unreachable at that moment. No source gives the interval either.

    With fail-open, QTSPs stay active during an outage. This also applies to a QTSP whose right was revoked during the outage. With fail-closed, the authorization server excludes all QTSPs during an outage. Two sub-questions are open:

    1. If the register is unreachable, is the behavior fail-open or fail-closed? If fail-open, after how much time does access close?
    2. At which interval does the authorization server check the right again? Or is a notification from the register on revocation sufficient?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The trade-off between availability of verification and timely exclusion of a party is a management and risk choice.

  • Options:
    • For an outage: (a) fail-open, (b) fail-closed, or (c) fail-open for a bounded time, then closed.
    • For the interval: (a) a periodic check, or (b) a notification from the register.
  • Current working assumption: Fail-open, with a check every hour by default (main.go#L101, registration.go#L226-L240, PR #522). If the register is unreachable at a registration, the authorization server refuses with 503.
  • Related: F-85, REQ-89, Q-31, Q-35, Q-41 (tokens after revocation).

docs.title: Q-35: Which identifier links a QTSP's access certificate to its register entry?
docs.text:
• Status: open

A QTSP registers at the ASI with a statement that it seals with its certificate and that points to its entry in the register. The authorization server must check that the entry belongs to the certificate holder, so that no QTSP can present the entry of another. Candidate identifiers are the EUID, the organization identifier with the KvK number, and the OIN. The question is which identifier the certificate and the entry share, and who sets it. In the working assumption, the organization identifier of the certificate must equal one of the identifiers of the entry.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK, and the operator of the Dutch register of relying parties. The sources that the GBO team read do not designate this operator.

  • Question: A QTSP registers at the ASI with a software statement. The QTSP seals the statement with its certificate, and the statement holds the registryURI of its entry. The authorization server must establish that the entry belongs to the holder of the certificate. Otherwise, every QTSP with a valid certificate can present the entry of another QTSP.

    ETSI/EUDI TS5 names the EUID as the standard identifier in the register. A certificate carries an organizationIdentifier, often NTRNL- plus the KvK number. FSC and PKIoverheid work with the OIN.

    Which identifier is in the access certificate of a QTSP and also in its entry in the Dutch register? An authorization server needs this identifier to compare the two. Who sets this identifier?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The register and the certificate profile (ETSI TS 119 411-8) decide which identifier applies. The ASI does not decide it.

  • Options:
    • (a) The EUID.
    • (b) The organizationIdentifier with the KvK number.
    • (c) The OIN.
  • Current working assumption: The organizationIdentifier of the certificate must equal one of the identifiers of the entry (REQ-88, registration.go#L211-L212).
  • Related: F-85, REQ-88, Q-07, Q-31, Q-34.

docs.title: Q-36: Which identification means does a Dutch ASI authorization server accept, and where does the identification data come from?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The ASI authorization server must identify the citizen, with the EUDI Wallet or another procedure under the ETSI identity proofing standard. It is open whether a Dutch server accepts the wallet, DigiD, or both. DigiD gives only a BSN, so it is also open whether the server can fetch the missing data from the BRP. In the working assumption, the demo accepts both, and the token carries more data after a wallet login than after DigiD. The demo refuses an identification without a BSN, which excludes foreign PIDs, but it accepts a PID with unknown or revoked status.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK, and a lawyer or DPO. PSA P-05, S03.
  • Question:
    1. Does the authorization server of a Dutch ASI accept the EUDI Wallet, DigiD, or both?
    2. A means can deliver only part of the data. DigiD delivers only a BSN, and the NL PID has no place of birth. In that case, can the authorization server get the other identification data from the BRP? Or is the BSN sufficient as "the required identification data"?
    3. Does DigiD count for the Dutch ASI as a procedure per ETSI TS 119 461 use case 9.2.4? If so, at which level (Baseline or Extended LoIP)?
    4. If the revocation status of a PID cannot be determined, or if the PID is revoked, can the PID lead to an identification?
    5. Does the chain support a PID without a BSN through identity matching (PSA S03)? If so, where is that function?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Two points are legal and policy choices: which means are allowed, and whether the authorization server can get data from the BRP.

    The standards set these rules. The authorization server identifies the citizen (REQ-AZSP-6.1.3.1-02). It uses the EUDI Wallet over OpenID4VP, or "an alternative electronic identification procedure according to ETSI TS 119 461" (-03). It puts "the required identification data" in the token (-08).

    TS 119 461 V2.1.1 has use case 9.2.4, identity proofing by authentication with an eID means (p. 57). This use case contains these rules:

    • The means is at least eIDAS LoA substantial for Baseline LoIP, and high for Extended LoIP (COL-8.2.4-02X and -02A).
    • The identity proofing practice statement lists the accepted means (COL-8.2.4-01X).
    • All mandatory attributes of the context are collected and identify the person uniquely (COL-8.2.1-01A and -02).
    • A reliable register, such as a population register, can be extra evidence (USE-9.2.4-04).

    So DigiD at level Substantial or High seems to fit. Fetching the other data from the BRP also seems to fit. The GBO team did not check whether DigiD is notified under eIDAS, and at which level. The NL PID has no place of birth, the fifth mandatory attribute (F-94).

  • Options:

    • For sub-question 1: (a) the EUDI Wallet, (b) DigiD, or (c) both.
    • For sub-question 2: (a) fetch the missing data from the BRP, or (b) the BSN alone is sufficient.

  • Current working assumption: The demo offers both: a DigiD mock and the NL Wallet (REQ-102, issue #544, issue #546). As a result, the token is asymmetric. With the wallet, the token carries the BSN and four PID attributes. With DigiD, it carries only the BSN and acr/amr (REQ-86).

    The wallet verifier accepts a PID whose revocation status is unknown or revoked. REQ-45, REQ-86, and REQ-102 refuse an identification without a BSN. This rule fits S03 ("only then can the source be queried"). But it excludes foreign PIDs and PIDs without a BSN.

  • Related: F-86, F-88, F-94, REQ-45, REQ-86, REQ-90, REQ-102, E7, Q-18, Q-29, Q-40.

docs.title: Q-37: What is GBO's role in the ASI: designated intermediary, technical supplier to bronhouders, or authentic source itself?
docs.text:
• Status: open

GBO builds one ASIP for several authentic sources, and the law allows an ASIP to be the source itself or a designated intermediary. The question is whether GBO becomes that designated intermediary, stays a technical supplier to each bronhouder, or becomes an authentic source itself. The role decides who seals the result and who answers for the correctness of the data. The working assumption is the intermediary model, which the GBO team saw as likely on October 14, 2026. The demo names an authentic source for every data service and uses one seal for all of them.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK (system responsibility), the bronhouders, and a lawyer or DPO.

  • Question: GBO builds one ASIP for more than one authentic source (F-89). The sources describe the role of an ASIP in these ways:

    • ETSI TS 119 478 says that the ASIP "can be an authentic source or an intermediary acting on its behalf" (clause 4.2).
    • CIR 2025/1569 art. 9(2) names "authentic sources or designated intermediaries recognized at national level".
    • Art. 9(4) lets the result name the source "or, where applicable, the public sector body designated to act on behalf of the authentic source".
    • 2026/1735 lets the source "or the designated intermediary" seal the result.
    • eIDAS art. 3(47) defines an authentic source as a system that "contains and provides" the data. That system is a primary source "or recognized as authentic in accordance with Union or national law".

    Does GBO (or the management organization) become the designated intermediary for ASI verification on behalf of the bronhouders? Or does each bronhouder stay ASIP itself, with GBO as technical supplier? Or is GBO itself recognized as an authentic source? In each case, who seals, and who answers for the correctness of the data?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The role follows from a designation and from the statutory responsibility for correctness. Those are administrative and legal decisions.

  • Options:
    • (X) GBO is the designated intermediary. provider is GBO, authenticSource is the bronhouder. GBO seals with one qualified seal of its own. This needs a national designation. The responsibility for correctness stays with the bronhouder.
    • (Y) Each bronhouder is ASIP itself, and GBO supplies the technology. provider is the bronhouder, there is no authenticSource, and each bronhouder seals itself. GBO is processor or technical service provider. GBO can possibly run one hosted service that has an identity and a seal per source.
    • (Z) GBO is itself the authentic source. provider is GBO, and there is no authenticSource. This needs statutory recognition of the GBO system as authentic. GBO then answers for data it does not manage, next to the base register that the law designates.

  • Current working assumption: Model X. In the team estimate of October 14, 2026, model X is likely and model Z is not. The demo has provider "GBO demo ASIP" (dataservices.json#L6). In its source description, the demo names the BRP as authentic source by its legal name. The demo uses one seal.

    The provider is set per data service, but a seal per data service is not built. Since issue #592 step 5, every data service names an authentic source. So the demo does not allow a data service with the ASIP itself as source.

  • Related: F-80, F-89, REQ-94, E3, Q-17 (who holds the seal), Q-28 (who the Netherlands designates), Q-32 (seal format), ADR 0037, ADR 0038.

docs.title: Q-38: How does an authentic source connect to the ASIP: by code, by configuration, or by a description it publishes itself?
docs.text:
• Status: partly answered

The ASIP must turn a verification request into a query on the source. One part is answered: the bronhouder manages the link between an attribute and its own schema, in the metadata that it publishes. The demo builds this: the ASIP derives one query per request from that description, and the code adapter for the BRP is removed. Still open is how many sources must connect and how fast, which is a management choice. The GBO team estimates that code fits fewer than about ten sources, and configuration or a published description fits tens of sources.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The management organization, the bronhouders, and GBO architecture.
  • Question:
    1. How many sources must the ASIP open up, and how fast must a new source connect?
    2. Who manages the link between an attribute and the schema of the source: GBO in the ASIP, or the bronhouder in a published description?

  • Answer so far: Sub-question 2 is answered (October 27, 2026): the bronhouder manages the link, in its published description. The team chose option c. The source describes the attributes that it offers for verification in its source metadata. It does this as capability asi, next to eudi, in the same document. As a result, the ASIP becomes generic (issue #592). The plan contains these choices:

    • Each attribute has a selection. The ASIP merges the selections of the requested attributes into one query (REQ-92 still applies).
    • There is no field for fuzzy matching. The ASIP applies MatchWithVariation only to text values. The value schema shows which values are text. ETSI leaves fuzzy matching to the ASIP and defines it as orthographic variation.
    • Activation does not check that the policy of the source allows the fields of each selection. That check is a later step.

    On one point, the demo deviates from the plan of October 27, 2026. On that point, the demo applies. The plan said that the metadata only copies values (gbo-simple-v1) and that the source sets the value schema. The demo lets the source map its own fields onto each value with pointer, join, const, and each. GBO keeps the value schema per attribute identifier in schemas/asi-attributes.json until the EU catalogue of attributes provides it. ADR 0039 records this deviation.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Sub-question 1 depends on how many sources come, how fast they must connect, and who manages the link. That is a management and organization choice. In the team estimate of October 14, 2026, code with good tests fits fewer than about ten sources. Configuration or a description by the source fits tens of sources or fast onboarding.

  • Options:
    • (a) A code adapter per source, with a contract test against the schema of the source.
    • (b) Query and mapping as configuration in the ASIP.
    • (c) The source publishes query and mapping per attribute as metadata.
  • Current working assumption: Option c is built through issue #592 step 5. For each request, the ASIP derives one query from the asi capability of the source. The ASIP then builds the attributes from the answer. The BRP code adapter is removed. The discovery records list the attributes of the current description. If there is no current description, verify, retrieve, and discovery return 503.
  • Related: F-89, REQ-64, REQ-92, REQ-94, Q-37, Q-70, Q-71, ADR 0016, ADR 0017, ADR 0039.

docs.title: Q-39: How does a data service contract name the authorization server, so a QTSP finds every ASIP the same way?
docs.text:
• Status: open

A QTSP finds a data service through the Discover Interface, and the record points to an OpenAPI contract. The ETSI standard requires that this contract names the OAuth authorization server, but OpenAPI has no field for it. The question is whether ETSI will fix a way, or whether the Netherlands sets one for its ASIPs. Without one shared way, a QTSP cannot find every ASIP the same way. In the working assumption, the demo uses its own extension in the security scheme, which no QTSP outside the demo knows.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: For sub-question 1: ETSI ESI, and BZK through the EUDI cooperation group. For sub-question 2: BZK and the management organization.

  • Question: A QTSP finds a data service through the Discover Interface. The record points to the contract with endpointDescription (REQ-99). REQ-DIP-5.3.3-03-02-01 requires that the contract specifies the metadata of the OAuth authorization server. But OpenAPI 3.0 has no field there for an OAuth server (RFC 8414) (F-91). Two sub-questions are open:

    1. Will a next version of ETSI TS 119 478 fix how the contract names the authorization server? Two examples are an extension in annex A or B, and the issuer in the record of the Discover Interface.
    2. If not, does the Netherlands fix one way for its ASIPs?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The field must be the same for all ASIPs in the EU. That needs an agreement in ETSI or at EU level.

  • Options:
    • (a) An extension in annex A or B of ETSI TS 119 478.
    • (b) The issuer in the Discover Interface record.
    • (c) A national convention.
  • Current working assumption: The demo uses the extension x-oauth-authorization-server in the oauth2 security scheme. The extension holds the URL at the location of RFC 8414 §3.1 (REQ-100, PR #534, PR #537, contract.go#L109). The reference QTSP reads the extension and checks it against the issuer. This extension is a choice of the demo. A QTSP from outside the demo does not know it.
  • Related: F-91, REQ-99, REQ-100, E1, Q-32 (same pattern), Q-67.

docs.title: Q-40: Must the citizen logging in at the QTSP provably be the same as the one logging in at the source's authorization server, and who checks?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The QTSP and the authorization server of the source each identify the citizen, and no specification links the two identifications. The question is whether the Netherlands requires that both are the same person. If so, the source side can check it in the verification request, or the authorization server can check it at login. It is also open whether the QTSP can rely on the identification by the authorization server. In the working assumption, the reference QTSP identifies the citizen itself with wallet data and no BSN, but the check itself is not built.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK, a lawyer or DPO, and ETSI ESI for the feedback on the specification (E6).

  • Question: The QTSP identifies the citizen to whom it issues a QEAA (eIDAS art. 24(1)). The authorization server of the source identifies the citizen for the verification (REQ-AZSP-6.1.3.1-02). No specification links the two identifications (F-93).

    CIR 2025/1569 art. 9(3) lets the verification request name the identification data of the subject. Art. 9(5) lets member states check that the QTSP acts at the request of a legitimate user. Three sub-questions are open:

    1. Does the Netherlands fix under art. 9(5) that the subject at the QTSP and at the authorization server is the same person?
    2. If so, does the source side check this through the verification request? In that case, the QTSP has its own identification data verified too. Or does the authorization server check it at login? In that case, the QTSP passes the data in advance.
    3. Can a QTSP use the identification by the authorization server as a "third party" in the sense of eIDAS art. 24(1a)? If so, the citizen logs in only once.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Three points are legal and policy choices:

    • whether the Netherlands imposes a check under art. 9(5)
    • which data the QTSP sends to the source side for this check
    • whether the QTSP can rely on the identification by the authorization server

    The demo can make each variant work, but it cannot make the choice.

  • Options:

    • (a) The QTSP identifies the citizen itself and has that data verified in the request.
    • (b) The QTSP passes its identification data to the authorization server before login.
    • (c) The QTSP relies on the data in the token. The team rejects option c. The token is meant for the ASIP, and the authorization server got the data for another purpose.
  • Current working assumption: The demo implements the team direction of October 19, 2026. The reference QTSP identifies the citizen itself before the verification (issue #560). It uses name, given names, birth date, and nationalities from the wallet, and no BSN. So option a is possible, but the check itself is not built. Issuance to the wallet is the subject of issue #549. REQ-104 is removed, because it is a QTSP duty under ETSI and eIDAS (see removed numbers).
  • Related: F-93, E6, REQ-88, Q-36 (identification means of the authorization server), Q-37 (who runs the ASIP and the authorization server).

docs.title: Q-41: What happens to the tokens of a QTSP whose right is revoked?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The authorization server checks the right of each QTSP again at intervals, but the ETSI standard says nothing about tokens that it already issued. The ASIP validates a token itself and does not ask the authorization server. The question is whether a QTSP can use its token after revocation until it expires, or whether the ASIP must learn of the revocation. How fast a revocation takes effect is a management and risk choice. In the working assumption, the server deactivates the client, and issued tokens stay valid until they expire, at most 10 minutes.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The management organization, BZK, and ETSI ESI for the feedback on the specification (E10).

  • Question: The authorization server re-checks the right of a registered QTSP in the register at intervals (ETSI TS 119 478 clause 6.1.3.2, figure 2). If the right lapses, the specification does not say what happens to tokens that are already issued. FAPI 2.0 §5.3.4 requires a resource server to check the revocation status of a token. The ASIP checks an RFC 9068 JWT itself and does not ask the authorization server. Two sub-questions are open:

    1. Can a QTSP use a token after its right is revoked, until the token expires? If so, for how long?
    2. If not, does the ASIP ask the authorization server for the status (introspection, RFC 7662)? Or does the ASIP keep its own list of revoked clients?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: How fast a revoked right must take effect is a management and risk choice. The technique follows from that choice.

  • Options:
    • (a) Accept the token lifetime as the delay.
    • (b) Introspection by the ASIP.
    • (c) A shorter token lifetime.
    • (d) A list of revoked clients at the ASIP.
  • Current working assumption: If the right is revoked, the authorization server deactivates the client. Tokens that are already issued stay valid until they expire, at most 10 minutes. The demo records this as "not met, open" in its security considerations (PR #574).
  • Related: REQ-89, F-84, F-85, Q-34, Q-66, E10.

docs.title: Q-42: When is a consent "retrieved", and how does the register learn that?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The functional requirements ask the consent register to record whether and when a source first retrieved data under a consent. The register cannot see a delivery, so the question is how it learns of one. It is also open whether retrieved means a delivery or a use of the consent. Each option changes what a source must build, from nothing to an extra interface (koppelvlak) to the register. In the working assumption, the demo shows no retrieved status, only Active, Expired, and Revoked.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The tech lead, and for option B also the bronhouders.

  • Question: FR-11 and FR-22 (FR-DvTP v0.9) require that the register records whether and when data was first retrieved under a consent. After the review of F-19, this information is a field in the register. The register does not derive it from the audit log. The open point is how the register learns of a successful delivery. It has three sub-questions:

    1. Does "retrieved" mean that data was delivered, or that a source used the consent?
    2. If the PDP denies after it requested the status, does the status change?
    3. For a consent that covers more than one source, is the status "retrieved" after the first delivery, or after all deliveries?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: What "retrieved" means for the citizen, and what a source must build for it, is a design choice. This choice changes the connection conditions.

  • Options:
    • (A) The first status query by the PDP of a source. The register sees this query itself. But a query is not a delivery: the PDP can deny after it, or the source can fail.
    • (B) A message from the source after a successful delivery. This option is exact, but every source builds an extra interface to the register.
    • (C) Derive the status from the LDV chain. This option needs no extra interface, but it depends on Q-08 and Q-25.
  • Current working assumption: The demo shows no "retrieved" status. The overview shows the statuses Active, Expired, and Revoked (issue #389, open).
  • Related: F-19, F-97, REQ-76, Q-08, Q-25, Q-47, Q-48.

docs.title: Q-43: For what purpose is a citizen's refusal recorded, and in which form?
docs.text:
• Status: partly answered

The functional requirements say that a refusal is recorded, but not where, what, or for whom. The purpose decides the form: a refusal in the citizen overview, a count per consumer as an abuse signal, or only a log line. A record under the citizen is personal data and needs a retention period. One point is answered: closing the window is no refusal, and nothing happens then. In the working assumption, the demo returns the citizen to the consumer with a denied status and records nothing.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The tech lead, a privacy officer or DPO for option a, and the management organization for option b.

  • Question: FR-DvTP v0.9, Flow A step A-13a, only says that the refusal is recorded. It does not say where, what, or for whom. The outcome (success, refusal, or error) already goes to the consumer in the return redirect (FR-14 criterion 3). That return needs no storage. Three sub-questions are open:

    1. Which purpose or purposes apply: a, b, c, or a combination?
    2. Is an abort (browser closed, time-out) a refusal or an outcome of its own?
    3. If a applies, can the citizen later change a refusal into a consent? Or does the consumer then start a new request?

  • Answer so far: Sub-question 2 is answered. Next to "agree", the citizen has only "refuse", as in FR-10 and Flow A-13a. There is no separate "abort" action. If the citizen closes the window or the session expires, nothing happens: no record and no return redirect. Sub-questions 1 and 3 stay open.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The purpose of the record is a design and privacy choice. The form follows from it.
  • Options:
    • (a) A record in the register with status "refused" under the citizen reference. The citizen sees it in the overview. This record is personal data, because it records that a consumer asked this citizen something. It needs a retention period.
    • (b) A count per consumer without the citizen, as an abuse signal for the management organization.
    • (c) Only a log line that accounts for the process.
  • Current working assumption: If the citizen refuses, the demo returns the citizen with status=denied and records nothing (PortaalConsent.tsx#L100-L106).
  • Related: Q-08 (retention), Q-42 (consent status), Q-44, Q-63.

docs.title: Q-44: What does the return redirect give back to the consumer, and how does the consent proof reach it?
docs.text:
• Status: partly answered

After every outcome, the consent portal (toestemmingsportaal) sends the citizen back to a registered address of the consumer. On success, the signed consent proof tells the consumer what is allowed, and on refusal or error a separate outcome is necessary. It is open which outcomes the consumer must tell apart, and whether the proof travels through the browser or as an exchange code. One point is answered: an abort is no outcome, because a citizen who closes the window does not return. In the working assumption, the demo puts the proof in the URL fragment of the return redirect.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The tech lead, and MijnOverheid for the redirect protocol.

  • Question: FR-14 requires a return redirect to a registered address after every outcome. The redirect carries the outcome (success, refusal, or error). On success, the signed proof binds the granted scopes, so the consumer knows what is allowed. On refusal or error, there is no proof, so a separate outcome is necessary. Two sub-questions are open:

    1. Which outcomes must the consumer tell apart: success, refusal, and error? On success, are the scopes in the proof sufficient? Or does the consumer also get the allowed data sets separately?
    2. Does the proof go through the browser (a), or through a code that the consumer exchanges (b)?

  • Answer so far: "Aborted" is not an outcome. There is no separate abort action (Q-43), and a citizen who closes the window does not return. So the consumer cannot tell a citizen who stopped from a citizen who is still busy. Two points stay open: the set of outcomes for success, refusal, and error, and the transfer of the proof.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The set of outcomes is a design choice that every consumer must implement. The transfer depends on the redirect protocol (OIDC, PAR, or an own extension) and on the check of the return address (issue #427).
  • Options for the transfer:
    • (a) The proof in the return redirect through the browser, as in demo v0.9.0. This option is simple. But the proof passes through the browser. Also, a URL has a limited length, and the proof carries a value per source.
    • (b) A short-lived code in the return redirect that the consumer exchanges for the proof over FSC (the OAuth authorization-code pattern). The proof does not touch the browser, but the consumer calls a service of the consent facility.
  • Current working assumption: The demo puts the signed proof in the URL fragment of the return redirect (PortaalBevestiging.tsx#L60). The demo deviates on one point. Next to "refuse", the consent screen has a "cancel" button. This button goes back to the login screen and does not return the citizen to the consumer (PortaalConsent.tsx#L108). The plan in issue #599 is to remove this button.
  • Related: FR-14, FR-34 criterion 1, REQ-37, REQ-119, Q-43, Q-60, Q-61.

docs.title: Q-45: Does the consent facility enforce the minimal mandatory set, and who decides which sets are mandatory?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The functional requirements keep the minimal mandatory set always on, but no source says whether the consent facility enforces it. It is also open who decides which sets are mandatory, and what happens when a consent lacks the mandatory set. The choice affects the service catalog and the initiation request of the consumer. If the consent facility enforces the set, both the UI and the backend enforce it. The demo has no mandatory set and enforces none.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The tech lead, and the management organization (service catalog).

  • Question: FR-10 says that the minimal mandatory set is always on. Optional sets can be switched on or off. A citizen cannot consent to part of a set. No source says whether the consent facility enforces this. Three sub-questions are open:

    1. Does the consent facility enforce that every consent contains the mandatory set?
    2. Who decides which sets are mandatory? The description of FR-10 answers this in part. The consumer sets the composition of the mandatory set, within the legal ceiling of the service catalog (FR-32). It is open whether the consumer does this per request or once at setup. If per request, the initiation request (REQ-37) must name the mandatory sets.
    3. If the consent facility enforces the set and the mandatory set is missing, what happens? Does the service deny with an error to the consumer, or does something else happen?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: A missing mandatory set can be an error, or a choice of the citizen with consequences for the consumer. That is a design choice. The decision on who sets "mandatory" affects the service catalog of the management organization. It also affects the initiation request of the consumer.

  • Options: See sub-questions 2 and 3.
  • Current working assumption: If the set is enforced, both the UI and the backend enforce it. The UI never enforces it alone. The demo has no mandatory set and enforces none.
  • Related: FR-10, FR-32, REQ-10, REQ-37, Q-44, Q-69.

docs.title: Q-46: Is the integrator in the consent proof, or only in the register?
docs.text:
• Status: open

An integrator acts on behalf of a consumer, with a mandate in the admission register. The question is whether the consent proof must also name the integrator, or whether that mandate is enough. With the integrator in the proof, only that integrator can use it, but a change of integrator makes running consents unusable. With only the mandate, every registered integrator of that consumer can use the proof. In the working assumption, the proof binds the consumer, and the PDP denies an integrator without a mandate.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The tech lead, the management organization (onboarding of integrators), and PSA B-19 (representation).
  • Question: Must the proof bind the integrator, or is the mandate in the register sufficient?
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo shows that both options work. The necessary binding is a balance between abuse risk and manageability.
  • Options:
    • (a) The integrator is also in the proof. Then only that integrator can use the proof. But if the service provider changes integrator, running consents become unusable.
    • (b) Only the mandate in the register, as in demo v0.9.0. A change of integrator needs no action from the citizen. But every registered integrator of that service provider can use the proof.
  • Current working assumption: Option b. The proof binds the represented party (the service provider). The integrator has its own mandate per service provider and rule in the admission register. Without a mandate, the PDP denies with INTEGRATOR_NOT_REGISTERED (engine.rego#L253-L259, PR #464, design from F-73). FR-DvTP v0.9 removed FR-06 (the citizen sees the integrator).
  • Related: FR-18, FR-37, REQ-106, AV-06, F-73, ADR 0034, Q-44, Q-68.

docs.title: Q-47: Which volumes must the chain handle, at start and later?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The chain needs volume figures for the consent register, the status query, and the BSNk link, at start and after a few years. The figures are citizens with a consent, new consents per day, and status queries per second at average and peak. They matter because every request does an online status query at the register without a cache, and every consent costs a BSNk transformation per source. Who supplies the estimate is open, and no figures exist. One demo measurement of the status query gave 14.5 ms at the median and 82 ms at most.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The tech lead, the management organization, the service providers and bronhouders (expected use per use case), and BSNk (transformation capacity).

  • Question: Which volumes must the register, the status query, and the BSNk link handle, at start and after a few years? Who supplies the estimate? These figures are necessary for each moment:

    1. Citizens with at least one consent.
    2. New consents per day.
    3. Status queries per second, on average and at peak.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo runs with a few test citizens. Volumes come from the expected use per use case.

  • Options: None, because the figures are input. Every request does a status query online at the register, without a cache (REQ-68). So the register is in the critical path of every request. Every consent costs one BSNk transformation per source, in groups of at most four recipients (BSNK-05).
  • Current working assumption: No figures exist. One demo measurement of the status query gave p50 14.5 ms and max 82 ms (note at REQ-75).
  • Related: REQ-75, REQ-68, Q-05 (propagation time, which decides whether caching is allowed), Q-42, Q-54.

docs.title: Q-48: Does the register record when a consent was revoked?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The functional requirements ask for status insight for the citizen and for a revocation that takes effect immediately. The question is whether the consent register keeps the moment of revocation with the consent, or whether the LDV log is enough. With the moment in the register, the overview and the status query can show it, and otherwise the portal must read the log. It is a choice about access and evidence. In the working assumption, the register keeps only active or revoked, and the moment is in the LDV record of the change.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The tech lead, and a privacy officer or DPO (citizen access).
  • Question: Must the register keep the moment of revocation with the consent, or is the LDV log sufficient? FR-22 asks for status insight for the citizen. FR-24 asks that revocation takes effect immediately.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo shows only "revoked". Whether the citizen or the source needs the moment is a choice about access and evidence. Technique does not decide it.
  • Options:
    • (a) Record the moment with the consent. The citizen sees it in the overview, and the status query can give it.
    • (b) Record the moment only in the LDV log. The register stays smaller, but the portal must read the log to show the moment.
  • Current working assumption: The register keeps only the status (active or revoked) per consent. The moment is in the LDV record of the change (REQ-72). The register writes that record through an outbox, in the same transaction as the change.
  • Related: FR-22, FR-24, REQ-68, REQ-72, REQ-109, Q-42 (same question for another moment), register data model.

docs.title: Q-49: Are the consent register and the consent portal backend one system, and who is the BSNk participant?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The PSA describes the consent register and the consent portal as capabilities and leaves their setup open. The question is whether the register and the portal backend become one system or two, and which party is the BSNk participant. The answer matters because a polymorphic value must not leave the party that requested it. With two systems at different parties, the register cannot store those values, and citizen recognition needs another route. In the working assumption, the portal backend requests the values at BSNk and the register stores them, under one participant.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The tech lead, the management organization, and BZK and Logius (BSNk management organization) for the recognition. PSA S01, S02.
  • Question: Do the register and the consent portal backend become one system or two? Which party is the BSNk participant? The PSA describes S01 and S02 as capabilities and does not describe them as systems. For S01, the PSA lists "central or federated setup" and "management organization" as open decisions.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo runs both as separate services under one operator. Which setup and which participant fit is a decision about management, recognition, and responsibility.
  • Options:
    • (a) One system, one BSNk participant.
    • (b) Two systems at one participant. That participant requests and stores.
    • (c) Two systems at different participants. Then the register must not store the polymorphic values, and citizen recognition must work differently. Route D (ADR 0040) then does not fit, and one of the routes A to C applies (routes compared).

  • Current working assumption: The demo follows option a or b. The portal backend is the requester at BSNk, and the register is storage (REQ-23). The register stores the polymorphic values that the portal requested (REQ-69). A polymorphic value does not leave the party that requested it (BSNK-03).

    The earlier working assumption on the BSNk preconditions page made the register the recognized party. REQ-22 is removed until this question is decided (see removed numbers). ADR 0040 stays proposed until then.

  • Related: REQ-23, REQ-69, BSNK-03, Q-26, Q-57, Q-58, register data model.

docs.title: Q-50: How does the consent portal backend inside MijnOverheid get the verified citizen identity?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The citizen logs in at MijnOverheid, and the backend of the consent portal runs inside it. The question is which evidence of that login MijnOverheid can give to the backend, and how the backend checks it. This matters because the backend must take the citizen identity from a validated login assertion and never from client input. MijnOverheid can pass a signed token, pass the BSN over an authenticated channel, or pass the BSN encrypted for BSNk. Until someone decides, the demo backend makes its own portal token after a mock login.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: MijnOverheid and the tech lead. PSA S02.

  • Question: Which evidence of the login can MijnOverheid give to the consent portal backend, and how does the backend check it? REQ-24 requires that the backend takes the citizen identity from the validated assertion of the authentication service (FR-01 criterion 2). The backend must not take it from client input.

    GBO builds the UI inside MijnOverheid, and the citizen logs in there. The working assumption on the BSNk preconditions page is that MijnOverheid passes the BSN after login. That page does not say how. It is unknown whether a token of the authentication service is available at that moment.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo has no MijnOverheid. What is available there depends on the setup of MijnOverheid and on the agreements with Logius.

  • Options:
    • (a) MijnOverheid passes signed evidence of the login (a token or assertion) that the backend validates itself.
    • (b) MijnOverheid passes the BSN over an authenticated channel between systems. The backend trusts MijnOverheid as caller.
    • (c) MijnOverheid passes the BSN encrypted for BSNk, and the backend does not see the BSN. This option is an open design choice in ADR 0040.
  • Current working assumption: In the demo, the backend makes its own portal token after a mock login.
  • Related: FR-01, PSA P-05, REQ-24, Q-26 sub-question 3 (does the MijnOverheid login count as authentication for BSNk), Q-44, Q-49, Q-59, Q-61.

docs.title: Q-51: Must it be provable which information the citizen saw when giving consent?
docs.text:
• Status: open

When a citizen gives consent, the portal backend requires an acknowledgment that the citizen saw the information. The question is whether it must also be provable afterwards what that information was, and where that evidence is kept. This matters because consent must be informed and provable, and the GDPR requires that the controller can show the consent. The existence of a consent proves the acknowledgment, but it does not show the text. The demo records nothing extra, so in effect only a versioned catalog can show what the citizen saw, and nobody has decided this.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: A lawyer, a privacy officer or DPO, and the management organization (versions of catalog texts). PSA S01.

  • Question: What must be provable afterwards about the information that the citizen saw, and where is it kept? Under REQ-107, the backend refuses a consent without an acknowledgment that the citizen saw the information (FR-08). So the existence of a consent proves the acknowledgment.
