It does not prove what the citizen saw.

    GO/PSA function F2 requires that consent is "informed" and "provable". PSA S01 requires "evidence of the interaction" in the consent record. GDPR art. 7(1) requires that the controller can show the consent.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Whether the existence of the consent is sufficient evidence is a legal decision. The demo can build each option.

  • Options:
    • (a) Record with the consent the version of the information shown: the version of the catalog text, or a fingerprint of the text.
    • (b) Record nothing extra. The acknowledgment is implicit. If the catalog keeps versions, what was shown follows from the catalog at that moment.
    • (c) Keep the text shown.
  • Current working assumption: The demo records nothing extra, so option b applies in effect. There is no decision.
  • Related: FR-08, REQ-107, REQ-117, REQ-121, Q-08, Q-63, register data model.

docs.title: Q-52: In which format does the citizen export the overview of consents?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The citizen can export the overview of consents. The question is which format the export uses, and whether GBO follows what MijnOverheid uses for export elsewhere. The requirement says "csv or pdf", which can mean both formats or only one of them. The content is fixed: what the overview shows, without the BSN or the name of the citizen. The demo has no export, so there is no working assumption for the format.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: MijnOverheid and the tech lead.
  • Question: Which export format does MijnOverheid use, and does GBO follow it? FR-20 v0.9 criterion 3 says: "The overview can be exported in csv or pdf format." This sentence can mean both formats, or one of the two. The content is fixed: what the overview shows, without the BSN or the name of the citizen.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The format depends on the conventions of MijnOverheid, and the demo has no MijnOverheid.
  • Options:
    • (a) Follow what MijnOverheid uses for export in other places.
    • (b) Both formats: csv to process, and pdf to keep or share.
    • (c) One format.
  • Current working assumption: The demo has no export (REQ-108 is not built).
  • Related: FR-01, FR-20, REQ-108, Q-50, Q-61.

docs.title: Q-53: Within which time and by which mechanism does suspension of a consumer take effect?
docs.text:
• Status: open

When a consumer is suspended or terminated, it must lose its access in time. The question is how fast that happens, by which mechanism, and who revokes its FSC contract: the source or the management organization. An expired or revoked consumer certificate must block access immediately, but FSC checks revocation through a cache. It is also open whether the citizen overview must show a consent at a suspended consumer as something other than Active. In the demo, a suspended party gets no new FSC contract, but it can still send requests with an existing contract.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The tech lead and the management organization. PSA S04.

  • Question: PSA S04 requires that suspension or termination leads "in time" to revocation of access. REQ-110 fixes the effect and leaves the consents as they are. Three sub-questions are open:

    1. Within which time must a suspension take effect, and by which mechanism? If the contract is revoked, who revokes it: the source or the management organization?
    2. If a consumer certificate expires or is revoked, access must be blocked "immediately" (FR-34 criterion 3). FSC refuses an expired or revoked certificate (REQ-46). But open-fsc checks revocation with a cache, so the effect takes as long as that cache. As long as the initiation is not bound to the certificate (Q-60), the consent process blocks through the status in the register (REQ-111). Does the same time limit apply as for a suspension?
    3. Must the overview of the citizen show a consent at a suspended consumer differently from "Active"? FR-30 criterion 3 asks that the status "trusted private service provider" is visible to the citizen. In demo v0.9.0, the citizen sees such a consent as Active, but the consumer cannot use it. A visible suspension affects the tone towards the consumer and the supervision.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The time limit is a management and supervision agreement. The mechanism depends on who manages the contracts.

  • Options:
    • (a) The source checks the admission status in the register on every request, as for an integrator in demo v0.9.0. This works immediately, but every source must call the register.
    • (b) If a consumer is suspended, its FSC contract is revoked. The source checks nothing extra. But an issued access token stays valid until it expires. After the suspension ends, a new contract is necessary.
  • Current working assumption: In the demo, a suspended party gets no new FSC contract. But it can still send requests with an existing contract.
  • Related: FR-31, FR-34, FR-36, REQ-61, REQ-110, REQ-46, REQ-111, Q-60, Q-62.

docs.title: Q-54: Which durability and recovery requirements apply to the register storage?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The consent register is the only place that holds the consents and the polymorphic values of a citizen. The question is which storage RINIS offers, and which requirements apply for durability, acceptable loss, recovery time and consistency after recovery. This matters because the source denies when a consent is lost, while the consumer still holds a valid consent proof. The demo register runs on Postgres when a database is set, and in memory otherwise. If RINIS offers Postgres as a platform service, Postgres is the obvious choice.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: RINIS, the tech lead, and the management organization. PSA S01 (availability, integrity, and auditability by the operator).
  • Question: Which storage does RINIS offer? Which requirements apply for durability, RPO, RTO, and consistency after recovery? The register is the only place for the consents and the polymorphic values of a citizen. If a consent is lost, the status query fails and the source denies (fail closed, REQ-68). The citizen then no longer sees the consent, but the consumer has a valid proof.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo has no production platform. The guarantees come from the agreements with RINIS.
  • Options: None. This input is necessary:
    • the storage that RINIS offers
    • the acceptable loss (RPO)
    • the recovery time (RTO)
    • how the record and the issued proof agree again after recovery (a proof for a consent that is missing after recovery)
  • Current working assumption: If DATABASE_URL is set, the demo register runs on Postgres (postgres_store.go#L71-L75). Otherwise, it runs in memory. If RINIS offers Postgres as a platform service, Postgres is the obvious choice.
  • Related: REQ-68, Q-47, Q-55, Q-63, register data model.

docs.title: Q-55: Where is the signing key of the consent proof, and how is it rotated and retired?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The consent register signs every consent proof, and the PDPs of the sources verify it with a public key. The question is where the signing key is stored, how it rotates, and how it is revoked after a leak. It is also open how the PDPs get the public keys. This matters because whoever has the key can make proofs for every citizen and every consumer. With a persistent store, the demo requires a fixed key from a file.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: The tech lead, RINIS (key storage), and the management organization.

  • Question: Where is the signing key? How is it rotated, and how is it revoked after a leak? How do the PDPs get the public keys?

    The register signs the proof (ES256). The PDPs of the sources verify the proof with the public key from a JWKS endpoint. They cache the key for five minutes. If a proof has an unknown kid, they fetch the key again (REQ-68). Whoever has the key can make proofs for every citizen and every consumer.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Key storage and key management belong to the platform and to operations. They are outside the scope of the demo.

  • Options: None. This input is necessary:
    • the storage (HSM, KMS, or other)
    • the rotation (overlap of old and new key, and the period)
    • the revocation after a leak (what happens to issued proofs)
    • the channel for the public keys to the PDPs (JWKS over FSC, or other)
  • Current working assumption: If the demo uses a persistent store, it requires a fixed key from a file (main.go#L84-L86).
  • Related: REQ-68, REQ-76 (status over FSC), ADR 0032, Q-54, Q-56, Q-62.

docs.title: Q-56: How do citizen references follow a rotation of the portal HMAC key?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The consent portal recognizes a citizen by an HMAC of the BSN under a secret key, and the register stores consents under that reference. With a new key, the same BSN gives a different reference, so the portal no longer finds the existing consents. The register cannot move them itself, because it sees no BSN. The question is how often the key rotates and how existing consents stay findable after a rotation. The design uses one key and the demo has no migration, so a new key hides older consents.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, and MijnOverheid for the case that citizen recognition works differently (Q-26 sub-question 5).

  • Question: How often does the HMAC key rotate, and why? How do existing consents stay findable after a rotation?

    The portal recognizes a citizen by an HMAC of the BSN under a secret key. The reference contains the key version (ADR 0040). The register stores consents and polymorphic values under that reference. With a new key, the same BSN gives a different reference. If nobody moves the existing consents, the portal no longer finds them. The register cannot move them itself, because it sees no BSN.

    Route D is a working assumption. There is no decision on it.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo knows one key. The choice depends on the key policy and on route D.

  • Options: The portal can handle a key rotation in one of three ways:
    • (a) Move the consents at the next login of the citizen. The portal computes both references and moves the consents.
    • (b) Keep both keys valid until all consents under the old key expire.
    • (c) Do not rotate, except after a leak. That case gets its own procedure.
  • Current working assumption: The design uses one key. A new SUBJECT_REF_KEY hides older consents. The demo has no migration.
  • Related: REQ-20, REQ-69, ADR 0040, Q-26, Q-55, Q-57.

docs.title: Q-57: Which protection do the stored polymorphic values get?
docs.text:
• Status: open

For each citizen, the consent register keeps the polymorphic identity and pseudonym of the first activation. From these values, BSNk makes an encrypted identity or an encrypted pseudonym for every party. As a result, a party that has the values and can call the portal can have values made for every source. The question is which protection the values get: encryption with a key outside the database, access control only, or both. The demo stores them unencrypted, in a table of their own.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, security officer.
  • Question: Which protection do the PI and PP in the register get? Who can read them? For each citizen, the register keeps the PI and PP of the first activation (REQ-69). From these values, BSNk makes an encrypted identity (VI) or an encrypted pseudonym (VP) for every party. As a result, a party that has the values and can call the portal can have values made for every source. Only the portal reads them.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The protection follows from the risk assessment and the security baseline.
  • Options: The register can protect the values in one of three ways:
    • (a) Encryption in the database, with a key outside the database.
    • (b) Access control only (database and network).
    • (c) Both.
  • Current working assumption: The demo stores the values unencrypted, in a table of their own.
  • Related: REQ-69, BSNK-03, ADR 0040, Q-49 (who stores), Q-55, Q-58, Q-63.

docs.title: Q-58: Must the register authenticate the consent portal backend, or is network isolation enough?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The consent portal backend is the only caller that creates, reads and revokes consents in the consent register. The question is whether the register must authenticate that backend, for example with mTLS or over FSC, or whether network isolation is enough. This matters because a party that reaches the register directly can create or revoke consents for every citizen. Network isolation alone requires that the register and the backend run at one participant, in one environment. The demo uses network isolation only, and the status query of the PDP has its own listener over FSC.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, RINIS (network design).
  • Question: Does the register authenticate the consent portal backend? If so, how? The backend is the only caller of the register to create, read, and revoke consents. Citizens reach the register only through the backend (REQ-39). REQ-76 requires authentication only for the status query by the PDP of the source. A party that reaches the register directly can create or revoke consents for every citizen.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo runs both components in one network, without authentication. The choice depends on the deployment.
  • Options: The register can rely on one of two protections:
    • (a) The register authenticates the backend, for example with mTLS or over FSC. The register also checks that only this caller can do these actions.
    • (b) Network isolation only. This option requires that the register and the backend run at one participant, in one environment (Q-49).
  • Current working assumption: The demo uses option b. The status query has its own listener and goes over FSC (REQ-76).
  • Related: REQ-39, REQ-76, Q-49, Q-57.

docs.title: Q-59: Which security requirements apply to the portal UI inside MijnOverheid?
docs.text:
• Status: open

GBO builds the UI of the consent portal inside MijnOverheid. The question is which security requirements apply to that UI, and which of them MijnOverheid already imposes. Examples are a content security policy, session management and protection against open redirects. The return to the consumer is a redirect, so the portal must check the return address. In the demo, only the frontend checks that address, against a fixed list of origins.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: MijnOverheid, tech lead, security officer.
  • Question: Which security requirements apply to the UI inside MijnOverheid? Which of them does MijnOverheid already impose? GBO builds the UI of the consent portal inside MijnOverheid. Security requirements apply to this UI, for example a content security policy, session management, and protection against open redirects. The return to the consumer is a redirect, so the portal must check the return address (issue #427).
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo runs outside MijnOverheid.
  • Options: None. The necessary input is the requirements that MijnOverheid sets for contributions to its code base, and the additions that GBO must make.
  • Current working assumption: In the demo, only the frontend checks the return address. It checks against a fixed list of origins (useRedirectContext.ts#L11-L26).
  • Related: FR-04 (trusted government domain), FR-14, REQ-24, REQ-111, Q-50, Q-61.

docs.title: Q-60: If name, purpose, return address, and status come from the registration, must the origin of the initiation request be provable?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The functional requirements say that the initiation request of a consumer must provably come from that service provider. The portal backend takes name, purpose and return address from the registration, so a forged request only gives a consent for the real consumer. A third party can still start a request for a consumer that asked for nothing. The question is whether that risk is acceptable, or whether the consumer must sign the request or send it in advance over FSC. The demo passes the context as query parameters, and its backend does not do these checks.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: owner of FR-DvTP, tech lead, MijnOverheid (what the login can keep).

  • Question: Besides the checks of REQ-111, is a provable origin of the initiation request necessary? If so, does the consumer sign the request in the URL, or send it in advance over FSC?

    FR-34 criterion 1 requires that the initiation request "provably comes from" the service provider. The criterion also requires verification of the request against the registered means of identification of the service provider. Under REQ-111, the backend takes name and purpose from the registration. The backend also checks the return address against the registered addresses, and it checks the status of the consumer. As a result, a forged request can only lead to a consent for the real consumer, with the correct name and for a registered scope. The return also goes to the address of that consumer.

    One risk remains: a third party can start a request on behalf of a consumer that asked for nothing. Only that consumer can use the proof (REQ-68).

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Whether the residual risk is acceptable is a decision. The demo can build each option (issue #427).

    • (a) Necessary, through a signed request in the URL. No FSC is necessary, but the content goes through the browser and MijnOverheid.
    • (b) Necessary, through a request that the consumer sends in advance over FSC. Only a reference goes through the browser (PAR, RFC 9126). This option needs an FSC service of the consent facility for consumers.
    • (c) Not necessary. Then FR-34 criterion 1 loses that part.

    Options: The question has three options:

    For options a and b, the request or the reference must survive the MijnOverheid login (FR-13).

  • Current working assumption: The demo sends the context as query parameters. It keeps the context in the browser session during the mock login. The backend in demo v0.9.0 does not do the REQ-111 checks.

  • Related: FR-12, FR-13, FR-34, REQ-37, REQ-111, Q-44 (transfer of the proof, same options), Q-50, Q-53, Q-61.

docs.title: Q-61: What must MijnOverheid deliver or allow for the portal UI and the link to the consent facility?
docs.text:
• Status: open

GBO builds the UI of the consent portal as a contribution to the MijnOverheid code base. Several requirements therefore depend on what MijnOverheid delivers or allows. This question collects the points without a question of their own, so that one meeting can discuss them all. They include the interface to the portal backend, the redirect protocol, the request context across the login, and ownership of the UI. Others are accessibility, house style, the switch to the apps, and delegation. There is no working assumption apart from the imitated shell in which the demo runs the portal.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: MijnOverheid (Logius), tech lead, PSA S02.
  • Question: GBO builds the UI of the consent portal as a contribution to the MijnOverheid code base. The citizen logs in there. As a result, several requirements depend on what MijnOverheid delivers. Some of them have their own question: the verified citizen identity (Q-50), the UI security requirements (Q-59), and the export format (Q-52). Q-60 covers what the login can keep for a signed or pre-sent request. This question collects the other requirements, so that one meeting can discuss them all:
    1. Interface: which form does the link between MijnOverheid and the consent portal backend get? How does this link relate to the interface DelenVanMijnGegevens?
    2. Redirect protocol: do initiation and return follow an existing protocol (OIDC, PAR), or a separate agreement?
    3. Contributions: on which stack does the GBO UI go into MijnOverheid? Which review and release process applies, who owns the UI, and who fixes bugs in production?
    4. Context across the login (FR-13): how does the request of the consumer stay available while the citizen logs in?
    5. Accessibility and house style: which accessibility standard applies to the whole UI, and who checks it? Which house style or component library does MijnOverheid prescribe?
    6. Web and app (FR-15): how does the switch to the DigiD app or the MijnOverheid app work? How does the citizen go back to the app of the consumer?
    7. Delegation (FR-02): does MijnOverheid pass on that the citizen acts on behalf of another person? In that case, who blocks: MijnOverheid or the consent facility?
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo has no MijnOverheid. The portal runs in an imitated shell.
  • Options: Each sub-question has its own options.
  • Current working assumption: None, apart from the demo shell.
  • Related: FR-02, FR-04, FR-13, FR-15, Q-44, Q-50, Q-52, Q-59, Q-60, Q-73.

docs.title: Q-62: What must the management organization record or deliver for the consent process?
docs.text:
• Status: open

Several parts of the consent screen and the overview depend on data or processes of the management organization. This question collects them in one place. They are the validity limits per service, the privacy officer per consumer, the voluntariness text, the owner of the texts, and the support contact. The incident processes for a failure of BSNk, MijnOverheid or the register, and for a compromised key, are also open. Until the management organization provides these, the demo uses fixed configuration values.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: management organization, tech lead.
  • Question: Several requirements on the consent screen and the overview depend on data or processes that the management organization must provide. This question collects these requirements:
    1. Validity limits (FR-11, FR-32): when a consent is recorded, which component enforces the limits per service? Where are the limits kept?
    2. GDPR reference (FR-25): where do the contact details of the privacy officer per consumer come from? How do these details reach the portal?
    3. Voluntariness (FR-36): which text does the screen show? Where does the alternative per consumer come from, and who receives complaints?
    4. Texts: who owns the B1 texts and the legal texts? How is the B1 level checked, and do all texts come from the catalog?
    5. Support (FR-04): which contact option does the page show?
    6. Incidents: which process applies if BSNk, MijnOverheid, or the register fails? Which process applies if a key is compromised (Q-55, Q-56)?
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo has no management organization. The demo fixes the values in configuration.
  • Options: Each sub-question has its own options.
  • Current working assumption: The demo uses fixed configuration values.
  • Related: FR-04, FR-11, FR-25, FR-32, FR-36, AV-14, AV-15, Q-13 (reopened: can the citizen change the default validity of the service?), Q-51, Q-53.

docs.title: Q-63: How long are consents, polymorphic values and citizen references kept?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The consent register keeps a record per consent, and the polymorphic values per citizen under a reference. The question is how long it keeps expired or revoked consents, the values of a citizen without a running consent, and empty references. It is also open how long the citizen sees old consents, and whether the citizen can ask to delete them. Retention and deletion must follow legal and audit requirements, so this is a legal decision. The demo keeps expired and revoked consents without a time limit.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: lawyer, privacy officer or DPO, management organization, PSA S01.
  • Question: PSA S01 requires that retention periods and deletion follow legal and audit requirements. Q-08 covers only the LDV, so this question covers the register. The register keeps the record per consent, and the PI and PP per citizen under a reference (register data model). The question has four parts:
    1. How long does the register keep an expired or revoked consent? How long does the citizen see it in the overview?
    2. How long does the register keep the PI and PP of a citizen without a running consent?
    3. If nothing is stored under a citizen reference any more, what happens to that reference?
    4. Can the citizen ask for the deletion of expired or revoked consents?
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Retention periods are a legal decision.
  • Options: None. The necessary input is a period per data item, and a rule for the end of the period.
  • Current working assumption: The demo keeps expired and revoked consents without a time limit.
  • Related: FR-20 (overview with consents that expired or were revoked a short time ago), Q-08, Q-43 (refusals), Q-51, Q-54, Q-57.

docs.title: Q-64: Must a Dutch ASIP also offer clause 6.2 (ISO 15000) besides clause 6.1, and with it deferred responses?
docs.text:
• Status: open

ETSI TS 119 478 lets an ASIP choose between clause 6.1 (HTTP and OAuth) and clause 6.2 (ISO 15000). Only clause 6.2 has a deferred response, for a source that cannot answer immediately. The question is whether a Dutch ASIP must also offer clause 6.2, and whether such slow sources exist. If so, it is open whether clause 6.2 can run over the eDelivery of the Basisinrichting OOTS. The working assumption is clause 6.1 only, which is synchronous.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: PSA/GO authors, bronhouders, BZK, PSA S08, S11.
  • Question: REQ-ASIP-4.3-04 (ETSI TS 119 478) lets an ASIP choose between two interfaces: the clause 6.1 interface (HTTP and OAuth) and the clause 6.2 interface (ISO 15000). For verify, Annex IV of CIR 2026/1735 designates clause 6.1.1, clause 6.2.3, or both. Only clause 6.2 has a deferred response (6.2.3.2.3, 6.2.4.3.3), for a source that cannot answer immediately. Clause 6.1 is synchronous. The question has three parts:
    1. Is clause 6.1 sufficient, or must a Dutch ASIP also offer clause 6.2?
    2. Are there sources that cannot answer immediately, so that they need a deferred response?
    3. If the answer to 1 or 2 is yes, can clause 6.2 run over the eDelivery of the Basisinrichting OOTS?
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: It depends on the QTSPs that will use the ASI, on the sources that cannot answer immediately, and on what GBO already has for eDelivery. PSA S08 places AS4/eDelivery at the side of the Basisinrichting OOTS.
  • Options: The ASIP can offer one of two sets of interfaces:
    • (a) Clause 6.1 only.
    • (b) Clause 6.1 and clause 6.2.
  • Current working assumption: Clause 6.1 only, synchronous (REQ-112). For the ASI profile, see the ASI requirements page.
  • Related: REQ-112, F-80, ADR 0037, Q-79.

docs.title: Q-65: Must the ASI support requests on behalf of another person (representation)?
docs.text:
• Status: open

With a mandate request, a QTSP asks the ASI for attributes of a subject while another person acts on behalf of that subject. ETSI makes support optional and leaves the details out of the specification. The question is whether the ASI must support such requests, and if so, whether the authorization server or the ASIP checks the evidence of representation. Support needs a legal basis, a source for the representation and an agreement on who checks it. The working assumption is no support, and the ASI answers such a request with status 501.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK, lawyer, PSA/GO authors, PSA S04, S11.
  • Question: REQ-ASIP-6.1.1.1-12 leaves an ASIP free to support requests with mandate. With such a request, the QTSP asks for attributes of a subject, and another person acts on behalf of that subject. ETSI leaves the details of mandate out of the specification (NOTE 3 at REQ-ASIP-6.1.1.1-13). The question has two parts:
    1. Must the ASI support requests on behalf of another person?
    2. If so, where does the evidence of the representation come from? Does the authorization server or the ASIP check it?
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Representation needs a legal basis, a source for the representation, and an agreement on who checks it. PSA S04 lists the governance of representation as an open point.
  • Options: The ASI can handle representation in one of three ways:
    • (a) No support.
    • (b) Support, with the check at the authorization server.
    • (c) Support, with the check at the ASIP.
  • Current working assumption: The ASI does not support representation. Such a request gets 501 (REQ-114).
  • Related: REQ-114, Q-73.

docs.title: Q-66: Which security profile does the authorization server of a Dutch ASIP get?
docs.text:
• Status: open

ETSI lets the authorization server of an ASIP choose its client authentication (mTLS, private_key_jwt or both) and its token binding (mTLS or DPoP). It also leaves open whether the server fully follows FAPI 2.0 with PAR. The question is which profile the Dutch ASIP picks. A profile stricter than ETSI excludes QTSPs that implement only ETSI, and a QTSP that serves several member states must support every variant. The demo uses private_key_jwt and DPoP without PAR, as a demo choice without a decision.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: management organization, security officer, PSA/GO authors.

  • Question: ETSI TS 119 478 lets the authorization server choose in two places. For client authentication, the server can choose mTLS, private_key_jwt, or both (REQ-AZSP-6.1.3.1-05). For token binding, it can choose mTLS or DPoP (REQ-AZSP-6.1.3.1-06). The QTSP uses what the authorization server chooses (REQ-TSP-6.1.3.1-02 and -03). The QTSP reads the choice from the metadata of the server (RFC 8414: token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported, and dpop_signing_alg_values_supported or tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens).

    ETSI also leaves open whether the server fully follows FAPI 2.0 (for example PAR). REQ-AZSP-6.1.3.4-01 only asks to take FAPI 2.0 "into account". The question has three parts: 1. Which client authentication: mTLS, private_key_jwt, or both? 2. Which token binding: mTLS or DPoP? 3. Does the authorization server fully follow FAPI 2.0, with PAR, or only ETSI?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The profile is a balance between security and the threshold for QTSPs. A profile stricter than ETSI excludes QTSPs that implement only ETSI. A QTSP that connects to ASIPs in several member states must support every variant. The form of the QTSP access certificates also matters, because a QTSP can use them as mTLS client certificate (Q-35).

  • Options: The sub-questions give the options.
  • Current working assumption: The demo uses private_key_jwt and DPoP, without PAR. This is a demo choice, and there is no decision on it (F-84). The demo security considerations explain the trade-off.
  • Related: F-84, F-96, Q-35, Q-41, E8, E9, and the ASI profile on the ASI requirements page.

docs.title: Q-67: How do Dutch data services get into the Discover Interface, and who registers them?
docs.text:
• Status: open

A QTSP uses the Discover Interface to find, per attribute, the data service that verifies it. ETSI intends this interface for the OOTS common services of the European Commission, such as the Data Service Directory. No document describes how a Dutch ASIP registers its data services there, or whether this goes through the Basisinrichting OOTS. The question is where QTSPs find the Dutch data services, and who registers them. The demo has a stub for the Discover Interface, and the ASIP publishes the records itself.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK, operator of the Basisinrichting OOTS, PSA/GO authors, PSA B-14, S08, S11.

  • Question: ETSI TS 119 478 clause 5 describes the Discover Interface. For each attribute, a QTSP uses this interface to find the data service that verifies the attribute. The requirements apply to the Discover Interface Provider (DIP), a role next to the ASIP. Clauses 4.2 and 5.1 intend the Discover Interface for the OOTS common services that the European Commission operates. These services are the Semantic Repository for attributes, and the Data Service Directory for sources and their data services.

    CIR 2025/1569 art. 10(2) lets the Commission reuse these services for the catalogue of attributes. No document describes how a Dutch ASIP registers its data services there, or whether this goes through the Basisinrichting OOTS. The question has two parts: 1. Does a QTSP find the Dutch data services in the OOTS Data Service Directory, or in a Discover Interface of its own? 2. Who registers a data service there? Does this go through the Basisinrichting OOTS?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Registration in the Data Service Directory is an agreement with the Commission and within the OOTS system.

  • Options: A QTSP can find the Dutch data services in one of two places:
    • (a) The OOTS Data Service Directory.
    • (b) A Discover Interface of its own.
  • Current working assumption: The demo has a DIP stub. The ASIP publishes the records itself (REQ-99).
  • Related: REQ-99, REQ-100, Q-31, Q-37, Q-39, Q-71, Q-79.

docs.title: Q-68: Can policy read the FSC Peer ID as the OIN of the consumer, or must that link come from the register?
docs.text:
• Status: open

In FSC, the Peer ID of a party is the serial number of its certificate, and with PKIoverheid that value is the OIN. The question is whether policy can treat "Peer ID = OIN" as a system rule, or must get the link between peer and organization from the admission register. The register is necessary when one peer acts for several organizations, as with hosting or an integrator, or when an organization changes certificate. The working assumption is the system rule: the DvTP policy compares the Peer ID directly with the consumer OIN in the consent.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, management organization (certificate profile and register), PSA S04.
  • Question: Is "Peer ID = OIN" a system rule that policy can build on? Or must the link between peer and organization come from the admission register? In FSC, the Peer ID is the serialNumber of the FSC certificate. With a PKIoverheid certificate, that value is the OIN. PSA S04 requires that the setup "links the technical identity to the admitted legal organization and role". REQ-67 fixes this link only for the bronhouder side.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: In the demo, every peer is one organization with an OIN as Peer ID, so both options behave the same.
  • Options: The link between peer and organization can come from one of two places:
    • (a) Peer ID = OIN as a system rule. The certificate profile guarantees this rule, and policy can read the Peer ID as OIN.
    • (b) The admission register records the OIN of the organization per peer. Policy compares the consent with that OIN. If one peer acts for more than one organization (hosting, integrator), option b is necessary. The same applies if an organization changes certificate.
  • Current working assumption: Option a. The DvTP policy compares the represented party (a Peer ID) directly with the consumer OIN in the consent (dvtp_helper.rego#L62-L65).
  • Related: FR-33, FR-34, REQ-61, REQ-67, REQ-106, ADR 0034, Q-06, Q-07, Q-46.
  • History: this question had the number Q-64 before.

docs.title: Q-69: Must the consent proof bind the purpose, so that the PDP checks it?
docs.text:
• Status: open

A consent binds one consumer, one service with its purpose, and at least one data set. The purpose is in the register record, but the consent proof does not carry it, so the PDP does not check it. The question is whether the proof must bind the purpose or service, and whether the PDP must check the admission of the consumer for it. The demo has one service per data set, so the difference is not visible there. The working assumption is that the service follows from the data set only.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, management organization (catalog).
  • Question: REQ-12 binds a consent to one consumer, one service with its purpose, and at least one data set. The purpose is in the register record, but the proof does not contain it. As a result, the PDP does not check the purpose. FR-17 criterion 1 names the purpose at retrieval. The question has two parts:
    1. Must the proof bind the purpose or the service? Or is the data set sufficient until the catalog exists?
    2. At the source request, does the PDP also check that the consumer is admitted for the service (FR-16 criterion 2)? At initiation, the consent portal backend already checks this (REQ-111). To do this check, the PDP must know the service. That depends on the same choice: the service in the proof, or in the contract.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo has one service per data set, so the difference is not visible.
  • Options: The PDP can learn the service in one of three ways:
    • (a) The proof carries the service or the purpose. The PDP denies a request that does not belong to that service.
    • (b) The service follows from the data set. The purpose stays a data item of the register and the screen.
    • (c) The service follows from the FSC contract. This option requires a catalog that links services to contracts (issue #382).
  • Current working assumption: Option b. The service follows only from the data set. The register gets the purpose from the redirect as use_case (PortaalConsent.tsx#L86).
  • Related: FR-09, FR-16, FR-17, REQ-12, REQ-68, REQ-111, ADR 0032, Q-45.

docs.title: Q-70: Which normalization applies in fuzzy matching per kind of value, and who sets it?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The ASI allows fuzzy matching only for free text, to accept spelling variations, and excludes dates, codes and numbers. The demo normalizes white space, case, hyphens and diacritics, but not every kind of value tolerates all of these rules. The question is whether the rules differ per kind of value, and who sets that kind: the ASIP, the source or the EU catalogue. In the demo, every string without a format gets the full normalization. Postal code and country code have no format, so they get it too, and that conflicts with the requirement.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, PSA/GO authors (ASI profile).

  • Question: REQ-113 limits fuzzy matching to free text. It excludes dates, codes, and numbers. ETSI TS 119 478 REQ-ASIP-6.1.1.1-10 names "orthographic variations" and leaves the rules free. The demo normalization has three rules: equal white space and case, equal hyphens, and removal of diacritics with transliteration per ICAO 9303.

    Not every kind of value tolerates all three rules. For a name, all three rules fit. A postal code that differs only in a space or in case (1234AB and 1234 ab) is clearly the same value. For a country code, case folding is the most that fits. The question has three parts: 1. Does the normalization apply per kind of value? Which rules belong to postal codes and to codes? 2. Who sets the kind of value: the ASIP, the source, or the EU catalogue of attributes? 3. Must REQ-113 then exclude codes, or name the rules per kind of value?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: What counts as the same value is an agreement between ASIP and QTSP. The QTSP must know in which cases it gets MatchWithVariation. The demo cannot make that agreement.

  • Options: The normalization can follow one of four rule sets:
    • (a) One normalization for every string without format.
    • (b) Normalization per kind of value. Names get the full normalization. Postal codes get only the white space and case rule. Codes get no normalization, or only the case rule. The ASIP sets the kind per attribute identifier.
    • (c) As option b, but the source gives the kind in value_schema, for example with format.
    • (d) The rules that the EU catalogue of attributes sets per attribute. This option needs the catalogue to exist (Q-38).

  • Current working assumption: Option a. Since demo issue #592 steps 1 to 5 (PR #624), the source describes its attributes. The ASIP takes the rule from value_schema.

    A string with a format matches exactly, for example the birth date (format: date). Every string without a format gets the full normalization (match.go#L31-L49, match.go#L137-L158). Postal code and country code have no format (asi-attributes.json#L44-L55). As a result, they also get the full normalization. This conflicts with REQ-113.

  • Related: REQ-113, REQ-84, REQ-85, F-92, ADR 0039, Q-29, Q-38, Q-71, E2.

docs.title: Q-71: Which form do address and name get as attributes, until the EU catalogue of attributes fixes it?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The ASIP compares an attribute in the form of a schema from the EU catalogue of attributes. Until that catalogue has schemas, GBO sets the schema per attribute, and each source maps its own fields to it. The BRP splits house number and surname into parts, while the amended PID puts the house number into the street. The question is which form address and name get, and who registers the Dutch attributes in the catalogue. The working assumption keeps a separate house number with letter and addition, and puts the surname prefix (voorvoegsel) in the family name.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK (registration in the catalogue), BRP bronhouder, PSA/GO authors (ASI profile).

  • Question: The ASIP compares an attribute as a JSON object. The object has the form of the JSON Schema that is registered for the attribute in the catalogue of attributes (ETSI TS 119 478 REQ-ASIP-6.1.1.1-06-02-01). As long as the catalogue has no schemas, GBO sets the schema per attribute identifier itself. In its source metadata, the source then describes how it maps its fields to that schema.

    The BRP splits the house number into the number (huisnummer), the letter (huisletter), and the addition (huisnummertoevoeging). It splits the surname into the prefix (voorvoegsel) and the main name (geslachtsnaam). The PID divides the address differently. CIR 2024/2977 first had a resident_house_number "including any affix or suffix". Since the amendment 2026/1731, that field is gone, and resident_street is "including the house number and any affix or suffix thereof".

    CIR 2025/1569 art. 7(5)(g) asks for the catalogue only "the data type of the attribute". Art. 7(3) lets the member state register the attributes of eIDAS Annex VI itself. The question has three parts: 1. Which form does the address get: (a), (b), or (c)? Which separator goes between house number, letter, and addition? 2. Does the name put the prefix (voorvoegsel) in family_name, or in a separate field? 3. Who registers the Dutch Annex VI attributes in the catalogue? Does the GBO schema then follow that registration?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The form must fit what QTSPs in other member states send. In the end, it must fit what the Netherlands registers in the catalogue. The demo can only pick a form.

  • Options for the address: The address can have one of three forms:
    • (a) As the PID after the amendment 2026/1731: street with house number, postal code, city, and country.
    • (b) As the demo: street, house number with letter and addition, postal code, city, and country. This form follows the original PID.
    • (c) As the BRP: huisnummer, huisletter, and huisnummertoevoeging as separate fields.
  • Current working assumption: Option b. For the name, the prefix (voorvoegsel) and the main name (geslachtsnaam) go together in family_name (asi-attributes.json#L44-L55). Since demo issue #592, the BRP source joins the parts in the asi mapping of its own source metadata. The source uses a space as separator (gbo-source-metadata.json#L219-L280). Since that issue, the ASIP has no BRP adapter in code.
  • Related: REQ-113, ADR 0039, F-94, Q-31, Q-38, Q-67, Q-70 (normalization: whether "12a" and "12 a" match).

docs.title: Q-72: Do GBO components write attributes outside the LDV core, and if so under which extension?
docs.text:
• Status: open

LDV allows attributes outside its core only within an approved extension. Several GBO components write local GBO attributes, such as the consent ID and attestation claims, and that extension has no approval. As a result, the demo does not log according to LDV. The question is whether the core is enough, or whether GBO must submit an extension to Logius for the consent ID that citizen access needs. The starting point is core only, but the demo still writes the local attributes.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, and Logius for option 2.
  • Question: Is the LDV core sufficient (option 1)? If citizen access needs the consent ID, is an extension at Logius (option 2) necessary only for that attribute? LDV allows an attribute outside dpl.core only within an approved extension (LDV, attributes). In demo v0.9.0, the consent register, the consent portal backend, and the EUDI adapter write dpl.gbo.* attributes. Examples are the consent ID, sourceId, typeId, the attestation claims, and the reason for pseudonymization. That extension is local and has no approval, so the demo does not meet REQ-72 ("according to Logboek Dataverwerkingen").
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo writes the attributes because it can. Whether they are necessary, and whether an extension gets approved, is a choice about conformance and an agreement with the operator of the standard.
  • Options: The GBO components can handle the extra attributes in one of three ways:
    • (1) Core only: the GBO components write no dpl.gbo.*. What is necessary follows from the processing activity, the status, or data_subject_id_type.
    • (2) Submit a GBO extension to Logius (extension template) for the attributes that add something, such as the consent ID for citizen access. The components write these attributes only after approval. Until then, option 1 applies.
    • (3) Accept the deviation and record it as a note at REQ-72 ("LDV core with local extension").
  • Current working assumption: The starting point is option 1. The demo still writes dpl.gbo.* (consent-register/main.go#L468, portal.go#L170, ldv_issuance.go#L173-L177). ldv-client/client.go#L44-L50 describes the local extension.
  • Related: REQ-72, F-64, ADR 0026, Q-08.
  • History: this question had the number Q-70 before.

docs.title: Q-73: Whose consent is a consent given by an authorized representative, and what does the register record?
docs.text:
• Status: open

If a service allows delegation, an authorized representative can give consent for another person. The requirements assume one person, who logs in, sees only their own consents, and gets polymorphic values while logged in. The question is in whose name the consent is, whether the register records the representative, and who can see and revoke the consent. It is also open whether BSNk can make a value for the represented person during the login of the representative. There is no working assumption, because the demo has no mandates.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, lawyer, MijnOverheid and Logius (mandates), BZK and Logius (BSNk), PSA B-19.

  • Question: If the legal basis of the service does not exclude delegation, FR-02 criterion 4 (FR-DvTP v0.9) lets an authorized representative give consent. Criterion 3 says that "the citizen" is then the representative. The requirements assume one person. The identity comes from the login (REQ-24), and the citizen sees only their own consents (REQ-40). The register knows the citizen under one reference, with the polymorphic values of that citizen (REQ-69). BSNk transforms only while the citizen is logged in (BSNK-04).

    For a mandate service, BSNk requires that the mandate is registered. With a mandate, the data belongs to the represented person, while the representative is logged in. If a service excludes delegation, the consent facility refuses (REQ-118). This question is about the services that allow delegation. The question has four parts: 1. In whose name is the consent: the represented person or the representative? 2. Does the register record that a representative gave the consent, and which representative? 3. Who sees the consent in the overview, and who can revoke it? 4. On the login of the representative, can the consent facility have BSNk make a value for the represented person? Or does that need another role (Q-26)?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo has no mandates. Who the data subject is, and who can view and revoke the consent, is a legal choice.

  • Options: The consent facility can handle a representative in one of three ways:
    • (a) The consent is in the name of the represented person. The register records the representative with it, and both persons see the consent.
    • (b) The consent is in the name of the represented person. The representative appears only in the LDV log.
    • (c) Allow delegation for no service, until a service asks for it.
  • Current working assumption: None. The demo has no mandates.
  • Related: FR-02, FR-20, FR-23, REQ-118, REQ-24, REQ-40, REQ-69, BSNK-04, Q-26, Q-61 sub-question 7, Q-65.
  • History: this question had the number Q-71 before.

docs.title: Q-74: Does GBO build the registration and onboarding facility for service providers, or the management organization?
docs.text:
• Status: open

Three requirements describe a facility where a service provider logs in with eHerkenning, applies with supporting documents, and gets its certificate checked. GBO builds the admission register, but that register knows only FSC Peer IDs and has no accounts or certificates. In this design, the registration and review process is with the management organization. The question is whether that organization builds or buys the facility, or GBO builds a self-service flow on top of the register. There is no working assumption, because the demo loads its participants into the register in advance.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead.
    • FR-03: login with eHerkenning or another recognized means. Onboarding functions are available only after authentication.
    • FR-29: start an application after login, with supporting documents.
    • FR-33 criterion 2: at registration, check validity, revocation status, and issuer of the certificate.

    Question: Three requirements describe a facility where a service provider registers and manages its connection:

    GBO builds the admission register (REQ-61). That register is keyed on the FSC Peer ID. It sees no certificate and has no accounts. In this design, the registration and review process is with the management organization (Q-22).

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo has no registration process. Participants are in the register in advance. Who builds the facility is a decision about the division of roles in the build phase.

  • Options: The facility can come from one of two parties:
    • (a) The management organization builds or buys the registration and onboarding facility. GBO delivers the admission register with its management interface.
    • (b) GBO builds the registration and review flow on top of the admission register, as self-service for service providers. With option b, FR-03, FR-29, and FR-33 criterion 2 become requirements on that component.
  • Current working assumption: None. The demo register has its participants loaded in advance.
  • Related: FR-03, FR-29, FR-30, FR-33, REQ-61, REQ-123, Q-06, Q-22.
  • History: this question had the number Q-72 before.

docs.title: Q-75: Does every source response get one seal, regardless of channel (DvTP, EUDI, ASI)?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The functional requirements ask the bronhouder to seal all outgoing data sets with a qualified electronic seal, without naming the standard. In the ASI, the ASIP already seals every result, and in issuance the attestation carries the seal of the issuer. A DvTP source response has no seal, and FSC mTLS protects only the transport. The question is whether every response gets one seal, which level and format apply, who holds the key, and what happens when sealing fails. The starting point is one seal for every channel, and in the demo only the ASI seals.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, owner of FR-DvTP, bronhouders.

  • Question: FR-27 requires that the bronhouder seals all outgoing data sets with a qualified electronic seal. The seal makes origin and integrity provable (criterion 1). The seal must meet "applicable system standards" (criterion 2), but FR-27 does not name the standard.

    In the ASI, the ASIP already seals every verification result (REQ-83). Q-32 covers the format. In issuance, the attestation carries the seal of the issuer (Q-17).

    For a source response in DvTP, no seal exists. FSC mTLS protects only the transport between peers. It does not protect the response after the consumer receives it, or after an integrator passes it on. The question has three parts: 1. Does every source response get one seal regardless of channel (a), a form per channel (b), or no seal (c)? 2. If so, which seal applies: qualified, or advanced with a PKIoverheid certificate? Which format applies, under which system standard (FR-27 criterion 2)? Who holds the key: the source, or a GBO component that seals on behalf of the source? 3. If sealing fails, what happens: no delivery, or delivery without a seal?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo can build each option. Which level is necessary, in which format, and who holds the key, is a choice about trust and management.

  • Options: The source responses can get one of three kinds of protection:
    • (a) One seal on every source response, regardless of channel. This option fits the ASI, where the ASIP already seals every response.
    • (b) A separate form per channel.
    • (c) No seal. FSC mTLS and the transaction log are sufficient, and FR-27 then applies to the transport only.
  • Current working assumption: Option a is the starting point. In the demo, only the ASI seals.
  • Related: FR-18 (integrator as processor), FR-27, REQ-08, REQ-46, REQ-83, AV-06, ADR 0041, Q-17, Q-32.
  • History: this question had the number Q-73 before.

docs.title: Q-76: Does the validity period apply per consent or per source within the consent?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The functional requirements give each consent rule its own validity period per source, while the register and the proof know one valid-until per consent. The question is which of the two levels applies. A validity per source changes the screen, gives the proof a valid-until per source, and lets a consent expire for one source only. The demo calls one source per consent, so the difference is not visible. The working assumption is one validity per consent, equal to the expiry time of the proof.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, owner of FR-DvTP, management organization (duration per service in the catalog).
  • Question: Must a consent have a separate validity per source? Or does one validity apply to the whole consent? FR-38 criterion 2 lets each consent rule refer to "(bronhouder, data element, validity period)". So FR-38 has a validity per source. REQ-19 and the register data model know one valid-until per consent. The proof has one expiry time, equal to that valid-until.
  • Why the demo cannot answer it: Under one consent, the demo calls one source, so the difference is not visible.
  • Options: The validity can apply at one of two levels:
    • (a) One validity per consent, as in REQ-19. FR-38 must then change.
    • (b) A validity per source within one consent. This option affects the screen, which shows the duration per source. It affects the proof, which has a valid-until per source, and the PDP of each source checks its own valid-until. It also affects the status: a consent can be expired for one source and not for another.
  • Current working assumption: Option a: one validity per consent. The proof exp equals the valid-until.
  • Related: FR-11, FR-38, REQ-19, REQ-38, REQ-68, REQ-117, Q-13.
  • History: this question had the number Q-74 before.

docs.title: Q-77: What is a change of a consent: a new consent or an amendment of the existing one?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The PSA asks the consent register to support granting, change, revocation and expiry of a consent, but no requirement covers change. The consent proof binds the data sets and the validity, so a change also affects the proof that the consumer holds. The question is which changes the citizen can make, who starts them, and whether the consumer then gets a new proof. The options range from no change, through restrictions only, to a new consent that replaces the old one. The working assumption is no change: the citizen revokes, and the consumer starts a new request.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, PSA S01.

  • Question: PSA S01 requires that the register supports "granting, change, revocation and expiry". REQ-12, REQ-14, REQ-19, and REQ-109 cover granting, revocation, and expiry. No requirement and no FR covers change. FR-DvTP v0.9 knows only giving and revoking.

    The proof binds the sets and the validity (REQ-68). As a result, a change also affects the proof that the consumer already has. The question has two parts: 1. Which changes must the citizen be able to make? Who starts them: the citizen in the overview, or the consumer with a new request? 2. Does the consumer get a new proof after a change?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: What the citizen can change, and what the consumer notices of it, is a design choice. This choice has consequences for the proof and the return redirect.

  • Options: The register can support a change in one of three ways:
    • (a) No change. The citizen revokes, and the consumer starts a new request.
    • (b) The citizen can only restrict: switch off an optional set, or shorten the validity. The restriction takes effect through the status query, and the consumer keeps the existing proof.
    • (c) A change makes a new consent with a new proof, and revokes the old consent.
  • Current working assumption: Option a. The demo has no change function.
  • Related: REQ-12, REQ-14, REQ-19, REQ-68, REQ-109, Q-13, Q-44.
  • History: this question had the number Q-75 before.

docs.title: Q-78: How does the reference policy show that it is not tied to one policy language or engine?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The PSA requires that policy is product-independent and not tied to one policy language or engine. The reference policy of GBO uses one language for one engine. A source with another PDP cannot take it over or show equal decisions. The question is how GBO shows independence: rules as data, a shared decision test set, or one open language with an exit path. There is no decision, and the demo has one engine and one policy language.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead, PSA S05, S06.

  • Question: Which option does GBO follow for its reference policy? Does the requirement also apply to policy that a bronhouder writes itself, or only as a guideline (RL)? PSA S05 requires that "the interface and the policy are product-independent". S06 requires that policy is "not tied to one specific policy language or implementation" (see also P-09). REQ-42 covers the interface.

    The reference policy that GBO delivers is in one policy language, for one engine. A source that chooses another PDP cannot take this policy over. That source also cannot show that its decisions are the same.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo runs one engine. Only a second engine can show whether the policy is portable.

  • Options: GBO can show the independence in one of three ways:
    • (a) The content of the rules (service, actor, sets, fields, regime) as data, apart from the engine code, with a thin layer per engine.
    • (b) A decision test set apart from the engine, which every PDP must pass, next to the policy in one language. Each test maps an AuthZEN request to the expected decision and reason.
    • (c) Accept one open policy language as sufficient, with a recorded exit path (D-13).
  • Current working assumption: No decision. The demo has one engine and one policy language.
  • Related: REQ-42, RL-01, ADR 0021, Q-16, Q-21.
  • History: this question had the number Q-76 before.

docs.title: Q-79: Does GBO build the OOTS adapter, or does the OOTS-V operator extend its facility with the GBO interface?
docs.text:
• Status: open

The PSA lets an OOTS adapter connect to the national interface of OOTS-V, and OOTS requests use the same authorization and logging as other requests. The question is whether GBO builds that adapter, or the OOTS-V operator extends its facility with the GBO interface. The choice decides the route to the source, the regime and evidence for OOTS, and the versioned mapping to OOTS-EDM. The PDP knows only the consent and PID regimes, so it denies an OOTS request without its own evidence. There is no working assumption, because the demo has no OOTS route.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: BZK and OOTS coordination, tech lead, PSA B-12, S08, S10.

  • Question: Does GBO build the OOTS adapter, or does the OOTS-V operator extend its facility with the GBO interface? Where is the boundary between OOTS-V and the mapping function?

    PSA S08 lets the OOTS adapter connect to the national interface of OOTS-V. OOTS requests use the same generic authorization and logging as other data requests. Bronhouders do not depend on AS4/eDelivery. The Basisinrichting OOTS stays responsible for transport, discovery, and the European process interaction. If the bronhouder configures a mapping, a central mapping function translates to OOTS-EDM.

    Who builds the adapter is an open decision of S08. This design has no OOTS requirement. Three items depend on the choice: - The route of an OOTS request to the source. - The regime and the evidence for OOTS. REQ-74 knows only the consent regime and the PID regime. As a result, the PDP denies an OOTS request without its own evidence. - The mapping to OOTS-EDM with traceable versions, as REQ-124 requires for issuance.

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: The demo does not touch OOTS.

  • Options: The OOTS adapter can come from one of two parties:
    • (a) GBO builds the OOTS adapter, behind the national interface of OOTS-V.
    • (b) The OOTS-V operator extends its facility with the GBO interface. GBO delivers only the generic source access.
  • Current working assumption: None. The demo has no OOTS route.
  • Related: REQ-04, REQ-44, REQ-46, REQ-74, REQ-124, ADR 0031, ADR 0020, Q-64, Q-67.
  • History: this question had the number Q-77 before.

docs.title: Q-83: Which authorization server identifies the citizen when an attestation is issued with the authorization code flow?
docs.text:
• Status: open

In the authorization code flow, an authorization server identifies the citizen and records consent, instead of the citizen sharing the PID with the issuer. HAIP 1.0 requires this flow, while ETSI TS 119 472-3 asks an issuer to offer at least one of the two flows. OpenID4VCI 1.0 leaves open how the authorization server identifies the citizen, and ETSI TS 119 478 covers only verification for QTSPs. GBO already plans an authorization server for the ASI that identifies the citizen and shows a request page per source. The question is which authorization server identifies the citizen if GBO offers this flow. It also asks what that means for the requirements that assume only a PID disclosure.

Options, working assumption and links
  • Forum: tech lead. PSA S11.

  • Question: HAIP 1.0 section 4 says that the wallet and the credential issuer must support the authorization code flow. ETSI TS 119 472-3, which Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1731 applies to the issuance interface, asks the wallet to support both flows (GEN-REQ-4.1-03). It asks an issuer to implement at least one of them (GEN-REQ-4.1-04). OpenID4VCI 1.0 section 3 leaves the authentication of the citizen to the authorization server. One example the specification gives is a credential presentation.

    1. Which authorization server identifies the citizen and records consent for issuance with the authorization code flow?
    2. If the authorization server of the ASI also serves issuance: which clients and resources does it accept? REQ-88 and REQ-89 admit only clients with the entitlement QEAA_Provider.
    3. REQ-45 takes the subject of a source query only from a verified PID disclosure. Which identification replaces it in this flow, and which identification means count (Q-36)?

  • Why the demo cannot answer it: It is a choice about components and responsibilities: which party identifies the citizen and records consent for issuance. The demo can build each option, but cannot choose between them.

  • Options:
    • (a) The issuer has its own authorization server, with its own login.
    • (b) The authorization server of the ASI is also the authorization server of the issuer. The wallet sends its authorization request and token request there.
    • (c) The issuer keeps its own authorization server toward the wallet, and is an OAuth client of the authorization server of the ASI. The citizen logs in and consents there. This is the proposal: one place where the citizen logs in and consents per source, in the same pattern as ETSI TS 119 478.
  • Current working assumption: None. The TO describes issuance only after a PID disclosure (ADR 0018).
  • Related: Q-28, Q-36, Q-37, REQ-45, REQ-88, REQ-89, REQ-91, ADR 0018, ADR 0037.

docs.title: Feedback on ETSI TS 119 478
docs.text:
The demo found gaps and conflicts in ETSI TS 119 478 V1.1.1. In increment SL-28, the demo built an Authentic Source Interface Provider (ASIP) mock to that standard. Each item gives the clause, the issue, and a proposal for the text. It also gives the related findings, open questions, and requirements. The finding or the open question holds the reasoning.

  • Audience: ETSI ESI, the group that maintains the standard.
  • Route: through the Ministry of the Interior (BZK) and the EUDI cooperation group, as for Q-32.
  • Who submits, and when: not decided.
  • State: collected and not sent.

Two kinds of items do not go to ETSI, so they are not on this list:

  • Choices that the Netherlands makes itself. An example is which identification means an authorization server accepts (Q-36).
  • Gaps in the NL PID (F-94).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The feedback has ten items:

# Clause Issue Related E1 5.3.3 No field for the authorization-server metadata in the contract F-91, Q-39 E2 6.1.1.1, 6.1.1.2 Value optional after Annex IV of 2026/1735, but the fuzzy-matching requirement stays F-92, Q-29 E3 6.1.1.2, 6.1.2.2 A response names one authentic source F-89 E4 6.1.1 No seal format for the verification result Q-32, F-80 E5 6.1.3.2 A token binds per operation and has no binding per attribute F-95, Q-33 E6 6.1.3.3 Identification by the QTSP and by the authorization server are not linked F-93, Q-40 E7 6.1.3.1 Identification data is readable for the QTSP in the token F-86 E8 6.1.3.4 Security profile left open, with conflicts on PAR and RS256 against the norms it references F-84 E9 6.1.3 RFC 9207 (iss in the authorization response) is missing F-96 E10 6.1.3.2 The meaning of a revoked right for issued tokens is not defined Q-41

docs.title: E1: No field for the authorization-server metadata in the contract
docs.text:
• Clause: 5.3.3.
  • Issue: REQ-DIP-5.3.3-03-02-01 requires that the contract behind endpointDescription specifies the metadata of the OAuth authorization server. OpenAPI 3.0 has no field for this. oauth2 has only endpoint URLs. openIdConnectUrl points to OpenID Connect Discovery. It does not point to RFC 8414 metadata.
  • Proposal: prescribe one fixed field. One example is an extension x-oauth-authorization-server with the URL of the RFC 8414 metadata. Another example is the metadata URL in the dataService record itself.
  • Related: F-91, Q-39, REQ-100.
  • Status: open (submitter not decided).

docs.title: E2: Value optional after Annex IV of 2026/1735, but the fuzzy-matching requirement stays
docs.text:
• Clause: 6.1.1.1, 6.1.1.2.
  • Issue: Annex IV of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1735 makes attributeValue optional for Match and MatchWithVariation. REQ-ASIP-6.1.1.1-10-01 still requires that an ASIP with fuzzy matching returns the stored value. An ASIP cannot satisfy both.
  • Proposal: change REQ-ASIP-6.1.1.1-10-01 to match the annex. The ASIP MAY return the stored value, but NEED NOT.
  • Related: F-92, Q-29, Q-70, REQ-85, REQ-113. The demo returns MatchWithVariation and never returns the stored value.
  • Status: open (submitter not decided).

docs.title: E3: A response names one authentic source
docs.text:
• Clause: 6.1.1.2, 6.1.2.2.
  • Issue: REQ-ASIP-6.1.1.2-08 and REQ-ASIP-6.1.2.2-04 let a response name one authenticSource. An ASIP that serves several sources cannot account for attributes of two sources in one response.
  • Proposal: allow authenticSource per attribute result. As an alternative, state explicitly that an ASIP offers one data service per source.
  • Related: F-89, REQ-94, REQ-95, ADR-0038. The demo follows the second option.
  • Status: open (submitter not decided).

docs.title: E4: No seal format for the verification result
docs.text:
• Clause: 6.1.1.
  • Issue: Art. 9(4) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1569, as amended by 2026/1735, requires a seal on each verification result. Clause 6.1.1 sets no format. Each ASIP chooses its own format, so a QTSP must build a different check for each ASIP.
  • Proposal: prescribe one seal profile. An example is JAdES baseline (ETSI TS 119 182-1) as a detached signature over the response body.
  • Related: Q-32, F-80, Q-75, REQ-83, ADR-0041.
  • Status: open (submitter not decided).

docs.title: E5: A token binds per operation and has no binding per attribute
docs.text:
• Clause: 6.1.3.2.
  • Issue: clause 6.1.3.2 defines the scopes verify and retrieve. A token is then valid for every attribute of the data service. The token does not show which attributes the citizen approved. The demo binds per attribute with RFC 9396 authorization_details and a type of its own. This works only between parties that know that type.
  • Proposal: define an authorization_details type for the ASI, with data service, operations, and attribute identifiers. A member state that authorizes per attribute (art. 9(5)) can then do so in an interoperable way.
  • Related: F-95, Q-33, REQ-103, ADR-0042.
  • Status: open (submitter not decided).

docs.title: E6: Identification by the QTSP and by the authorization server are not linked
docs.text:
• Clause: 6.1.3.3.
  • Issue: the specification has no link between the two identifications:
    • In figure 3 of clause 6.1.3.3, only the authorization server identifies the citizen. Those identification data go into the token (steps 7 to 10 and 16).
    • The QTSP must identify the citizen to whom it issues (eIDAS art. 24(1)). The specification does not describe that identification and does not link the two.
    • Art. 9(3) of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1569 lets the request name the identification data of the subject. ETSI fills this in through the token.
  • Proposal: describe how the QTSP shows that the subject of the request is the citizen it identified. For example, the QTSP sends its own identification data for verification too.
  • Related: F-93, Q-40.
  • Status: open (submitter not decided).

docs.title: E7: Identification data is readable for the QTSP in the token
docs.text:
• Clause: 6.1.3.1.
  • Issue: REQ-AZSP-6.1.3.1-08 lets the token carry the identification data of the user. The QTSP can read the token. It then also sees a national identification number that it is not allowed to process. In the Netherlands, this number is the BSN.
  • Proposal: allow or prescribe that the identification data are encrypted for the resource server (JWE), or that the token carries a pseudonym.
  • Related: F-86, REQ-86. ICTU/GBO-demo#595 holds the demo work to protect the BSN in the token.
  • Status: open (submitter not decided).

docs.title: E8: Security profile left open, with conflicts on PAR and RS256 against the norms it references
docs.text:
• Clause: 6.1.3.4.
  • Issue: clause 6.1.3.4 asks only to take RFC 6819, RFC 7636, RFC 9700, and FAPI 2.0 "into account". NOTE 3 at the PKCE requirement refers to FAPI 2.0 §5.3.2.2, which requires PAR. ETSI does not require PAR. RFC 9068 §2.1, mandatory through REQ-AZSP-6.1.3.1-08, lets resource servers support RS256. FAPI 2.0 forbids RS256. As a result, a QTSP meets a different profile at each authorization server.
  • Proposal: fix one profile: client authentication, token binding, PAR or no PAR, and the algorithms.
  • Related: F-84, Q-66. The demo records its choice per point in conformance/security-considerations.md.
  • Status: open (submitter not decided).

docs.title: E9: RFC 9207 (iss in the authorization response) is missing
docs.text:
• Clause: 6.1.3.
  • Issue: a QTSP talks to one authorization server for each ASIP. RFC 9700 §2.1 then requires a defense against mix-up attacks, preferably with iss per RFC 9207. FAPI 2.0 requires that the authorization server returns it. Clause 6.1.3 does not name RFC 9207.
  • Proposal: prescribe RFC 9207 for the authorization server, and the check of iss by the QTSP.
  • Related: F-96.
  • Status: open (submitter not decided).

docs.title: E10: The meaning of a revoked right for issued tokens is not defined
docs.text:
• Clause: 6.1.3.2.
  • Issue: clause 6.1.3.2 and figure 2 let the authorization server check the right of a QTSP again at intervals. The clause does not say what happens to tokens that are already issued when the right lapses. FAPI 2.0 §5.3.4 lets the resource server check the revocation status.
  • Proposal: state how fast a revocation takes effect. The standard can choose one of two options:
    • Tokens stay valid until they expire, with a maximum lifetime.
    • The ASIP uses token introspection.
  • Related: Q-41, REQ-89, Q-34.
  • Status: open (submitter not decided).

docs.title: Traceability
docs.text:
• Requirements: REQ-83, REQ-85, REQ-86, REQ-89, REQ-94, REQ-100, REQ-103, REQ-113
  • Findings: F-80, F-84, F-86, F-89, F-91, F-92, F-93, F-95, F-96 (all open)
  • Open questions: Q-29, Q-32, Q-33, Q-39, Q-40, Q-41
  • Demo increments: SL-28
